OceanofPDF.com Introduction What Albert Einstein Can Teach You About Improving Your Advertising Results _____________________________ “The irresistible offer is an identity-building offer central to a product, service, or company where the believable return on investment (ROI) is communicated so clearly and efficiently that it’s immediately apparent you’d have to be a fool to pass it up.” — Mark Joyner _____________________________ I assume you are a small-business owner, marketing manager, Internet marketer, direct marketer, ad agency creative director, copywriter, product manager, advertising manager, or any other marketer concerned with generating leads and orders, and not just communicating brand messages. In this book, we will explore ways to dramatically improve response rates to your promotions anywhere from 10 percent to as much as 900 percent — just by creating and testing different offers. As you know, an “offer” is simply what your prospects get when they respond to your ad or mailing — combined with what they have to do to get it. In its simplest form, an offer might be “Call us toll-free for a free booklet on adjustable beds.” The booklet is what prospects get. Making the phone call is what they have to do to get it. “Give your reader something to do and make it easy for him to do it,” writes G. Lynn Sumner in his book How I Learned the Secrets of Success in Advertising (North Audley Media). “Tell him where to get what you have to sell, how much it costs — and why he should do it now.” An irresistible offer promises prospects something so compelling or desirable that they can’t help but call, write, or go online to get it. “The irresistible offer is an identity-building offer central to a product, service, or company where the believable return on investment (ROI) is communicated so clearly and efficiently that it’s immediately apparent you’d have to be a fool to pass it up,” writes Internet marketing pioneer Mark Joyner. Or, to paraphrase Marlon Brando in The Godfather, it’s an offer your prospect can’t refuse. What’s the biggest difference between general advertising and direct marketing? In my view, it’s that direct marketers recognize the critical importance of the offer, while general marketers, by and large, do not. More than that, direct marketers focus their efforts on driving the largest volume of qualified prospects to accept their offers. General advertisers spend their time agonizing over the messaging in their ads and finding creative ways to express it. General advertisers are concerned with image and brand. What image of the company does their advertising convey? Are consumers aware of their brand and what it stands for? What brand messages do they want to communicate? How can they make those brand messages memorable? Direct marketers focus on presenting compelling reasons why consumers should buy their products right then and there, as well as overcoming any objections the consumers may have. They are concerned with the action they want the consumer to take — and how to get him or her to take it. General advertisers sit in conference rooms, brainstorm what they want to say about the product, and then spend large amounts of money communicating those messages in their advertising. They often ask consumers for their opinions of products, brands, and advertising through focus groups, surveys, and other market research. Direct marketers do not assume they know what consumers want to hear or what will sell best. They test everything: lists, media, key sales appeals, headlines, envelope teasers, direct-mail package size, mailing formats, Web page colors, banner designs, and offers. Many direct marketers eschew market research in favor of live tests of actual promotions, believing the only opinion expressed by consumers that has any meaning is the one they vote on with their checkbooks and credit cards. So which approach is better — the brand-driven approach of the general advertiser or the offer-driven approach of the direct marketer? A recent study by The Kern Organization found that when marketing sells the offer instead of the brand, it generates approximately 10 times more orders and sales: (Source: Target Marketing, 4/08) Figures are based on direct mail promotions to sell offers with high lifetime customer values including cable TV subscriptions, long-distance and cell phone service. The wisdom of stressing the offer in advertisements has been known for well over a century. In 1902, three years before he wrote his groundbreaking paper on the theory of relativity, a young Albert Einstein ran newspaper ads offering his services as a tutor in math and physics. The ads prominently offered a “free trial lesson” — showing that free offers really are a smart marketing tactic! The two areas in your promotional copy where you can get the most leverage — the greatest lift in responses and orders — are the opening and the closing. The opening is mainly the headline and lead of your copy, as well as its graphic design and presentation. In his book The Architecture of Persuasion, Michael Masterson shows you how to write compelling headlines and leads. The closing of your copy is largely the offer and its presentation. In How to Create Irresistible Offers, I’ll show you how to craft strong offers that make your marketing make more money for you. I do have one favor to ask. If you’ve used a great offer that works, why not send the promotion to me so I can share it with readers of the next edition of this book? I also welcome your comments and questions on How to Create Irresistible Offers. You can reach me at: Bob Bly Copywriter / Consultant 590 Delcina Drive River Vale, NJ 07675 Phone: (201) 505-9451 Fax: (201) 573-4094 E-mail: rwbly@bly.com Web: www.bly.com OceanofPDF.com 1 Offers That Bring in a Flood of New Leads There are two major categories of direct marketing: lead generation and order generation. Order generation, also called “mail order,” seeks to generate an order for a product directly from the promotion. Mail order is “one-step marketing,” because you make the sale in a single step. As Bill Bonner of Agora Publishing describes it, “You send strangers a letter, and they send you money.” Lead generation seeks to produce an inquiry or sales lead — to get qualified prospects to metaphorically raise their hands and say, “Hey, I might be interested in this product. Tell me more.” Lead generation is “twostep marketing.” The first step is sending the promotion and generating the inquiry. The next step is following up on the inquiry and closing the sale. Strong offers are critical to the success of both lead generation and mail order marketing. The strategic planning, selection, and testing of offers can make or break a campaign, regardless of how well designed or well written the piece is. In this chapter, we’ll look at the offers that work best for lead generation. Creating a Simple Offer That Works A typical offer for a lead-generating promotion might be “Call us tollfree for a free catalog on adjustable beds plus a copy of our free booklet: How to Get a Good Night’s Sleep.” The catalog and booklet are what prospects get. Making the phone call is what they have to do to get it. As a rule, the more valuable and risk-free the offer seems to the reader, the better your response. The presentation of the offer — the copy used to describe it, the graphics, its position in the promotion — is also important. Usually, the more you emphasize and stress the offer in copy and graphics, the higher your response rate. Another rule of thumb: The clearer and more understandable your offer, the better your response. The lack of a clear, distinct offer can significantly depress response. The simplest, most popular offer in lead generation is probably the offer of a brochure describing the product or service. In direct mail, this typically reads: “For a free brochure on the Widget 2000, complete and mail the enclosed reply card today.” What the prospects get is a brochure describing the product. What they have to do to get it is fill in and mail a reply card. The offer of a free brochure can and does work for numerous products and services. However, you can often come up with a much more attractive offer — one that will get many more people to be interested in your proposition and respond to your ad or mailing. In lead generation, there are four fundamentally different types of offers: soft, hard, negative, and deferred. Get More Leads With a Soft Offer In a soft offer, the prospect requests some type of printed material that is mailed or shipped to him or downloaded online as a PDF document. The prospect makes this request by using a reply card or other response mechanism that does not require face-to-face or other personal communication between him and the seller. For example: For a FREE copy of our white paper on Best Software Audit Practices, complete and mail the reply card today. Want our latest catalog? Call toll-free 800-XXXXXXX. We’ll rush a copy first-class as soon as we hear from you. To download our new free white paper, “Calculating ROI From ERP Implementation,” click here now. The important thing to note about the soft offer is that it’s the most painless, risk-free way for the prospect to raise his hand, get in touch with you, and say, “I may be interested — tell me more” … without having to subject himself to sales pressure of any kind. The typical soft offer in a direct-mail letter reads as follows: “If you’re interested in learning more about what Product X can do for you, just complete and mail the enclosed reply card for a free brochure.” The prospect checks off a box on a reply card and mails it to you. You mail the requested literature back. The prospect has expressed interest, responded, and received information without making personal contact. The soft offer appeals to prospects who do not have an immediate need and are “just looking,” and to those who have an immediate need but want to gather preliminary information without speaking to agents or sales reps. The soft offer generates a high level of response, because there is no sales pressure or risk of being pitched by high-pressure sales types. It promises details that can be reviewed by the prospects at their leisure. Many marketers mistakenly believe that all people who respond to soft offers are just collecting brochures or white papers, and are therefore not real prospects. For this reason, they avoid soft offers. They say, “If the prospect doesn’t pick up the phone and call me, she’s not really interested. I don’t want to waste time and money sending her expensive color brochures that she’s just going to file or throw away.” While there’s some validity to this point of view, it usually turns out not to be true. Soft leads can be extremely profitable, and often the conversion rate is just as good as it is with hard leads. In a survey of IT professionals, for instance, 57 percent said that white papers influenced their buying decisions. For most promotions, the best strategy is actually to give the reader a choice of several offers, not just a soft offer or a hard offer. Target Your Best Prospects With Hard Offers The opposite of the soft offer is the hard offer. A hard offer in lead generation requires or results in face-to-face or other personal contact between buyer and seller. Whether in person or on the phone, the seller has the prospect “captive” for purposes of doing some selling. In the hard offer, the prospect typically calls or writes the advertiser to arrange a meeting, demonstration, initial consultation, or appointment. There is direct person-to-person contact between buyer and seller — initially over the telephone and, usually, later face to face. During these contacts, outbound telemarketing representatives or salespeople attempt to persuade prospects to buy the product or service being offered. Examples of hard offers: * To get a no-obligation estimate for adding a new family room or den to your house, just complete and return the Free Estimate Request Form enclosed. * For a free analysis of what you’ll need to save to put your children through college, call XXX-XXX-XXXX today. The hard offer is ideal for prospects who have a serious interest, an immediate need, or a desire to buy something fairly soon and want to sit down and talk with vendors. The prospect responding to a hard offer, especially if doing it by telephone, typically feels a fairly urgent need to gather more information for an immediate or upcoming purchase. With a hard offer, the prospect is taking a definite (if tentative or uncommitted) step toward purchasing the product. A soft offer, by comparison, gets more of a “Let me look you over” or “We’ll wait and see” response. Turn a “No” Into a “Maybe” With a Negative Offer In addition to soft and hard offers, there are two other basic categories of offers: negative and deferred. The negative offer reads as follows on the reply element: Not interested right now because: (Please give reason — thank you.) Typically, reference to the negative offer is made in the P.S. or elsewhere in the body of the sales letter, using the following language: P.S. Even if you are not interested in [name of product or service], please complete and return the enclosed reply card. Thank you. The negative offer provides a response option for people who qualify as prospects — that is, they have a need or problem your product addresses — but, for whatever reason, are not ready to take the next step in the buying process: getting more information on your product. A negative offer instructs the reader to respond even if she does not want to learn more about your product, which is disarming and unusual. By using a negative offer option, you can often get a response from a small portion of your prospects. That response can be increased by giving the reader a logical reason to reply: P.S. Even if you are not interested in [name of product or service], please complete and return the enclosed reply card so we can give your free [whatever is being offered] to another person on our list. Thank you. The negative offer should be used when you are testing a mailing on a new product, service, or offer you haven’t promoted before using direct mail. The reason you use the negative offer is that, without it, if you get a low or no response to your mailing, you don’t know whether it’s the mailing piece that’s ineffective or the product, service, or offer that isn’t right for the market. With the negative option, people will tell you why they are not interested in your offer. Perhaps the price is too high. Or your technology is not compatible with the systems they are already using. Or they don’t like your type of product or don’t use it. This information not only helps you readjust your marketing plans, it demonstrates that the mailing was unsuccessful for reasons other than ineffective copy and design — something that’s good to know if you’re the person who wrote or designed it. A second benefit of the negative option is that it can slightly increase your overall response rate. You might object and say, “But all the people who check the negative option box have told us they are not prospects.” But quite the opposite is often true: If people take the time to tell you why your offer isn’t right for them, they may be prime prospects. They’re telling you they have some sort of need, but your product as described in the mailing doesn’t seem quite right … and that they want you to get back to them with a product, service, or offer that is right for them. Actually, your product or service may be ideal for them, but your ad or mail copy may not have communicated that effectively — or they misunderstood or didn’t read carefully enough. That’s okay. By completing the negative offer option box, your prospects have set themselves up for follow-up and closing by a skilled salesperson. If you have ever been a salesperson, you know the most difficult prospect to sell is the one you can’t reach — the one who never responds to your letters, never returns your phone calls, or says he is not interested but won’t say why. A prospect who fills in the blank space on your reply card where it says “Please give a reason why you are not interested” has framed a specific objection, which can be overcome with the proper selling argument. Get Non-Responders to Reply With a Deferred Offer A deferred offer is a variation on the negative offer. Here’s how it’s phrased on the reply element: Not interested right now. Try us again in (month/year) The deferred offer encourages responses from prospects who do not have an immediate need but may have a future requirement for your product or service. Some of these prospects won’t check off the soft offer option box (“[ ] Please send me a brochure”) because they think, “If I check off this box, they’re going to follow up with a phone call and pester me. I don’t have a need right now.” The deferred offer option box says to this prospect, “If you have no immediate requirement but may have a future need, you can use this box to let us know that you have a future need, without getting calls and annoying follow-up from salespeople now.” When do you use the negative as opposed to the deferred offer option? Use the negative offer when you are testing a new offer or when you think many prospects might not respond for specific reasons. Use the deferred offer when you think a significant number of prospects might need your services at some future date rather than right away. Increase the Odds of Sales Success With Multiple Offer Options A common mistake in lead-generating promotions is to have only one offer option. In most instances, you should have two or three options. In lead generation, the best results usually come from having three offers: a soft offer, a hard offer, and either a negative or a deferred offer. At minimum, you should have both a soft and a hard offer, with one of the two being primary and the other secondary. The primary offer is the one you hope your prospects will respond to and the one you emphasize in your copy and graphics. For example, if you want a face-to-face meeting with your prospects, you would urge them to call and arrange an appointment. A “free, no-obligation initial appointment” would be your primary offer, the one you stress in your letter or e-mail. The secondary offer is included to give those prospects who will not take you up on your primary offer a second reason to respond. If a prospect is not willing or ready to take you up on your offer of a free initial meeting, introduce the secondary soft offer at the end of your ad or letter copy. (“P.S. For a free special report outlining six tax-saving strategies offered by our firm, just complete and mail the enclosed reply card.”) _____________________________ Your Primary Offer: Hard or Soft? Which offer should be your primary offer? Make your soft offer — the offer of free literature or information — the primary offer when: You know requesting a brochure or catalog is the typical first step in the buying process in your particular industry or field — and that circumventing that step would be counterproductive. You feel many prospects would be reluctant to meet or talk with you, so you need some sort of brochure or other literature to create a reason for them to respond to your mailing. Your product or service is complex and requires a lot of explanation that is best communicated in a standardized written format, such as a brochure or data sheet. You have limited staff for telephone contact with prospects, and your operation lends itself more to the mailing of a standardized inquiryfulfillment brochure or package. Your prospects are far away, and you do not have regional branch offices or sales reps who can call on them in person. You have a great brochure or inquiry-fulfillment kit already in place that has proven its ability to (1) screen out unqualified prospects and (2) sell effectively to qualified prospects. Industrial equipment manufacturers are a good example of marketers who stress soft offers. Their prospects — engineers and purchasing agents — require a lot of detailed information on technical products before making a buying decision. This technical information is communicated more easily in a printed brochure than over the telephone. Also, having a brochure on an industrial product is standard practice in the industry. Most purchasers won’t buy without having a brochure or other technical literature in their files. So a logical next step in industrial direct mail and ads is the offer of such a brochure or catalog, at no charge. The hard offer should be the primary offer when: You would prefer to get a phone inquiry rather than a written inquiry because your salespeople are more likely to close when they receive a hot lead via an inbound telephone call. You believe sending printed material, such as a brochure or catalog, is an unnecessary step that only gets in the way and slows down the selling process. There is not a lot of information or detail to communicate about your service or product, and you can sum it up quickly and easily in a twominute phone conversation. You have a free trial offer or other special offer that enables prospects to try your service or product on a small scale for free or for a nominal fee, and you feel you can get prospects to accept this offer if you can sell them on the phone or face to face. Your product or service is unique, unusual, and difficult to communicate in printed material, and you can more easily communicate it in person, either over the phone or via demonstration. Your audience is not comprised of readers or information seekers. An example of an industry that doesn’t tend to use brochures is adult vocational training. One such marketer told me, “We have learned through experience that offering a brochure is a waste. To sell the prospect on taking our program, we have to get him to come to our facility in person for a free introductory class. Otherwise, it won’t work.” _____________________________ Once you have the soft and hard offer options in place, you add either a negative option (if you want to learn why prospects are not responding as you had hoped) or a deferred option (if yours is the type of product or service that is likely to be bought at a future date rather than immediately). How will the response be split? In one mailing I did to promote my freelance copywriting services, the following letter generated a 10 percent response: Dear Marketing Professional: “It’s hard to find a copywriter who can handle directresponse, business-to-business, and high-tech accounts,” a prospect told me over the phone today, “especially for landing pages, white papers, direct mail, and other long-copy assignments.” Do you have that same problem? If so, please complete and mail the enclosed reply card and I’ll send you a free information kit describing a service that can help. As a freelance copywriter specializing in direct marketing, I’ve written hundreds of successful ads, sales letters, directmail packages, landing pages, e-mail marketing campaigns, brochures, case studies, feature articles, press releases, newsletters, and websites for clients all over the country. But my information kit will give you the full story. You’ll receive a comprehensive “WELCOME” letter that tells all about my copywriting service — who I work for, what I can do for you, how we can work together. You’ll also get my client list (I’ve written for more than 100 companies) … client testimonials … biographical background … samples of work I’ve done in your field … a fee schedule listing what I charge for sales letters, white papers, and other assignments … helpful article reprints on copywriting and marketing … even an order form you can use to put me to work for you. Whether you have an immediate project, a future need, or are just curious, I urge you to send for this information kit. It’s free … there’s no obligation … and you’ll like having a proven copywriting resource on file — someone you can call on whenever you need him. From experience, I’ve learned that the best time to evaluate a copywriter and take a look at his work is before you need him, not when a project deadline comes crashing around the corner. You want to feel comfortable about a writer and his capabilities in advance … so when a project does come up, you know who to call. Why not mail back the reply card TODAY, while it is still handy? I’ll rush your free information kit as soon as I hear from you. Regards, Bob Bly P.S. Need an immediate quote on a copywriting project? Call me at (201) 385-1220. There is no charge for a cost estimate. And no obligation to buy. Of the total response, most people (more than 90 percent) checked the soft offer box (“Please send more information”) on the card. Fewer than one in 10 (less than 10 percent) checked the hard offer box (“Give me a call”). Only a couple selected the deferred offer. I can convert between 10 and 25 percent of leads from this letter to sales within six months of receipt of the inquiry … if I want that much business. Interestingly, there is no difference in the quality of the lead (seriousness of the prospect) between those who check the soft offer box and those who check the hard offer box: Percentage conversion to sales is the same in both categories. Almost all of the response to this mailing is from the reply card. I give my telephone number in the letter, but do not encourage phone calls. (I prefer to speak to prospects only after they have received a complete package of information about my services.) I do not give a fax number or encourage fax responses. People check the deferred offer box (“Not interested right now”) infrequently, and I mail so few of these letters that I can’t give you a statistical result. Qualitatively, however, I can tell you that having the third box for the deferred offer has paid off. I can recall specific instances where a prospect checked the “Try us again” option, and, when I followed up, I found they did indeed have a specific project in mind to be started at a specific date. Immediate follow-up with literature and a later phone call at the time requested resulted in a sale in at least two cases. OceanofPDF.com 2 Hook More Prospects With a “Bait Piece” — and Double Your Response _____________________________ “The free booklet offer is so effective and so important that, for most marketers seeking to generate leads, I think it’s a mistake not to have such an offer as part of their promotions.” — Bob Bly _____________________________ The most effective method of increasing the response rate of a leadgeneration campaign is to use a “bait piece.” The term bait piece refers to free information the advertiser offers in a mailing piece or e-mail to generate a higher number of inquiries. The word bait is used because the free content is given not just to educate the reader (as the reader is led to believe) but to “hook” the reader by generating a response or inquiry, which can then be followed up by telephone or field sales personnel. To make this strategy work, the content of the bait piece should be relevant, valuable, desirable, and specific to the prospect’s interests and needs. There are a number of ways to enhance the soft offer by giving away a bait piece. The most popular, and probably still the most effective, is with a free booklet, special report, white paper, or other printed content. Where does the free bait piece fit into the sales cycle? The diagram above tells the story. Your initial e-mail, direct mail, or other promotion offers the bait piece. Some of those who read your promotion respond by asking for the bait piece. You fulfill these inquiries by sending the bait piece along with sales materials (e.g., a brochure) on your product or services. Then you follow up. Depending on the nature and cost of your product or service, anywhere from 10 to 35 percent or more of those requesting the free bait piece will ultimately do business with you. _____________________________ Here is a fact many direct marketers do not know: Just by adding a free bait piece to your offer, you can often double the response to your ads and mailings over what the response for essentially the same ad or letter copy would be without the free information offer. _____________________________ Why are free content offers so effective? For several reasons. First, today’s prospects, despite being overloaded with reading material, are information seekers, always on the lookout for advice, ideas, and information to help them do their jobs better and more efficiently, or save time and money at home, or lead happier lives. Many publishers charge handsomely for such information sold as seminars, audio CDs, DVDs, books, newsletters, and manuals. So when people see that they can get similar information from you in the form of a free booklet or special report, they respond. After all, if it’s free, they have little to lose. Second, many folks are so busy that they flip through mail, e-mail, and ads at a frantic rate. The free booklet offer, with perhaps a cutout coupon in the ad and a picture of a free booklet in an HTML e-mail, has attentiongrabbing power. It forces the reader to slow down, stop, and peruse your copy. The reader thinks, “Oh, this is one of those ads offering something free. Let me look for a second and see what I can get.” So she calls or clips the coupon and requests the booklet. Third, people love getting things for free. In the direct-marketing seminars I give nationwide, there is always someone in the audience who says, “Aren’t free offers much less effective today? Come on, really, how excited can an executive get about a free booklet or white paper?” The fact is, whether or not they get excited is irrelevant. They do get interested — and giving away free information in your advertising dramatically increases online and offline response rates. The free booklet offer is so effective and so important that, for most marketers seeking to generate leads, I think it’s a mistake not to have such an offer as part of their promotions. The reason is simple: Unless prospects have an immediate, urgent need to pick up the phone and call you, your mailer or e-mail is largely of little interest to them. It’s just another “sales pitch,” one of many they will receive by mail or phone that day. The prospect feels no need to respond — and doesn’t. But a free booklet can solve this problem. It says to the prospect, “Even if you have no immediate need, don’t have time to read our mailing, and don’t want to think about our product right now, at least mail back the reply card. You’ll receive something of value in return.” Bottom line: Giving away a bait piece containing valuable content can double response rates to your leadgeneration campaigns. Make the offer of the free content prominent in your copy and graphics. The business reply card below features the free offer, not the product or service, in the headline: “Send me your FREE White Paper.” It is illustrated with a picture of the free white paper, not the product or service. Rule of thumb: The more you emphasize your offer in your marketing, the greater your response. 7 Steps to Creating Winning Free Content Offers Here are the seven steps to creating and using free content offers: 1. Pick an appropriate topic for your free booklet, report, or white paper. The topic should be something that interests the reader while helping to sell the reader on your system, product, service, or idea. _____________________________ The more you emphasize your offer in your marketing, the greater your response. _____________________________ For instance, to promote a line of business software, IBM published a free 200-page paperback book telling small businesses what to look for when evaluating software packages. The book helped readers by showing them which features to look for when shopping for software. At the same time, it helped IBM promote its software, because the comparison checklist in the book highlighted many of the features of the IBM products. I ghostwrote the book for IBM, working with their software developers to give readers a useful checklist of features they should make sure they get in the business software they buy. IBM hired me because of my reputation as a book author, not a copywriter. They instructed me to write the book as if it were to be sold in a bookstore for $20, not given away as a bait piece. They wanted it to be detailed, useful, and full of content — not a “puff” piece. The book gives readers specifications they can use to evaluate potential software purchases. The information is believable because it is packaged in the form of a book rather than a promotional brochure. In their minds, IBM has become a credible source for business software because, after all, IBM “wrote the book.” (My name is not on the cover.) When prospects check out IBM’s software, they find (surprise!) that it fulfills the specifications outlined in the book. Therefore, it must be good and a sale is made. The topic you select for your bait piece can persuade the reader to favor your product or service, but the sell must be soft and subtle. Typically, the free report or booklet explains a certain way to do a thing or how to select a product to do it. “The ‘silver bullet’ I include in every white paper is a section on how to select or what to look for when buying the particular type of product my client is selling,” says white paper writer Michael Stelzner. “Of course my client’s product fills all the requirements spelled out in the white paper.” While a product selection guide must appear unbiased and editorially neutral, you will slant it so the reader comes away favoring your approach to doing the thing, solving the problem, or selecting the product. The booklet you write contributes to the selling process in two ways: first, by predisposing the reader to accept your methods as standard and desirable; second, by positioning you and your firm as experts on the topic. The topic must be interesting and relevant to the reader. A smallbusiness owner would not be interested in “How IBM Designs and Codes Its Software Systems,” but he would be interested in “How to Choose the Right Software for Your Business.” The booklet must appeal to the reader’s self-interest while promoting your own. That’s the balance you must achieve. _____________________________ “The ‘silver bullet’ I include in every white paper is a section on how to select or what to look for when buying the particular type of product my client is selling,” — Michael Stelzner _____________________________ 2. After selecting a topic, you need a catchy title. A title with the words “how to” in it (e.g., “How to Reduce Costs and Increase Productivity by Implementing Electronic Data Interchange”) can be effective. People want to know how to do things and they want solutions to their problems. Number titles (e.g., “7 Ways,” “6 Steps,” “14 Winning Methods”) also make your booklet more attractive to the reader because they arouse curiosity. People want to know what the 7 ways, 6 steps, or 14 methods are. Here are some titles from successful free booklets offered in actual direct-mail promotions and print ads: 15 Ways to Improve Your Collection Efforts (RMCB) Should I Personalize? A Direct Marketer’s Guide to Personalized Direct Mail (Fala Direct Marketing) Choosing Business Software (IBM) Aldus Guide to Desktop Design (Aldus) Family-Owned Businesses: The 3 Most Common Pitfalls… and How to Avoid Them (Consulting Dynamics) The Special Report: Productivity Breakthrough Projects (JMW Consultants) 33 Ways to Make Better Displays: What Every Marketing Executive Should Know About Point-of-Purchase Display Marketing (Display Masters) Steel Log: Glossary of Metal Terms (Specialty Steel) 7 Questions to Ask Before You Invest in DP Training… and One Good Answer to Each (Chubb Institute) The title of your bait piece is all-important, because it determines, in large part, whether you can get prospects interested enough to send for your free content. So choose the title with care. If you are selling e-mail distribution software and your target market is advertising agencies, how about a downloadable white paper titled “What Every Ad Agency Executive Should Know About Maximizing E-Mail Delivery Rates”? If you owned an ad agency and your clients were complaining about low e-mail response rates, would you send for that free report? I should think so! When choosing a topic and title, it’s better to make it narrow and more targeted than broad and general. By narrowing the focus, you can cover one specific topic of great interest to your prospects with sufficient detail to gain their attention and whet their appetites for further contact with you. For example, Fala’s booklet — “Should I Personalize? A Direct Marketer’s Guide to Personalized Direct Mail” — is effective because it zeros in on one specific topic of interest to direct marketers (personalizing direct mail) rather than on the broader, less meaningful topic of “Direct Mail.” It specifically positions Fala as the expert in personalized direct-mail production. Here are some conventions for titling bait pieces: 3. After selecting the topic and title, think about media and format. Do you want to publish a booklet, report, fact sheet, downloadable PDF white paper, kit, folder, folio, monograph, CD-ROM, PowerPoint presentation, flash presentation, podcast, Webinar, or poster? Or how about a book or manual? Or do you plan on putting your information on audio CD, DVD, or computer disk? A fact sheet or tip sheet is the most basic format. In a fact sheet, your information is desktop-published or typeset and printed on one or both sides of a single sheet of 8 1/2 x 11 inch paper. Such sheets can be produced quickly and inexpensively. For example, you can offset print or photocopy 500 single-sided tip sheets for $30 to $50. To enhance their perceived value, print on yellow, gold, or other brightly colored stock rather than white. Or you can offer reprints of articles you’ve written, calling them “tip sheets.” Tip sheets can be effective, but some marketers think they look cheap. One solution is to print your tip sheet as a poster, using a larger size and better stock of paper suitable for framing. The Communication Workshop, a New York consulting firm, has had great success promoting its business-writing seminars with a series of one-page posters on grammar, sexist language, and similar writing topics. Most marketers offer free information in the form of a booklet or special report. A booklet implies a smaller-size publication, either folded or saddle-stitched (staples through the spine). The information is more detailed than a tip sheet but less detailed than a book or scholarly article. The booklet page size can be 4 x 9 inches to fit a standard No. 10 business envelope or 5 1/2 by 8 1/2 inches to fit a 6 x 9 inch envelope. A special report is similar to a booklet except it has full-size (8 1/2 x 11 inch) pages and is mailed in a 9 x 12 inch envelope. The report can be mailed physically to the prospects or made available for immediate download online as a PDF file. Printed reports can be run off on a photocopier or offset press, collated, and put in a clear plastic or other attractive cover. If you want to tailor versions of the report to different audiences, you can keep the body of it the same and simply change the introduction and front cover for each one. 4. Write an enticing description for your bait piece. How you describe the bait piece in your offer copy can affect the response rate. For instance, years ago, when the Clintons were in office, American Spectator magazine offered as a subscription premium “The Bill & Hillary Clinton ‘Inside the White House’ Report.” Sounds important and impressive. Of course, the special report consisted of recycled content: a few long articles on the Clintons that had run in past issues, nicely reprinted and saddle-stitched together. The free “Inside the White House Report” was offered in radio commercials selling the magazine. Imagine how much less impressive and desirable it would have been for the radio announcer to describe the premium literally and say: “Subscribe to American Spectator today, and we’ll rip some old articles out of back issues, staple them together, and mail them to you.” Clearly, the wording of the offer, and that includes the descriptions of premiums, matters. As Bob Hemmings notes in an article in Direct (12/08, p. 34): “The same offer stated differently is perceived as being a uniquely different offer and can give a substantial boost to results.” _____________________________ “The same offer stated differently is perceived as being a uniquely different offer and can give a substantial boost to results.” — Bob Hemmings _____________________________ Here are some suggestions on how to label your premium in your offer copy: You can argue that we are talking only about semantics here. But words sell, and semantics matter. For example, as a consumer, are you more interested in getting a “brochure” or a “consumer awareness guide”? Is a CEO more likely to send for and look at a “white paper” or an “executive briefing”? 5. Even though you intend to give away your booklet or report for free, put a price on the front cover in the upper right-hand corner. This serves a couple of functions. First, it adds to the perceived value of the booklet or report. People are more interested in getting a $29 item for free than they are in getting a free item for free. Second, it allows you to charge for the item when you get inquiries from those who are not potential customers: students, brochure collectors, and so on. Third, it allows you to gracefully request payment from the occasional person who calls you up and wants multiple copies for a seminar, presentation, or class. (This does happen every once in a while, and it can be costly to oblige.) What should the pricing be? I suggest $1 or $2 for a tip sheet, $3 to $10 for a booklet, $7 to $29 for a special report (depending on length), $15 to $25 for a book, $15 to $25 for a manual. These prices seem credible and fair. If you make the price too high, the prospect realizes it’s a scam to make the offer seem better than it is. Quick Tip: Post all your bait pieces on a page on your website so that visitors can order them online, for the full cover price, through your shopping cart. (If you need a shopping cart, visit www.automateyouronlinebusinessnow.com.) Even without proactively promoting these pieces as information products, the traffic on your site will yield occasional orders. The purpose is not to make money selling your bait pieces. It is to legitimate the dollar amount you list as a cover price. All my bait pieces are posted online at http://www.bly.com/reportslibrary.html, and we do get orders for them. So I can honestly say in my copy that the price is real, not made up. 6. Now decide how you will package and reproduce your premium. If your report is long (50 pages or more), you can increase its perceived value still further by putting the pages in a three-ring binder and calling it a manual. You can duplicate your manual in small quantities using your office copier. If you are going to produce the manual in volume, don’t print the manual cover directly on the binder. Instead, leave the binder cover blank and use a title page. Or print the cover on a separate glossy sheet and buy notebooks with a front cover “trap-in” (a clear plastic sleeve that allows you to easily insert and remove the cover). This way, if the report changes or becomes dated, you are not stuck with hundreds of unusable (and expensive) custom-printed binders. If the free information bait piece is lengthy and a proven success, you may want to go to the next step and produce it as a self-published book. IBM did this with the Choosing Business Software book. CoreStates Financial Corporation similarly promoted its expertise and technology in EDI (Electronic Data Interchange) by giving away a self-published paperback book on the subject. Even with Internet-savvy prospects like IT professionals, free book offers can work extremely well: A conventional paperback book requires more of an investment in effort, typesetting, and printing than a booklet, report, or manual. Because of printing economics, you will have to order a minimum of 500 copies of your book and will probably get the best price/volume deal when you order 2,000 or 3,000. Be sure to get quotes only from printers that specialize in short runs (less than 5,000 copies). General printers charge two to three times as much because they are not set up to print books. For a directory of book printers, contact Para Publishing at 800-PARA-PUB. Or consult the reference book Literary Marketplace, available in your local library. If you are promoting your free book to a small niche market and do not want to print a lot of copies all at once, consider Print on Demand (POD) technology. POD printers enable you to print and bind your paperback book one copy at a time, though the per-copy cost is many times higher than with a short-run book printer. A book has a high perceived value and is also seen as being an unbiased, legitimate source of information. Because you want to keep the cost reasonable, you should plan to publish a small book rather than a big one. A small paperback can contain as few as 60 to 80 pages with as little as 15,000 words of text (the equivalent of 60 double-spaced typewritten pages). Again, don’t forget to put a cover price on the book. About $10 to $15 for a slim paperback seems right. 7. You have selected the topic, title, and format. Now it is time to determine the contents, make an outline, and write the copy for your booklet or report. The most important thing to keep in mind when writing informational premiums like free booklets or reports is that the contents must deliver on the promise of the headline, convey useful information helpful to the reader, and be accurate. It is not necessary for the contents to be revolutionary or give the reader all new information. Many people read to affirm current beliefs or reinforce existing knowledge. So if your booklet mostly repeats what they already know, they’ll be happy with it. More important, they’ll think you’re a wise, knowledgeable expert on the topic. However, if you can give the reader one or two genuinely new ideas or things they may not have thought of before, so much the better. It will make your booklet or report even more valuable to them. Do not include your advertising message in the body of the booklet. The contents should be pure information. You promised the reader knowledge; you impress the reader by conveying that knowledge. If you turn the booklet into a sales pitch, the people who sent for it expecting helpful advice will be angry, disappointed, turned off, and not inclined to do business with you. You can insert an ad or promotional copy on the pages in the back of the book, at the end of the regular text. How much information should be included in your bait piece? It depends on the length and format. A full-length book, for example, must obviously provide more detail than a one-page tip sheet. As a rule, make your booklet or report helpful and fascinating, but don’t overdo the detail. You want to tell the prospect enough to get her interested in hiring you to solve a problem. You don’t want to tell so much in your report that it eliminates the need for the prospect to hire your firm or buy your product. If the body is pure information, can you do any selling in the booklet? Yes, but keep it low key. On the front cover, under the title, put your firm as the author, giving the address and phone number. Repeat this information on the back cover, adding a more complete description of your company, your product or service, how you can help the reader, and the next step she should take to learn more about your product or service. This should read like the “About the Author” bios you find on how-to books written by business experts, giving enough information to whet the reader’s appetite without being blatantly sales-oriented. Increase Perceived Value With an Electronic Bait Piece One way to generate additional interest and make your bait piece stand out even more is to offer your information in the form of an audiocassette, audio CD, DVD, or software CD-ROM. One advantage of these formats is that they are not as widely used as print and downloadable PDF files. Therefore, they are a bit unusual and likely to attract more attention. Also, CDs and DVDs tend to stand out in an in-basket crowded with paper. Other advantages? CDs and DVDs usually get past secretaries who screen and throw away lots of paper mail. Because a CD or DVD has a higher perceived value than paper and is a tangible object, it won’t get thrown away. Experience has shown that prospects will take the time to listen to or view the audio CD or video, or at least make sure it gets passed on to the right person within the organization. Printed pieces are not treated with the same degree of importance. Finally, even if the prospects don’t immediately listen to or view the tape or disk, they will probably keep it in a desk drawer rather than throw it away. So every time they open the drawer, they will see the tape or disk imprinted with your company name and phone number. Audio CDs Sell Your Products to Prospects While They Drive Audio CDs are the easiest and least costly audiovisual medium to use as information bait pieces. Some marketers using audio CDs think that briefer is better and limit the message to 10 or 20 minutes. But if the audio contains pure, useful information, it can be much longer. I have been successful promoting both my seminars and my consulting and copywriting services using audio CDs that are 30 to 90 minutes long. Prospects must set aside valuable time to watch a DVD. But they can listen to your audio CD while driving the car, exercising, or doing household chores. Audio CDs do not require the high level of production that videos do. You can record a live presentation or speech given at work, a meeting, or an industry event, edit it in a studio, and offer it as an attractive bait piece. What will all this cost? To hire someone with professional-quality equipment to record a presentation costs $200 to $400 plus travel expenses. Studio time goes for $75 to $95 per hour, and should take less than half a day. To duplicate my audio CDs with a laser-printed label in a vinyl case or sleeve costs about $1.25 per unit. Create Visual Excitement With a DVD Videos are another story.

You can record a live presentation or speech given at work, a meeting, or an industry event, edit it in a studio, and offer it as an attractive bait piece. What will all this cost?
