 You can expect to pay a professional at least $1,000 or $2,000 to record you on location or in a studio. If you want a fullblown production with sets and special effects, an eight-minute video can cost $5,000 to $15,000 or more, just for production. The cost to duplicate 1,000 copies of an eight-minute video is about $2.50 per cassette with a cardboard box and typed label. Plastic boxes and four-color packaging can run much higher. But do you need to hire expensive pros to create your marketing videos? Or can you do it yourself with a camcorder or even a webcam? For many years, conventional wisdom was that the quality of a marketing video had to be equal or nearly equal to the quality of broadcast television. Reason: The viewer is accustomed to watching TV, and therefore rejects anything with lesser production values as inferior and cheesy. But all that has changed. The overwhelming majority of small Internet marketers who post videos on their sites shoot homemade clips, with minimal production values, using hand-held digital cameras. Internet users watch millions of videos on YouTube and other video-sharing sites, all similarly produced by amateurs. As a result, the Internet user is very accepting of low production values on Web videos. So you can shoot your own video and eliminate the need to spend hundreds or thousands of dollars to hire a professional. _____________________________ If you’d like to find out more about how to use video to market your products and services online, check out American Writers & Artists Inc.’s (AWAI) program Marketing With Video Online for Profit at www.awaionline.com/video-marketing/. AWAI teamed up with award-winning videographer, Jessica Kizorek, to give you everything you need to: Write, shoot, edit, and distribute a video and make it look professional, even if you have no experience or have only used YouTube™ for fun in the past; Why people expect more from the marketing materials and advertisements they see, and what you can do to deliver on their expectations; What it takes to persuade someone to take a desired action in a video and how that translates into a video script and shooting; How to measure the success of your video (even a simple YouTube™ video); The legal considerations to keep in mind when shooting and distributing your videos; Business models they can use to build a successful video marketing business; Video-marketing techniques for marketing your services, including a “vlog” (video blog); and How you can make sure you have a never-ending stream of clients ready to pay for your services and much more! _____________________________ An Offer With Incredibly High Perceived Value Sales and informational presentations can be put on CDs or USB drives that the prospect can view using a personal computer. Disks and flash drives containing software or data files have a high perceived value and, therefore, make effective bait pieces. They work well with businesspeople, PC users, and others who have access to a personal computer. I would not use them for audiences that don’t have computers or are not computer literate. Many software marketers generating leads offer demos or evaluation copies of their software on CD or via download as the bait piece. Alex Plavocos, Marketing Director of Computron Software, used Excel to organize the information on his marketing CD. This enabled prospects to easily find information on the particular product, service, or application they were interested in. Software has an extraordinarily high ratio of perceived value to actual cost. Since a software program can sell for $49 to $499 or more, the consumer considers it a valuable product. Yet your cost per premium is about a dollar with a CD, or virtually zero if you offer a download online. Where to Get Free Content for Your Bait Piece One reason that marketers give for not using the bait piece offer despite its proven effectiveness is this: “It sounds good, but I have a limited budget and staff. I don’t really have the time to write and design or commission someone to write, design, and print a really good booklet or special report.” There are several solutions to this problem. One is to write and place a feature story on your preferred topic in an industry trade journal, and then simply reprint that article as a tip sheet or booklet. This eliminates the need for you to write, typeset, and design an original piece. Be sure you retain reprint rights or get reprint permission from the magazine in which the piece is first published as an article. When submitting an article to a newspaper or magazine, type “First rights only” in the upper left corner of the first page of your manuscript. This tells the publisher that, once they run the article in their magazine, you own all rights and can do with it as you please. When you offer an article reprint as a bait piece, call it a tip sheet or special report, not an article reprint, as the former convey higher perceived value. Somewhere in small type on the reprint, you can cite the publication and date of the article’s original appearance. A second strategy for offering free reports as bait pieces without paying to create them yourself is to reprint existing material relevant to your product or market. For instance, if you are a member of a professional society or trade association, many such organizations offer informative publications that members can distribute or reprint without charge or for a reasonable sum. When reprinting, add your own front and back cover with your logo, company name, description, and contact information. Many medical societies and associations, as well as some pharmaceutical companies, for example, offer informative booklets on various aspects of health care that member physicians can reprint. Most doctors simply leave copies for patients on a table in their waiting room. But one orthodontist in my town reprinted one of those booklets with his office address and phone number, added a personal cover letter, and mailed it, with good results, to potential patients. If you’re an agent, representative, distributor, or dealer, your manufacturer or wholesaler may provide you with booklets and other literature you can reprint or add your label to. These can be offered to prospects as bait pieces with no creative or other development costs on your part. Another well-kept secret: The U.S. government is one of the biggest producers of informational booklets and special reports — and a large number of those government publications are not copyrighted and may therefore be reprinted and used by you for promotional (or any other) purposes. The government asks, but does not require, you to acknowledge them as the original source of the material. One local radon-testing firm, for example, offers a report on “Radon in the Home,” which is simply a reprint of a government publication with the firm’s name and phone number imprinted on the top. For catalogs of the various government publications available for free or at reasonable cost, contact: Superintendent of Documents U.S. Government Printing Office Mail Stop IDCC 732 N. Capitol Street NW Washington, DC 20402 Phone 202-783-3238 http://www.pueblo.gsa.gov/cic_text/smbuss/cpyright/circ01.pdf www.gpoaccess.gov _____________________________ The U.S. government is one of the biggest producers of informational booklets and special reports. _____________________________ Using existing publications as bait pieces works if you have a product or service for which a more generic bait piece would be an effective promotional device. For instance, if you’re generating leads for an executive fitness program, you could probably increase response by offering a free package of booklets on health, diet, and exercise that are reprints of some of the copyright-free publications offered by the U.S. government. On the other hand, if you are selling a highly specialized technical product, there is probably not an existing report you can use, and you will have to create your own. While in many cases you can use existing publications as bait pieces, I often recommend to clients that they create their own customized information premiums because an original publication can be made more interesting to their audience and more relevant to their product or service. 5 Common Objections to Free Booklet Offers — and One Good Answer to Each Offering a free booklet, report, or other free information piece in your ads and direct mail can dramatically boost response. In fact, this is one of the few direct-response rules that works almost every time. In virtually every campaign where I have added a free booklet offer to the marketing program, sales lead generation has increased substantially and marketing costs were reduced. I know of few other strategies that are so basic, simple, and easy to use while consistently delivering such excellent results. Despite this, many marketers avoid using free booklet offers, based largely on the following erroneous beliefs. If you are not using the bait piece strategy because of one of these fears, this list may be helpful in overcoming your particular objection. The five erroneous beliefs are: 1. “It’s a cliché.” The number one reason marketers avoid free booklet offers is that they think it’s old hat and are looking for something original. They say to me: “Offering a free booklet isn’t original. Can’t you think of something more creative?” My answer is simple: So what if it’s old hat? So what if it’s a formula? The reality is, it works consistently and repeatedly for companies in all industries. The fact that free booklet offers are not original is true but unimportant. What’s important is that they will generate more leads per ad or mailing, producing more inquiries and more sales while lowering marketing costs. 2. “It’s overused.” Another common objection is, “I like the idea, but free booklet offers are so overused in our industry. Take a look at the magazines serving our niche, and you see free booklet offers in every other ad. Every other mailing I receive offers a free booklet. So how could our offer compete with all this clutter?” This argument makes sense but is refuted by experience. While there are some marketing techniques that do lose effectiveness in the face of clutter and overuse, the free booklet offer is not one of them. In fact, the opposite is often true: Prospects in a particular industry become accustomed to seeing ads with free booklet offers and eagerly seek out such ads in their trade publications. If your ad lacks such a bait piece, prospects are more likely to pass it by. 3. “Our competitors already offer a free booklet.” The natural tendency is to think, “Our competitor has already published a booklet on the topic we were thinking of, so they’ve beaten us to it. There’s no sense going ahead with ours.” Free content offers can establish you as a thought leader in your industry and increase response to your marketing campaigns. But the bait piece itself is almost never a branding strategy or unique selling proposition (USP). The fact that your competitors also give away bait pieces is largely irrelevant and certainly not a reason to avoid the technique. If anything, it demonstrates that the tactic works in your market. The right strategy is to go ahead with your own booklet and either (1) choose a topic that’s different but still helps promote your product or (2) choose the same topic and produce a report or booklet that’s better. How do you make your booklet better? Give tips and strategies the competition does not. Include a helpful glossary, charts, conversion tables, bibliography, checklists, names and addresses of resources, graphs, and other useful references. Use pictures and illustrations to make your point clear. Reveal inside information and details the competition keeps secret. Even if the topic is similar, select a title that’s clearly different from the competition’s. Having the same or a similar-sounding title confuses prospects and isn’t good for either you or your competitor. Without a free booklet offer, your prospects are likely to respond only to your competitors’ ads, which do offer booklets, while skipping over yours. Adding a free booklet offer helps ensure that you, too, will hear from prospects with a need to buy what you are selling. 4. “My prospects already have too much to read.” The fourth argument against free information offers is either “My prospects already have too much to read, so the last thing they want is another booklet or report” or “My prospects are not readers.” While it is true that many prospects already have too much to read, they will still seek out and send for yet another booklet or report if they perceive that it contains information that is relevant, helpful, and tailored to their needs. A prospect may have six inches of paperwork stacked in his inbasket, yet if his most pressing problem is cutting energy costs in the plant, he will respond to an ad or direct-mail package offering a free report on “6 Proven Ways to Cut Energy Costs in Your Plant This Year.” Ideally, you want your prospect not only to send for but also to read your booklet or report. However, even if a prospect sends for but does not read your free information, the bait piece offer has still done its job: It’s generated an inquiry from a prospect who would otherwise have tossed your ad or mailing aside. Therefore, the fact that your prospects are too busy or not inclined to read the material you send is not a good reason not to offer such information. The key is to overcome inertia and get them to respond. Once you receive the inquiry, you can start the selling process to convert the lead to a sale. But with no response, you get nowhere. And free booklet offers increase response. 5. “If we give away free content, we’ll generate a large volume of poor-quality leads from freebie seekers.” If this is a concern, you can qualify the leads more up front and generate a better quality lead using some or all of the following techniques: Charge a nominal fee for your catalog, brochure, or other literature. Ask the prospects to answer a lot of questions about themselves. Make them fill out a survey or complete a questionnaire. Make the prospects pay the postage on the return envelope or postcard. Tell prospects you will not fulfill inquiries if they do not provide their phone number. Say, “Serious inquiries only, please.” Do not stress guarantees, money-back offers, free offers, and risk-free trials or estimates. If you offer a premium, do not send the gift in response to the inquiry. Instead, tell prospects they will be given the gift in person when they meet with your salesperson or that the gift is sent when they make a purchase. Bait Pieces: Free or Fee? In most cases, I recommend that you do not charge for your bait piece. If you’re offering a booklet or report to generate leads, the booklet or report should be free. Unless your primary business is selling books or reports by mail and you are offering this booklet or report to build your mailing list, charging for it will dramatically decrease your response rate and slow down the flow of leads. And that defeats the reason for offering the bait piece in the first place. One argument for charging is the theory that people who pay for the booklet or report are better-qualified prospects. This isn’t true (unless, again, your main business is selling books or reports by mail). For businessto-business lead generation, you can qualify prospects by asking them questions (e.g., “What type of business are you in?” or “What is your immediate need?”) on your ad coupon or direct-mail reply card. But does asking them to pay $5 for your booklet make them more qualified to buy your widget? I don’t think so. In fact, it only serves to prevent a lot of qualified prospects who would have requested your widget booklet if it were free from doing so. (The reason is not the cost but the added trouble of writing a check and sending it to you.) The basic offer options for bait pieces are as follows: Booklet or report free to prospects who call or mail the reply card. Booklet or report available free only to qualified prospects. Booklet or report free with self-addressed, stamped envelope. Booklet or report free with self-addressed, stamped envelope and $1 or $2 to cover handling. Booklet or report for $5 (or whatever you want to charge). Booklet or report free to qualified prospects; $5 (or whatever you want to charge) to the general public and others who are not qualified prospects. CD or DVD free, with $5.95 charged to credit card for shipping and handling. If the cost of printing and distributing booklets is a real hardship for you, you can recover that cost by requesting that the reader supply a selfaddressed, stamped envelope and $1 or $2 to cover shipping and handling. But I don’t recommend this. For 99.99 percent of marketers, the free booklet offer should be just that — entirely free. SR, one of my mentors in freelance copywriting, told me an interesting story about charging prospects for information. Many years ago, SR promoted his freelance copywriting services with small display ads in The Wall Street Journal. The ads offered a “copywriting information kit” that included reprints of helpful marketing articles. SR’s small ad generated dozens of inquiries when he offered the information kit free. Many of the inquiries were serious. Some turned into business. A few, of course, were from freebie seekers who had no interest in hiring SR and just wanted the free articles. This frustrated SR, because it wasted his time and money to fulfill those inquiries. To cut down on freeloaders, SR changed the ad, requiring respondents to send him a nominal sum — just three dollars — to get the information kit. The response dwindled from dozens of inquiries to two or three per ad … and no business. Charging for his bait piece certainly did away with freeloaders. But it also discouraged legitimate prospects from inquiring about his services. Lesson learned: With rare exceptions, the bait piece should be free. That’s especially true today, when offering a print, audio, or video bait piece as an online download reduces fulfillment costs to practically zero. OceanofPDF.com 3 Using Hard Offers to Capture Hot Prospects Okay. In lead generation, we have two major kinds of offers. The soft offer is designed to generate leads from qualified prospects — folks who could surely benefit from your product but are not ready to buy it. It does this by offering them information: a product brochure, white paper, or other free content. The hard offer captures inquiries from hot prospects who have an immediate need and want to buy now instead of later. It results in a face-toface or telephone meeting between the seller and the potential buyer. A marketing manager once told me that prospects are like submarines: They are submerged most of the time and surface only occasionally. The soft offer ferrets out prospects who are submerged by getting them to raise their hands and say, “I might be interested. Tell me more.” But the hot prospect has surfaced. She is actively looking for a product or service to solve a specific problem, fill a pressing need, or handle a particular application. The hard offer is the weapon that helps us spot hot prospects “swimming on the surface” and reel them in. In this chapter, we’ll review five time-tested rules for creating winning hard offers that capture more hot prospects that you can meet with and convert into sales. Rule 1: Do Not Involve “Salespeople.” A typical hard offer in lead generation is a check-off box on the business reply card or ad coupon that says, “Have a salesperson call me.” By choosing this offer option, the prospect is saying, “I have sufficient interest in your product or service that I am willing to have your salesperson make a presentation to me or at least chat with me over the phone for a few minutes.” This is a more aggressive, active response toward initiating the next step in the selling process than the soft offer of “Send me a brochure.” “Have a salesperson call” is probably the most widely used hard offer in lead generation. It paves the way for the in-person sales visit that, for many marketers, is a crucial step in getting the prospect to buy their product or service. In many cases, however, very few prospects select this offer option. Reason: Prospects don’t view salespeople as helpful or beneficial. In fact, the word salesperson signals to the prospect that sales pressure will be exerted — something most prospects want to avoid. The word “salesperson” has a negative connotation, implying that the prospect will be subjected to high-pressure selling tactics aimed at benefiting the seller, not the buyer. The solution is to repackage the “Have a salesperson call me” offer, using skillful copywriting and a change in tactics, to convert what is perceived as a sell job into what is perceived as a meeting that will be beneficial and helpful for the prospect. In a nutshell, this is done by replacing the words sell and sales with words that are more prospectoriented. To start with, do not use the term salesperson when referring to the person who will contact or follow up with the prospect. Replace salesperson with any of the following (or create your own title, as appropriate): Account Representative Senior Consultant Technical Specialist Account Manager Account Supervisor Industry Specialist Program Manager Program Planner [name of product] Specialist [description of application] Specialist For example, if you are selling financial services, don’t say, “Have a sales representative call.” Instead, say: “Have a financial consultant call” or “Have a financial planner call” (if your salespeople are truly financial planners). If you are selling a relational database, say, “Have a database specialist call.” If you are a consultant teaching firms how to sell by using social networking, say “Have a social networking specialist call.” Rule 2: Do Not Offer to Do a “Sales Presentation.” Do not use the words sales call, sales pitch, or sales presentation when referring to the initial appointment you are seeking with the prospect, because of the negative connotation of the word sales. Instead of a sales call or sales presentation, suggest to prospects that they contact you to arrange one of the following: Initial appointment Free, no-obligation consultation Free estimate Free analysis Needs assessment Audit Exploratory meeting Evaluation of their requirements Initial planning session Free demonstration Free executive briefing Free seminar Your hard offer might now read: Please have a technical consultant call to arrange a free analysis of my network requirements. I understand there is no cost for this initial analysis — and no obligation. If you phrase your offer this way (or in a similar fashion), you will get more response than if you simply say, “Have a salesperson call” or “Call me to arrange a sales presentation.” Why does this technique work so well? If you think about it, you’ll realize that any initial contact between buyer and seller is not merely a selling opportunity for the marketer — it has value to the buyer independent of whether he buys the product or service. For example, if a printer makes a presentation and gives you a price quotation, that price information is of value even if you do not hire the printer, since it provides a benchmark against which you can judge other quotes. You might also gain some helpful pointers on the print production process, and the printer is not compensated for giving this knowledge to you unless you actually hire him to do the job. Say you have an initial meeting with a financial planner during which you ask questions about investment options, your financial situation, and so on. In order to convince you that she is knowledgeable, the financial planner will probably answer many of those questions. You can put that information to work even if you decide not to hire that particular person. Therefore, the initial sales meeting has value inherent in the meeting itself and independent of the product or service. The strategy of offering a “free consultation by our expert,” as opposed to the traditional “sales presentation by our salesperson,” simply recognizes this inherent value — and it increases response by highlighting the value of the initial meeting or contact itself, rather than asking for a sales opportunity. Rule 3: Do Not Charge for the First Meeting. If you are actively prospecting for new customers or clients, I assume that you need the business. If you always had more leads than you could ever hope to handle, you would not need to proactively generate more. Given that you want or need new business, you can get more appointments by offering the initial meeting or conversation for free. Some prospects may represent an account so potentially lucrative that it is worth traveling to meet them. With prospects whose value is more marginal, you may decide that the only way you can “meet” with them for free is over the phone. When your prospect requests an initial meeting, make it clear that the meeting or consultation is free. This alone may give you an advantage over your competitors, some of whom may charge for the first meeting. For instance, we once called three landscape architects to get a quote on landscaping the front lawn of a home we owned. All three have good reputations in our county. Two were willing to visit us, inspect the property, and give us a free quote. The quote included a free preliminary drawing, showing us the landscapes they proposed to create for us. The third vendor explained that he charged $100 for a landscape drawing, so his quote could not include one unless we paid his fee. “I can still come to your home and give you an estimate for the landscaping for free,” he said. “You just won’t get my drawing until you retain me.” His position seemed reasonable, so we had him come and give us a free estimate. But when we reviewed the three quotes, the other two had beautiful drawings and his had none. Given that the pricing was fairly equivalent, he had no chance of winning our business. We chose one of the other landscaping firms. If you are in a field where it is not unusual for some vendors to charge for initial meetings, estimates, or preliminary recommendations, your prospects may assume you charge too. So your marketing copy must make it clear that you do not charge, as this gives you an advantage over your competitors. Especially when your offer sounds too good and generous to be true, prospects become suspicious that there is some hidden charge or implicit agreement requiring them to buy something. Always stress in your copy: “This initial consultation is absolutely free, with no obligation of any kind.” Rule 4: Add Value to the Initial Meeting. Offering the initial meeting for free is good. But it’s even more attractive if you convince the prospect that the initial meeting has a high value. People like getting free stuff, but they don’t get too excited when that stuff is always free and widely available. If you convince them that you are giving away an exclusive and valuable service worth $100 or $1,000 for free, they become much more eager to acquire it. For instance, one of the more interesting hard offers I wrote copy for was a free “network topology analysis” by Timeplex, a manufacturer of multiplexers, switches, and hubs for telecommunications and data networks. When a prospect accepted this offer, we’d send a sales representative to visit. Using proprietary network design software and his laptop, the rep would sketch the prospect’s network layout or “topology.” Then, the rep would click an “optimize” button. The software would reconfigure the network by adding Timeplex multiplexers. By doing so, it reduced the number of voice and data lines. The software, as I recall, calculated the monthly cost savings from this line reduction, as well as the ROI of adding the Timeplex network elements. Just by meeting with the Timeplex “networking specialist,” the prospect could get “a FREE network topology analysis that can reduce your monthly line costs 10% to 20% or more.” That made the offer hard to resist, and extremely successful for Timeplex. Rule 5: State That There Is No Obligation to Buy. Tell the prospect that your offer is free and without obligation. State it in your sales letter and again on the reply form. People can be skeptical of free offers. They have heard and heeded the old saying, “If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.” Let your prospect know that there are no strings attached. The prospect wants assurance that agreeing to meet with you — or even replying to your promotion — does not obligate him in any way to buy from you or pay you any money. Don’t assume that your prospects understand this to be so. Say it plainly using these phrases: No obligation No commitment No risk Risk-free No strings attached There’s no obligation of any kind There’s nothing to buy You pay nothing You won’t be billed Without charge OceanofPDF.com 4 Offers That Make You More Money in Mail Order Marketing _____________________________ “Nothing is worse for your business reputation than a customer who did not understand your offer and feels he is being cheated when you refuse him a refund.” — Bob Bly _____________________________ In mail order selling, a hard offer is an offer that requires the prospect to pay for the product in advance. It is also referred to as “cash with order,” though almost no customers send cash. Most pay by check or credit card. The seller ships the product only after payment is received via check, money order, credit card, PayPal, or another method of payment. Use of a hard offer eliminates credit and collection problems because there is no billing. Everyone pays up front. By comparison, the soft offer in mail order selling is the classic “billme” offer. Here, the prospect can order and receive the product with no money up front. The seller sends a bill and is paid later. The Offer Should Not Be an Afterthought When creating a direct-response promotion, many copywriters give the closing copy — especially the formulation and working of the offer — short shrift. The writer simply picks up the boilerplate from previous promotions, without thinking through whether the offer and its wording make sense. Often, they don’t. More and more we see offers that are confusing, deceptive, unfair, or illogical — if we look carefully. Here’s an example: A number of publishers permit the new subscriber to cancel at any time and receive a prorated refund on what they call “unmailed issues.” By that they mean the following … Say your annual subscription costs $96. It entitles you to 12 monthly issues, which works out to $8 per issue. After three issues, you cancel. That means nine issues that you paid for have not been mailed to you and, now that you are canceling, will not be mailed to you. So you are entitled to a $72 refund on those unmailed issues. But here’s where it can get a bit confusing. If the publisher offers both a bill-me option (soft offer) as well as a payment with order option (hard offer), such a prorated refund guarantee actually gives his customers an incentive not to take the hard offer and pay up front — the opposite of what the publisher desires. Say the customer checks the “bill-me” option for a monthly newsletter, gets his first issue, and then writes “cancel” on his invoice. The publisher doesn’t send him a bill for one issue, nor does the publisher ask for the magazine or newsletter back. So the customer gets a free issue. But if the customer pays in advance and then cancels after the first issue, he theoretically gets a refund for eleven-twelfths of the subscription price (for the 11 unmailed issues) and therefore ends up paying for the issue received. (I have talked with many publishers about this. Some give the customer a full refund. But a surprising number actually give only a refund for the 11 unmailed issues less the cost of the one issue sent.) Why should the bill-me customer get a free issue but not the paymentwith-order customer? It doesn’t make sense, considering a cash-with-order customer is more desirable than a bill-me customer. How can you fix this problem? Offer a full money-back guarantee within the first 30 days, then a prorated refund thereafter. That way, everyone gets the first issue free if they decide not to become subscribers, whether they enclose payment with their order or chose the bill-me option. Make Your Offer Crystal Clear To paraphrase Ralph Waldo Emerson, it is not enough to state your offers clearly enough to be understood. You must state them so plainly that they cannot possibly be misunderstood. Reason: Nothing is worse for your business reputation than a customer who did not understand your offer and feels he is being cheated when you refuse him a refund. Let’s take the famous “lifetime guarantee.” On the surface, this seems simple and direct. For as long as you own the product, you can return it for a refund at any time. But really, at any time? Of course you can return it if it wears out or falls apart. But what if it becomes damaged through your own negligence? What if it works fine but you are simply bored with it and wish to have a newer model or different color? Does lifetime mean the lifetime of the seller or the lifetime of the buyer? The wording in lifetime guarantees is at times ambiguous, unclear, or even misleading. For instance, in subscription marketing, the old standard lifetime offer used to be “a prorated refund on the unused portion of your subscription” or on “unmailed issues.” No problem there. You knew that if you cancelled after six months and the newsletter cost $100, you would get $50 back. Now, promotional copy says the publisher offers “a full refund on the unused portion of your subscription.” Are they offering 100 percent of your money back? No. By “full,” they mean the full amount of the cost of the unmailed issues. Again, for a $100 subscription cancelled after six months, that’s a $50 refund. But when consumers read “full,” they may interpret that to mean “all my money back.” If you really are giving back the subscriber all of her money, make it clear — e.g., “We’ll refund your entire subscription fee in full” or “We’ll refund every penny you paid.” Another gray area is the offer of a free issue. Many subscription offers with a 30-day money-back guarantee promote the first issue, sent within 30 days, as a “free issue.” In reality, that issue is free only if you do not become a subscriber. If you do subscribe, you are paying for that issue, because it is one of a total of 12 you will get as part of your one-year subscription. So for those who pay and do not request a refund, there is no free issue. In that case, “free issue” is not wholly accurate. More correctly, the offer should say “risk-free issue” or “no-risk issue.” To make it a truly free issue, the publisher would have to give them the first issue plus, if they subscribe, 12 more issues — a total of 13 issues for the price of 12. Very few magazine or newsletter publishers do that, but if you have a how-to newsletter, you could, quite easily. Just create an evergreen “first issue” and include it in your welcome kit. Then begin the regular subscription with the next issue mailed. Can Generous Premiums Work With Bill-Me Offers? Those of us who use premiums know the danger of offering an overly generous premium with a bill-me option: The subscriber responds, gets the free gift, cancels, pays nothing, and keeps the great freebie. The solution is to phrase the bill-me option check-off box this way: “Bill me. (Bonus gift sent upon receipt of payment.)” The subscriber can still (if he wishes) pay, get the bonus, cancel within 30 days, get a refund of that payment, and keep the premium. But that’s going to a lot of trouble to get a free special report. Asking for the money before you send the premium requires more of a commitment from the subscriber. The result: fewer replies from people who have no intention of subscribing but just want something for free. At least two publishers have approached me recently with the idea of offering a bestselling book on a topic covered by their publication as a premium. A popular book is a bad choice, however, because many of the people receiving your mailing may already own it. You could offer the choice of an alternate premium, and ask the subscriber to pick one — either the book or the alternate item. In theory, it sounds good, but it seldom works. The more choices you ask the buyer to make, the more she has to think about before making her buying decision. And a decision deferred is a decision not made. The typical guarantee offers a full refund if you cancel the service or return the product within 30 days, but some experts suggest a longer period. How long? Some recommend a lifetime guarantee. Boardroom Inc. offers a full refund on the full subscription price of its publications, even if you cancel on the last day of your subscription. “It is a great selling point,” says Boardroom’s Michael Feldstein. “And since very few people cancel on a bill-me offer after they pay, the risk is minimal.” Business-to-Business Mail Order Offers That Bring in the Big Bucks Business-to-business mail order is a little different from consumer mail order. In consumer mail order, you can get away with having a hard offer only, and indeed many consumer mail order marketers do not offer a billme option. They want to avoid the hassle and headache of collections, and so require payment for the product up front. Also, with the price tag on many consumer mail order purchases being so low, it often doesn’t pay to go after deadbeats who keep your product but don’t pay your bill. The deadbeat realizes it’s not worth your time and effort taking him to court for a $12 past-due balance, and therefore doesn’t feel an urgent need to respond to your dunning letters. I know from decades of experience that pay-ups are a huge issue for marketers selling products with bill-me offers. The true measure of profitability is not how many orders you get, but how many of those buyers pay for what they ordered. Some buyers quickly return the merchandise. Less scrupulous buyers keep it without paying. So while bill-me offers usually lift front-end response, the gross revenues, once you subtract for the no-pays, can actually be less than cash-with-order. So you do not necessarily need to have a bill-me option for consumer mail order marketing. In many cases a bill-me offer will increase gross response, but the question is, how many of those who order on a bill-me basis ultimately pay up? A test gives you the surest answer. Many consumer mail order firms, especially smaller ones, do quite nicely without a bill-me option. They know it’s easy for the consumer to write a check, send a money order, or charge it to her American Express, Visa, or MasterCard. I run a small but profitable part-time mail order business selling books, manuals, and audio albums to writers and would-be writers, and we have not had a problem with our payment-with-order policy. In business-to-business direct marketing, on the other hand, I believe it is a mistake, in most instances, not to include some type of soft bill-me offer to supplement the hard pay-up-front offer. Why? Because the recipient is ordering for his or her company, not for personal use. Most B2B companies are not set up to issue advance checks. Their usual procedure when making a purchase is to issue a purchase order, receive the product, be satisfied with it, get an invoice, then pay you when they are ready — hopefully in 30 days but more often in 60 or 90 days. If your selling method forces business buyers to go against their company system, they may decide that buying from you is too difficult or just not worth the aggravation and effort, and take their business to a competitor who is more flexible about payment terms and options. If you demand payment up front, the prospect may not even know how to get the accounting department to issue and send you an advance check. Therefore, when selling to businesses, you should offer both a soft bill-me option as well as a hard payment-with-order option. Fortunately, there is a way to structure an offer that meets your business customer’s needs as well as your own requirements. It is done by extending a traditional hard offer (payment up front), as well as a second one that is conditional, rather than a pure “soft” bill-me offer. The traditional soft offer says, “We’ll send you our product and bill you. If you like it, you can keep it and pay the bill. If you don’t, you may return it, tear up the invoice, and you will not owe us any money.” Perhaps your product is expensive or easily damaged, and you are afraid that people will take advantage of you by ordering the product, keeping it, and not paying for it. One solution is to use a modified bill-me offer, in which you agree to send an invoice but do not ship the product until the invoice is processed and payment is received. This would read as follows: [ ] Bill me. (NOTE: Product not shipped until payment is received.) The modified bill-me is similar to a soft offer in that it allows the prospect to respond without enclosing any payment and to receive an invoice from you that he can put through the system for payment. At the same time, it is similar to a hard offer in that the product is not shipped until it is paid for. A variation of the modified bill-me is to agree to ship the product right away but to withhold shipment of any gift item or other premium until payment is received. There is a danger, if your premium is too attractive, that people will send for your product on a bill-me basis just to get the premium, then return the product and keep the free gift. To prevent this, you use a modified bill-me offer as follows: [ ] Bill me. (NOTE: Bonus Gift is shipped when payment in full for your order is received by us.) Even if you allow prospects to keep the premium if they return the product, this modified bill-me offer cuts down on freebie seekers. It requires ordering and paying for the product in order to get the gift, and few will go to that trouble just to get a free item from you — unless the premium is truly fantastic. You can go even further and state in your offer that, if they don’t want to keep the product and decide to return it for a refund, they must return the premium as well as the product. This provides an added degree of protection and is useful when the premium is fairly costly to you. Another way to modify the bill-me offer so that you reduce the number of prospects who send for the product and don’t buy it is to ask prospects to initial or sign the order card or provide a purchase order number or actual purchase order. For example: [ ] Bill me. Our purchase order number is: ______________ Signature (required for all bill-me orders): ______________ For phone and online orders, you can’t get a signature, but you can still ask for a purchase order number. I recommend that you avoid requiring prospects to send you an actual purchase order. The purchase order number itself is sufficient. If you insist on getting an actual purchase order, you will lose sales from prospects who are too busy to generate the paperwork. In general, your mailings should never force prospects to read a lot of instructions or fine print or fill out a lot of complicated paperwork. The more work you force your prospect to do to respond to your mailing, the lower your response will be. The two basic categories of premiums are merchandise and free content or “information premiums” (as discussed in Chapter 2). The legendary adman David Ogilvy, after working as a chef in the kitchen of a French hotel, began his career in marketing by selling stoves door to door. He offered the homemaker six cooking lessons for three guineas, but gave the lessons free if you bought the stove. (Source: Kenneth Roman, The King of Madison Avenue: David Ogilvy and the Making of Modern Advertising, page 40) Offering one or more premiums is a standard ploy used in direct mail and online marketing to sell magazines, newsletter subscriptions, and other information products. But which premiums work best? What are your choices? Most premiums for newsletter and magazine subscriptions are print products — typically special reports. They can be mailed through the U.S. Postal Service as hard copies or made available for download online as PDF files. Here are some of the more popular premiums for newsletter and info product marketing: The super-premium. A super-premium is a special report that delivers all or most of the information, secrets, or strategies promised in the mailing piece. Example: A magalog for Weiss’s Safe Money Report offers a super-premium, “Grow Up to 1,000% Richer in the Great Stock Market Panic of 2002,” that delivers on the big promise of the mailing. The offer of the super-premium is made on just about every other page of the 24-page magalog. The owner’s manual. An owner’s manual advises the subscriber how to use the service for maximum results and benefits. An options trading program, for instance, will typically have a premium explaining terms (e.g., “puts” vs. “calls”) and the types of trades the service makes (e.g., “straddles”). The vertical premium. A vertical premium is a report covering, in depth, one specific area the newsletter deals with rather than the bigger picture. A newsletter on Information Technology, for instance, might have a special report on supply chain management (SCM) or enterprise resource planning (ERP). The resource guide. A resource guide is a mini-directory of vendors, suppliers, associations, websites, and other resources of interest to the newsletter’s target audience. Be sure to include addresses, phone numbers, e-mail addresses, and Web URLs for listed resources. Surveys. The results of subscriber surveys are of great interest to potential subscribers. When Hospital Admitting Monthly added the offer of a salary survey premium, response to its control mailing jumped 50%. “Best of’s.” If you have a regular column that is highly popular with subscribers, collect a dozen or so of them in a “best of” premium. Newsletters covering regulatory or legal issues have done this with monthly columns on court cases and their outcomes (e.g., “The Best of ‘You Be the Judge’”). The editor’s magnum opus. Be careful of offering a book by the editor as a premium, especially if the book is a bestseller or the newsletter is expensive. If the book is a bestseller, many potential subscribers will already own it. If the newsletter is expensive, you’re better off offering a premium with a higher perceived value than a book. E-zines. If you send weekly e-mail updates between monthly print issues, talk about the “free e-zine” they get as a bonus for subscribing. E-alerts. Some newsletters offer periodic, unscheduled e-mails when there is important news or instructions that cannot wait for the next print issue or ezine. If you do this, position it as a value-added premium service. Online archives. Access to your password-protected subscribers-only website is a bonus for subscribers to your print or online newsletter. One feature that subscribers look for is an online archive of back issues. If it is searchable by keyword, even better. Forums and chat groups. Hosting a forum, chat group, or other online community where subscribers can network and share best practices is another nice little online extra. The postings are also very helpful for your marketing and editorial people. Telephone hotlines. Many monthly newsletters offer subscribers a telephone hotline they can call to hear current news and advice. Such hotlines are typically updated weekly. Conference invitations. You can offer potential subscribers invitations to exclusive conferences, workshops, and seminars. They should get these invitations early, before the general public — and a subscriber’s discount on the registration fee wouldn’t hurt. Transcripts. Transcripts of conferences, seminars, teleseminars, webinars, speeches, lectures, even TV or radio appearances by the editor can make attractive premiums. Audio CDs and DVDs. You can tape your editorial staff when they give presentations and offer audios or videos as premiums. Videos have a higher perceived value. I prefer audiotapes because busy people can listen to them in the car. CD-ROMs. A CD-ROM can present multimedia material that’s difficult to reprint in a printed report. The CD-ROM that comes with my book Public Relations Kit for Dummies, for example, includes samples of video news conferences. Software. At least one financial newsletter I’ve seen recently includes trading software as a premium for new subscribers. Software has a high perceived value. Is there a simple spreadsheet, such as a cost calculator, that you can put on a disk or CD-ROM and offer as a premium? Three-ring binders. For a newsletter that has lasting shelf value as a reference, you can offer a free three-ring binder that the subscriber can use to store all his issues in one convenient location. Merchandise. Merchandise, a common premium for magazine subscriptions, is seldom used in newsletter promotions. There are rare exceptions. Release 1.0, a technology newsletter aimed at high-level decision-making executives, offers a Release 1.0 baseball cap as a “payment with order” premium. Consumer magazines are more likely than newsletters to offer merchandise premiums. For many years, Business Week gave away a free solar calculator with a subscription to the magazine. Sports Illustrated offered a free video of the photo shoot for its annual swimsuit issue. 6 Steps to Irresistible Offers The more of the following characteristics your offer incorporates, the more irresistible it will be, and the higher your response rates: 1. Different or unique. The best offers are fresh and new. When copywriter Bill Jayme wrote the direct-mail package that launched New York magazine, he proposed a sweepstakes. Sweepstakes had long been used to sell magazine subscriptions, but none had ever offered the prize Jayme dreamed up: dinner at Gracie Mansion with New York City’s mayor. Most investment newsletters offer free special reports as premiums. The Sovereign Society, a newsletter on offshore investing, offered something different: a free Swiss bank account — a gift not given by any other investment newsletter. Most business magazines offer either discounted subscription rates or standard premiums like special reports, tote bags, or calculators. Advertising Age had a successful control where the premium was a ceramic coffee mug. Coffee mugs are nothing special. But this one was imprinted with a mock-up of an Ad Age cover. If the subscriber was Jan Smith, the headline on the mock issue of Ad Age was personalized to read: “Jan Smith Chosen as Marketing Genius of the Year.” 2. Desirable. An unusual offer works only if it’s something people really want. The Sports Illustrated swimsuit video is a great example. Every red-blooded American male who wasn’t dead would have liked to see it. Sex sells! Another example: A publisher was selling a loose-leaf service on how to manage Novell NetWare local area networks. Response rates doubled when a new direct-mail promotion offered a disk with free software — a collection of utilities for Novell networks. The 100 percent increase in orders confirmed that these software programs were tools network administrators obviously wanted to get their hands on. The outer envelope teaser read: “Yours FREE! — 5 Powerful Programs to Help You Manage Your Novell NetWare Network More Efficiently and Easily — See Inside for Details on This Special TimeLimited Offer.” On the other hand, when a financial newsletter mailed a renewal promotion that offered as a premium a pack of playing cards with the editor’s picture on them, it flopped. No surprise. Who would want that? 3. Has a high perceived value, especially in relation to your fulfillment cost. Free software has traditionally worked well as a premium. Software has a high perceived value in relation to the cost of the goods. In a store or online, software packages can easily sell for $49 to $300 or more. Yet a CD with code on it can be duplicated for about a dollar. That’s why the promotion offering a pack of playing cards with the newsletter editor’s picture on them didn’t work. After all, how much do you pay for a deck of playing cards at your local stationery store? About a dollar, right? Therefore, the perceived value of the playing cards was only a dollar — hardly a motivator to renew a newsletter subscription that costs $79 a year. In a promotion tied in with their sponsorship of the Olympics, IBM offered a special IBM Olympic pin as a premium. In reality, the pin probably only cost (and was worth) a buck or so. But the mailer copy hinted that it could become a collectible, creating the impression of potentially high value. 4. Dramatizes the brand or USP. The symbol for offshore investing has long been Swiss bank accounts. Therefore, the offer of a free Swiss bank account with a subscription to The Sovereign Society supported and dramatized the newsletter’s USP: making money and increasing privacy by investing offshore in things like Swiss bank accounts. Even when the offer does not at first glance seem closely related to the product, a clever copywriter can find a connection. Example: Years ago, Newsweek offered a free radio as a premium for new subscribers. It would seem that a radio was a poor choice for a premium: In the news area, radio and magazines compete with one another. But copywriter Milt Pierce used the differences between these media to make a logical connection between the premium and the product: Dear Reader: What’s the fastest way to get the news? It’s on the radio. That’s why Newsweek wants you to have — as an introductory gift for new subscribers — this superb AM/FM radio. But what’s the best way to get the news? You won’t get just headlines and a rough outline of the news, with Newsweek; you’ll get the news in depth … 5. Easy to take advantage of. You should make it as easy and convenient as possible for the prospect to accept your offer.

jobs.source_name: How to Create Irresistible Offers The Easiest Way on Earth to Make Your Marketing Generate More Leads, Orders, and Sales (1).docx
