vesting has long been Swiss bank accounts. Therefore, the offer of a free Swiss bank account with a subscription to The Sovereign Society supported and dramatized the newsletter’s USP: making money and increasing privacy by investing offshore in things like Swiss bank accounts. Even when the offer does not at first glance seem closely related to the product, a clever copywriter can find a connection. Example: Years ago, Newsweek offered a free radio as a premium for new subscribers. It would seem that a radio was a poor choice for a premium: In the news area, radio and magazines compete with one another. But copywriter Milt Pierce used the differences between these media to make a logical connection between the premium and the product: Dear Reader: What’s the fastest way to get the news? It’s on the radio. That’s why Newsweek wants you to have — as an introductory gift for new subscribers — this superb AM/FM radio. But what’s the best way to get the news? You won’t get just headlines and a rough outline of the news, with Newsweek; you’ll get the news in depth … 5. Easy to take advantage of. You should make it as easy and convenient as possible for the prospect to accept your offer.

 How? To begin with, offer multiple response mechanisms: toll-free phone number … fax number … a hyperlink to a landing page (see www.thelandingpageguru.com) … e-mail … even (gasp!) a postal address. Different prospects respond in different ways. In a direct-mail package, enclose a fax-back form or business reply card (BRC) with your sales letter. If you want customers to enclose payment with their order, or privacy is a concern, also include a business reply envelope (BRE). In a print ad, consider including a coupon or a bind-in BRC opposite the advertisement. On the Web, your landing page should ask for the minimum information from the prospect when collecting leads. If you are building your opt-in e-list, ask for name and e-mail address only. When you have multiple fields for the user to complete, use an asterisk (*) to indicate which are mandatory, and make as many fields as possible optional. Conversion rates decline incrementally for each additional field you force the prospect to fill out. The ease and convenience of accepting the offer can even be highlighted in the copy as a benefit. In a letter selling the Board Report, a newsletter for graphic designers, copywriter Sig Rosenblum makes a benefit out of the fact that the reply element is a BRC: Please complete the card enclosed and drop it in the mail today. It’s already addressed. And the postage is paid. 6. Minimizes the buyer’s risk and obligation. Do whatever you can to minimize sales pressure on the prospect. If you follow up leads by phone instead of with a field sales force, say in your copy “No salesperson will visit.” If you do not follow up leads by phone, say “No salesperson will call.” When offering anything free — a white paper, a webinar, even a brochure — say that it is free. Do not substitute the weaker “complimentary” when writing to a high-level business audience because you think “free” is not professional or will offend them. It won’t. Everybody wants free stuff, and businesspeople and professionals are no exception. A health care agency sent a direct-mail piece inviting doctors to attend a symposium. They did an A/B split test of two versions. The only difference was that B offered a free pocket diary as a gift for attendance. Version B out-pulled version A — with no free gift — six-fold. Busy doctors were persuaded to give up an afternoon by a free pocket diary that cost about a dollar! Does the buyer have to agree to sit through a presentation or demonstration or complete a survey? If he is not required to take further action once he accepts the offer, note this in your copy by saying: “There’s no obligation … nothing to buy … and no commitment of any kind.” How Many Premiums Should You Offer? Should you offer a single premium, two premiums, many premiums? In his book Secrets of Successful Direct Mail (NTC, 1992), the late Dick Benson said: “Two premiums are frequently better than one.” Newsletter and magazine subscribers and other information product buyers especially like multiple premiums. To promote one of my books, we offered almost a dozen free special reports — all downloadable PDFs, so they cost us nothing to deliver. The promotion worked, and the book became the #1 nonfiction bestseller on www.amazon.com, with more than 900 orders in a single day. In an online promotion for Men’s Health, Rodale offered 10 free reports: Assign a dollar value to special reports you give away as premiums by putting a price in the upper right corner of the front cover. Demonstrate that the price is real, not made up, by putting up a page on your main website where you sell all your bonus reports in an online shopping cart for the actual price on the cover. You will get some orders from your site visitors, so you can say in your copy: “We are not making this price up. We actually sell this report at this price on our website.” Michael Bell of Phillips Publishing suggests that the total value of the multiple reports you are giving away should exceed the price of the newsletter subscription. That way, the buyer is getting his money’s worth with the premiums alone, so, in a sense, he is getting the newsletter free. Premiums can be used to get customers to make their first purchase as well as to motivate them to continue buying. Franklin Mint had a brilliant offer for their Civil War chess set. The customer signed up to get one piece per month. After purchasing all 32 pieces, the customer got a free chessboard. This gave the buyer incentive to collect the whole series. Gevalia offers a subscription service for monthly delivery of gourmet coffee. One incentive they’ve used to get people to sign up was a 12-cup coffeemaker free with their first order. Here are a few additional observations and rules of thumb from Benson’s book concerning offers: Sweepstakes will improve results by 50 percent or more. A credit or bill-me offer will improve results by 50 percent or more. Memberships renew better than plain subscriptions by 10 percent or more. The addition of installment payments for items over $15 will increase results by 15 percent. If you have to choose only one, premiums work better than cash discounts. Subscriptions sold at half-price for at least eight months will convert at renewal time just as strongly as subscriptions sold for a full year at full price. Offers of subscriptions giving a choice of terms (e.g., one year vs. two years) will pull more gross dollars but 10 percent fewer subscriptions. Offering an incentive to pay cash when you offer both cash and credit options reduces net response. OceanofPDF.com 6 Pricing Strategies That Pump Up Your Profits We’ve talked about the offer, how to make it more attractive, and the tremendous advantage you get with premiums. Premiums are important, but they are not the only factor determining your response rates. The key components of a mail order offer are: The price The payment terms The premium The guarantee All four elements can make a dramatic change in your response rates. All are important. Of these components, price is probably the most important to test. Pricing is often counterintuitive, meaning what you think is the best price often is not. For example, which price do you think would sell best — $79 or $129? Most of us assume a low price always attracts more buyers than a higher price. But experienced marketers know this is frequently not the case. One software company selling to both consumers and professionals priced their software at $79 per desktop, which they thought would appeal to both segments of their market. But it appealed to neither. Consumers found it too high, and it communicated “not a serious tool” to professionals. The company decided to focus on the professional market and raise the price to $129. When they did so, sales soared (Brown, Dennis, “10 Common Pricing Mistakes,” Atenga, p. 3). How to Make Your Pricing More Palatable to Prospects Discount offers work well in direct marketing. And it is usually better to state the cost savings as a dollar amount rather than a percentage savings. For instance, a company tested two e-mail subject lines: (a) $50-off coupon vs. (b) 15%-off coupon (equivalent to a $50 discount). Result: The “$50- off” offer generated nearly three times more revenue than “15%-off” (The Marketing Report, 9/8/08). Does that mean percentage discounts don’t work? No. Sometimes you have a sale or savings that is a fixed percentage discount where the dollar value of the discount varies with the product, model, or options selected. For example, Geico advertises a “free rate quote,” where the consumer can quickly get a rate quote online. Their promise: “15 minutes could save you 15 percent on your insurance.” If you’re selling a high-priced item, you can overcome price resistance by presenting it in a way that makes it seem less expensive than it really is. For instance, Georgia Publishing’s American Speaker — a loose-leaf service aimed at business executives — comes in a three-ring binder with quarterly supplements and sells for $297. By dividing $297 by 365 days for a full year’s subscription, they could say that the service costs “just 81 cents a day.” Which sounds more affordable to you — $297 or 81 cents a day? Another way to do it is to compare the price of your product to products that are in other categories addressing the same purpose or need. For instance, a gym membership, a personal trainer, an ab machine, an exercise bike, a jump rope, and an exercise video all serve the same purpose — to get you fit and in shape. So the commercial for the ab machine might say, “Why spend thousands on an expensive gym membership when our Ab-Strengthener can give you six-pack abs for three easy payments of just $19.95?” Many financial newsletters cost $49 to $99 for a one-year subscription. Some of the editors of these investment newsletters also manage money for clients. If the minimum size of a managed account is $100,000 and the management fee is 2 percent, the editor of your newsletter could say something like this in the promotional copy: “It gives you the same stock recommendations that my private clients pay $2,000 a year for at a small fraction of that cost.” The principle here is to talk about higher-priced options and alternatives first, so that when you give the actual price of your product, the reader is almost relieved to hear how low it is. In his book Influence, Robert Cialdini tells of a retailer who wanted to sell a line of expensive sweaters. He put tables of even more expensive sweaters at the front of the store, where every customer coming in had to pass them. By the time they got to the table of sweaters he really wanted to sell, the customers felt that those sweaters were a bargain compared with the ones they saw first. Clever Pricing Can Skyrocket Your Sales As I said, you can make the price of a product more palatable through the use of clever language and phrasing. But you can also get significant increases in response rates by experimenting with the actual terms of payment. For example, a company selling an options trading course as a home business opportunity used a subscription model, charging $29.95 a month for full access to its online training videos, other course materials, and its online commodities price charts. By charging $29.95, they could say that getting into this business cost “less than a dollar a day.” The company decided to add a 14-day trial to the offer. The service was still $29.95 a month. But when you signed up, you paid just one dollar for the first 14 days, using your credit card. At the end of the 14 days, you could cancel or continue. If you cancelled, you were not billed further, and your dollar was even refunded. (Actually, the card was never charged, since it’s not worth processing an order for a dollar. The reason for making the 14-day trial a dollar instead of free was to get the buyer to submit his credit card information online.) If you did not cancel, your credit card would be billed $29.95 until you said to stop. The $1 offer worked very well and significantly increased sales. When you offer any kind of installment payments, the prospect psychologically reacts to the price of the first installment. He tends to discount the cost of any future payments when making his purchase decision, perhaps because he knows he has the option to cancel and avoid making those payments. In the above example, the seller of the options trading course could literally say “Get started in this great home business for just one dollar.” Which price do you think is best — $49 or $156? Is this a trick question? Well, a financial publisher did an A/B split test of two price offers for one of its investment newsletters: (a) $49 for one year vs. (b) four quarterly payments of $39 each, which equals $156 for one year. This is not a misprint. This was the actual test. The result? Offer “B,” four quarterly payments of $39, was the winner, even though it worked out to more than three times the cost of offer “A.” Why did this happen? Most likely, the prospects mentally compared a $49 payment to a $39 payment, instead of the actual price of $49 a year vs. $156 — more evidence that the buyer psychologically tends to pay attention only to the price of the first payment. Rodale has used this technique for years to sell books by mail. A typical Rodale offer might be three payments of $9.95. That means the book costs almost $30, which is not cheap for a book. But the reader doesn’t hear “This book costs $30” in her head. She hears “$9.95,” which seems affordable. The technique of relying on the buyer’s tendency to discount future payments also works well in Internet marketing. Rich Schefren of Strategic Profits sells high-end educational programs on a monthly payment plan. In the third month, he offers an upsell — an additional product or an upgrade to the deluxe version of the product the customer already has. But the customer does not have to pay for the upsell when he buys it, though it is shipped immediately upon ordering. Instead, half a dozen additional monthly payments are added to the end of his payment schedule. Why does Schefren wait to do the upsell until the third month? He says that if the buyer has not cancelled after the third month, the likelihood that he will cancel drops astronomically, and so it is safe to sell him something more at that point. “Free” is often cited as the most powerful word — and the most powerful offer — in direct marketing. But nearly as powerful is an offer for a dollar or a penny. In fact, old-school direct marketers have a name for these offers: “the magic of a dollar” and “the magic of a penny.” A commercial cleaning company was marketing its janitorial services through direct mail. The offer was that they would come to your facility and clean it for free to demonstrate the quality of their service. Their marketing advisor advised them not to offer the cleaning for free but instead to charge one penny. Why? So they could use a time-tested direct-mail gimmick: spot-gluing a penny to the top of the first page of the sales letter. The package was very successful. The letter began: “We will clean your offices or plant for only a penny … and we’ve even enclosed the penny to get you started!” A gimmick, but it worked. _____________________________ “Free” is often cited as the most powerful word — and the most powerful offer — in direct marketing. But nearly as powerful is an offer for a dollar or a penny. _____________________________ A software company was selling an integrated accounting software package for $249 by direct mail. It included general ledger, accounts payable, accounts receivable, payroll, inventory control, and a few other modules. But none of the modules would work on their own. They could run only if you had the general ledger. The company sent out a mailing advertising “accounting software for a dollar.” They priced all modules — accounts payable, inventory, and the others — at one dollar each, and the general ledger at $244. In a way, it was pure semantics. The combined cost of all the modules was still $249, and without the $244 general ledger, none of the others would work. So the buyer was still paying $249 for the integrated accounting software suite. But this pricing scheme allowed the company to promote “accounting software for a dollar” in their marketing copy. (If you insisted, they would have sold you the accounts payable module for just a dollar. But it was not an option on the order form, and no one asked for it.) The “accounting software for a dollar” mailing generated 10 times more orders than the company’s control mailing of “integrated accounting software for $249.” That’s how powerful the magic of a dollar can be. The Drop-in-the-Bucket Technique for Overcoming Price Resistance Have you ever been shopping for a major purchase, and when the salesperson told you the price, you said incredulously, “What? HOW much!?” This phenomenon is known as “sticker shock.” In sticker shock, the prospect is so put off by the purchase price that he is nearly traumatized. This is a bad sign for the seller, because a prospect in sticker shock can seldom be convinced to buy. The reason the prospect suffers from sticker shock is not because of the high price. It is because the seller has failed to communicate the true value of the offer. To overcome this, you can use what copywriter Mike Pavlish calls the “drop-in-the-bucket” technique. With this technique, your marketing copy convinces the prospect that the price you are asking — whatever it may be — is a “drop in the bucket” compared to the value he receives. And, you do this before you give the price. I use it for every offer, not just high-priced products. Reason: Before I give the price, I want to feel confident the prospect won’t be shocked by it. For instance, I sell a $79 e-book of business forms for freelance copywriters. I worried that prospects might think $79 is a lot to pay for an e-book on freelance writing, many of which sell for between $9 and $29 online. To combat this, I built the perception of high value using the drop-inthe-bucket technique. Specifically, I explained that this is not a conventional book, but a collection of forms. I then showed the value of ready-made forms and the money savings they offer. Here is the “drop-inthe-bucket” copy from my landing page for this product: What will my Copywriter’s Toolkit cost you? If I added up all the hours spent planning, writing, testing, and refining the tools in this collection, and then multiplied that by my current hourly rate, it would come to well over $25,000. Of course, you could hire a lawyer to draft some of these forms for you, at about $200 an hour. But most lawyers don’t know or understand the copywriting business. But my Copywriter’s Toolkit won’t cost you $25,000 … or $1,000 … or even $200. Instead, the price is just $79 — less than I charge for just 5 minutes of my time! The Copywriter’s Toolkit is a 140-page e-book … which means it’s available for immediate download. No shipping costs. And no waiting. As a licensed purchaser, you get the e-book as well as unlimited rights to use the forms, model letters, and other tools in the toolkit as is … or customize them to fit your own copywriting business. It’s your choice. Information marketers have long understood the importance of making the price of their products seem like a drop in the bucket compared to what they’re worth. A standard line in marketing copy for information products has been: “Just one idea from this program can pay back its cost 10 times over or more!” If your service helps buyers pass regulatory audits, talk about the cost of failing such an audit — fines, penalties, even a shutdown. If your manual on energy efficiency in buildings cuts heating and cooling costs 10 to 20 percent a year, the prospect with a $10,000 fuel bill for his commercial facility will save $1,000 to $2,000 this year and every year — more than justifying the $99 you are asking for the book. More Ways to Avoid Sticker Shock When selling specialized information products — newsletters, conferences, online services — we often ask prices that are many multiples of what trade publishers charge for books and magazines. The higher the price, the more the prospect is likely to experience “sticker shock” — a resistance to paying that much money for information, no matter how much he wants it. In addition to the drop-in-the-bucket technique, here are twelve things you can do to help overcome your prospect’s sticker shock: 1. Compare the cost of the product to the cost of hiring the author. That’s what I did in my landing page copy above for The Copywriter’s Toolkit. As a consultant, I charge $500 an hour, which works out to approximately $42 for five minutes. Therefore, I can say that the e-book, at $39, costs “less than I charge for just five minutes of my time.” 2. Make the prospect feel relieved to hear how little you are charging. Do this by stating higher prices for other services or products first, then giving your price, which is less. For instance, if you are selling reading glasses, mention that laser eye surgery is $1,000, new eyeglasses can run $300 at an optician’s, but your buy-by-mail reading specs are just $19.95. If you are selling an options trading course on video, first mention your $1 million minimum private managed accounts ... your $5,000 seminars ... and by the time you get to the videos, the prospect will actually be relieved to hear that they are only $299. 3. Make an apples-to-oranges comparison. Don’t compare your newsletter to another newsletter. Compare it to another information resource, such as private consultation or expensive training. Promotions for Georgetown Publishing’s American Speaker compare the $297 price to the $5,000 a top speechwriter would charge to write just one speech. Leeb’s Index Options Alert notes that the $2,950 it charges for its options trading fax service is like paying a 2.95 percent fee on a $100,000 managed options account — and that it’s actually lower than the total fee such a managed account would charge. 4. Spread out the payments. Rodale and Franklin Mint are well aware of the sales-closing benefits of offering several smaller payments vs. one large lump sum. One publisher of a financial advisory service costing thousands of dollars found that offering subscriptions on a quarterly basis reduced sticker shock and increased sales. If yours is an Internet service, consider offering it for so much a month with credit card payment on a till forbid basis. (“Till forbid” means you bill the subscriber’s credit card monthly until they tell you to stop.) Which sounds better to you — “$19.95 a month” or “$240 for one year of service”? 5. State the price in terms that make it seem as small as possible. Even if you want full payment up front, state the price in your promotion in terms that make it seem smaller. A $197 annual subscription, for instance, gives the buyer access to vital information for just 54 cents a day. Warning: Divide the price by length of service or subscription, but avoid a price per book or price per page comparison. Reason: Specialized information products always have a higher price per page than the trade books or periodicals that the buyer will invariably compare them with. 6. Value the component parts. If you are selling an investing course for $200, list the individual elements and show that the retail prices of each (videos, workbook, telephone hotline, website access) add up to much more than $200 — therefore, the buyer is getting a great deal. Even better: Position one or two of the elements as premiums the buyer can keep even if he returns the product or cancels the subscription. Offering “keeper” premiums usually increases response. Example: Instead of selling your eight-cassette audio album for $69, say it is a six-cassette album for $69. Then position the other two cassettes as premiums. 7. Add an element that cannot easily be priced by the buyer. Loose-leaf services, for instance, face built-in resistance from the buyer: “Why is it X dollars if it’s just a book?” Supplying periodic supplements helps differentiate these services from regular books, but publishers have found it even more effective to include a CD-ROM with the three-ring binder. The CD-ROM is perceived as a high-value item with an indeterminate retail price. (Software on CD-ROM can cost anywhere from $19 to $499.). So it destroys the “book to book” comparison. 8. Find a solution with your pocket calculator. With intelligent manipulation, you can almost always make the numbers come out in support of your selling proposition. Example: A highpriced trading advisory specializes in aggressive trades with profits of around 20 to 30 percent with average holding periods of less than a month. The challenge: Overcome resistance to paying a big price for modestsounding returns. Solution: Dramatize the profits the subscriber can make with numerous quick trades: “If you could earn 5 percent each month for the next 10 years, a mere $10,000 investment would compound to a whopping $3.4 million. At 10 percent, it would be an almost unimaginable $912 million!” 9. Pre-empt the price objection. Most mailings for expensive products build desire and perceived value, then reveal the price once the prospect is sold. An opposite approach is to state the price up front and use the exclusivity of a big number to weed out non-prospects. Example: “This service is for serious investors only. It costs $2,500 a year. If that price scares you, this is not for you.” An element of exclusivity and snob appeal is at work here. Also, the more you tell someone they do not qualify, the more they will insist they do and want your offer. The classic example is Hank Burnett’s famous letter for the Admiral Bird Society’s fund-raising expedition. The second paragraph states: “It will cost you $10,000 and about 26 days of your time. Frankly, you will endure some discomfort, and may even face some danger.” 10. Use a false close. Bring the prospect to the point of asking for the order. Then, instead of doing so, say “But wait, there’s more …” and then present another irresistible benefit. THEN ask for the order. 11. Add a sweetener. Add an extra incentive — a special premium, extended warranty or guarantee, free service or support, two for the price of one, or other special offer to close the deal. 12. Establish yourself as the leading expert in your field. Price resistance diminishes in direct proportion to the prospect’s belief that you are the unchallenged expert in your field or niche. Reason: They perceive you offer solutions unavailable from other sources, and that your solutions work as promised. The Good, Better, Best Strategy for Boosting Average Order Size Another way of overcoming price resistance is by offering multiple pricing options and levels of service. If you’re an information marketer or coach, for example, you might offer the following options and price levels to buyers interested in getting your advice: Best deal: The premium consulting service — a high level of personal service rendered by you or another top specialist and priced accordingly … in the thousands of dollars. Great deal: The midrange coaching service — where the customer does most of the work, but you offer advice, support, and encouragement through weekly telephone calls, online help, or some other mechanism with a service component. Good deal. Perhaps a package of information — where you sell a manual, DVD, or audio learning system that teaches people how to solve the problem themselves. It’s entirely packaged, reasonably priced (say, anywhere from $100 to $300), and involves little or no personal service or support on your part. Starter package. Maybe a book — a how-to e-book or traditionally published book giving advice on your topic … selling for anywhere from $10 to $50. Kick-the-tires. Free content — how-to information delivered at no cost via your blog, podcasts, free webinars, e-newsletters, special reports, content-rich websites, or some other advice you give away. Having the low-priced options above — the inexpensive book and the free e-newsletter — makes it virtually impossible for consumers to complain that you are too expensive or unfairly priced. You simply point out that if they can’t afford your high-priced products and services, they can avail themselves of your knowledge through your books or free online content. By doing so, you avert potential criticism of you as a greedy opportunist, and can sleep nights knowing bitter people who can’t afford your premium offers are not going around besmirching your reputation. You also get them into a sales funnel through which you can move them up to higher and higher packages and price points. Marketers selling dietary supplements by mail order typically offer three options. The highest-price option and best value is a six-month supply at a discounted price with some free premiums and free shipping and handling. The mid-priced choice is a three-month supply, maybe with one free bonus gift and free shipping and handling. The low-priced option is a single bottle of the supplement, a one month supply with no premiums and the buyer pays shipping and handling. The average unit of sale in this example is a three- or four-month supply. And this rule holds with almost every other product: If you offer the prospect three choices — good, better, and best — the majority will take the middle one. They perceive the cheapest option to be not good enough, and the most expensive option to be too expensive. The middle option seems to offer the right combination of quality, value, and affordability. OceanofPDF.com 7 Iron-Clad Guarantees That Make Your Product or Service Irresistible Would you buy a product, sight unseen, from a total stranger located in a city halfway across the country or even the world? Well, neither would your prospects, which is why you need to back your products with a strong guarantee of satisfaction. Recall from Chapter 6 that the key components of a mail order offer are: The price The payment terms The premium The guarantee I discussed price and payment terms in Chapter 6 — and premiums throughout the book, especially in Chapter 2. Now let us move to the final component of the offer, the guarantee. The key considerations when creating your guarantee are: Length Conditionality Coverage Activation Let’s take a brief look at each one in a bit more detail: Length refers to the time period for which the guarantee is in force. In general, the longer the guarantee, the greater your response rate will be. The minimum guarantee period used by direct marketers is 10 days. Many sellers of trading services and other high-priced information offer a two-week guarantee. Reason: They want the guarantee period to end before the customer has buyer’s remorse and can ask for a refund. The most common guarantee in direct marketing is the 30-day guarantee. Based on the notion that a longer guarantee is better, I prefer 60 or 90 days. The longest guarantee is the lifetime guarantee — e.g., L.L. Bean’s. I don’t like the lifetime guarantee for solo entrepreneurs, because it leaves a financial liability permanently hanging over your head. Some of my information products become dated with age. I wouldn’t want someone to return a program on, say, Internet marketing 10 years after he bought it — a program he had liked and profited from — because the information was no longer current. Some products should never have a lifetime or even a one-year guarantee. The most obvious is an annual directory. If it were guaranteed for a year, the buyer could use it for a year, return it for a refund, buy the new edition, and repeat the cycle ad infinitum. For directories, I like a 30- day money-back guarantee. Then there is the double-your-money-back guarantee, where a dissatisfied customer who returns a $100 product is entitled to a $200 check from you — $100 to cover the refund and $100 to (presumably) compensate him for his trouble. I know from experience that double-your- money-back guarantees can be very powerful and significantly increase sales. One marketer who sold a workshop to help doctors pass their oral board exams had trouble filling seats — until he added a guarantee promising double their money back if they failed the exam after taking the workshop. Attendance and revenues tripled. Conditionality refers to any conditions or limitations you impose on your guarantee. For example, I am sure you’ve seen promotions where the merchant says they will give you a full refund if the product is returned “in saleable condition.” This makes the buyer wary. How do you define “saleable condition”? The buyer fears that if he returns your book for a refund, you will claim that there is a tiny tear in the dust jacket or a smudge on page 78 and refuse to give him his money. Conditional guarantees sound like a good idea, at least to the seller, but when you use them, you are asking for headaches. Trading services, home business start-up kits, and other educational products often say they will refund your money in full “as long as you show you have made a sincere effort to follow our program.” How could a dissatisfied customer seeking a refund prove that he complied with that condition? Some sellers of business opportunity products and trading systems require the customer to return worksheets, completed forms, or other documents proving they attempted to make the program work for them but were not successful. Buyers fear that, instead of getting a prompt refund, the seller will tell them they did not use the materials correctly and instruct them to go back and try again. Bottom line: Consumers distrust conditional guarantees, and using them can depress sales. The best guarantee is the unconditional guarantee. If your guarantee is unconditional, say so in your marketing copy — e.g., “This is our unconditional, iron-clad, money-back guarantee of satisfaction.” Or “We’ll refund your money in full — no questions asked.” An unconditional guarantee of satisfaction, boldly stated, works equally well whether you’re selling information products or merchandise. “We sold custom-lettered work uniforms by mail,” says Lewis Elwin. “We gave a guarantee of complete satisfaction. There was some concern at first because when a lettered garment came back, there’s wasn’t a whole bunch of options for us. But not many came back on the satisfaction issue. Our experience with small business owners was that most of them were honest.” Coverage refers to the part of the purchase that is covered by the money-back guarantee. For merchandise, the seller typically gives the customer his money back when he returns the product. But does that refund include the shipping and handling fee he paid on top of the cost of the merchandise? If it does not, be clear about that in your copy. Instead of saying “full refund” use the phrase “product refund.” A product refund does not include a refund of the shipping and handling charges. Should you refund shipping and handling? I don’t. Some direct marketers not only refund the shipping and handling charges, they also pay for return shipping of the product from the dissatisfied customer. If it’s a small item, they might include a postage-paid return shipping label with the product. If it’s larger, they may give you a return label for UPS or even send a freight company to take the product back. You will occasionally have a customer who says he tried your product and, not only does he want a refund, he wants you to compensate him for lost time or money spent using it. I am not a lawyer and cannot give you legal advice. So if you run into a problem like this with a persistent customer, you should consult an attorney. But, in general, I would say you are not responsible for any damages beyond the cost of the product except in extraordinary circumstances. (If, for example, the customer uses your shampoo and his hair turns permanently purple.) Guarantee coverage can be an issue for seminar marketers. Will you allow a person to take the entire seminar and, if he is then not satisfied, give him a refund? He may be able to return his workbook and other materials, but he can’t return the seminar itself, because he has already absorbed the information. Some seminar promoters tell attendees that if they are not satisfied, they should let the seminar leader know by the first break on the first day of the event. At that point, they can turn in their materials, leave, and get a full refund. After that, it’s too late. Activation refers to the time period when the guarantee goes into effect, as well as to what the customer has to do to take advantage of it. Does the 30 days for a month-long money-back guarantee start the day the order is placed or the day the product is delivered? Your customer expects it to be 30 days from receipt of goods, and that’s the way your guarantee should be written. Your guarantee should also spell out exactly how to get a refund. Companies selling nutritional supplements by mail, for instance, usually tell the customer that they must return the “unused portion” of the product or “even the empty bottles.” Years ago, a mail order company was selling corncob pipes by mail. Their guarantee was, “If you are not 100 percent satisfied, break the stem off the pipe and mail it back to us for a refund.” This eliminated the trouble and expense of returning the whole pipe, but also emphasized the company’s confidence in its product: If you didn’t agree it was great, they wanted you to destroy it. In his classic ad for “The Lazy Man’s Way to Riches,” the late Joe Karbo made this guarantee famous: “Send us a check and we will send you the product. We won’t cash your check for 30 days. If you return the product within 30 days, we will send your uncashed check back.” This ploy can, in fact, generate incremental improvement in response, giving you another few orders per thousand pieces mailed. However, it may also increase the number of bad checks you receive. At least one major seminar promoter has used a similar guarantee. When you arrive at the seminar venue, there is a table with a pile of checks on it, including yours. If you are not satisfied, you may leave. On the way out, pick up your uncashed check for a full refund of the seminar fee. What happens when a customer wants a refund after the guarantee period has expired? Be reasonable but firm. If someone wants to return one of my products and they missed the cut-off by a few days or even a week, I let it slide. However, if they are asking for a refund months after the guarantee expired, I tell them sorry but it’s too late. If they are reasonable or have been a regular customer, I may offer them a credit for a future purchase rather than a refund. Two More Tips for Strengthening Your Guarantees There are two other things to consider when creating your guarantee: Clarity. Make certain the terms and conditions of the guarantee are clearly stated and spelled out. Be careful about wording that the consumer can misinterpret. For instance, a performance-based guarantee — “If you do not earn extra money trading options with our program, return it for a refund” — sounds good but raises a potential concern. Namely, does it mean that if I DO make some extra money with the product, I can’t return it — even if I only made 10 bucks? Rewrite the guarantee so there is no condition or ambiguity stated or implied: “If you do not make extra money trading options with our program, or you are not 100 percent satisfied for any other reason — or for no reason — just return the program within 90 days for a full refund.” Make it stand out. The guarantee should be graphically emphasized within the promotion. Don’t bury it in body copy or put it in an asterisked footnote in 8-point type. Print the guarantee in 12-point type with a large, bold headline. Put a box or even a certificate-style border around it to make it stand out. Boost Orders Up to 21 Percent With an “Unfair Advantage” Offer E-books and other downloadable PDF information products present a unique problem as far as guarantees and refunds are concerned. With a hardcover or paperback book, if you want a refund you have to return the product. When you do, the seller has the book (which he can resell), you don’t, and you get your money back. But how do you return an e-book? The seller has the original PDF file, so they won’t want or need your copy. Even if you send it, how do they know you didn’t keep a copy on your hard drive? Some e-book sellers require customers requesting refunds to delete the PDF from their hard drive (and, I would suppose, throw away or rip up any printouts of the document). How do they know the buyer has complied? They don’t. Since there is no way to know whether a customer has deleted and destroyed their copy of my e-book, I don’t make them do it. In fact … I tell them they can keep it! Here — taken from the landing page for The Copywriter’s Toolkit — is my standard guarantee for the e-books and other downloadable PDF information products I sell online: _____________________________ Our 100% iron-clad guarantee of satisfaction I totally guarantee your satisfaction with this toolkit. If you aren’t convinced that The Copywriter’s Toolkit is the smartest investment you’ve made in your freelance copywriting business this year, just let me know within 90 days. I’ll send you a prompt refund of your $39. And you can still keep the e-book with my compliments. That way, you risk nothing. So what are you waiting for? To order The Copywriter’s Toolkit on a 90-day risk-free trial basis, just click here now: _____________________________ With such a policy, you might think that people would take advantage of me that and my refunds on e-books would be huge. Why should they pay for my e-books when they can essentially get them for free? The answer is that people are basically honest. Yes, a few do take advantage. But that small number is far outweighed by the increase in orders this strong guarantee generates. The proof: My e-book refund rate is a tiny fraction of 1 percent. And conversion rates increased once I added this copy to my sales pages. Internet marketer David Powers tested it, and found that telling buyers they could keep his e-book either way increased conversion rates and sales by 21 percent. My e-book offer allows the prospect to take unfair advantage of me: If they order the e-book and request a refund, they get it for free. Not only does my offer allow the prospect to take unfair advantage of me, my copy actively encourages them to do so: I’ll send you a prompt refund of your $39. And you can still keep the e-book with my compliments. We call this the “unfair advantage offer” — an offer where, if the prospect accepts it, he benefits unfairly … and the seller incurs loss. The reason to test an unfair advantage offer is its potential to boost response far in excess of the losses incurred from the few customers who exercise the guarantee. Another example: In 1999, one of my clients, a software publisher, was selling a tool that automatically recoded software to be Y2K compliant. When I suggested a 30-day money-back guarantee, the marketing manager balked. She was concerned that the buyers could use the tool to recode their software and then send it back, getting the benefit for free. “Let them,” I replied. In our marketing copy, we explicitly pointed out that they could use the tool during the 30-day trial to recode their systems. And that, after doing so, they could return the tool without paying for it, thereby “taking unfair advantage” of the software publisher. It was very profitable, and returns were no higher than normal. _____________________________ People are basically honest. Yes, a few do take advantage. But that small number is far outweighed by the increase in orders this strong guarantee generates. _____________________________ OceanofPDF.com 8 Getting Your Prospects to ACT NOW! _____________________________ How do you get the prospect to act now instead of later? The simplest mechanism is to put a time limit on your offer. _____________________________ Michael Masterson, copywriter, entrepreneur, and consultant for newsletter publishing giant, Agora, Inc., has a formula for creating compelling headlines. His Secret of the Four U’s © requires a headline to be unique, ultra-specific, useful (offering a benefit), and urgent. Without a sense of urgency, your promotion may not generate as many responses as you had hoped. And one of the most effective ways to get the prospect to “act now” is to build an element of urgency into your offer. Why It’s Important to Get Prospects to Act Now Instead of Later Your prospect is bombarded by direct mail, e-mails, telemarketing calls, radio commercials, TV spots, and other sales messages and offers. Which means that your best chance of getting her to respond to your offer is to give her sufficient motivation to do it right now, while the piece is still in her hands. There is an old saying among direct marketers: “A decision deferred is a decision not made.” If there is no “respond now” incentive, the prospect may think, “I’ll put this aside and get to it later.” Unfortunately, a directmail package is similar to the Sunday newspaper: If you don’t read it within 48 hours of getting it, chances are you never will. Too many other things surface to compete for your attention. How do you get the prospect to act now instead of later? The simplest mechanism is to put a time limit on your offer. This can either be (1) a specific date (“Offer expires March 15, 2009”) or (2) a generic time limit (“You must reply within 15 days to take advantage of this special free offer”). Both types of deadlines are effective. Which is better? A specific date is good if you have enough control over the timing of your promotion to ensure that delays in printing and mailing don’t make the date obsolete. For instance, you don’t want prospects to get a “Reply by April 15th” mailing on April 21st. If you do not have precise control over timing, or if you print your sales letters in large quantities and mail them regularly, a generic “Respond within the next 15 days” offer may be better. That way, no matter when the mailing arrives, it always works. How long should the time limit be? Which is best? 12 days, 20 days, 25 days, 30 days, two months, or something else? Obviously, the shorter the timeframe, the more pressure there is on the prospect to respond quickly. On the other hand, too short a timeframe may make the prospect feel rushed and uncomfortable. For direct mail, a 15- to 21-day deadline seems reasonable: short enough to motivate action, long enough to allow some breathing space. In e-mail marketing, deadline timeframes can be shorter. E-mails can say “Good this week only” or “Offer expires in 48 hours.” Sending one or two follow-up e-mails reminding prospects that the offer is about to expire as you approach the deadline can be very profitable in generating additional orders. On a landing page, you can have a clock or counter displaying, in real time, the days or hours remaining until the offer expires. Decades ago, Dennis R., a seller of mainframe utility software, used the standard 30-day free trial offer. Then he did a split-test of a 30-day free trial vs. a 60-day free trial. The 60-day offer outperformed the standard 30- day offer by 10 percent. “I concluded that the standard 30-day trial period was not sufficient for a busy IT professional to test our software,” said Dennis. “It would sit on the prospect’s desk for weeks. Then he would put off testing it for another week or two. And by that time, he felt he had to send the software back before he got billed for it. By extending the trial period from 30 days to 60 days, we gave the prospect sufficient time to install and test the software without fear of the free trial period expiring before he did so.” Apparently, 60 days was more than sufficient time for the software trial. When Dennis tested 90 days vs. 60 days, there was no further lift in response. Run all promotional copy past your attorney for vetting, especially time-limited offers. Once you state in your marketing that a certain offer expires on a certain date, you are generally not allowed to extend the offer beyond that date. Word Your Offer for Maximum Impact As I pointed out elsewhere in this book, the language you use to describe your offer can also affect response rates. In another mailing, Dennis tested the 60-day free trial vs. 60-day free use. This time, “free use” outperformed ”free trial” by 15 percent. Dennis concluded that the word “trial” had negative connotations for the IT tech who would be using the software. It meant screwing up batch files and coming in nights and weekends to do the testing. “But,” he said, “everyone wants to use a product — so who wouldn’t like ‘free use’?” For consumer mailings, the offer should require the recipient to reply within the next seven, 11, or 15 days. A common offer in direct mail is an additional “quick-response bonus” — usually a free report or other premium given as an incentive to reply within seven days. Offer expiration moves much faster in television infomercials. Merchandise is often offered on a payment plan — e.g., four easy payments of $19.95. The quick-response incentive is the elimination of one of the payments — the equivalent of a 25 percent discount — for viewers who call within a certain timeframe, usually 20 to 30 minutes. This time element can also be used online to establish a sense of urgency. To promote its annual copywriter’s conference, FastTrack to Copywriting Success Bootcamp & Job Fair, American Writers & Artists Inc. (AWAI) has used a digital display counting down to the expiration date for their early bird registration discount on their bootcamp home page. A variation of the specific timeframe offer is the limited number offer: “This offer is limited to the first 200 people who respond to this letter.” This tactic gets prospects’ attention because they have no idea how many pieces you mailed — and, therefore, are motivated to reply right away to ensure they are one of the first 200. Other variations? The limited offer is most effective when you can give a legitimate, credible reason why the offer is limited. Scarcity can be one such reason: The supply of what you are offering is limited, and, once it is gone, no more will be available. The late Bill Jayme had a clever scarcity line he used in direct-mail packages selling subscriptions to new magazines. It read: “Only so many copies of the premiere issue will be printed — no more.” That statement would be true no matter how many copies were printed. Nonetheless, it communicates a definite sense of limited supply. One computer company offered free prototyping of the prospect’s application. Because prototyping takes time and the company had a limited staff, it could handle only so many prototypes at one time. The sales letter made a point of this, saying, “We urge you to hurry. Based on response to previous mailings, we will get many requests for this free prototyping offer. If you are not one of the first to respond, you may well have to wait longer than we’d both like.” This worked because it was specific, credible, and true. If you don’t have a real reason why the offer is limited, you can invent one, and that can work. But when doing so, respect the intelligence of your prospects. For instance, one mailing I received many years ago told me I had to request a certain report right away because “We have printed only 1,000 copies and supplies are limited.” I suspected, of course, that if requests exceeded 1,000, the company would simply print more. So its act- now incentive lacked credibility for me. (The “limited quantity” offer is especially suspect when the premium can be downloaded as a PDF or MP3 file.) Another effective way to add a sense of urgency is to limit the total number of members, participants, or buyers. For a conference, seminar, or workshop, there really are only so many seats available — and no more. Tell prospects these limited seats are available on a first-come, first-served basis. In a promotion for a new $1,500 financial advisory service, a publisher told prospects that they had to act quickly because he could only take on 1,000 subscribers. Reason: With more than that, he could not make sure his subscribers got good execution on their trades. In his marketing copy he said, quite honestly: “If you apply after I have 1,000 members, I’ll have to return your thousand dollar check to you uncashed, as much as it pains me to do so.” Early-bird discounts are effective for events, and for pre-publication offers for directories, books, and other information products. For a weekend seminar costing $2,497, you might offer a $500 early bird discount, bringing the price to $1,997. For a book or directory selling for $100, even a $5 or $10 pre-publication discount is usually all you need to lift response rates. Give a Gift for Prompt Response A premium is a free gift the prospect gets for responding to your mailing. Does the premium have to relate to the product or service being sold? That depends on whether the purpose of the mailing is to generate leads or to make sales. Dick Benson, a successful consultant and entrepreneur, writes in his book Secrets of Successful Direct Mail (NTC) that it is not necessary for the premium to relate to the product being sold. The most important criteria for premium selection, according to Benson, are the perceived value and desirability of the premium. If the premium relates to the product, fine, but that’s of secondary importance. In lead generation, I agree that having a desirable premium is important, but I put more weight on trying to select a premium related to the product. Also, you have to be careful with premiums because many companies, especially defense contractors and subcontractors, have policies forbidding employees to accept gifts from vendors. In fact, a firm selling custom-imprinted business gifts by mail tested a straight 25 percent discount vs. a 25 percent discount combined with the offer of a free clock radio. Not only did the premium not increase response, it actually depressed it. Why? We can’t know for sure. Perhaps the buyers didn’t want to be perceived as accepting a gift or bribe for giving that vendor his company’s business. Whenever a mail order company attempts to bribe buyers with an expensive gift, some prospects might assume the merchant is inflating the price of their product to make up for the cost of the free gift — and they would rather pay less for the product and not get the gift. In business-to-business marketing, the corporate employee increasingly looks good to management by being a sharp buyer. That means getting the product at the lowest price possible. A larger discount might therefore work better than a free gift intended for personal use. If you do offer a premium to a business buyer, especially one working in a corporate setting, consider making it something related to the product and of value to the buyer’s company. For instance, a publisher selling highpriced technical journals and information databases on CD-ROM offered a free CD-ROM stacker and reader with the purchase of a group of its highpriced CD-ROM—based information products. The premium had high perceived value, was closely related to the product, and made the prospect look like a smart buyer. For lead generation, I think the best use of a premium is to offer something directly related to the product or service. My experience is that unrelated premiums of high value bring in large numbers of “freebie seekers” and other unqualified leads.

A larger discount might therefore work better than a free gift intended for personal use. If you do offer a premium to a business buyer, especially one working in a corporate setting, consider making it something related to the product and of value to the buyer’s company. For instance, a publisher selling highpriced technical journals and information databases on CD-ROM offered a free CD-ROM stacker and reader with the purchase of a group of its highpriced CD-ROM—based information products. The premium had high perceived value, was closely related to the product, and made the prospect look like a smart buyer.
