 Modest premiums that are directly related to the product or service increase the total number of responses. While you will always get some inquiries from those people who seem to send for anything and everything that’s free, you will also get a greater volume of qualified leads from good prospects. I personally like the offer of a free booklet or report related to the product or service. This is most often used in the soft offer (“Send for free report”), but it could conceivably be tied to a hard offer. For instance, you can offer an impressive report with the condition that it will be handdelivered by a salesperson. Ricoh did this many years ago when selling fax machines, copiers, and other office equipment via direct mail. You would get a little gift as an incentive for replying to the mailing. Ricoh would call to set up a time for a sales rep to come to your office and demonstrate the machine. The gift item was delivered personally by the sales rep, and you got it only after the demonstration. Samplings, Trial Offers, and Product Evaluations Are All Great Offers Three additional incentives you can use in your marketing are samples, trial offers, and product evaluations: Samples. You offer to render your service or allow the customer to use your product on a sample basis. This may be for purposes of demonstrating your service or product or for analyzing the customer’s needs to determine which of your services or products is right for them. For example, a company selling equipment that turns chemical powders into pellets says in its sales letter, “Send us a five-pound bag of your compound and tell us what size pellets you want. We will run it through our pelletizer and return it to show you the quality of the pellets it can produce.” Graver Chemical makes a similar offer for Ecosorb, a carbon-based filtration medium for purifying water supplies. Their letter states: “Is Ecosorb right for your application? We’d be delighted to evaluate a water sample to see if Ecosorb can handle your particular requirements.” Another company, a computer firm, sells a software program that businesses can use to quickly create customized applications that work with their databases. One potential buyer was skeptical and asked, “How long would it take to develop a so-and-so application for our database using your product?” Instead of answering, the software firm’s rep sat at the computer, started pressing keys, and had the application prototyped and working with the database within 30 minutes. The prospect’s response? “Decision made! We’re buying it!” Trial offers. A trial offer allows the prospect to use your product or service for a specified period at no cost and with no obligation to buy. The pelletizer manufacturer’s letter went on to say that if the sample pellets were satisfactory, they would ship a pelletizer to the prospect’s plant and let them us it for a month with no obligation. Then the company would have the option of sending it back (at the manufacturer’s expense) or buying it. A trial offer can also work with a service. If you have an online database, a long-distance telephone service, or another service where users are billed by the hour, you could offer “30 minutes of use free.” In his book Profitable Direct Marketing, Jim Kobs shows two ads from MCI. The first offers $5 off the prospect’s long-distance phone bill. The second offers 30 free minutes of long-distance calls. The “30 free minutes” offer pulled roughly twice the response of “$5 off” because customers perceived 30 free minutes of long-distance calling to be the greater value. The 30 minutes of free service is, in essence, a free trial of the long-distance phone service. Product evaluations. Similar to the free trial is the product evaluation. The gist of this offer is: “Let us send you the product at no cost, and you can perform whatever technical evaluation is required to help you decide whether it is the right product for you. If it is not, send it back and owe us nothing. If it is, you can buy it for the list price of $X.” One problem with free trials and evaluations is that prospects send for the product — and then, because of inertia, laziness, or lack of time, they don’t do anything with it. One way to overcome this problem is to combine the free trial or evaluation with an incentive to make a buying decision within a specified period of time. For instance: “If you accept our free trial offer and then decide to invest in the so-and-so system within the next 30 days, you will get 10 percent off the regular purchase price.” Mention of this time-limited offer in your ad or mailing can increase overall response. Periodic reminders to prospects via mail or phone during the evaluation period can help get more of them to try the product and increase the conversion rate of leads to sales. Creating Urgency With a Loss Leader Strategy Have you ever read an ad offering a product at a price so low that it seems impossible for the seller to be making a profit? Any item sold at or below cost to attract new customers is called a loss leader. Retail and mail order merchants sell items at or below cost to entice you to their store or get you to place an order. (Retailers refer to these discounted items as “door busters,” because they can whip consumers into such a frenzy that they will literally bust down the door to the store to get one.) Once you purchase the loss leader or door buster, you have made the transition from shopper to paying customer. And the merchant makes his profit by selling existing customers like you additional products with a regular mark-up. An example is mail order coin dealers who offer, say, an American Silver Eagle for $19.95, which they say is “our cost.” They might get 10,000 first-time customers to order the Silver Eagle. With the coin, they send out literature advertising a set of silver coins for $200. Of the initial 10,000 first-time customers, 1,000 buy the set of silver coins, generating $200,000 in revenues. Well, the same loss leader strategy that merchants have been using off line for decades to build their customer lists can now be profitably applied online. Here’s how it works. First, create your loss leader. If you are an online information marketer, it could be an e-book. This e-book should have wide appeal for all segments of your market. The topic should be one that all your customers will find interesting enough to make them want to own the e-book. And be sure it is a truly valuable product. No matter what your intent is, you always want to give your customers great value for their money. That way, they’ll come back to you for more information again and again. Assign a $39 list price to the e-book, for reasons I will make clear in minute. Next, approach your affiliates — other online marketers that you have a commission agreement with — and suggest that they sell your $39 e-book to people on their lists for $19, giving them a special $20 discount offer. Tell your affiliates that you won’t pay the customary 50 percent commission. Instead you’ll give them 100 percent commission for every book that’s sold. That’s right. They get all the money. Reason: If you give them the usual 50 percent commission on the $19 sale, their cut would be only $9.50 — too little to interest them. But 100 percent commission on a $19 sale is equivalent to a 50 percent commission on a $38 sale. And the fact that you are giving them all the commission makes them stand up and take notice. This is why I suggested assigning a retail price of $39 to the e-book. It allows you to offer the consumer a $20 discount, which has strong appeal, and still give the affiliate a $19 commission per sale, which also has strong appeal. What you end up with is a win, win, win situation. The customer gets a great $39 product for $19. The affiliate gets 100 percent of the sales. And you get a valuable list of subscribers. Where to Feature the Offer in Your Copy The offer must be featured prominently on the response device. (In Chapter 9, I will give you copy and graphics guidelines for creating winning reply elements that highlight the strong offers you build.) Of course, the offer is usually mentioned elsewhere in the copy, too. For an offer that is strong but standard, we typically write copy describing it in the closing section of the promotion. The more compelling or unusual the offer is, the more prominently you should feature it. A mailing for the McGraw-Hill Chemical Engineer’s Book Club featured an unusually generous offer: a free copy of Perry’s Handbook, a large and expensive reference book. The buyer paid only a nominal fee plus shipping and handling to get the handbook, and in exchange was enrolled in the club with a commitment to buy a few additional books. The publisher felt the handbook was such an attractive incentive that they featured it on the outer envelope of the promotion with this teaser: “Why are we giving away this 50th Anniversary Edition of Perry’s Handbook practically for free?” An advertisement for an application development tool used by programmers used the headline: “Develop applications up to 6X faster — guaranteed or your money back.” Putting the guarantee in the headline helps address skepticism for a big promise right up front. OceanofPDF.com 9 How to Write and Design Reply Elements That Flood Your Mailbox With Orders One of the most labor-intensive, time-consuming marketing tasks is copywriting. Not necessarily writing the copy … but agonizing over what has been written. As a copywriter, I do this all the time. I fret to an insane degree over every sentence, reading the copy over and over again, questioning whether the wording could be stronger. Many marketers do the same thing. They mark change after change on a nearly finished promotion, worrying about whether the copy says exactly the right thing, in exactly the right way. The irony, of course, is that in most situations, all this suffering is for naught. I don’t mean to say that copy is unimportant. But most of the time, the changes we make — punctuation, grammar, spelling, and minor word choice (e.g., whether to use “the” or “a”) — are so insignificant, it wouldn’t make one iota of difference in response whether we went with “version A” or “version B.” That said, I do think you should put in the time to carefully fine-tune your promotion … but only a small fraction of it. Specifically, here are the three “hot spots” in your promotion where what you say — and how you say it — really, really matters: The first critical portion of the copy is determined by its position in the promotion. The most important copy in a #10 direct-mail package is the outer envelope teaser — and the headline and lead of the sales letter. In a magalog, it’s the front cover … the inside front cover … the headline and lead … and the back cover. On a landing page, it’s the banner, headline, salutation, and lead. In an e-mail, it’s the subject line and the first paragraph. These sections are worth agonizing over, because different wording can result in dramatic increases or decreases in your response rates. Given the importance of the headline, should it focus on the offer instead of the product or the prospect? Do we present our offer on the front cover of a self-mailer or in the lead of a sales letter? Not usually. But if the offer is particularly powerful or unusual, then yes, you might lead with that. Here’s how I did it with a letter I used to promote my online copywriting services to a couple of hundred newsletter publishers. (It generated a 3 percent response.) _____________________________ Dear Fellow SIPA Member: A proven process for selling thousands of new subscriptions entirely over the Internet … at a tiny fraction of the cost of direct mail … … is described in a new, informative Mini-Report, “7 Steps to Selling More Newsletter Subscriptions Online.” It is yours FREE, with my compliments, when you complete and mail the card enclosed. In our new FREE special report, you’ll discover how to: ** Adapt the “Agora Model” to increase online subscription sales while slashing your marketing costs. ** Build a large and profitable opt-in e-list with a “free-onfree name-squeeze page.” ** Find the right balance of content to promotion in your email marketing — and the optimal frequency of e-mail distribution. ** Maximize conversion of “freebie seekers” to paying customers within 90 days of acquiring new online names. ** And many other ideas for boosting your online clicks, conversion rates, orders, and revenues. For nearly 3 decades, I’ve helped dozens of newsletter, book, magazine, and software publishers beat their controls — and increase their revenues — online and offline. “In one test, your promotion actually had a 14% conversion to sale,” says David Galland of Casey Research. “You can’t ask for much better than that.” But a landing page I wrote for an e-book recently generated a conversion rate of 32%. To get your FREE Online Marketing Report … free facts on my copywriting services … and samples of successful promotions I’ve written for Phillips, KCI, Weiss Research, Agora Publishing, Brownstone, Medical Economics, Ken Roberts, and other clients, just check “Copywriting Information Kit” on the enclosed reply card — and mail it today. No obligation, of course. Sincerely, Bob Bly P.S. To get an immediate cost estimate for a copywriting project, call me today at 201-385-1220. The quote is free. And there’s no commitment of any kind. _____________________________ The second critical area is the copy describing the central message, theme, or idea of your selling proposition. For instance, do you position your newsletter on energy stocks as a way for your reader to hedge his portfolio against a bear market triggered by rising oil prices? Or do you talk about how he can profit from the “next big thing” in energy investing — which, according to your editor, is that crude oil will reach $200 a barrel by the end of the decade? The “big idea” of your promotion — and the way you express it — really matters. The third critical area is the copy in the offer — specifically, how the offer is expressed on the reply element. Offering a “free information kit,” for instance, usually generates more leads than the vaguer “send for more information” — the idea of a “kit” somehow being more tangible and valuable. On the order form, changing even one word in the copy — if changing that word results in changing the offer itself — can mean the difference between a winner and a disaster. For instance, “$100 a year” vs. “$500 a year” or “10-day money-back guarantee” vs. “90-day money-back guarantee.” It is worth your time to keep polishing your headlines, leads, offer copy, theme, and big idea until you finally feel confident that what you’ve written can work. For my money, the final step in creating an irresistible offer is creating an irresistible order device. By “order device,” I mean the mechanism through which you present the offer to the prospect and with which he responds. The simplest order device, used in lead-generating direct mail, is the reply card. In Chapter 1, I introduced this simple reply card I use for mailings promoting my freelance copywriting services, shown below: The prospect indicates with a checkmark which offers he wants, fills in his contact information, and returns the reply card to me in the mail. (You can require your prospects to affix their own postage, or you can use a prepaid business reply card.) An effective variation on the basic business reply card is to add a perforated tear-off stub, as shown in the diagram below. The stub can spotlight the premium (with a picture of the bonus gift). Or you can tell the prospect to keep it as a record of his order, leaving space for him to fill in the date of the order and his check number. The tear-off stub can also highlight the guarantee. Another variation is to create an 8 1/2 x 11 inch order form. The bottom third is a tear-off business reply card (for a bill-me offer) or order card (for a mail order offer). The top two-thirds (both front and back) give the copywriter and designer additional space for selling copy: A growing number of marketers are omitting the reply card from their lead-generating direct-mail promotions. They reason that, in the Internet Age, prospects would rather reply online or call. I disagree. You should still enclose a reply card in your mailings, even if, in fact, the majority of prospects don’t use it. Reason: The reply card graphically signals to the prospect that he is supposed to reply to the mailing. Enclosing a business reply card with your sales letter actually lifts total response, including responses by phone and online, not just responses by snail mail. Years ago, a large percentage of direct-response space ads, both for mail order and lead generation, had response coupons. These days, reply coupons in print ads are a rarity. I still like them, though, for the same reason I like business reply cards in direct mail: They tell the prospect: “Hey, this is one of those ads you are supposed to respond to — and if you do, you get something.” In my experience, adding a reply coupon to a space ad increases response by approximately 10 to 15 percent. The reply coupon appears in the bottom right corner of the ad. In your insertion order, you require the ad to be placed on a right-hand page so the coupon is easy to clip out, as in this classic ad for Dale Carnegie’s book, How to Win Friends and Influence People : Do not assume that your prospects will always prefer to contact you by phone or online. Your order device should offer multiple response options, including: Mail back the reply element. Fax back the reply element. Order or request more information on the Web. Reply via e-mail. Call a toll-free phone number. For direct mail written to generate an order, the response mechanism is usually an order card or form. A #9 business reply envelope (BRE) is included so the recipient can return the order form with his payment. For years, the standard reply element in a #10 direct-mail package was a 4 x 9 inch order card, which the recipient placed with payment in the BRE without folding it. Today, many marketers are switching to an 8 1/2 x 11 inch order form that folds like a letter for placement into the BRE. The larger order form has space for more copy. One popular style is to make the order form resemble an invoice on which all the features or benefits of the product are listed as separate “items,” with a price or value for each one. This creates the perception that the prospect is getting a lot for her money. Here is a layout for creating one of these invoice-style order forms: Invoice-style order forms are widely used in direct mail to sell newsletter and magazine subscriptions. Here’s an example from Kiplinger’s: Some marketers I know swear by “messy” order forms. They say the busier and more cluttered the order form looks, the greater the response. Others prefer cleanly designed order forms that are easy to fill out. With membership, mortgage, insurance, and other offers where the prospect is applying for a service he may or may not qualify for, you can design the reply elements to look like a membership application or official enrollment form: Often-neglected, tokens, peel-off stickers, stamp sheets, and other physical devices on the order form are a proven response-booster. With multiple products, such as magazine subscriptions, you can have a stamp sheet with the name and picture of each magazine on the sheet. The customer affixes the stamps for the magazines she wants to receive on the order form. An even more-overlooked variation is the “yes/no/maybe” offer, which may be done with or without peel-off stickers. The prospect who wants to order affixes the “yes” label to the order sheet. The prospect who is less certain can request a free trial with the “maybe” sticker. The negative offer (see Chapter 1) may be selected with the “no” sticker. You can also use “yes/no” stickers — or even just “yes.” Following are two examples: Order Devices That Increase Response Here are nine proven techniques for creating reply elements that effectively present your offer for maximum response: 1. Show a picture of the premium. If you are giving away merchandise, show a photo of the item you are giving away. If the premium is a free special report, show an image of the front cover. If you are giving away multiple special reports, spread their front covers out in a fanfold. 2. Highlight your guarantee on the order device. Put a certificate-style border around the guarantee. Add the signature of the company owner beneath the guarantee copy. Print the guarantee in clear, legible type. 3. Leave sufficient space on the order form for the prospect to write in his name and address. If the area is too cramped, he may give up in frustration. 4. If you want to track response with a key code on the mailing label, design your mail piece so the label is returned with the response device. This requires the mailing label to be affixed to or imprinted upon the reply element. 5. You can track phone responses without having a special phone number for each promotion. After your phone number on the order form, put something like “Ask for Betty” or “Ask for Extension 112” as a code. Your operators should ask each caller which extension or person they want. Their answer tells you which promotion they’re responding to. If you’re having people order or request more information on the Web, send traffic for each promotion to a unique URL. 6. Create domain names that are easy to remember, like www.myveryfirstebook.com or www.beer.com, which get more traffic than longer ones that do not connect logically with the product. 7. When you are using a Web-based form to generate leads, like registering for a free webinar or downloading a free white paper, it’s important to ask the minimum number of qualifying questions. Reason: The more information you require the prospect to fill in, the lower your conversion rate (the percentage of prospects who will complete the transaction). According to an article in DM News (10/20/08, p. 11), approximately 20 percent of visitors abandon the form for every field or question that is presented. So ask only what is necessary. For consumer online marketing, that’s usually just name and e-mail address. For B2B, it might include company name and phone number. If your sales process requires an inbound phone call to the lead, then collecting the phone number is mandatory. 8. Web-based forms can also be used for e-commerce or online mailorder marketing. The online order form may be the actual shopping cart order page or a custom-designed page preceding the shopping cart order page. A frequent problem with online ordering is “AVS mismatch.” The customer’s card is rejected, which irritates the customer who complains she’s using a valid card. To combat this problem, add copy to your order page reminding the reader to make sure the name they enter on the page matches exactly the name on the credit card they are using. 9. Online and offline, color can make a difference in your response rate. In one test, a marketer tested identical landing pages, with the only difference being that the order buttons on version “A” were red and on version “B” they were ochre. Surprisingly, the subdued ochre buttons outperformed red by 27 percent. And you can get a lift in direct mail by printing the order card or form on a paper stock that’s a different color than the outer envelope and letter. I particularly like canary yellow or robin’s egg blue. Testing Offers and Offer Devices The Florida Marlins, with 23 wins and 14 losses, once had the best record in Major League baseball. But that means the best-performing team in professional baseball still lost four out of every 10 games it played. And remember: That was the best record in baseball at the time. What’s ironic is that businesspeople who accept this statistical fact about baseball without a second thought … absolutely go bonkers when even one of their marketing programs fails. Experienced direct marketers know — and expect — that a percentage of their test campaigns will under-perform the control or even lose money. They accept this fact without despair, because they know that if one test mailing in every two … or every three … or even every five is a winner — they can make a lot of money. Inexperienced direct marketers don’t get this, however. As a result, countless small businesses test direct-marketing offers only once every few years, making it difficult if not impossible to identify the winning offer — the one offer that can multiply their sales two, three, even fivefold or more. If they don’t hit a home run the first time at bat, they loudly proclaim that “direct marketing doesn’t work” … and abandon it wholesale. If you’re a business owner or marketing professional, is there a better way to get direct marketing to work for you? Yes. Simply do more testing — of offers, reply elements, copy, prices — than you do right now. Let’s say you are planning to mail 5,000 postcards to drive people to a Web page. You just can’t decide which of two headlines you like — “Tastes Great” vs. “Less Filling.” If you subjectively pick just one, your risk of selecting the wrong sales appeal — and, therefore, having your postcard mailing bomb — is 50 percent. A much better approach is to split the postcard mailing into two batches, half with the headline “Tastes Great” and the other half with “Less Filling.” _________________________ “Don’t let personal preferences get in the way. What’s important is not what you think, like, believe, or prefer … it’s what your prospects think, like, believe, and prefer.” — Peter Betuel _________________________ Each postcard in this test drives traffic to a different URL, so you can measure the click-through and conversion rates, and then see which generates the most leads. In this type of test, it’s important for the headline on the landing page to match the headline on the postcard. Especially on the Web, testing variations — of headlines, copy, graphics, formats, and offers — is relatively quick, easy, and inexpensive. So if you create a landing page to sell a product on the Internet and your conversion rate is poor, don’t give up on the product. Instead, test different headlines, visuals, pricing, bonuses, guarantees, subheads, and copy leads. You’ll notice that one headline pulls slightly better than another … or one price generates more orders. Start incorporating the winners of those tests into your landing page, and in no time flat, you can take the promotion from marginally profitable to a real winner — all courtesy of testing. I am amazed at how many marketers, large and small, online and offline, invest significant sums in developing products — and then promote each product with just a single promotion … with no testing of any kind. If you are doing this, you are essentially hoping you’ll get a hit with only once chance at bat. In baseball, a .250 hitter who gets only one at-bat has a one in four chance of getting on base. In reality, for product launches, the success rate is often as low as 10 percent — which means that a single promotion has only a one in 10 chance of making money. That makes the odds of winning with a one-shot promotion 10 to one against you. _________________________ “Advertising arguments should only be settled by testing, not arguments around a conference table.” — Claude Hopkins _________________________ By testing different copy, offers, designs, and formats, you can significantly tip those odds in your favor. Giving your marketing multiple chances to score a winner is clearly the way to go. Copywriter Peter Betuel advises marketers: Don’t let personal preferences get in the way. What’s important is not what you think, like, believe, or prefer … it’s what your prospects think, like, believe, and prefer. No one can predict which offer will work best, and the least effective way to make marketing decisions is through subjective judgment. But as a direct marketer, you don’t have to rely on subjective judgment. You can put almost any proposition — e.g., offer “A” vs. offer “B,” or long copy vs. short copy — to a direct test with a statistically valid A/B split. For instance, a company that rented automobiles by the week tested two offers. Offer “A” was a free upgrade to a larger size model. Offer “B” was a rental discount given in exchange for purchasing multiple weeks of rentals in advance. (Customers would get a book of tickets they could redeem at the car counter.) To almost everyone’s surprise, offer “B” outperformed offer “A” significantly, generating nearly a tenfold increase in revenues. As advertising legend Claude Hopkins once said: “Advertising arguments should only be settled by testing, not arguments around a conference table.” And that includes the answer to the question: Which offer is best? In Conclusion … The way an offer is worded and presented is tremendously important. The right offer can boost response rates by 10 to 900 percent. The more you stress your offer in your promotional copy, the more leads and orders you will generate. Testing different prices and terms can yield big improvements in sales, and the results are often surprising. For example, the lower price is frequently not the winner of the test. The easiest way to increase response rates is to offer a premium — a free gift with order or inquiry. Free information — e.g., a free special report, CD, or video — can work extremely well as a premium. Guarantees should be at least 60 and preferably 90 days, and they should be unconditional. (Return the product and you get your money back.) Create a sense of urgency by giving the prospect a deadline or other incentive to respond to your offer now instead of later. Design your offer so all the risk is on the seller’s shoulders, not the buyer’s. Make buying entirely risk-free. You can never predict which offer will get the best response. Only by doing a series of A/B split tests will you find the winning offer for your product or service.

Goes here. Strategic offer structuring for e-commerce to increase conversion and LTV. Covers front-loaded subscription offers (high initial discount/low recurring, welcome kits), bundle psychology (BOGO, middle-option anchoring), and welcome pop-up mechanics ($ vs. % discounts based on AOV thresholds, mystery discounts, and stacking concurrent site offers into a single advertised value). Not here. • The email or SMS welcome sequence that delivers the pop-up discount code -> 14-EML • Landing page layouts and section order for displaying the bundle -> 07-LPG • Unit economics and sourcing for the physical welcome kit items -> 18-COG

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Defines exact mathematical thresholds for switching between percentage and dollar-off discounts, and reveals the margin-saving mechanic of front-loading subscription discounts instead of using flat recurring rates. modules: [OFF] topics: [subscription offers, bundle mechanics, welcome pop-up offers, discount psychology, offer stacking] tier: 2 scope_hint: growth

Topics.

Subscription Offers: Front-loaded discounts, recurring vs. initial margin, strategic welcome kits, consumption-enhancing gifts.

Bundle Mechanics: Middle-option anchoring, BOGO vs. percent-off psychology, same-SKU bundling, flash deal urgency.

Welcome Pop-Up Offers: Dollar vs. percent off thresholds, mystery discounts, store credit framing, combining site-wide discounts with welcome codes.

Offer Measurement: 90-day LTV tracking for offer validation, opt-in rate vs. placed order rate.

Look for.

AOV Threshold Rule: If AOV is >$100, use Dollar Off (e.g., $25 off). If AOV is <$100, use Percent Off (e.g., 20% off) to maximize perceived value.

Front-Loaded Subscription Formula: High initial discount (e.g., 25-30% off first order) + low recurring discount (e.g., 5-10% recurring) to incentivize the initial opt-in without destroying long-term margin.

Welcome Kit Criteria: Free gifts must directly contribute to the consumption or experience of the core product (e.g., a frother and specialized spoon for a coffee product), completely avoiding unrelated swag (e.g., tote bags).

Bundle Anchoring: Auto-selecting the middle option (e.g., a 6-pack) and anchoring the price against the single-unit cost to force the bundle as the baseline standard. "Free" (Buy 2 Get 1 Free) mathematically outperforms the exact equivalent "33% off 3 items".

Offer Stacking Math: Combining an evergreen site discount (e.g., 15% off subscription) with a welcome code (10% off) to advertise a massive aggregate dollar-off claim in the pop-up (e.g., "Up to $50 off your first order").

Skip. Generic advice like "make an offer they feel stupid saying no to." Discount depth testing that merely swaps percentages (10% vs 20% vs 30%) without changing the structural benefits of the offer. Promotional pitches for agencies, analytics platforms, or paid communities.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (having a basic welcome pop-up), 90% growth (complex welcome kits, mystery discounts, BOGO bundling, front-loaded subscriptions). Volume. ~400 words.

How is it that two brands can sell the exact same product, but one hits nine figures and the other stays at seven figures forever? It's not the team. It's not the ads. It's definitely not the product. It is the offer. Multi-9igure brands like AG1, Grunes, and True Classic have figured out the art of the offer. And this is what separates the true winners like that as well as some of the other brands that I've been able to play a part in their growth. I've watched the same pattern across every single category from subscriptions to apparel, accessories, CPG, everything. and I've been a part of several brands who have gone from the 8 figure mark to the nine figure mark, seeing everything play out. So, in this video, I'm going to be breaking down the three offer types that have helped these brands scale to nine figures. I'll walk you through the brands that are running each one and then how it can fit inside of your business. See, most brands are thinking about offers wrong entirely. They'll do something like slap on a regular 10% off offer and leave it at that. Maybe they'll always have a 20% off sort of seasonal sale always on their website or just give a discount for somebody's email. But that's not what the fastest scaling brands are doing. They are actually putting real strategic thought and ad money behind testing the offer and making it the forefront of their business. They test it religiously because they know that if you can make an offer that just hits a different psychological nerve with the customer that will get them to buy more than any other creative can. Just like Alexi says, the offer is everything. Make an offer that people feel stupid saying no to. A lot of you might be thinking, "Okay, perfect. Let's throw up 50% off or 90% off and that'll get you sales." It probably will, but it's not going to last you very long. A lot of other people out there are just going to test different discount percentages like 10% off, 20% offers, 30% off. That's not offer testing. That is discount testing. And that is the biggest reason why brands don't break through the ceiling. An offer is not necessarily a discount. A discount is percent off. An offer is a series of benefits and advantages [clears throat] that a customer gets from buying with you. And so the real lift and test comes from testing different offers, not discount depths. There are three core offers that I want to go over today. Now, this blew my mind once when I saw this with a client who was around the seven figure mark and they wanted to get to eight figures as fast as possible. All they were doing was they were just running a plain discount on their product. They're a CPG brand and they were just doing, "Hey, get an extra 20% off if you subscribe to our product." That was boring and that does not grab your attention. In the days of people scrolling meta and there are discounts being thrown everywhere, you need to have an offer that actually grabs people's attention. That's what this brand did. If you subscribed to their product, here's what you got. You got $10 off, you got three free gifts, and you got a $20 gift card of future credit that you can use at that store. With all the gift value, it essentially made the product free and instantly their CAC dropped and they were able to scale like crazy. And the fact that it was subscription means that they got higher repeat order rates. So, their LTV drive considerably. This brand is now one of the fastest growing in the space and they are multi-ight figures. So, let's break down the first offer type, which is the front-loaded subscription offer. So, you may have seen that a lot of the fastest growing brands like Marsmen, IMA, Grunes, and AG1 are all subscription brands, and they really try to get you to subscribe on that first order. Why do you want people to subscribe? Well, subscribers repeat order at a much higher rate. This is our custom analytics platform, and we're looking at cohort LTVs of people who are subscribers or non-subscribers. If somebody is a subscriber, their month 6 LTV right here is around $226 on average. But if we switch to people who did not do subscription, on average they're worth $138 just at month six alone. That's why getting people to subscribe on their first order is so important. And that's why these brands create banger offers around subscription. And that does not mean 10% off. It means building an actual offer. Discount bundle value. And all that goes away if you try to one-time purchase. The best example of this right now is I amate who has been scaling like crazy. Take a look at this offer that you get if you subscribe to their product. It's $91 every single month for this 90-day supply. You get exclusive access to a 90-day IM8 transformation program, which is right here, which is a quarterly sort of complete mastermind with some of the biggest health experts in the space. You get a free welcome kit, which you can see right here. $100 in value. Look at all this stuff right here that the customer sees. You get absolute maximum savings. So, it's $91 compared to $130 if you did a onetime order. And you get this 90-day money back guarantee. And again, you're reminded of all these discounts. That is a banger offer. It is 30% off. So, they're really incentivizing 90-day versus 30-day is 20% off right here. You still get some similar stuff. You get a welcome kit of €81 in value, but you don't get access to this other sort of stuff. That is an offer. You think that is going to convince people to buy compared to this, no offense, but just a regular subscribe and save 15% off. This does not grab anybody's attention. They're relying just on the product. Whereas this will get people to convert no matter the product because of the value that's been stacked in. So how are they able to economically make this work? They just jack up their prices and then you stack up the value. AG1 follows the similar playbook right here with subscription first. You can see just how low the buy once is and it's $99 compared to if you do the one month you get all these free gifts. $43 value right here and you get 20% off. Application of the Value Equation to physical products, pre-purchase offer architecture, risk reversal and guarantee mechanics (money-back guarantees, Try-Before-You-Buy layaway structures), scarcity and urgency implementation (live stock count displays, lightning deals, limited-edition drops), zero-marginal-cost bonus stacking (video styling guides, digital education, usage protocol add-ons), and outcome-driven product naming conventions. Also covers the three core mechanisms for trading unit margin: trading margin for conversion rate (discounts, free shipping), trading margin for higher AOV (multi-pack tiers, volume thresholds, cross-sell bundles), and trading margin for LTV/repeat purchases (front-loaded subscription discounts, free gifts on opt-in, prepaid annuals). Not here. • Unboxing experience, physical inserts, and post-purchase customer handling -> 17-CXP • The underlying avatar discovery, trigger moments, and interview methodologies -> 02-AVT • Visual section layouts, wireframes, and page hierarchy that house the offer -> 07-LPG • Base product manufacturing spec, unit economics, and physical production cost -> 01-PRD • The email or SMS welcome sequence that delivers the pop-up discount code -> 14-EML

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Translates info-product offer architecture into physical DTC by mapping the four Value Equation variables directly to e-commerce mechanics, and explicitly outlines how to trade unit margin for AOV or LTV using mystery discounts, bundle anchoring, and front-loaded subscriptions. modules: [OFF] topics: [value equation in e-commerce, guarantee mechanics and risk reversal, scarcity and urgency ratchets, digital bonus stacking for physical goods, dream-outcome product naming, margin trade-offs, bundle mechanics, subscription offers, welcome pop-up offers, discount psychology] tier: 2 scope_hint: growth

Topics. offer mechanics / physical product value equation (dream outcome, perceived likelihood of achievement, time delay, effort and sacrifice); margin trade-offs (unit margin for conversion, AOV, or LTV); guarantees and risk reversal / table-stakes money-back guarantees, try-before-you-buy 7-day layaway billing, demystification via unboxing and styling demos; scarcity and urgency / live SKU inventory countdowns, time-gated lightning deals, drop-model constraints; bonus stacking / informational add-ons (video styling guides, usage protocols, recipe/combination guides) to lift perceived value without adding COGS; product naming / outcome-explicit naming vs. generic product categorization; bundle mechanics / multi-pack tiers, middle-option anchoring, BOGO vs. percent-off psychology, same-SKU bundling; subscription offers / front-loaded discounts, recurring vs. initial margin, strategic welcome kits, consumption-enhancing gifts, prepaid annuals, the auction math of LTV; welcome pop-up offers / dollar vs. percent off thresholds, mystery discounts (scratch-offs, spin-to-win), store credit framing, combining site-wide discounts with welcome codes.

Look for. Specific conversion levers mapped to each variable of the Value Equation:

Perceived Likelihood of Achievement: Inclusion of third-party reviews and explicit multi-use demonstration videos (e.g., 3-way pairing videos) to eliminate application friction.

Time Delay Compression: Shift from standard shipping windows to expedited fulfillment protocols (1-day/2-day shipping) and immediate consumption assets.

Effort & Sacrifice Minimization: Friction removal at checkout via accelerated payment rails (Shop Pay, 1-click checkout).

Risk Reversal Tiers: Dual-guarantee structures combining unconditional returns with delayed-capture billing (Try-Before-You-Buy).

Bonus Economics: Integration of digital companion assets with 0% incremental COGS that resolve immediate post-purchase implementation anxieties.

AOV Threshold Rule: If AOV is >$100, use Dollar Off (e.g., $25 off). If AOV is <$100, use Percent Off (e.g., 20% off) to maximize perceived value.

Front-Loaded Subscription Formula: High initial discount (e.g., 25-30% off first order) + low recurring discount (e.g., 5-10% recurring) to incentivize the initial opt-in without destroying long-term margin.

Welcome Kit Criteria: Free gifts must directly contribute to the consumption or experience of the core product (e.g., a frother and specialized spoon for a coffee product), completely avoiding unrelated swag (e.g., tote bags).

Bundle Anchoring: Auto-selecting the middle option (e.g., a 6-pack) and anchoring the price against the single-unit cost to force the bundle as the baseline standard. "Free" (Buy 2 Get 1 Free) mathematically outperforms the exact equivalent "33% off 3 items".

Offer Stacking Math: Combining an evergreen site discount (e.g., 15% off subscription) with a welcome code (10% off) to advertise a massive aggregate dollar-off claim in the pop-up (e.g., "Up to $50 off your first order").

The "Mystery" Pop-Up Mechanic: Converting a static 10% off pop-up (which may yield a 7% opt-in rate) into a "mystery discount" (e.g., scratch-off or game) can push opt-ins to 15-17.46%, effectively 3x-ing total email revenue while offering the exact same 10% discount.

LTV Ceiling Math: In a subscription acquisition auction, your maximum CAC is bound by LTV. If Month 6 LTV is $289 on a $40 product (roughly 3:1), you can afford to spend $95 to acquire the customer, accepting a first-order loss to outbid competitors relying on single-purchase ROAS.

The "Death" Offer: Offering free shipping on a low-AOV item (e.g., a $14 sock) will spike conversion rate but crush net profit because the brand absorbs the shipping cost without offsetting it with cart volume.

Skip. Generic mindset commentary, references to the My First Million podcast banter, promotional pitches to buy the book on Kindle for 99 cents, service-based business examples not directly translated to physical DTC, generic advice like "make an offer they feel stupid saying no to," discount depth testing that merely swaps percentages (10% vs 20% vs 30%) without changing the structural benefits of the offer, and promotional pitches for agencies, analytics platforms, or paid communities.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (standard risk reversal, transparent stock states, having a basic welcome pop-up), 90% growth (conditional bonus stacking, try-before-you-buy financing, drop-urgency mechanics, complex welcome kits, mystery discounts, BOGO bundling, front-loaded subscriptions). Volume. ~700 words.

03-OFF / offers Goes here. Pre-purchase subscription offer architecture and first-order take-rate optimization. Structuring welcome kits with consumption-focused free gifts, pricing disparities between one-time and recurring purchases, and manipulating product page (PDP) layouts to bias subscription selection. Not here. • The onboarding and transactional emails sent after the subscription is active -> 14-EML • The cancellation flow mechanics inside the customer portal -> 17-CXP

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Flips standard discount logic by removing all one-time purchase discounts and auto-selecting subscriptions, while using consumption-focused free gifts to reduce downstream churn.

modules: [OFF]

topics: [subscription offers, welcome kits, take-rate optimization, bundle mechanics]

tier: 2

scope_hint: growth

Topics. subscription offers / front-loaded welcome kits, consumption-focused free gifts (e.g., frothers, custom spoons), removing one-time discounts entirely; take-rate optimization / auto-selecting subscriptions on load, 3-option pricing anchoring (e.g., 90-day sub, 30-day sub, 1-time purchase), popup and PDP offer alignment.

Look for. Consumption-focused gift criteria (gifts must explicitly aid in using the product to build the habit, avoiding generic swag). The 3-option pricing display rule (making two out of the three choices subscription-based to force a default bias). The baseline LTV multiplier (first-order subscriptions driving a 50% increase in Month 6 LTV).

Skip. Mentions of the Bobby baby formula ad shutdown story. Vague advice on "having a good product." Promotional pitches for agencies or paid communities.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (having a subscription option), 90% growth (welcome kits, 3-option anchoring, pop-up alignment).

Volume. ~300 words.

14-EML / email lifecycle Goes here. Subscription onboarding sequences, transactional email optimization (billing reminders and order confirmations), and subscriber-specific campaign segmentation. Covers habit-stacking education, customizing emails by refill number, and post-cancellation win-back flows. Not here. • The subscription offer structuring on the PDP -> 03-OFF • In-portal cancellation mechanics and dynamic save-rate logic -> 17-CXP

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Maps out a counter-intuitive onboarding sequence that front-loads education in days 1-7 before delivery to prevent day-0 churn, and redesigns transactional emails to bury the cancel button.

modules: [EML]

topics: [subscription onboarding, transactional emails, billing reminders, subscriber segmentation, win-back flows]

tier: 2

scope_hint: growth

Topics. onboarding sequences / pre-delivery heavy education (days 1-7), habit-stacking pushes (e.g., creatine in coffee), long-term pacing expectations (telling customers it takes 90-120 days for results); transactional emails / migrating Shopify confirmation emails to native ESPs, customizing billing reminders by refill number, highlighting upcoming free gifts; UI manipulation in emails / prominent "delay order" CTAs vs. buried "cancel" CTAs; subscriber segmentation / limiting generic campaigns to 1-3 times monthly, excluding active subs from standard promos, offering exclusive 1-time add-on cross-sells; win-back flows / 30-60 day delayed win-back with aggressive discounts (30-50% off).

Look for. Email cadences (daily emails explicitly placed in the first 7 days post-purchase, backing off during days 7-14 to avoid triggering cancellation reminders). Billing reminder structural rules (Delay CTA at the top, Cancel CTA at the very bottom). Win-back timing (waiting 30 to 60 days post-cancellation rather than sending immediately).

Skip. Platform tutorials (e.g., how to contact Shopify Plus support to turn off native emails). Promoting custom retention dashboards.

Scope mix. 20% baseline (having basic billing reminders), 80% growth (customizing by order number, habit-stacking education, delayed win-backs).

Volume. ~400 words.

17-CXP / post-purchase Goes here. Subscriber retention mechanics and churn deflection inside the customer portal. Cancellation flow structures, save rate tracking, and dynamic offer logic based on the user's selected cancellation reason. Not here. • The billing reminder emails sent before the charge -> 14-EML • The physical unboxing experience or physical package inserts -> 03-OFF / 17-CXP (physical)

rights: public_reference

why: Details the exact logic tree for subscription cancellation flows inside platforms like Skio or Recharge to hit a 15%+ save rate.

modules: [CXP]

topics: [cancellation flows, subscription portal, save rate, churn deflection]

tier: 2

scope_hint: growth

Topics. cancellation flows / founder video splash screens, loyalty point loss-aversion; churn deflection logic / mapping cancellation reasons to specific actions.

Look for. Save rate benchmarks (Target: 15%+, Red flag: <10%). The specific branching logic for cancellation reasons: "Too much product" -> Delay/Skip CTA; "Don't like taste" -> Swap product CTA; "Too expensive" -> Discount offer CTA.

Skip. Generic advice on making customers "feel part of something."

Scope mix. 10% baseline (allowing users to cancel), 90% growth (dynamic deflection logic, founder videos).

Volume. ~250 words.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the operationalization of subscription acquisition, emphasizing that subscription churn is fundamentally an acquisition problem that must be solved through continuous offer testing and persona-driven funnels, rather than relying solely on post-purchase retention tactics. modules: [ADC] topics: [offer testing, persona mapping] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. offer testing / The philosophy that "your ceiling is an acquisition problem wearing a retention costume"—arguing that focusing primarily on retention (e.g., trying to bump month-3 cohort retention from 60% to 65% via expensive gifts) is inherently capped and less efficient than improving initial subscriber opt-in rates (e.g., from 40% to 45%) through rigorous offer testing. Testing mechanisms to move beyond simple "Subscribe & Save" discounts (which attract discount hunters) by utilizing "Buy More, Save More" bulk options, or bundling high-margin secondary SKUs as free gifts. persona mapping / Testing different funnels tailored to specific customer personas and desired outcomes (e.g., marketing protein powder distinctly to bodybuilders versus individuals managing perimenopause). Gathering persona data via pre-purchase quiz pop-ups (e.g., Alia or KnoCommerce) to segment traffic (e.g., athletes vs. coaches) and dynamically reallocating ad spend toward the cohorts that demonstrate higher front-end conversion rates or stronger LTV.

Look for. The specific mindset shift regarding churn: "Subscription is not a retention problem, it's an acquisition problem." The specific reason to test bulk discounts (e.g., Buy More, Save More) over simple percentage discounts: they dissuade "cheap" discount hunters and attract buyers looking for value, increasing AOV and LTV. The specific method to uncover personas: using pre-purchase quiz pop-ups to ask the user's primary goal or identity (e.g., athlete vs. coach) and tracking subsequent conversion rates by cohort.

Skip. Plugs for "The Cancel Page" website, the "Subscription Prescription" agency, or the "Email Marketing Mastery" community. Discussions about WooCommerce versus Shopify. The specific customer onboarding sequences (e.g., X Endurance challenge) or post-purchase Dunning email flows, as those relate strictly to retention (01-EML or 21-OPS) rather than acquisition/offer frameworks.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 15 to 20.

03-OFF / offers

Goes here. Pre-purchase offer architecture and scaling mechanics. Layering multiple offer types (e.g., combining pre-built starter kits with quantity breaks), subscription-only gating, scaling free gifts proportionately to unit volume, and cognitive cost reduction via price-per-serving or price-per-bottle displays.

Not here.

• Wireframing the product page accordions or side-cart UX -> 07-LPG

• Evaluating the statistical significance of the offer test -> 09-CRO

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Demonstrates how to layer multiple offer mechanics (subscription gating + quantity breaks + tiered gifts) while using per-serving pricing to eliminate sticker shock on high-AOV bundles.

modules: [OFF]

topics: [layered offers, quantity breaks, price anchoring, subscription gating, tiered bonus stacking]

tier: 2

scope_hint: growth

Topics. offer mechanics / layered offers, subscription-only gating, quantity break tiers; price anchoring / per-serving breakdowns, per-bottle display; bonus stacking / unlocking sequential free gifts tied to volume (e.g., 1 gift per bag, 3 gifts for 3 bags).

Look for. The AOV and Conversion Rate benchmark formula for scaling: $\text{AOV} \times \text{Conversion Rate} > 250$ (removing the percentage sign). Exact mapping of free gifts to quantity break tiers to increase perceived value.

Skip. General agency pitches, promotional intros, and claims about $10M revenue without structural offer breakdowns.

Scope mix. 20% baseline, 80% growth.

Volume. ~300 words.

07-LPG / landing pages

Goes here. Product page layout, listicle advertorial structures, heatmap-informed CTA placement, delivery expectation promises, side-cart optimization, gamified cart progress bars, and cart reservation urgency timers.

Not here.

• The economic structure of the quantity break offer itself -> 03-OFF

• Post-purchase email flows triggering from an abandoned cart -> 14-EML

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Details the exact friction-removal and AOV-boosting UX elements for side carts (progress bars, 1-click cross-sells) and listicle landing pages (high CTA placement).

modules: [LPG]

topics: [listicle structure, cart optimization, friction removal, social proof placement, UX/UI elements]

tier: 2

scope_hint: mixed

Topics. page types and section order / listicle advertorials ("7 reasons why"); above the fold / early CTA placement based on heatmaps and scroll depth; proof placement / featured review carousels followed by bulk reviews; friction removal / specific delivery date expectations, organized product detail accordions; cart optimization / sticky checkout buttons, side-cart 1-click cross-sells, gamified free-shipping/gift progress bars, reservation urgency timers (e.g., "reserving order for X minutes"), in-cart subscription upgrades.

Look for. Specific UX placements, such as moving CTAs higher up on listicles because heatmaps reveal low scroll depth. Gamification steps in the cart (unlocking tiers like free shipping, then a free gift).

Skip. Agency self-promotion, vague statements about "crushing it with ad creatives," and general e-commerce platitudes.

Scope mix. 60% baseline (friction removal, accordions, sticky buttons), 40% growth (listicles, gamified carts, in-cart upsells).

Volume. ~350 words.

04-BRD / brand and marketing Goes here. A comprehensive analysis of "Buyology" by Martin Lindstrom. Covers the application of functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) and Steady-State Topography (SST) to neuromarketing, challenging traditional market research methods by revealing the subconscious drivers of consumer behavior, brand loyalty, and advertising effectiveness. Not here. • Paid media campaign setup or Facebook Ad targeting -> 06-MEA • Landing page visual design or layout conversion rate optimization -> 07-LPG

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the neuroscientific foundation of consumer purchasing decisions, explaining how subconscious factors like somatic markers, mirror neurons, and sensory branding override rational thought—crucial insights for brand positioning and advertising strategy. modules: [BRD] topics: [neuromarketing, consumer behavior, brand positioning, fMRI, SST, mirror neurons, somatic markers, sensory branding, subliminal messaging] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. neuromarketing vs. traditional research / why traditional surveys and focus groups fail (consumers cannot accurately articulate their subconscious motivations) and how brain scanning (fMRI and SST) reveals the hidden drivers of purchasing; the failure of health warnings / discovering that graphic cigarette warnings stimulate the brain's "craving spot" (nucleus accumbens) rather than deterring smoking; product placement / finding that overt, storyline-integrated brand placement (e.g., Coca-Cola on American Idol) is highly memorable, while passive, non-integrated placement (e.g., Ford) is easily forgotten and can even suppress memory; mirror neurons / how observing an action or an attractive model triggers the same brain regions as if the consumer were performing the action or embodying the model, driving the desire to purchase the associated brand; subliminal messaging / demonstrating that logo-free imagery (e.g., a red Ferrari or a sunset) can trigger stronger brand cravings than the actual logos themselves, bypassing conscious defensive filters; ritual, superstition, and religion / exploring how brands create "stickiness" by establishing comforting rituals (e.g., the Corona lime) and how powerful brands activate the exact same brain regions as religious icons; somatic markers / how the brain creates emotional "bookmarks" based on past experiences (e.g., the sound of a closing car door or the shape of a bottle) that unconsciously steer future buying decisions; sensory branding / proving that sight is not the most powerful sense in advertising; combining congruent smells and sounds with visuals exponentially increases brand recall and pleasantness, while incongruent or annoying sounds (e.g., the Nokia ringtone) can actively damage a brand; sex and beauty in advertising / revealing the "Vampire Effect," where overtly sexual or highly attractive models suck attention away from the actual product or brand message, reducing recall.

Look for.

The Nucleus Accumbens Activation: The counterintuitive finding that graphic health warnings on cigarette packs actually stimulated the brain's reward and craving center, effectively acting as marketing for tobacco companies.

The "Vampire Effect": The phenomenon where highly sexualized imagery or extreme physical beauty in an advertisement distracts the viewer so much that they fail to remember the brand or product being advertised.

Somatic Markers: The concept of subconscious cognitive shortcuts or "bookmarks" created by past experiences (reward or pain) that instantly guide a consumer's purchasing decision without rational thought.

Mirror Neurons: The brain cells that fire both when an individual acts and when they observe the same action performed by another (e.g., seeing someone drink a refreshing beverage), explaining empathy and the urge to mimic behavior through purchasing.

Skip. Personal anecdotes about the author's travels (e.g., his childhood illness and Lego obsession, meeting the CEO in Switzerland) unless they directly introduce a specific neuromarketing concept.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (traditional marketing research concepts), 90% growth (neuromarketing, behavioral psychology, and advanced brand strategy). Volume. ~450 words.
