Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the dual purpose of quiz funnels in e-commerce, explaining how they function as both a front-end conversion rate optimization (CRO) tool and a critical back-end data-gathering mechanism for refining ad creative, messaging, and product-market fit. modules: [MEA] topics: [conversion rate optimization, business and marketing analytics, creative strategy] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. conversion rate optimization / Utilizing quiz funnels to dramatically increase e-commerce conversion rates by masking the sales process behind a personalized assessment. Structuring quizzes to intersperse data-gathering questions with educational "nurture" screens, visual trajectory graphs (e.g., charting a timeline of expected hair regrowth), and authoritative social proof to build conviction before the user ever sees the final product offer. Highlighting the critical role of A/B testing the first three questions of a quiz, treating them as the "hook" that dictates the overall completion rate and throughput of the funnel. business and marketing analytics / Leveraging quiz funnels as a scalable, automated first-party data engine. Replacing slow, unreliable research methods (e.g., reading Reddit threads or competitor comments) with real-time quantitative data sourced directly from paying customers. Analyzing aggregated quiz submissions (e.g., pulling reports every 100 submissions via AI) to identify the most common pain points, the average age demographic, and the user's specific stage of awareness based on their "failed past solutions," providing actionable insights that inform future business decisions. creative strategy / Translating back-end quiz data directly into front-end paid media strategy. Ceasing the practice of blindly copying competitor ads, and instead using aggregated customer pain points (e.g., discovering that 70% of respondents struggle specifically with "chin fat" rather than general skin tightening) to craft highly targeted, data-backed ad hooks and angles. Adjusting the "frame" of the marketing message—whether to lead with doctor authority, raw social proof, or logical statements—based entirely on the psychographic data gathered in the quiz.

Look for. The dual purpose of a quiz funnel: to increase front-end conversion rates through personalization, while simultaneously gathering back-end first-party data to inform marketing strategy. The importance of the first three questions in a quiz: they act as the "hook" of the funnel and must be A/B tested to maximize the completion rate. The definition of marketing "frame": the specific angle or authority lens through which a marketing message is presented (e.g., leading with a doctor's endorsement vs. raw customer reviews). How to use quiz data for creative strategy: identifying the most frequently selected pain points (e.g., 70% selecting "chin fat") and turning them directly into the hooks for new ad creatives.

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a call with the speaker's agency.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 5 to 10.

07-LPG / landing pages and funnels

Goes here. A diagnostic breakdown of common landing page conversion killers across B2B, digital products, and e-commerce, offering actionable CRO (Conversion Rate Optimization) fixes such as optimizing the above-the-fold, restructuring navigation, and visualizing product bundles.

Not here.

• Technical SEO or blog content strategy -> 05-SEO

• Automated email marketing flows -> 09-EML

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Details specific, recurring UX and copywriting mistakes that depress conversion rates across different business models, providing actionable remedies grounded in behavioral psychology and A/B testing data.

modules: [LPG]

topics: [conversion rate optimization, landing page design, e-commerce, B2B lead generation, digital products, above the fold, copywriting, visual hierarchy, FUD reduction, navigation design, bundle pricing]

tier: 3

scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. ad-to-page congruency / explaining that the primary promise in the ad copy (e.g., "Lose 6-20 lbs") must be mirrored exactly in the landing page headline, preventing the immediate bounce caused by generic messaging; optimizing B2B and lead-gen pages / breaking down the ideal above-the-fold structure: benefit-driven headline, descriptive sub-headline, stacked social proof, FUD reducers (Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt), and a conversion-focused CTA (e.g., "Lose Fat Fast" instead of "Contact Us"); removing navigation leaks / advising the removal of top navigation bars (About, Explore, Blog) on dedicated landing pages to force users toward the primary conversion event; the Problem-Agitate-Solve (PAS) framework / structuring mid-page copy to identify the user's struggle, agitate the emotional pain, and present the product as the exact solution; selling digital products and courses / shifting from a transactional feature list (e.g., "5 hours of video") to an outcome-driven offer ("Land six-figure gigs"), utilizing "Value Stacking" to assign monetary worth to bonuses and modules to make the price feel like a no-brainer; optimizing e-commerce homepages / identifying the "View Product Rate" as the most critical homepage metric and prioritizing visual navigation (using icons/images for categories) while keeping menu items under seven to prevent analysis paralysis; e-commerce product page (PDP) fixes / exposing image thumbnails (avoiding hidden dots), placing reviews above the product title, keeping the "Add to Cart" and FUD reducers (warranties, free shipping) above the fold, and explicit bundle savings (e.g., "Save $20" in the bundle title so users don't have to do math); skimmable design / transforming dense paragraphs of product information into visual, icon-driven infographics to accommodate the 80% of users who scan rather than read.

Look for.

Ad-to-Page Congruency: The strict CRO rule that the exact quantifiable promise made in the ad creative must be the very first thing the user reads in the landing page headline.

The "Value Stacking" Framework: A pricing presentation strategy for digital products where every module and bonus is assigned a specific dollar value, making the final bundled price appear heavily discounted.

The "Don't Make Them Do Math" Rule: The pricing psychology tactic of explicitly stating the exact dollar amount saved in the headline of a product bundle (e.g., "3-Pack: Save $20") rather than just showing the discounted price.

Visual Navigation Menus: The UX strategy for e-commerce of replacing text-only drop-down menus with images or icons representing the product categories, which significantly increases click-through rates to product pages.

Skip. The intro hook promoting the speaker's audits of 1,000 pages, generic promotional links to a Figma swipe file, and the outro teasing the next video.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of above the fold and digital products), 85% growth (advanced UX optimization, direct response copywriting, and B2B/E-com specific CRO tactics).

Volume. ~400 words.

07-LPG / landing pages and funnels Goes here. A breakdown of seven core conversion rate optimization (CRO) principles for designing high-performing landing pages, focusing on UX design, copywriting, and psychological triggers to maximize leads and sales. Not here. • Driving top-of-funnel traffic or scaling ad accounts -> 06-MEA • Automated email sequences and abandoned cart flows -> 09-EML

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides a data-backed, actionable framework for structuring landing pages, detailing exactly what elements belong "above the fold" and how to use visual hierarchy and behavioral psychology to increase conversion rates. modules: [LPG] topics: [conversion rate optimization, CRO, landing page design, above the fold, copywriting, visual hierarchy, social proof, Jakob's law, UX design] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. the 5-second rule and above the fold / ensuring the topmost section of the page immediately answers "why should I care?" using a benefit-driven headline, USP sub-headline, social proof, and a clear CTA; emotional decision making / leveraging imagery and the Problem-Agitate-Solve (PAS) copywriting framework to tap into customer frustrations or desires before rationalizing the purchase with logic; landing page length / debunking the myth that long pages hurt conversions, arguing instead that pages should act like a comprehensive digital salesperson, provided no crucial information (like reviews) is hidden in drop-downs or carousels; designing for scanners / structuring copy with descriptive headlines, bullet points, and bold text to accommodate the 80% of users who scan rather than read; authentic social proof / combating consumer skepticism by adding specific quotes to "featured on" logos and using verifiable reviews with real names, photos, and platform sources; visual hierarchy / guiding the user's attention toward the CTA using contrasting colors, font weights, and proximity while avoiding analysis paralysis; Jakob's law and simplicity / favoring familiar, standardized web design layouts over overly creative or minimalist structures that sacrifice clarity.

Look for.

The "Above the Fold" Formula: The mandatory elements for the hero section: a benefit-driven headline tying to a dream outcome, a USP sub-headline, at least two forms of social proof, a clear CTA, FUD (Fear, Uncertainty, Doubt) reducers, and a complementary image.

FUD Reduction Placement: The highly effective tactic of placing risk-reversal elements (e.g., "free trial," "money-back guarantee," "easy returns") directly underneath the primary CTA button to instantly alleviate purchase anxiety.

Descriptive Scanning Headlines: The copywriting rule to abandon generic section headers (e.g., "How it Works" or "Our Services") in favor of full, benefit-driven statements, assuming the user will only read the headlines.

Jakob's Law in UX: The psychological principle that users spend most of their time on other websites, meaning they expect your landing page to look and function in a familiar, standard way rather than reinventing the wheel.

Skip. Plugs for the speaker's CRO agency, mentions of specific client results without the accompanying strategic context, and the outro teasing the next video.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of landing page elements), 85% growth (advanced UX psychology, CRO testing methodologies, and copywriting frameworks). Volume. ~400 words.

But if that creativity comes at the cost of clarity, you're going to lose conversions. There's actually a concept in CRO and UX design called Jacob's law, which basically states that people expect a landing page or website to look and feel and function on a similar level to what they're already familiar with because they spend a lot of time on other websites. And so when you look at this example here, right, it completely deviates from a common design pattern to what most people are used to. There's two different headlines instead of one. There's social proof that is gigantic on the page and underneath the headline and then the body text is completely separate and far away from the headline further down in the page or these examples here where they simply have a headline with no body text and no CTA button whatsoever. All in the hopes of achieving minimalism. Just cut all of this out, right? Just stick with the basics and what people are already used to. If you care about conversions, that means one clear headline, one clear body text in close proximity to the headline, social proof right at the very top of the site, your CTA button right underneath. You're going to reduce your FUDs underneath the CTA button, and then you're going to have an image or video. So, in this video, I went over what's working right now and some of my key learnings. And now you could go and make your own landing page based on what I've shown you here. Or you could click right here to watch the next one where I apply all of my best learnings to build a real landing page for my own business. And because it's a real landing page that I'm actively using for my agency, I'm not holding anything back. If you want to follow along and use my process to build your own landing page, I'll see you

07-LPG / landing pages and funnels Goes here. A breakdown of five UX and psychological strategies to reduce "cognitive friction" on e-commerce websites. Covers navigation simplification, bundle pricing psychology, visual hierarchy, and the effective use of images and badges to increase conversion rates and AOV. Not here. • Paid media campaign setup or top-of-funnel ad targeting -> 06-MEA • Automated email marketing flows or SMS strategies -> 09-EML

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details specific, actionable UX optimizations to simplify the customer journey, from reducing navigation clutter to streamlining the cart experience, demonstrating how minimizing cognitive load directly increases conversion rates. modules: [LPG] topics: [conversion rate optimization, CRO, cognitive friction, cognitive ease, UX design, e-commerce, visual hierarchy, bundle pricing, navigation design, A/B testing] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. cognitive friction vs. ease / defining the core CRO concept that high mental effort (due to cluttered navigation or too many choices) kills conversions, while cognitive ease (streamlined design, clear benefits) drives sales; the paradox of choice / identifying that offering too many navigation links (over seven) or too many product bundles (e.g., five instead of three) overwhelms users, and how cutting options actually increases both conversion rate and Average Order Value (AOV); visual selling / leveraging the fact that the brain processes images 60,000 times faster than text by replacing generic navigation text and long product descriptions with scannable icon graphics and lifestyle infographics; benefit-driven copywriting / accommodating the 80% of users who only scan by ensuring that headlines communicate the ultimate benefit ("Why should I care?") rather than just stating the product name; visual hierarchy / guiding the user's attention from the most important element (a bold, large headline) to the Call to Action (CTA) using font size, color contrast, and spacing, avoiding the trap of emphasizing everything; optimizing the product selection process / reducing friction on product detail pages by explicitly stating the exact dollar amount saved on bundles (instead of making users do the math), adding images to bundle variants, and utilizing "Best Seller" or "Most Popular" badges to guide decision-making; the sliding cart drawer / replacing disruptive, page-reloading cart confirmations with frictionless slide-out drawers that offer immediate feedback and integrated cross-sell/upsell progress bars.

Look for.

The Paradox of Choice Reduction: The specific A/B testing strategy of reducing product bundle options (e.g., from 5 to 3 tiers) to eliminate analysis paralysis, which simultaneously boosts conversion rates and Average Order Value (AOV).

The 7-Item Navigation Rule: The UX heuristic that placing more than seven items in a top navigation menu creates diminishing returns; non-essential links (About, Contact, Blog) should be moved to sub-menus or the footer.

The "Don't Make Them Do Math" Rule: The pricing psychology tactic of explicitly stating the exact dollar amount saved in the headline of a product bundle (e.g., "Save $20") rather than just listing the percentage discount or requiring the user to calculate the difference.

Visual Navigation Menus: The strategy of replacing text-only navigation bars with images or icons representing the product categories, significantly increasing click-through rates.

Skip. The promotional hooks offering free website audits, generic client percentage lifts without the full testing context, and the outro teasing the next video.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of cognitive load and visual hierarchy), 85% growth (advanced UX optimization, A/B test case studies, and behavioral pricing tactics). Volume. ~400 words.

Cognitive friction might be destroying your website's conversion rate. So, in this video, I'll explain why that actually is and give you the five-step guide that you can use every single time you create any website page so that you can sleep at night knowing you're not leaving any money on the table. So, let's start by understanding what cognitive friction actually is and why it's important. Cognitive friction simply means how much brain power, thinking or mental effort does someone have to use in order to make a decision and shop on your website. The human brain has something called a cognitive threshold, which is basically how much information can somebody think about and process all at once. If cognitive friction is high and you're above that threshold, that means that your navigation is confusing and hard to use. There's way too much information and there's too many choices. And so people are just frustrated and they're probably not going to buy. What you want to aim for instead is the opposite of cognitive friction, which is also known as cognitive ease. Cognitive ease can be achieved on multiple different levels, including a streamlined navigation, having crystal clear articulation of your benefits, having scannable and digestible text, having an easy product selection process, and having images that complement and reinforce your value prop. When you have all of this, people are way more likely to buy on your website. So, now let's go through my five-step hyperactionable checklist of things that you can do to completely eliminate cognitive friction and instantly increase your conversion rate. The first step to reduce cognitive overload is to actually remove elements on your site, not add more. There's something called the paradox of choice, which basically states that when you give people too much choice, it equals no choice at all. This can happen on multiple different levels on your website. The first low-hanging fruit is by simply cutting down the number of items on your navigation menu. Here's an example of a poor navigation where there's a total of 12 different items that I can choose from, many of which are not even critical to the core conversion action of buying a product. Here's another example where I'm completely overwhelmed by the number of options and I have no idea where to start. My advice is to install a tool called Microsoft Clarity where you can literally see exactly what navigation items people are clicking on. Based on my experience, you can easily cut out two to three items from your navigation because you'll see through Microsoft Clarity that they're getting close to 0% of clicks. Easy example and lowhanging fruit is getting rid of home on your navigation menu. People already know that they can access the homepage by clicking on the logo on your website and this is universally known. The other big thing is if your focus is on conversions, all of these secondary menu items that are not critical to buying products like about, contact, blog, FAQ, all of that can be either entirely removed or put on a submen in much smaller text and much less prominent. My rule of thumb is to never show any more than seven items on the navbar. This is when we start to see diminishing returns and very poor conversions. If you have a lot of products and collections, then I recommend leveraging a nested menu where you're basically limiting the number of products that you're displaying at one time. Also, do not add redundant clicks. Your shop menu does not need to be hidden, right? You can just expose this up front and you're basically saving people an extra click. Reducing elements should also occur on your product pages. This website has so many different elements on the screen that I'm completely overwhelmed and I have no idea what to do next. Compare that to this where it's a nice, clean, and organized layout where I can digest all of the content and I know exactly what to do next. One of my favorite examples is an AB test we ran for a client, Wild Men Drinking, where we noticed on their product page in user recordings that people were getting overwhelmed by the five different bundle options they had. They would either choose one of the lowerpriced options or they were seen in recordings to completely exit the website altogether. And so what we hypothesized is let's cut down from five bundle options to three. And what we saw from that very simple AB test was a 53% increase in conversions and a 13.5% increase in the average order value. So not only were people purchasing more products, but they were also purchasing the higher price options as well, like the three-pack and five pack. The other big thing is to simplify your cart menu. If you look at this example, they have a very poor cart where everything is screaming at me at once. And they've basically tried to add all these CRO best practices with upsells and crossells and it just looks so overwhelming. And the irony is that it's actually probably hurting their conversions rather than helping them. Just strip that all down and go with the basics with a simple cart that shows you the higher tiered options, the items in your cart with some minor upsells and crossells, and then simple next steps. The second step is to use images and icons wherever possible instead of just text. As humans, we're naturally visual creatures, right? The human brain processes images 60,000 times faster than text. Yet, most e-commerce brands don't understand this, and they litter their pages with tons and tons of paragraphs of text that no one ever actually reads. The first critical place to use images and icons is in your navigation menu. Here are some examples of what not to do. These navigation menus are fully textbased and they have nothing exciting or engaging about it. Why should I click further into any of these items and take action? Compare that to these examples that do an excellent job of showing the product in the navigation menu itself through images or icons where I can actually visualize what the product looks like and it's going to make the buying decision for me as a user a lot easier, thus reducing cognitive friction. We actually ran this as an AB test for parcel safety where their original version just had a generic textbased menu. And what we did was we added images and icons and added nested layers. And what we saw was a 60.7% increase in the conversion rate and a whopping 92% increase in the revenue per visitor. Another place you can use icons is what I call the social media icon test where it basically resembles stories on common social media platforms. So basically, you put all of your navigation items out in the open, so you're saving people an extra click, and it's also giving people a visual snapshot very quickly of all of the different product offerings you have. We did this for a pet client as an AB test, and we saw a 72% increase in the conversion rate and an 82% increase in the revenue per visitor. It also generated them an incremental six figures in annual projected revenue, which is absolutely massive considering it's just one small test. Your product images are also crucial. Whenever we look at heat map data on any website, we always notice that the product images are one of the most clicked elements on the page. The big mistake people do is similar to bum where they basically show different angles of their product that adds no substantial value to me whatsoever, and it's a massive waste of real estate in one of the most crucial important sections of the page. What you want to do instead is transform your photos into infographics where you're basically taking your product photos, but you're combining it with scannable value props and USPS on the image itself. We did this for Wild Men Drinking where we took their boring product images and transformed them into custom infographics highlighting all of their different value props, their benefit driven sections, their social proofs, how the product works. And all of this led to a 32% increase in their conversion rate. The last big thing you want to avoid is using large blocks of text that no one is going to read. Chunk all of that content into scannable icons, into bullet points, and into sub headlines. We did this for Wild Men Drinking where we took all of their large blocks of text and put them into scannable icons. And we saw a 25% increase in conversions and a 34% increase in the revenue per visitor. For Fiddler's Green, their entire landing page had large blocks of text. So, we completely transformed it with compelling icons and images and digestible content. And we saw a 158% boost in store orders. As I'm going through all these steps, if you need help in figuring out exactly what's wrong with your website and how to increase your conversion rate, you can apply for a free audit where I'll do a deep dive into all your conversion blockers and give you actionable areas of improvement for your website. Just use the link in the description below and you can apply. The third step is to avoid using vague messaging on your website. Although images and icons are important, you still need to have text to convey the benefit of your product. The big mistake I see a lot of brands make is that they don't understand that people don't read, they scan. In fact, people will only read 20% of the content on your website or page actually read. The other 80% they just scan. So, you need to operate under the framework that somebody will only read the headlines on your landing page or website alone, nothing else. The biggest mistake I often see every single day are generic headlines that are vague, use jargon that have no meaning whatsoever. And the biggest conversion mistake of all time, which is simply explaining who they are and what they do in the headline. I can literally pull up hundreds of examples like these and it's absolutely killing your conversion rate. I cannot honestly believe that people are running paid ads to these. It's literally burning money down the drain. The only thing you need in your headline is why should I care? I want you to put yourself in the shoes of your user and think, what is that one hard-hitting benefit that makes people think and say, take my money? These are examples of pages where every single headline communicates the end benefit and assuming that this is the only thing I read, I actually have an incentive to go and purchase the product just based on the headlines alone. The best headlines in my experience when doing tons of AB testing for our clients are the headlines in which you can quantify the value in the headline itself. So instead of just saying trusted by happy customers, you could put trusted by 700,000 happy customers, which one do you think is going to be more impactful? For Parcel Safety, we completely redid their landing page and took their headlines, which were just generic, and simply explained who they are and what they do, and took it to a completely different level where every headline communicates that end benefit that somebody can receive. Through this new landing page, we saw an 80% lift in conversions. Same thing for Carolina. We completely revamped their page and took all of their headlines to make them benefit oriented and communicating the benefit in the headline itself. and we saw a 157% increase in conversions. Step number four, avoid overwhelming people with poor visual hierarchy. Have you ever wondered why some websites look super chaotic and confusing to look at while other websites seamlessly and naturally guide you to take action? This is due to a concept called visual hierarchy and it's basically the art of guiding the flow of information to the most important elements down to the least important elements using things like font, size, color, weight, etc. For example, here are some pages that are the exact opposite of what you want to do when it comes to visual hierarchy. Everything screams out to you on the page with all different colors, font, sizing. The irony is that in trying to emphasize everything, they've emphasized nothing at all. Compare that to this example where there's a clear flow of information from top to bottom. And the elements that I actually want to stand out on the page actually do stand out. I always like to use this example when explaining visual hierarchy to clients, right? You can see the distinction between all the different elements based on things like font size, weight, color, etc. A great example of visual hierarchy is prepared hero. You can see as you go from top to bottom, the headline stands out on the page and is bold. The body text has slightly less weight and is subdued. The icons and images are clearly separated. And the button stands out on the page and is prominent. To implement visual hierarchy, you just want to logically think what are the most important things I want to emphasize on the page and then actually do that through things like font, color, weight, etc. Likewise, whatever you want to emphasize less, make sure that those are less prominent on the page. Here's a real life AB test example that we did for parcel safety. The old version of their above the fold had no visual hierarchy. The colors clashed with one another, the messaging was subdued, and there was no clear direction of what action they wanted users to take. Compare that to the after version we designed where there's one large headline that stands out on the page and is bold. The badges are on a gray bar that doesn't compete with the main call to action, which is that red button, and there's just overall a clear flow of information from top to bottom. We ran this as an AB test and we saw a 64% lift in conversions and a 72% increase in the revenue per visitor. Step number five, make the product selection process as simple as possible and don't make people think. So, there are a couple different dimensions and levels to this. The first is when you're presenting your different product bundles. While I love Javi's Coffey's website in general, one of the big mistakes that they make is they don't show people exactly how much they're going to save by going with one product version over the other. You never want to make your users do math, right? Trust me, we've tested this a lot. For Wild Man Drinking, we actually ran an AB test where the before version simply just had the savings as a percentage and in small text hidden in the sub headline. And what we did in the after version was we communicated the exact dollar amount that people would save in the headline itself. We saw a 25% increase in the conversion rate and a 28.5% increase in the revenue per visitor just from this one small change. The other big mistake with Javi Coffey's bundles is they don't show people an image of what the product bundles actually are. If they simply added an image of the three-pack, the fourpack, etc., it would substantially reduce the cognitive load to process the differences between all of the different bundle options because of the fact that people process images a lot faster than tech. If you look at Yeti, they do a great job of this by basically showing people what the product looks like, not only when changing color, but also changing the size itself. We actually did this for Wild Men Drinking by adding images to their bundles where they didn't have it before, and we saw a 32% lift in conversions. It seems really trivial, but all of these small differences make a really big difference, especially when you consider how low people's attention spans are. The next big tactic is to guide your users on what actions they should be taking. One of the most effective ways to do this is to utilize badges. The first place you can do this is on your collection page, right? Simply just highlight which products are new, which are the most popular, and the most critical of all, which is best sellers. Naturally, as humans, we want to buy products that other people are already buying and that are already high in demand. And so, from a new user perspective, I'm going to probably gravitate towards those products first. And it's going to reduce the cognitive load in choosing the right product. The next big area badges can be super effective are on product variance itself. You can see with I restore laser, they have the for faster results badge on the second bundle option which basically adds contextual relevance and gives me an incentive to go and choose that option over the first option. And obviously they know what they're doing because that second option is actually an additional cost which is going to increase their average order value. Another great example is perfect snacks where they have the most popular tag which is going to naturally gravitate me towards that option subconsciously and thus lead me to spending more money which means more revenue for perfect snacks. The final critical thing on your product pages to reduce cognitive load is to give people immediate feedback when something has been added to their cart. Take for example this website which reloads the entire page just to notify me that something's been added which is a completely disruptive process. Compare that to this example where as soon as you add to cart it gives you immediate feedback that something's been added through the form of a sliding cart drawer. But it also gives you the opportunity to upsell and cross-ell people directly in the cart itself. If you look at Perfect Snacks again, they reduced a cognitive load by having the progress bar at the very top to indicate what exactly I need to do in order to unlock higher discounts, which is completely brilliant. Now, if you're wondering how I would go about implementing all the things we talked about in this video, click here for the next one where you can watch me performing real life data analysis on an e-commerce brand, showing you exactly how you can pull these same data and basically identify conversion blockers, how to come up with design ideas and run AB test and drastically improve your conversion rate in just a matter of weeks.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details Craig Clemens' "7 Human Hijacks" for creating category-defining marketing campaigns, emphasizing behavioral change, dramatic demonstrations, and rebellious positioning over standard feature-benefit selling. modules: [ADC, PRD] topics: [copy frameworks, unique mechanism and blue ocean] tier: 2 scope_hint: growth

Topics. copy frameworks / The "7 Human Hijacks": 1) Make it about them (selling the transformation, e.g., "Little Mario vs. Super Mario shooting fireballs"). 2) Make it an event (tapping into "nothing attracts a crowd like a crowd"). 3) Powerful demonstration (e.g., Otis cutting the elevator cable, Dr. Oz popping fat-cell balloons, or cutting a bullet in half with a sword). 4) Unquestionable proof (e.g., 4,500 doctors agreeing on a hearty bacon breakfast, or influencers validating a product). 5) Change a daily behavior (e.g., adding MCT oil to morning coffee, or taking a daily probiotic). 6) Sell the dream (e.g., the "movie star smile" behind the film on your teeth). 7) Help them rebel or feel superior (e.g., "Torches of Freedom" for women smoking, or wearing barefoot shoes to rebel against Nike). unique mechanism and blue ocean / The three stages of market awareness: 1) Clueless (requiring education on the problem first, like explaining the microbiome before selling probiotics), 2) Curious (intercepting existing knowledge, e.g., "Doctor says throw your probiotics in the trash" because they lack enough strains), 3) Saturation (highly commoditized, requiring a strong unique mechanism or personality to break through).

Look for. The "Mario Marketing" analogy: Do not sell the Fireflower (features); sell the customer becoming Super Mario shooting fireballs (the benefit/transformation). The rule for product awareness stages: When the market is "clueless," start with the problem they care about (e.g., digestive issues) before introducing the solution (probiotics). The definition of a "Powerful Demonstration": a dramatic, often exaggerated visual event that proves the product's efficacy so viscerally that it bypasses logical skepticism (e.g., Otis Elevator braking system, Mini Katana sword tests).

Skip. General banter about video backgrounds or the hosts' ages. The specific history of Sigman Freud or Edward Bernays, unless it directly ties to the marketing principles discussed. The detailed political analysis of Donald Trump or Barack Obama's speechwriting, keeping the focus strictly on the underlying marketing mechanics ("soundbites" and "rebellion").

Scope mix. Almost entirely growth.

Volume. 15 to 20.

07-LPG / landing pages and funnels Goes here. A masterclass on the data-driven framework for e-commerce conversion rate optimization (CRO). It covers quantitative analysis (Google Analytics 4, Microsoft Clarity) and qualitative analysis (UserBrain, review mining, surveys) to identify friction points, formulate hypotheses, and execute A/B tests using the PXL prioritization framework. Not here. • Paid social media ad buying or ROAS scaling strategies -> 06-MEA • Automated email marketing flows or deliverability -> 09-EML

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a comprehensive, data-backed methodology for diagnosing e-commerce conversion leaks, providing actionable tutorials on using GA4, heatmaps, and qualitative surveys to form high-impact A/B testing hypotheses. modules: [LPG] topics: [conversion rate optimization, CRO, e-commerce, Google Analytics 4, Microsoft Clarity, UserBrain, heatmaps, A/B testing, user research, PXL framework, visual hierarchy] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. GA4 funnel analysis / utilizing the "Purchase Journey" report in Google Analytics 4 to benchmark drop-offs at key stages (View Product, Add to Cart, Begin Checkout) against e-commerce industry standards; user path exploration / using GA4's "Path Exploration" to map how users navigate between the homepage and collection pages, identifying navigation loops (e.g., Homepage -> Collection -> Homepage) that signal UX friction; GA4 tech overview / segmenting conversion rates and average order value (AOV) by device type (mobile vs. desktop) to uncover hidden UX issues; behavioral analytics with Microsoft Clarity / deploying heatmaps (Area Maps) and scroll maps to discover what elements receive the most clicks (e.g., hidden category filters) and where users drop off (e.g., 60% dropping off before viewing products); identifying friction via session recordings / watching Clarity session recordings to pinpoint UX disconnects, such as users scrolling back and forth between a color selector and the main product image; qualitative surveying / implementing two specific surveys: a post-purchase survey ("What almost stopped you from buying today?") and a mid-session product friction survey triggered at 60% of average session duration; qualitative user testing / using UserBrain to recruit targeted demographics and instruct them to complete specific site tasks (like adding to cart) while speaking their thought process aloud; review mining / exporting product reviews (from Amazon, Trustpilot, etc.) to categorize customer sentiment by motivation, value, and anxiety to feed directly back into landing page copy; the CRO hypothesis framework / structuring A/B test ideas using the formula: "If we do [X], we will generate more [KPI] because [Rationale]"; the PXL prioritization framework / scoring A/B test hypotheses based on impact and effort (e.g., is it above the fold? does it address user testing data?) to systematically prioritize tests with the highest ROI potential.

Look for.

The Post-Purchase Survey: A critical qualitative data gathering tool that asks recent buyers, "Did you have any concerns or doubts that almost stopped you from buying today?" to uncover hidden friction points.

The Mid-Session Friction Survey: A survey specifically timed to fire at 60% of the average session duration, asking active users, "Is there anything holding you back from buying this product right now?"

GA4 Purchase Journey Benchmarks: The specific industry benchmarks used to diagnose funnel leaks: View Product Rate (50-70%), Add to Cart Rate (12-20%), Begin Checkout Rate (40-60%), and Purchase Rate (45-60%).

The PXL Prioritization Framework: A scoring system for ranking A/B test ideas based on binary questions (e.g., Is it above the fold? Is it supported by heatmaps? Is it easy to implement?) to objectively identify high-impact, low-effort CRO tests.

Skip. The intro/outro promotional hooks, plugs for the speaker's free audits and agency services, and repetitive mentions of specific percentage lifts without the full context of the before-and-after tests.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of CRO and GA4 navigation), 85% growth (advanced behavioral analytics, statistical testing frameworks, and qualitative UX research). Volume. ~450 words.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the deep psychological and structural mechanics of writing direct-response advertorials, moving beyond generic AI prompts to explain how to bridge product mechanisms with urgent market trends using visceral metaphors and editorial framing. modules: [ADC] topics: [advertorials, direct response, copywriting, Big Idea, metaphors, copy blocks, awareness levels, massive proof, ChatGPT prompting] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. urgent pain points / prioritizing problems that carry high emotional urgency (e.g., bloating and weight loss over general low energy) to drive immediate direct-response conversions; the Big Idea framework / constructing a unifying marketing angle at the intersection of the unique product features (e.g., chlorophyll dropper), the target prospect's pain, and the current market zeitgeist (e.g., microplastics); intermediary mechanisms / using a bridge concept (like "detox") to link broad, high-urgency health concerns (like fatty liver or blood sugar) back to the specific product mechanism; metaphor specificity / avoiding sloppy or abstract metaphors (like "a mop" for a filter or "a factory" for a liver) in favor of visceral, accurate imagery (like "a sticky hand" or "a clogged filter") that reduces cognitive load; the technology adoption curve / surfing the zeitgeist by adopting emerging mainstream fears (like seed oils or microplastics) while they are in the high-momentum "early/late majority" phase; copy block symphonies / weaving curiosity, proof, and constraints into the opening lead rather than relying solely on generic pain points, ensuring the reader is hooked immediately; avoiding academic and AI copy / identifying and fixing "staccato" AI-generated sentences, overly complex grammar, and presumptuous pain-agitation that lacks conversational rhythm or "permission"; massive proof translation / transforming dry clinical study data into visceral marketing claims (e.g., translating a "0.45 to 0.24 drop" into "slashed by nearly 50%") while leveraging the credibility of the researching institution; advertorial identity / ensuring the copy mimics a specific editorial news format (e.g., breaking news, whistleblower, or discovery story) rather than just reading like a standard Video Sales Letter (VSL).

Look for.

The Big Idea Intersection: The strategy of finding a unique, high-converting angle by overlapping the specific product features, the target prospect's urgent pain, and current market trends (like microplastics).

Symphony of Copy Blocks: The copywriting technique of opening an advertorial by layering curiosity, proof, and constraints, rather than making the amateur mistake of leading purely with generic pain points.

Metaphor Specificity: The rule that marketing metaphors must be extremely precise and easy to visualize (e.g., a "clogged filter" rather than a "slow factory") to prevent cognitive friction for average readers.

Advertorial Identity: The requirement that an advertorial must adopt a recognized journalistic frame (e.g., Warning, Discovery, or Whistleblower) rather than reading like a standard sales pitch.

Skip. Plugs for the creator's "Copy Blocks" training program, mentions of the Genesis AI bot, and the general intro/outro requests for comments and copy submissions.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (basic definitions of advertorials and awareness levels), 90% growth (advanced direct-response theory, mechanism creation, and psychological copywriting rules). Volume. ~450 words.

07-LPG / landing pages and funnels Goes here. A breakdown of a three-pillar framework for building high-converting landing pages: Offer/Copywriting, Design Structure, and Iterative A/B Testing. Covers Voice of Customer research, the PAS (Problem-Agitate-Solve) copywriting framework, and specific layout sections (Hero, Pain Point, Social Proof, Value Props). Not here. • Paid media campaign setup or top-of-funnel traffic generation -> 06-MEA • Automated email marketing flows -> 09-EML

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides a strategic, three-pillar framework for diagnosing and rebuilding underperforming landing pages, detailing how to extract Voice of Customer data and translate it into specific copywriting formulas and visual layouts. modules: [LPG] topics: [landing page design, conversion rate optimization, CRO, copywriting, problem-agitate-solve, above the fold, social proof, A/B testing, user research, Microsoft Clarity] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. diagnosing landing page failures / identifying that simply checking boxes (adding random reviews or generic pain points) without a cohesive, offer-driven strategy results in wasted ad spend; the three-pillar landing page system / outlining the framework: (1) Offer & Copywriting derived from deep research, (2) High-Converting Design built around that copy, and (3) Iterative A/B Testing; Voice of Customer (VoC) research / utilizing Reddit, sales team interviews, and qualitative testing tools (UserBrain) to harvest exact customer phrasing, pain points, and objections before writing a single word of copy; crafting the hero section / using the formula "[End Result] + [Time Period] + [Emotional Payoff]" for the main headline, and the "Stop doing X, no more Y [pain] -> Our solution does Z [benefit]" formula for the sub-headline; reducing FUDs / mitigating Fear, Uncertainty, and Doubt directly beneath the Call to Action button (e.g., "Cancel anytime," "100% Guaranteed") to immediately lower perceived risk; executing the pain point section / utilizing the Problem-Agitate-Solve (PAS) framework for long-form sales letters on complex offers, versus using scannable visual comparisons (e.g., "Old Way vs. New Way") for transformative/visual offers; social proof strategies / abandoning generic "Our Reviews" headers in favor of benefit-driven titles (e.g., "Helping 110,000 members achieve [Dream Outcome]") and utilizing "Walls of Love" that blend video and text testimonials with clear source attribution; feature-to-benefit translation / requiring that all value propositions answer the "So What?" question until the core benefit is reached, and ensuring that benefit is explicitly stated in the section headline (since 80% of users only scan); the necessity of continuous CRO / emphasizing that the landing page that gets a business to $1M will not get them to $10M without continuous iteration using tools like Microsoft Clarity (heatmaps/recordings), Google Analytics, and A/B testing platforms (Intelligems, Go Stellar).

Look for.

The "So What?" Feature-to-Benefit Translation: A copywriting technique that takes a product feature and repeatedly asks "So what?" to drill down to the ultimate customer benefit (e.g., Feature: "Clear reports" -> So what? -> "Make smarter decisions" -> So what? -> Benefit: "Grow your bottom line").

The Problem-Agitate-Solve (PAS) Framework: A copywriting structure for the "Pain Point" section where you identify the struggle, agitate the emotional consequences of that struggle, and then introduce the product as the clear solution.

The "Wall of Love" Social Proof Layout: The design strategy of inundating the user with a dense grid of mixed media (video reviews, text reviews, before/after photos) that clearly displays the verifiable source (e.g., Google, Trustpilot) to instantly build massive credibility.

The Hero Headline Formula: The specific copywriting framework for the main headline: "[End Result] + [Time Period] + [Emotional Payoff]" (e.g., "Get 20/20 Vision in 10 Minutes and Feel Safe").

Skip. Plugs for the creator's swipe file, generic lists of client ROI percentages without strategic context, and the outro teasing the next video.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of landing page sections), 85% growth (advanced copywriting formulas, VoC research techniques, and UX design frameworks). Volume. ~400 words.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the exact structural, psychological, and technical processes required to build high-converting landing pages, including how to use specific software tools (Clarity, UserBrain, Elementor, FigPii) to gather data and deploy A/B tests. modules: [LPG] topics: [conversion rate optimization, landing page design, Microsoft Clarity, A/B testing, UX design, B2B lead generation, above the fold, Elementor, FigPii, user testing] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. the ROI of conversion rate optimization / arguing that doubling conversion rates is vastly superior to doubling traffic because it amplifies the return on all existing ad spend and lowers customer acquisition costs; above the fold structure / defining the essential elements: benefit-driven headline, pain-to-solution sub-headline, stacked social proof, FUD reducers (fear, uncertainty, doubt), and a reinforcing image; traffic-aware sequencing / matching the page layout to the audience's awareness level (e.g., placing the "Pain/Proof" section first for problem-aware Meta Ads traffic, but placing "Social Proof" first for solution-aware Google Ads traffic); data analysis with Microsoft Clarity / a tutorial on using session recordings, scroll maps, and click maps to identify user drop-offs, rage clicks, and ignored CTA buttons, leading to immediate UX fixes like removing navigation bars; qualitative user testing / using UserBrain to recruit targeted demographics to perform specific tasks on the site while narrating their thought process aloud; WordPress and Elementor setup / the technical stack recommendation of using Flywheel for premium hosting and Elementor Pro for flexible, custom landing page development; deploying A/B tests with FigPii / a walkthrough of setting up visual A/B tests (changing headlines via the editor) versus split URL tests (routing traffic 50/50 to completely different page URLs), emphasizing that testing is only viable for sites with over 25,000 monthly visitors.

Look for.

The Microsoft Clarity "Rage Click" Filter: The specific tactic of filtering session recordings for "Rage Clicks" to instantly identify broken UX elements (e.g., users trying to click non-hyperlinked review stars) and fix conversion leaks.

The "Wall of Love" Social Proof Layout: The strategy of combining video testimonials, text reviews, and verifiable platform logos (Google, Trustpilot) into a fully exposed grid, completely avoiding low-engagement carousel sliders.

The 25k Visitor A/B Testing Threshold: The explicit warning that split testing (A/B testing) is mathematically useless for landing pages receiving less than 25,000 to 30,000 visitors a month due to a lack of statistical significance.

Traffic-Aware Layouts: The strategic rule to organize landing page sections based on traffic intent: leading with Problem/Agitate/Solve copy for interruption-based social traffic, but leading directly with Social Proof and forms for high-intent search traffic.

Skip. Plugs for the speaker's agency (Thrilllex), the promotional intro/outro hooks, and the rapid-fire lists of generic client wins.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of landing pages and above the fold), 85% growth (advanced UX analytics with Clarity/UserBrain, technical WordPress/FigPii setup, and traffic-aware CRO frameworks). Volume. ~400 words.

Topics. creative strategy / Deconstructing the architecture of an advertorial funnel, which sits between the prospecting ad and the checkout to pre-sell the consumer through education. Mapping the optimal flow of an advertorial page: Hook/Trust Above the Fold → Skimmable Listicles (e.g., "5 Reasons Why") → Origin Story & Unique Mechanism → Social Proof & Proof Story → Risk Reversals (Guarantees) → The "Two Options" Close. messaging and positioning / Applying direct-response copywriting principles within advertorials by defining the "Unique Mechanism" (e.g., "fear-based feedback technology") that differentiates the product from failed past solutions. Utilizing Tony Robbins' concept of the "pain threshold": recognizing that mild problem agitation is insufficient; copy must aggressively stack pain points (e.g., embarrassment, wasting money on training aids, dreaded slices) until the consumer is emotionally compelled to act. Structuring social proof intentionally so that every testimonial counters a specific buying objection, rather than just providing generic praise.

Look for. The primary use case for an advertorial: a pre-sell landing page that sits between an ad and the checkout to educate and build desire before asking for a sale. The concept of the "pain threshold" in copywriting: people won't take action until their pain exceeds a certain threshold, meaning copy must aggressively stack pain points to motivate a purchase. The definition of a "unique mechanism": the specific, named feature or technology (e.g., "fear-based feedback") that explains why the product works when others have failed. The correct way to structure social proof: each testimonial should systematically dismantle one specific buying objection.

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a call with the speaker's agency or watch their other SOP videos.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 5 to 10.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the psychology and mechanics of high-converting quiz funnels, explaining how to use micro-commitments, psychological seeding, and pre-handled objections to optimize conversion rates for cold traffic. modules: [MEA] topics: [conversion rate optimization] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. conversion rate optimization / Deconstructing the psychological mechanics that make quiz funnels highly effective for converting cold traffic. Explaining that the true value of a quiz funnel is not just product personalization, but the ability to place the customer into an "emotionally primed" or highly suggestible state through a sequence of micro-commitments (clicking "yes" or progressing sliders) before presenting the final offer. Utilizing quizzes to subconsciously "seed" buying beliefs (e.g., reframing a symptom as a severe quality-of-life issue) and proactively handle sales objections (e.g., asking how quickly they expect results to pre-handle the "it takes too long" objection). Establishing a target KPI of a 30% quiz completion rate, and advising against the use of high-friction "input" questions (where users must type an answer) unless deliberately introducing friction to qualify buyers.

Look for. The three core functions every question in a successful quiz funnel must serve: getting a micro-commitment, seeding a belief, or pre-handling an objection. The definition of "seeding" in a quiz funnel: subconsciously influencing the user's beliefs to align with the beliefs required to buy the product. The definition of Eugene Schwartz's "gradualization": starting a quiz with highly non-invasive questions and slowly building up to more invasive or personal questions to prevent drop-off. The target KPI for a successful quiz funnel completion rate: approximately 30%. The reason input questions (typing out an answer) should generally be avoided: they represent a much higher perceived effort than multiple-choice buttons and cause massive drop-off.

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a call with the speaker's agency or access their foundational docs.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 5 to 10.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the structural and copywriting framework for constructing high-AOV, multi-step e-commerce sales funnels, emphasizing the psychological necessity of selling transformational outcomes over product features and maximizing post-purchase profit contribution via one-time offers (OTOs). modules: [LPG] topics: [landing pages, funnel architecture, average order value, conversion rate optimization, sales pages, order bumps, one-time offers, OTOs, copywriting, Voice of Customer, VSSL, TSL] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. funnel architecture / the transition from sending traffic directly to a standard Product Detail Page (PDP) to routing through a dedicated Sales Page, an Order Page, and sequential post-purchase One-Time Offer (OTO) upsell pages; ugly lander theory / the premise that landing page visual aesthetics matter far less than clean copy and frictionless performance, provided conversion rate and AOV are optimized; post-purchase OTO psychology / leveraging the customer's immediate post-transaction emotional peak and high price elasticity to introduce high-margin upsells (e.g., 10x pricing tiers) that drastically increase profit contribution per customer; Voice of Customer (VoC) research / utilizing AI-driven research prompts and foundational documentation (research docs, offer briefs, avatar sheets, and necessary belief lists) to harvest real consumer language from forums and reviews rather than writing through marketer bias; sales page essentials / structuring landing pages around benefit-driven headlines, urgency, scarcity, risk-reversal guarantees, unique mechanisms, embedded social proof, and FAQs; order page friction reduction / prioritizing speed and minimal friction on checkout pages through quantity breaks and checkout order bumps (e.g., shipping insurance or expedited delivery); OTO structures / utilizing Video Sales Letters (VSLs) or Text Sales Letters (TSLs) driven by core product placement strategies, specifically selling "more of the same" or products that "solve one problem and create another."

Look for.

The Funnel Architecture Shift: Moving away from standard PDP-to-checkout flows toward Sales Page -> Order Page -> OTO1 -> OTO2 architectures to capture high-margin post-purchase revenue.

The Price Elasticity OTO Rule: The concept that right after a transaction, customer price elasticity is at its highest, allowing brands to offer high-ticket or multi-unit upsells that scale Average Order Value (AOV) significantly.

The "Ugly Lander" Principle: The core argument that copy clarity, speed, and conversion metrics override aesthetic design—ugly landing pages print money if conversion and AOV are healthy.

Solve One Problem, Create Another: The strategic framework for choosing OTO products where the initial front-end product solves a specific customer pain point while naturally creating a brand-new, adjacent problem that the upsell immediately fixes.

Skip. Plugs for the creator's Instagram DM automation, Brand Builders Academy, and references to exterior YouTube videos on quiz funnels.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (landing page definition and basic conversion metrics), 90% growth (advanced direct-response funnel architecture, post-purchase OTO optimization, and Voice of Customer research). Volume. ~450 words.

11-ADC / ad copy Goes here. A tutorial on using AI (specifically ChatGPT-4.5) to write direct-response advertorials. It covers a five-step framework: deep research, creating foundational documents (avatar sheet, offer brief, necessary beliefs), swiping competitors, AI drafting, and the "chiefing" (editing) process. Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides a highly structured, prompt-engineering blueprint for generating long-form direct-response copy (advertorials) using AI, emphasizing the necessity of feeding the LLM deep qualitative research rather than just asking it to rewrite existing copy. modules: [ADC] topics: [advertorials, copywriting, ChatGPT, deep research, avatar sheet, offer brief, necessary beliefs, AI prompting, direct response, chiefing] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. the fatal flaw in AI copywriting / explaining that simply asking ChatGPT to rewrite a competitor's ad without feeding it foundational research results in terrible, low-converting copy; the five-step advertorial framework / outlining the process: (1) Research via AI, (2) Foundational Docs, (3) Swipe an existing competitor, (4) Write the advertorial, and (5) Chief (edit) the copy; feeding context to AI / demonstrating how to convert a brand's sales page into a PDF and upload it to ChatGPT to ground the AI in specific product details before prompting; ChatGPT's Deep Research feature / using AI to write its own deep research prompt to crawl the web for customer pain points, generating a massive qualitative research document in 10-15 minutes; building foundational documents / turning the raw research into three specific PDFs: an Avatar Sheet (demographics, pain points, direct quotes), an Offer Brief (funnel architecture, stage of awareness, unique mechanism), and a Necessary Beliefs doc (the specific mindset shifts required for a customer to buy); swiping and drafting / uploading a successful competitor's advertorial as a structural reference (the "swipe"), and prompting the AI to write the new advertorial in chunks (first half, then second half) to bypass token limits and ensure high quality; the slippery slide principle / referencing the copywriting rule that copy must flow so naturally that the reader slides down it without friction; the AI "chiefing" process / uploading the final drafted advertorial back into ChatGPT to evaluate it against the foundational documents, ensuring it hits all necessary beliefs, unique mechanisms, and objection handling before human editing.

Look for.

The Deep Research AI Inception: The specific prompt-engineering tactic where you ask ChatGPT to write the prompt that will be used to trigger its own "Deep Research" feature, ensuring the most comprehensive data scrape possible.

Token Limit Chunking: The rule that you must never ask an LLM to write a full 2,000-word advertorial in one prompt due to token limits drastically lowering the output quality; always prompt it to write the "first half," review it, and then prompt the "second half."

The Slippery Slide Copywriting Principle: The editorial benchmark that copy must flow so naturally and logically that the prospect slides from the headline to the Call to Action without hitting any "bumps" (illogical phrasing or friction).

The Necessary Beliefs Document: A foundational copywriting asset outlining a maximum of six specific beliefs a prospect must hold to positively buy the product (e.g., "I believe my current method is inefficient").

Skip. Plugs for the creator's swipe file, generic rants about why ChatGPT is better than Claude, and mentions of specific product details (e.g., the space heater example) that don't serve the broader prompt-engineering lesson.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of advertorials), 85% growth (advanced AI prompt engineering, qualitative research methodologies, and direct-response copywriting frameworks). Volume. ~400 words.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides a purely statistical and financial business case for speed optimization, defining baseline benchmarks for Core Web Vitals (TTFB, FID, FCP) and quantifying the revenue impact of slow load times and peak-traffic brownouts. modules: [SPD] topics: [core web vitals, benchmarks] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. benchmarks / The financial and behavioral impact of site speed: a 1-second reduction in load time increases conversion rates by 5.6% and decreases bounce rates by nearly 12%. The "3-Second Rule": 40% of shoppers abandon a site if it takes more than 3 seconds to load. Recognizing the disparity between desktop and mobile performance, where mobile sites take 87.8% longer to load on average despite mobile comprising 59% of all web traffic. core web vitals / Understanding Google's recommended thresholds for specific speed metrics. Time to First Byte (TTFB): the time taken for the first byte of HTML to respond (benchmark: under 800ms). First Input Delay (FID): the time from a user's first interaction to the browser's response (benchmark: under 100ms). First Contentful Paint (FCP): the time taken for a page to load enough readable content (benchmark: under 1.8 seconds). traffic management / Diagnosing "IT brownouts"—severe traffic-induced slowdowns or dynamic area errors (like cart or checkout failures) that occur during high-traffic events, rather than complete site crashes. Mitigating brownouts using virtual waiting rooms, as 87% of consumers prefer a short queue over a buggy, slow site.

Look for. The specific benchmark for TTFB: 800 milliseconds or less. The specific benchmark for FID: 100 milliseconds or less. The specific benchmark for FCP: 1.8 seconds or less. The definition of an IT brownout: a slowdown or error occurring in dynamic areas of the site (cart, login) caused by high traffic spikes. The exact conversion rate impact of a 1-second load time improvement: 5.6%.

Skip. The hypothetical math scenario calculating an extra $1.8 million to $5.5 million in revenue based on arbitrary 50,000 daily visitor metrics. The specific survey percentages of what marketers are currently prioritizing (e.g., "57% say they’ve optimized images"), as they represent survey opinions rather than operational frameworks.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 10 to 15.

When it comes to ecommerce speed, time really is moneyA slow site loses you sales, loyalty, and visibility. It wastes marketing spend and drives customers to competitors.

But few marketers see site speed as the priority it is. Most changes to ecommerce websites add fancy new animations and features that make pages slower, not faster.

That’s why we’ve scoured the web and found 93 powerful statistics that speak to the importance of ecommerce site speed. Get the concrete numbers you need to prove to your team just how crucial site speed is.

Table of contents

Why is site speed important?

Ecommerce site speed statistics

How page speed boosts ecommerce revenue

Ecommerce page load time benchmarks

The importance of website speed for mobile

Website load time statistics

Page load time breakdown

Marketers' perspectives on page load speed

How high traffic can slow down your site

Why is site speed important?

1. 40% of shoppers won’t wait more than 3 seconds before abandoning an ecommerce site.

2. 80% of users said a slow loading website is more frustrating than a temporarily down website.

3. Stress levels increase by 33% when content takes more than 6 seconds to load, the equivalent of a math test or watching a horror movie.

4. Almost 70% of consumers say page speed impacts their willingness to buy from an online retailer.

5. Half of online users surveyed say they’d prefer to miss out on animation and video if it meant getting faster load times.

6. Sites that appear on the first page of Google search results take an average 1.96 seconds to load. This means the better your speed, the better your Google ranking.

7. 83% of people expect websites to load in 3 seconds or less.

8. 73% of consumers would likely try an alternative site if the one they were on was too slow.

When an ecommerce page loads slowly:

9. Almost 50% of shoppers say they’ll try to refresh the page at least once.

10. 22% of shoppers say they’ll close the tab.

11. 14% say they’ll visit a competitor’s site.

12. 64% of online shoppers will shop elsewhere if they have a poor user experience.

13. 44% of online shoppers share negative online experiences with others.

14. 1 in 3 consumers say they’ll leave a brand they love after just one bad experience.

15. 65% of consumers trust a business less when they experience a problem.

RELATED: Boost Your Customer Experience with These 9 CX Tips & Tricks

Ecommerce site speed stats

16. A 1 second reduction in load time results in a conversion rate increase of 5.6%.

17. A site that loads in 1 second has a conversion rate 5x higher than one that loads in 10 seconds.

18. A 1 second reduction in load time decreases bounce rates by nearly 12%.

19. If an ecommerce site takes more than 4 seconds to load, 63% of shoppers will bounce.

20. If your ecommerce site takes 6 seconds to load, 2 out of 3 shoppers will leave.

21. Shoppers visit 8.9 pages when load time is 2 seconds, versus just 3.3 pages when load time is 8 seconds.

22. A 0.1 second improvement in mobile site speed increases retail conversions by 8.4%.

23. 9.1% more shoppers added items to their basket when mobile site speed increased by just 0.1 seconds.

When a page loads slowly:

24. 45.4% of shoppers are less likely to make a purchase

25. 36.8% of shoppers are less likely to return.

26. 11.9% are likely to tell a friend.

RELATED: 79 Staggering Statistics That Show the Power of Loyalty Programs

How page speed boosts ecommerce revenue

Let’s say your ecommerce site has 50,000 daily visitors, a conversion rate of 3.5%, and an average order value of $50. Your average page loads in 6 seconds.

That would give you 1,750 orders per day and a daily revenue of $87,500.

Now, if we improve your average page speed by 1 second, your conversion rate jumps to 3.7%.

Suddenly your daily orders are 1,850 and your daily revenue is $92,500.

Fast forward one year, and that 1 second improvement has made you an extra $1.8 million.

Get your site down to Google’s recommended 3 second load time, and you’ll have an extra $5.5 million a year later.

And that’s just based on conversion rates. It doesn’t include the improvements to Google rankings, customer loyalty, and word-of-mouth marketing.

Ecommerce page load time benchmarks

27. Google’s recommended mobile page load time is 3 seconds, but the faster the better.

28. U.S. retail sites take an average of 6.3 seconds to load on mobile, more than twice Google’s benchmark.

29. In the U.K., ecommerce sites take a slightly better 6 seconds to load.

30. 86% of ecommerce sites load in 5 seconds or less on desktop.

31. The average web page load time of the top 100 websites worldwide is 2.5 seconds on desktop.

32. On mobile, the top 100 sites take an average of 8.6 seconds to load.

33. The highest ecommerce conversion rates (an average of 3.05%) occur on pages that load in 1 or 2 seconds.

34. The average unoptimized product detail page (PDP) takes 6.1 seconds to load.

35. Optimized PDPs load a full 2 seconds faster than unoptimized PDPs, taking 4.1 seconds to load.

36. PDPs and category pages make up 72% of all page views during the shopper journey.

37. Retail sites have the highest average pages per session out of any industry, with 5.01 pages per session on desktop.

38. This means optimized sites save buyers 23 seconds per shopper journey.

Importance of website speed for mobile

39. Traffic from mobile devices makes up 59% of all web traffic.

40. The average webpage takes 87.8% longer to load on mobile than on desktop.

41. Decreasing mobile page load speed by 1 second improves conversion rates by 5.9%.

42. That same 1 second improvement decreases bounce rate by nearly 9%.

43. 46% of people say waiting for pages to load is what they dislike most about browsing the web on mobile.

44. 85% of mobile users expect pages to load as fast or faster than they do on desktop—which almost never happens.

45. 64% of mobile users expect pages to load in under four seconds.

46. 53% of mobile visitors will leave a page if it takes more than 3 seconds to load.

47. 74% of mobile users say they’d abandon mobile sites that don’t load within 5 seconds.

48. Mobile users have an average bounce rate of 56.8%, compared to the average desktop bounce rate of 50%.

49. The average website takes around 15 seconds to load on mobile.

50. 95% of mobile users said they’d return to a fast site, compared to just 62% for a slow site.

51. 73% of mobile users have encountered websites they consider too slow.

Website load time statistics

52. When page load times goes from 1 to 3 seconds, the chance of a bounce increases by 32%.

53. When it goes from 1 to 5 seconds, the chance of bouncing jumps 90%.

54. If a site jumps from 1 to 10 seconds to load, the chance of a bounce increases 123%.

55. Pages that load in under 2 seconds have an average bounce rate of 9%.

56. Pages that take 5 seconds to load have an average bounce rate of 38%.

57. When load time is 2 seconds, users visit an average of 8.9 pages.

58. When load time is 8 seconds, they visit just 3.3 pages.

59. Large pages take 318% longer to visually load compared to small pages.

60. Every third-party script on a site adds an average of 34.1 milliseconds to load time.

61. 25% of pages could save more than 250kb simply by compressing images and text.

62. 10% of pages could save more than 1mb by compressing images and text.

63. For every extra second of load time, the BBC loses 10% of its users.

64. When Yahoo! sped up its page load time by just 0.4 seconds, traffic increased by 9%.

Page load time breakdown

These next stats break down some of the specific measures that make up page load speed. They get a bit into the weeds and technical terms, so we’ll pair the stats with some basic definitions.

Fully Loaded: The time it takes for a site to display as 100% loaded and usable.

65. The average time it takes fully load a webpage is 10.3 seconds on desktop.

66. On mobile, the average time is a massive 27.3 seconds.

Time to First Byte (TTFB): The time it takes for the first byte of HTML to respond.

67. The average Time to First Byte (TTFB) speed is 1.286 seconds on desktop.

68. On mobile, TTFB averages 2.594 seconds.

69. Google recommends a TTFB speed of 800ms or less.

First Input Delay (FID): The time it takes from when a user first interacts with your site (when they click a link or hover over an interactive feature) to when the browser responds.

70. The average First Input Delay (FID) speed is 12.73 milliseconds on desktop.

71. On mobile, FID speed averages 59.73 milliseconds.

72. Google recommends an FID score of 100 milliseconds or less.

First Contentful Paint (FCP): The time it takes for a page to load enough for a user to be able to read the content on the page.

73. Google recommends your FCP should appear in 1.8 seconds or less.

Optimizing the Queue-it home page got our FCP down to 0.8 seconds. You can check your own score on Google’s PageSpeed Insights tool.

Marketers' perspectives on page load speed

74. 81% of marketers know speed impacts conversions, but don’t prioritize optimization.

75. Only 3% of marketers say faster load speed is their top priority.

76. But 73% of marketers think improving page speed is somewhat or very urgent.

How are marketers improving page speed?

77. 57% say they’ve optimized images, videos, or other media files.

78. 43% have implemented backend fixes like caching.

79. 39% have run speed tests.

80. 38% have reduced their dependence on JavaScript and CSS.

81. 22% implemented Accelerated Mobile Pages.

82. 14% began using a Content Delivery Network.

RELATED: Optimize Your Website Performance with These 11 Expert Tips

How high traffic can slow down your site

Everyone knows high traffic can crash your site. But few know that it can also cause slowdowns and errors.

The traffic-induced slowdown is sometimes called an IT brownout. A brownout typically results in slow load times or errors on dynamic areas of your site—such as when customers add items to cart, use site search, or log in.

During Black Friday, for instance, Pet Smart’s load speed almost doubled, jumping from 7.7 seconds to 13.84 seconds.

RELATED: How High Online Traffic Can Crash Your Site

Brownouts and traffic-induced slowdowns like these are more common than you’d think:

83. 50% of ecommerce consumers have experienced slowdowns during “high-traffic” occasions.

84. 82% of those who experienced slowdowns reported being unable to access their target website because of this.

85. 97% of enterprises experienced an IT brownout in the past three years.

86. The average number of brownouts for enterprises is 19 per year.

RELATED: The Cost of Downtime: IT Outages, Brownouts & Your Bottom Line

87. Costs are up to 16x higher for companies that have frequent outages and brownouts compared with companies who have fewer instances of downtime.

88. 53% of IT professionals think their company will experience a brownout or outage so severe that it makes national media headlines.

89. 31% of IT professionals say they have experienced brand/reputation damage due to IT brownouts.

90. 30% said brownouts and outages lowered their stock price.

A recent survey found that consumers prefer to wait in a virtual waiting room for a reliable online experience:

91. 87% prefer a short wait for a reliable site over instant access to a slow or buggy one92. 84% would rather queue than face a crash or error page93. Consumers are willing to wait in an online queue for an average of 53 minutes for limited-inventory sales
