Ecommerce Site Speed Optimization: Complete Guide for 2026

Learn how a 0.1-second improvement can boost conversions by up to 8.4%. Complete guide to Core Web Vitals, image optimization, caching, CDN, and hosting for ecommerce stores.

25 min read

Published March 25, 2026

A 0.1-second improvement in page load time can increase retail conversions by up to 8.4%, according to Google and NitroPack research. For ecommerce stores, this translates directly to revenue. Yet most online stores still load slower than customers expect.

This guide covers the technical and strategic aspects of ecommerce site speed optimization. You'll learn why speed matters for both conversions and SEO, what slows down online stores, and how to fix the most common performance issues. The focus is on practical solutions for Shopify, WooCommerce, and other major platforms.

Where to Start: The Speed Fix Priority Ladder

If you can only tackle three things, focus on these in order:

Images first - Compress and convert to WebP. This single change often cuts page weight by 40-60% with minimal effort.

Third-party scripts second - Audit installed apps and remove what you don't actively use. Each unnecessary script competes for browser resources.

Hosting and CDN third - If you're still on shared hosting with meaningful traffic, upgrade. Add a CDN if you serve customers across multiple regions.

Everything else in this guide builds on these three foundations. Get them right before optimizing JavaScript bundles or fine-tuning cache headers.

For a prioritized checklist of what to tackle first in 2026, including current Core Web Vitals benchmarks and real store case studies, see ecommerce site speed best practices for 2026. For Shopify stores specifically, our Shopify audit checklist covers speed alongside 27 other SEO, UX, trust, and CRO checks, and the comprehensive Shopify speed audit walks through 8 platform-specific issues with detection criteria before you reach the fixes in this guide.

Why Site Speed Matters for Ecommerce

If you're wondering why your ecommerce website is slow, you're not alone. Most store owners notice the symptoms, such as high bounce rates, abandoned carts, and declining organic traffic, before identifying speed as the cause.

Speed affects every metric that matters to online stores. Customers abandon slow sites, search engines rank fast sites higher, and the gap between winners and losers continues to widen.

The Conversion Connection

The relationship between page speed and conversions is well-documented. Cloudflare reports that stores can lose around 4% in conversions for every 2 seconds of load time. Put differently, a site that loads in one second converts roughly five times more visitors than one that loads in ten seconds.

Mobile performance matters even more. Google's research shows that approximately 53% of mobile visitors abandon sites that take longer than three seconds to load. With mobile traffic now accounting for the majority of ecommerce visits, this represents a substantial revenue leak.

Real-World Results

When companies invest in speed, results follow. Vodafone ran an A/B test and found that a 31% improvement in their Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) metric led to a 15% improvement in lead-to-visit rate and 8% more sales. Rakuten 24's case study shows even more dramatic results: after optimizing Core Web Vitals, they achieved a 33% increase in conversion rate and 53% improvement in revenue per visitor.

These aren't outliers. Around 70% of consumers say page speed affects their decision to buy from a website. Industry research consistently shows that customers expect pages to load in under three seconds, with many abandoning sites that fail to meet this threshold.

The Bounce Rate Problem

Slow sites bleed traffic before customers even see your products. If an ecommerce site takes more than four seconds to load, around 63% of shoppers will leave, per Queue-it statistics. These visitors rarely return. They simply find a faster competitor.

Mobile Performance Gap

Mobile ecommerce traffic now exceeds desktop for most stores, yet mobile sites consistently perform worse. Smaller screens hide some issues, but slower processors and variable network conditions amplify others.

A slow mobile site loses more than half its potential customers before they even start shopping. The three-second threshold that matters on desktop becomes even more critical on mobile, where users are often multitasking or dealing with spotty connections.

Test your mobile performance separately from desktop. Use PageSpeed Insights to see real mobile user data, and test on actual devices rather than just browser emulation. What feels acceptable on a development machine often frustrates real customers on mid-range phones.

How Google Measures Site Speed

Google uses Core Web Vitals as part of its ranking algorithm. While content relevance remains the primary factor, Core Web Vitals serve as a tie-breaker between pages with similar quality. Understanding these metrics helps prioritize optimization efforts.

Lighthouse vs PageSpeed Insights: What's the Difference?

Both tools use the same Lighthouse engine under the hood, which can cause confusion. The key difference is data source.

Lighthouse (available in Chrome DevTools or as CLI) runs a simulated test on your machine. It measures how your site performs in a controlled environment with throttled CPU and network speed.

PageSpeed Insights runs Lighthouse tests but adds real user data from the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX). This shows how actual visitors experience your site over the past 28 days.

For a detailed breakdown of how to interpret your Lighthouse report, see the guide to reading Lighthouse reports.

For optimization decisions, focus on the metrics rather than the tools. Both report the same Core Web Vitals. PageSpeed Insights simply provides additional context from real users.

Speed is one ranking signal. To check the on-page SEO side at the same time, the free ecommerce SEO audit reviews indexability, meta tags, and structured data alongside Core Web Vitals on a page you enter.

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)

LCP measures how quickly the largest visible element on your page loads. For product pages, this is often the main product image. For category pages, it might be the hero banner or the first visible product grid.

The target threshold is under 2.5 seconds. Pages that exceed 4 seconds receive a "poor" rating from Google. Most ecommerce sites struggle with LCP because of unoptimized images and slow server response times.

Interaction to Next Paint (INP)

INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) as a Core Web Vital metric. It measures how quickly your site responds when visitors interact with it. This includes clicking buttons, tapping links, and using filters on category pages.

The target is under 200 milliseconds. Ecommerce sites often fail INP because of heavy JavaScript from apps, plugins, and tracking scripts. When a customer clicks "Add to Cart" and nothing happens for half a second, they wonder if the click registered.

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)

CLS measures visual stability. When page elements shift around while loading, visitors accidentally click the wrong thing or lose their place. This frustrates users and damages trust.

The target is under 0.1. Common CLS culprits on ecommerce sites include late-loading images without defined dimensions, dynamically injected content like cookie banners, and font loading that causes text to reflow.

The SEO Connection

According to HTTP Archive data, approximately 50% of mobile sites pass the Core Web Vitals assessment, meaning half still fail to meet Google's thresholds. Google uses mobile-first indexing, meaning your mobile performance determines your ranking potential.

For competitive keywords where multiple pages offer similar content quality, better Core Web Vitals scores can push you above competitors. This "tie-breaker" effect makes speed optimization a genuine SEO advantage.

Check your store's real speed score

1350+ stores audited

Run Free AuditNo credit card needed

What Slows Down Ecommerce Websites

Before optimizing, identify what's actually causing slowdowns. Most performance issues fall into a few common categories.

The Biggest Culprits

Unoptimized images cause more speed problems than anything else. Product photos, category banners, and promotional graphics are often uploaded at full resolution without compression. A single uncompressed hero image can exceed 2MB, longer than some customers are willing to wait.

Too many apps and plugins accumulate over time. Each app adds JavaScript that runs on every page load. A store with 30 apps might have 30 separate scripts competing for resources. Removing unnecessary third-party tools often delivers noticeable speed improvements. In our Shopify Speed Benchmark 2026, the correlation between third-party service count and performance score was r = -0.66, the strongest signal in the dataset. See our detailed third-party impact analysis for blocking time data per service and a step-by-step audit guide.

Industries with heavier app stacks feel this more acutely. Beauty stores load a median of 31 third-party services per page and rank last among 9 Shopify industries for mobile speed. Automotive parts stores, by contrast, load a median of 15 and rank first. Fashion & Apparel stores fall in between, with return-prevention tools like sizing charts and shipping insurance adding a performance layer unique to the category.

Excessive JavaScript and CSS from themes, page builders, and customizations bloat page size. Unminified code contains comments, whitespace, and formatting that browsers don't need. Minification alone can reduce JavaScript file sizes by up to 80%.

Platform-Specific Issues

Shopify stores often slow down from app overload. The platform handles hosting and basic optimization, but apps bypass these optimizations. Review apps, upsell popups, and analytics tools each add their own scripts. Product pages are especially affected because they load PDP-specific functionality (variant selectors, review widgets, BNPL calculators) that other page types don't need. See our product page speed analysis for per-page-type benchmark data.

WooCommerce sites face different challenges. Shared hosting, unoptimized databases, and plugin conflicts create bottlenecks. WordPress flexibility becomes a liability when every feature requires another plugin.

Gradual Degradation

Performance problems rarely appear suddenly. More products get added. More apps get installed. More tracking scripts get layered on. Without monitoring, stores gradually slow down until customers start complaining or conversions drop noticeably.

Which Pages Matter Most for Speed

Not all pages affect conversions equally. Prioritize optimization based on traffic volume and conversion impact.

Homepage Speed

Your homepage creates the first impression. Visitors decide within seconds whether to stay or leave. A slow homepage loses potential customers before they see a single product.

Homepage LCP is critical because it's often the entry point for brand searches and direct traffic. Large hero images, rotating carousels, and promotional banners frequently cause problems here.

Product Page Performance

Product pages convert browsers into buyers. Every delay between clicking a product and seeing its details increases the chance of abandonment.

The main product image drives LCP on these pages. Customer reviews, related products, and variant selectors add JavaScript that affects INP. Keep product pages lean by loading secondary content only after the primary image and buy button render.

Category Page Challenges

Category pages display many products simultaneously. Each thumbnail needs to load, filters need to respond quickly, and pagination must work smoothly.

Lazy loading is essential for category pages. Load visible products immediately but defer images below the fold. Implement responsive images that serve appropriately sized thumbnails rather than full-resolution photos.

Checkout Speed

Slow checkout pages directly cause abandoned carts. When customers have decided to buy, any friction pushes them toward competitors.

Payment gateway integrations, address verification, and fraud detection scripts all add load time. Cart calculations need to feel instant. Test checkout flows specifically, as overall site speed scores don't capture the full checkout experience.

Image Optimization for Product Pages

Images account for most page weight on ecommerce sites. Optimizing them delivers the biggest speed gains for the least technical effort.

Modern Image Formats

WebP format offers approximately 25-35% smaller file sizes than JPEG at equivalent visual quality. All modern browsers support WebP, making it the recommended default for web images. AVIF offers even better compression but has narrower browser support.

Keep original images in JPEG or PNG formats. Use build tools or CDN services to automatically convert and serve WebP or AVIF to supported browsers, with fallbacks for older browsers.

Compression Guidelines

Target file sizes under 100KB for product images and under 200KB for hero banners. Tools like Squoosh, TinyPNG, and ShortPixel compress images while preserving visual quality. Most visitors can't perceive quality differences after intelligent compression.

For product photography, 80% JPEG quality typically balances file size and appearance well. Avoid compressing images multiple times, as quality degrades with each pass.

Lazy Loading Implementation

Lazy loading defers image loading until visitors scroll near them. This reduces initial page load time and saves bandwidth for images visitors never see.

Modern browsers support lazy loading natively with the loading="lazy" attribute on image tags. Shopify, WooCommerce, and most platforms handle this automatically for product grids.

One exception: never lazy load images that appear above the fold. The hero image and first visible products should load immediately. Lazy loading above-the-fold content actually hurts LCP scores.

CDN-Based Image Optimization

Content Delivery Networks like Cloudflare, Imgix, and Cloudinary offer automatic image optimization. They resize images based on visitor device size, convert formats automatically, and serve from edge locations near visitors.

For stores with thousands of product images, CDN-based optimization saves hours of manual work. The slight monthly cost typically pays for itself in improved conversions.

JavaScript and CSS Performance

Code optimization requires more technical knowledge but delivers substantial speed improvements, especially for stores with heavy customization.

Minification Basics

Minification strips unnecessary characters from code. Whitespace, comments, and long variable names get removed or shortened. Research indicates minification can shrink JavaScript files by up to 80%.

Popular minification tools include Terser for JavaScript and CSSNano for stylesheets. Most modern build tools (Webpack, Vite, Parcel) minify automatically in production mode.

For Shopify stores, minification typically requires apps like Hyperspeed or TinyIMG. WooCommerce stores can use plugins like Autoptimize or WP Rocket.

Code Splitting Strategies

Code splitting breaks large JavaScript bundles into smaller chunks that load on demand. Instead of loading all site functionality on every page, visitors only download what they need.

Product pages don't need checkout code. Category pages don't need product zoom functionality. Splitting code by page type reduces initial load time for every visitor.

Modern frameworks like Next.js, Nuxt, and Gatsby handle code splitting automatically. For traditional themes, manual configuration through Webpack's dynamic import feature achieves similar results.

Critical CSS

Critical CSS extracts styles needed for above-the-fold content and inlines them directly in the HTML. This eliminates the render-blocking effect of external stylesheet requests.

The rest of the CSS loads asynchronously after the initial render. Visitors see a fully-styled page faster, improving perceived performance and LCP scores.

Tools like Critical and PurgeCSS automate this process. WP Rocket and other WordPress caching plugins offer built-in critical CSS generation.

Third-Party Script Management

Analytics, chat widgets, review systems, and marketing tools each add scripts that compete for browser resources. Audit your third-party scripts regularly. Remove tools you no longer use actively. Ecomhint data from 1,533 Shopify stores shows that stores with 0-5 third-party services score a median 74 on mobile, while stores with 21-30 services drop to 44 (full industry breakdown).

For necessary scripts, consider deferring or async loading. Scripts that don't affect initial page rendering can load after the main content. This improves INP scores by reducing JavaScript execution during page load.

Caching Strategies for Ecommerce

Caching stores copies of content to serve visitors faster on repeat requests. Effective caching reduces server load and improves response times dramatically.

Browser Caching

Browser caching instructs visitor browsers to store files locally. When someone returns to your store or navigates to a second page, their browser loads cached files instantly instead of downloading again.

Set appropriate cache durations through HTTP headers. Static assets like images, CSS, and JavaScript can cache for a year since filenames change when content updates. HTML pages need shorter durations to ensure visitors see current content.

CDN Edge Caching

CDN edge caching stores content at servers distributed globally. A visitor in Tokyo receives files from an Asian edge server instead of waiting for data from a US origin server.

Cloudflare explains that effective CDN caching reduces latency by 200-800ms for geographically distant visitors. For stores with international customers, this improvement matters substantially.

Configure your CDN to cache static assets aggressively. Set shorter TTL (time-to-live) values for pages with dynamic content like prices or stock levels.

Server-Side Caching

Server-side caching stores generated HTML pages or database query results. Instead of building each page from scratch for every visitor, servers return cached versions.

For WooCommerce, plugins like WP Rocket, W3 Total Cache, or Redis Object Cache handle server-side caching. Shopify manages server caching automatically but provides limited control.

What Not to Cache

Ecommerce has unique caching challenges. Cart pages, checkout flows, and account pages must never be cached because they contain visitor-specific data.

Session cookies complicate caching further. Salesforce documentation recommends deferring session creation until visitors actually need it, typically at first add-to-cart or login. This keeps anonymous browsing cacheable.

Product prices and stock status need careful handling. Cache pages but update these elements dynamically via JavaScript, or use short cache durations with rapid invalidation when data changes.

CDN Implementation Guide

A Content Delivery Network distributes your content across servers worldwide. Proper configuration maximizes the performance benefits.

How CDNs Work

When a visitor requests your site, the CDN routes them to the nearest edge server. That server either returns cached content instantly or fetches fresh content from your origin server.

The first visitor from each region experiences normal load times. Subsequent visitors receive cached content with dramatically lower latency. For stores with traffic from multiple regions, CDNs provide substantial speed improvements.

Choosing a CDN

Major CDN providers include Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, AWS CloudFront, and BunnyCDN. Most offer free tiers or affordable entry-level plans suitable for small and medium stores.

Evaluate based on your traffic geography. If most customers are in one region, a basic CDN suffices. Global stores benefit from providers with extensive edge networks.

Also consider additional features. Cloudflare includes DDoS protection and image optimization. Fastly offers advanced edge computing capabilities. BunnyCDN provides competitive pricing for high-bandwidth stores.

Configuration Best Practices

Start with static assets: images, CSS, JavaScript, and fonts. These files change infrequently and benefit most from caching.

Configure cache keys carefully. Include query parameters that affect content (like page numbers) but exclude tracking parameters that create unnecessary cache fragmentation.

Set up automatic cache invalidation. When you update a product image or deploy new code, outdated cached versions should clear immediately. Most CDNs offer API-based purging or URL-based invalidation.

Monitor cache hit rates. A well-configured CDN should serve 80%+ of requests from cache. Low hit rates indicate configuration problems or excessive dynamic content.

See exactly what's slowing your store down

1350+ stores audited

Run Free AuditNo credit card needed

Hosting: From Shared to Cloud

Hosting infrastructure affects speed more than many store owners realize. The cheapest option often costs more in lost sales than the price difference.

Shared Hosting Limitations

Shared hosting places multiple websites on the same server, sharing CPU, memory, and bandwidth. When neighboring sites experience traffic spikes, your store slows down.

Shared hosting costs approximately $1-15 per month, making it attractive for new stores. However, BlueHost documentation notes that resource limitations make shared hosting unsuitable for stores with meaningful traffic.

VPS as Middle Ground

Virtual Private Servers provide dedicated resources within a shared physical server. Your store gets guaranteed CPU and memory regardless of neighboring activity.

VPS hosting starts around $20-50 monthly for managed options. This level suits growing stores that have outgrown shared hosting but don't need dedicated hardware.

The setup complexity exceeds shared hosting. Managed VPS providers handle server administration, while unmanaged options require technical expertise.

Cloud Hosting Advantages

Cloud hosting distributes your site across multiple servers with automatic scaling. Traffic spikes get absorbed without performance degradation.

Hostimul analysis explains that cloud environments integrate better with load balancing and handle growth without manual server upgrades.

Major cloud platforms include AWS, Google Cloud, DigitalOcean, and platform-specific solutions like Shopify's infrastructure or managed WooCommerce hosts like Kinsta.

Recommendations by Store Size

New stores with minimal traffic can start on shared hosting temporarily. Plan to upgrade within the first year of growth.

Stores processing 100+ orders monthly should use VPS or cloud hosting. The improved reliability and speed pay for themselves in reduced cart abandonment.

High-volume stores benefit from cloud infrastructure with auto-scaling. Peak traffic during sales or promotions gets handled automatically without pre-provisioning extra capacity.

Speed Testing and Monitoring

Testing reveals what needs fixing. Ongoing monitoring catches degradation before it affects customers.

Ecomhint Store Speed Test

The Ecomhint store speed test runs a Lighthouse-based performance audit and presents mobile and desktop scores with ecommerce-specific context — telling you not just the number but what it means for conversions. Useful as a starting point before a deeper investigation with PageSpeed Insights or GTmetrix.

PageSpeed Insights

Google PageSpeed Insights combines lab data with real user metrics from the Chrome User Experience Report. It tests both mobile and desktop performance, providing scores and specific recommendations.

A score of 90+ indicates good performance. Scores between 50-89 need improvement. Below 50 signals serious problems requiring immediate attention.

Pay attention to Core Web Vitals metrics shown prominently. The recommendations section lists specific issues in priority order.

GTmetrix Deep Dive

GTmetrix provides more detailed analysis than PageSpeed Insights. The waterfall chart shows exactly which resources load when and how long each takes.

Create a free account to test from different locations and connection speeds. This reveals how international customers or mobile users experience your site differently.

Focus on the "Top Issues" section first. GTmetrix highlights the changes that will have the most impact.

WebPageTest for Advanced Analysis

WebPageTest offers the most detailed testing available. Run tests from specific locations, on specific device types, over specific connection speeds.

The filmstrip view shows visual progress at each stage of loading. The connection view reveals server response times and resource loading sequences.

WebPageTest requires more interpretation than simpler tools. It's most useful for diagnosing specific issues rather than general monitoring.

Setting Up Monitoring

Don't rely on occasional manual tests. Set up automated monitoring to track performance over time.

Free options include PageSpeed Insights API with scheduled runs, GTmetrix monitoring (with account), or Lighthouse CI for automated testing during deployments.

Paid services like DebugBear, SpeedCurve, and Calibre provide more detailed tracking, alerting, and historical analysis. For stores where speed directly affects revenue, these investments typically pay off.

Common Speed Mistakes to Avoid

Understanding what goes wrong helps prevent problems before they occur.

Uploading Unoptimized Images

The most common mistake is uploading product photos directly from a camera or design tool. A 4000x3000 pixel image at full quality can exceed 5MB. Resize to actual display dimensions and compress before uploading.

Installing Apps Without Speed Audits

Each app adds code that runs on every page. Before installing, check reviews for speed complaints. After installing, test page speed to measure impact. Remove apps that degrade performance without providing proportional value.

Ignoring Mobile Performance

Desktop tests don't reflect mobile experience. Mobile devices have less processing power and often slower connections. Test mobile performance specifically and prioritize mobile optimizations.

Misconfiguring Caching

Caching configuration errors cause either stale content or missed optimization opportunities. Too-aggressive caching serves outdated prices or stock status. Too-conservative caching fails to provide speed benefits.

Audit cache headers after changes. Verify that updated content appears correctly while static assets remain cached.

Forgetting Font Optimization

Custom fonts improve branding but slow loading when misconfigured. Host fonts locally or use font-display: swap to show fallback text while custom fonts load. Subset fonts to include only characters you actually use.

Neglecting Database Optimization

WooCommerce and other database-driven platforms slow down as data accumulates. Old revisions, expired transients, and orphaned metadata bloat the database. Schedule regular cleanup using plugins like WP-Optimize.

No Performance Budget

Without defined limits, performance degrades gradually. Set a performance budget: maximum page weight, minimum speed scores, maximum third-party scripts. Review before approving changes that exceed limits.

Testing Only Once

One test provides a snapshot, not a trend. Performance varies based on server load, network conditions, and cached state. Test regularly and track changes over time.

Get a full speed and conversion audit

1350+ stores audited

Run Free AuditNo credit card needed

Research Summary

The data consistently shows that speed drives ecommerce success.

Conversion Impact:

A 0.1-second improvement in load time can increase retail conversions by up to 8.4% (NitroPack/Google)

One-second delay leads to roughly 7% fewer conversions (Cloudflare)

Sites loading in one second convert around 5x more than ten-second sites (Queue-it)

Mobile Behavior:

Approximately 53% abandon sites taking more than three seconds on mobile (Google/NitroPack)

Around 70% of consumers say page speed affects their purchase decision (Unbounce)

Core Web Vitals:

Approximately 50% of mobile sites pass the Core Web Vitals assessment (HTTP Archive 2025)

Rakuten 24 achieved 33% higher conversion rate and 53% more revenue per visitor after CWV optimization (web.dev)

Optimization Potential:

WebP images are approximately 25-35% smaller than JPEG at equivalent quality

JavaScript minification can reduce file sizes by up to 80%

Removing unnecessary apps often delivers noticeable speed improvements

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a good page speed for an ecommerce site?

Aim for pages that load in under three seconds, with two seconds or less being the target for competitive performance. Google PageSpeed Insights scores of 90+ indicate good performance. Core Web Vitals should meet thresholds: LCP under 2.5 seconds, INP under 200 milliseconds, CLS under 0.1.

How does page speed affect SEO?

Page speed is part of Google's ranking algorithm through Core Web Vitals. While content relevance remains more important, speed serves as a tie-breaker between pages with similar quality. Google uses mobile-first indexing, so mobile speed particularly affects rankings.

What tools can I use to test my site speed?

The store speed test gives you mobile and desktop scores with ecommerce-specific context in one click. Google PageSpeed Insights provides free testing with both lab data and real user metrics. GTmetrix offers detailed waterfall analysis and location-based testing. WebPageTest allows advanced testing with specific device and connection configurations.

Why is my Shopify store slow?

Common causes include too many installed apps, unoptimized product images, heavy theme with excessive features, and third-party scripts from marketing and analytics tools. Audit installed apps and remove those providing minimal value. Compress images and consider a speed optimization app like Hyperspeed or TinyIMG.

How can I improve my WooCommerce speed?

Start with hosting. Shared hosting limits performance significantly. Add caching through plugins like WP Rocket or W3 Total Cache. Optimize images with ShortPixel or Imagify. Minimize plugins and use a lightweight theme. Consider a CDN for global visitors.

What are Core Web Vitals?

Core Web Vitals are three metrics Google uses to measure user experience: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures loading speed, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures responsiveness, and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures visual stability. Meeting the thresholds for all three positively affects search rankings.

Does site speed really affect conversion rate?

Yes, substantially. Research consistently shows that faster sites convert better. A one-second delay can reduce conversions by approximately 7%. Companies that invest in speed optimization typically see measurable revenue increases. The effect is particularly strong on mobile where customers have less patience.

How often should I test my site speed?

Test at minimum monthly to catch gradual degradation. You can test your store speed in a click, without any setup. Test immediately after installing new apps, changing themes, or making site-wide updates. Set up automated monitoring for ongoing tracking. Before major sales events, run speed audits to ensure your site handles increased traffic smoothly.

Is it worth paying for premium hosting?

For most ecommerce stores, yes. The difference between $5/month shared hosting and $30/month quality hosting often represents a meaningful speed improvement. If that improvement prevents even a few abandoned carts monthly, the investment pays for itself. Calculate your cart abandonment rate and average order value to estimate ROI.

Should I use a CDN for my store?

If you have customers across multiple regions, a CDN provides substantial benefits. Even for single-region stores, CDNs offer image optimization, security features, and reduced server load that justify the cost. Free tiers from Cloudflare make testing easy before committing.

Why is my ecommerce website so slow?

The most common causes are unoptimized images, too many installed apps or plugins, inadequate hosting, and accumulated database bloat. Start by testing with PageSpeed Insights to identify specific issues. Often a single problem, such as a 3MB hero image or a dozen unused apps, causes most of the slowdown. Fix the biggest issues first rather than trying to optimize everything at once.

What is the difference between Lighthouse and PageSpeed Insights?

Both use the same Lighthouse engine to measure performance. Lighthouse runs a simulated test in a controlled environment. PageSpeed Insights runs that same test but adds real user data from the Chrome User Experience Report, showing how actual visitors experience your site. For most store owners, PageSpeed Insights provides more actionable information because it includes real-world performance alongside lab results.

Which pages should I optimize first?

Start with your highest-traffic pages, typically homepage, top product pages, and main category pages. Then prioritize checkout because slow checkout directly causes abandoned carts. Use analytics to identify which pages get the most visits and focus optimization efforts there. A 0.5-second improvement on a page with 10,000 monthly visitors matters more than a 2-second improvement on a page with 100 visitors.

Summary

Site speed directly affects ecommerce revenue. Customers abandon slow sites, search engines rank fast sites higher, and the performance gap between optimized and unoptimized stores continues to widen.

Key takeaways:

Aim for page loads under three seconds, with Core Web Vitals meeting Google's thresholds

Start with image optimization for the biggest gains with the least effort

Audit and remove unnecessary apps and plugins regularly

Implement proper caching at browser, CDN, and server levels

Monitor performance continuously rather than testing occasionally

Consider hosting upgrades as traffic grows

Start identifying your store's speed bottlenecks today with Ecomhint to find the specific issues affecting your performance and conversions.

Topics. core web vitals / Differentiating between Field Data and Lab Data in PageSpeed Insights. Field Data (View Data): aggregated from the Chrome UX Report (CrUX) over 28 days based on real user interactions; includes First Input Delay (FID) and Interaction to Next Paint (INP). Lab Data (Lighthouse Data): simulated using a mid-tier device on a mobile network; used for immediate optimization feedback; measures Total Blocking Time (TBT) instead of FID. resource optimization / Resolving Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): fixing dynamic content injections by using placeholders and explicitly defining image dimensions, or using the "Add missing width and height attributes" setting in WP Rocket. Resolving Total Blocking Time (TBT): reducing the time the "main thread" is occupied by tasks taking longer than 50 milliseconds. Utilizing WP Rocket's "File Optimization" tab to minify JavaScript, combine files, and defer/delay JS execution to unblock the main thread.

Look for. The definition of the Main Thread: the browser's primary worker responsible for parsing HTML, rendering content, and processing user inputs. The definition of Total Blocking Time (TBT): the accumulated time that long tasks (>50ms) prevent the main thread from responding to user interactions. The specific testing protocol when minifying/deferring JavaScript: activate the setting, clear the cache, test the live site in incognito, and uncheck if the UI breaks. The specific reason why Field Data might display "Origin" instead of "URL": the specific page tested did not receive enough traffic over the past 28 days, so PageSpeed Insights defaults to the site-wide average.

Skip. General SEO philosophy about content depth mattering more than a perfect 100 score. Plugs for the Rank Math SEO plugin or other YouTube videos. Broad explanations of accessibility or standard SEO metadata checks.

Scope mix.

Almost all baseline.

Volume.

10 to 15.

Google wants to create an all-inclusive environment to allow even the visually impaired to view web pages. So the Accessibility Audit will look at things like if buttons have any descriptive labels that will help people who use a screen readers to understand it, or if there is a clear contrast between the background and foreground colors. Topics. benchmarks / The financial and behavioral impact of site latency: a 100-millisecond delay can reduce conversion rates by 7% (according to Akamai). The 3-second threshold: 53% of mobile visitors abandon pages taking longer than 3 seconds to load, while 47% of online shoppers expect load times to be 2 seconds or less. core web vitals / Understanding key performance metrics used by Google. First Contentful Paint (FCP): the time required to render the first visible element, such as text or an image. Time to Interactive (TTI): the time until the website is fully interactive and usable. Total Blocking Time (TBT): the elapsed time between First Contentful Paint and Time to Interactive. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): the time required for the main page content to fully load from the user's perspective. resource optimization / Implementing "lite embeds" for videos, which load only a static thumbnail initially and defer the heavy video player code until the user clicks. Delaying third-party scripts and integrations so they only execute after the main page (product images and info) has fully loaded. Compressing images and serving device-specific dimensions (e.g., preventing XXL desktop images from loading on small smartphones). rendering and architecture / Utilizing Server-Side Rendering (SSR) to handle complex rendering tasks directly on the server, reducing the processing burden on the user's browser and reliance on their internet connection speed. Using a hybrid rendering approach where the server handles heavy processing and the client-side browser handles lighter, immediate interactions. Distributing static content via globally distributed Content Delivery Networks (CDNs). Implementing fast, well-structured APIs that allow for precise data selection, thereby reducing response payloads and mitigating over-reliance on caching.

Look for. The exact conversion impact of a 100ms delay: a 7% reduction in conversion rate. The definition of Total Blocking Time (TBT): the time elapsed between First Contentful Paint (FCP) and Time to Interactive (TTI). The specific technique for video optimization: "lite embeds," which only load a thumbnail until the user interacts. The specific API optimization rule: using well-structured APIs to select exactly which data should be loaded, reducing payload sizes and response times.

Skip. Plugs to download the "Marketing ROI: How to Increase Your Profit Return by Five" guide. Generic advice to use tools like GTmetrix or Pingdom without explaining the underlying mechanical fixes.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 10 to 15.

Key Takeaways

Page speed directly impacts conversion rates, revenue, and SEO, so slow shops lose customers and visibility fast.

Retailers should measure performance first (mobile and desktop) using tools like PageSpeed Insights and focus on Core Web Vitals.

Key optimizations include image compression, lite embeds, fewer third-party scripts, and CDNs to reduce load times globally.

Fast infrastructure, efficient APIs, caching, and server-side rendering help scalable shops deliver consistently fast experiences.

Why is page speed optimization so important for online retailers? If websites are too slow, customers quickly become impatient. And it’s not just sales that suffer. Search engines such as Google and Ecosia also attach great importance to fast loading times and rate a website’s performance accordingly as good or poor. The result: bad search engine rankings for slow websites. Nor does this necessarily promote sales for online businesses. But how can you tell when you should optimise your page speed? Only a performance check can help. This will give you some initial insights into where your shop’s optimization potential lies. Some changes can be implemented very quickly, others need some time or fundamental adjustments. But they all have one thing in common: They are worth it.

Why Page Speed Optimization Is Important

Slow sites are a lesson in patience. One of the reasons online shopping is so popular, though, is because it’s fast. At least in theory. It’s not uncommon for potential customers to quickly abandon a site if it’s too slow. So they head off to online shops with higher performance – and make their purchases there. Online retailers are therefore missing out on sales if they do not optimise their page speed. The high bounce rate also sends negative feedback to Google and other search engines. And that ensures a poorer ranking in organic search engine results. In contrast, those who have fast loading times are rated positively. Page speed is not the only ranking factor, of course, but it is an important one.

A three second page load is for many mobile shoppers reason enough to leave your online shop.

Website Speed Influences Conversion Rates

Studies show a direct correlation between eCommerce site speed and revenue. Every second counts. A study by Akamai, for example, shows that a delay of just 100 milliseconds in loading time can reduce the conversion rate by seven percent. 53 percent of mobile visitors would leave a page immediately if it took more than three seconds to load. Internet users are often impatient and erratic. And they have high expectations: 47 percent of online shoppers expect a page to load in two seconds or less. 79 percent would be less likely to shop again on a page that they thought was too slow. Reasons enough, then, to prioritise page speed optimization.

A shop system that supports optimized page speeds isn’t just nice to have — it’s essential to your ROI. For more important insights on how to maximize your ROI, download our guide, Marketing ROI: How to Increase Your Profit Return by Five.

Google’s PageSpeed Insights help you to check the performance of your site and make adjustments.Content Delivery Networks (CDN) speed up online shops because they provide information where customers actually are.

The Essentials of Measuring Website Loading Speed

Before you start optimising, you should check your performance: How fast is the page currently and how many adjustments do you need to make? With Google’s PageSpeed Insights, you can measure the website loading time for free. The result scores can be displayed for desktop and mobile. In many cases, these two types differ significantly. It is therefore worth keeping an eye on both. For example, if you have a lot of customers shopping on mobile, you can focus on mobile page speed optimization first. PageSpeed Insights not only provides the mere figures, but also a classification of which scores are good, mediocre, or poor. What’s particularly practical: The tool directly provides recommendations for improvement and even estimates how much time adjustments can save.

Various key figures play a role in measuring performance and are weighted differently. These include:

First Contentful Paint: Time to get to the first element that a user sees on the website, e.g., text or an image

​​Time to Interactive: Time until the website is interactive, i.e., the user can use it

Total Blocking Time: Time between First Contentful Paint and Time to Interactive

Largest Contentful Paint: Time until the page is loaded from the user’s point of view

Tip: Check your website speed in other tools like GTmetrix or Pingdom’s Website Test to get a reliable, comprehensive overview.

Don’t just rely on Google when optimising your page load. Also take a look at other tools, e.g., GTmetrix.

First Steps in Page Speed Optimization

There are many different ways to improve the loading time of websites. An important basic is, for example, a stable infrastructure with fast and reliable hosting. Online shops in particular want to convince customers with appealing and high-quality images. But big images are often responsible for long loading times. Compressing them saves time. Images should also always be optimised for the device that is currently loading them. It makes little sense to deliver an XXL image to a small smartphone. Different image sizes depending on the page, usage and device are recommended.

Embeddings and Third-Party Providers as Performance Killers

If you embed a lot of videos, e.g., to show products in action, you quickly run the risk of losing page speed. So-called lite embeds may be the solution: Only the thumbnail image is loaded, the video player is only loaded when a user actually clicks on it. This approach also works for third-party integrations. They are additional content and code that might cause pages to slow down. So you should always ask yourself if all of them are really necessary and get rid of unnecessary ones. To make the page faster, the remaining integrations are loaded only after the main page has been loaded, e.g., product images and information.

Taking Page Speed Optimization Further

In addition to these steps, you can also ensure faster loading times by making a few adjustments in the setup of your website:

server-side rendering (SSR): There are two ways to render JavaScript pages. Either the main work is done in the browser of the page visitor loading and rendering all elements (client-side). Or all this is already done on the server and the page is directly displayed faster. The first one is highly dependent on the user’s internet connection. The second demands more power from the server but is more reliable. Often a combination of both is the best choice. Complex tasks are handled by the server. For anything else, the browser takes over and reduces the load on the server.

content delivery networks: A content delivery network (CDN) is a network of globally distributed servers on which content such as images or files are temporarily stored. This way, they can be fetched from the server that is closest to the user. It saves time and makes the website faster.

caching: During caching, information such as product data and other content is temporarily stored so that it is available more quickly. Caching is possible both in the user’s browser and on the server.

fast and well-structured APIs: interfaces through which information is retrieved and exchanged should work quickly and efficiently. If this is the case, it, in turn, requires less caching to provide all content. A clear structure is also very helpful. It allows you to select exactly which data should be loaded. This reduces response and loading times and thus contributes to page speed optimization.

Volume. 10 to 15.

The load time (page speed) of your ecommerce store has a direct impact on conversion rates. Visitors often abandon poorly optimized stores immediately. Well-optimized stores, by contrast, see a measurable uplift in revenue.

Page speed in ecommerce: the essentials at a glance

Why page speed matters: Even a one-second delay can reduce conversion rates by up to 7%. Fast stores (under one second load time) convert up to three times better than slow sites.

Core Web Vitals: Google measures user experience using metrics such as LCP (loading speed of the main content), CLS (visual stability), and INP (responsiveness to interactions). These metrics are official ranking factors.

Improving page speed: Optimizing images (WebP format, responsive sizes) and reducing third-party scripts (tracking, plugins).

Technical foundation: High-performance caching (e.g., Redis or Varnish) and modern server technologies (PHP 8.2+, HTTP/3) form the foundation for all further optimization.

Shopware: Shopware 6 automates many processes such as WebP generation, thumbnail management, and full-page caching.

Why page speed is so critical for online stores

In ecommerce, page speed matters because it bridges technical performance and purchasing psychology. Faster load times demonstrably lead to higher conversion rates, lower bounce rates, and stronger rankings in Google search results.

Direct impact on conversion rates: There is a clear correlation between load time and revenue. Online stores that load in under one second achieve conversion rates up to three times higher than stores that take five seconds.

Google rankings and Core Web Vitals: Google has made page speed an official ranking factor under the Core Web Vitals framework. This means a slow store will rank lower in search results even if its content or products are excellent.

Higher efficiency of advertising spend (ROI): With paid advertising (e.g., Google Ads or social media ads), you pay for every click. If a user clicks an ad but the page loads too slowly, they often leave before seeing your offer.

Mobile shopping: 66% of online revenue comes from smartphones and tablets. Page speed optimization is therefore especially critical for these devices.

Which metrics define page speed in ecommerce?

Google evaluates the speed of your store using the Core Web Vitals, a set of metrics that reflect real user experience. These include Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and Time to First Byte (TTFB).

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) – perceived loading speed

LCP measures the time it takes for the largest visible element on the page (typically the hero image on the homepage or the product image on a product detail page) to fully load.

Target value: Under 2.5 seconds.

Ecommerce relevance: If the product image does not appear immediately, customers may question the credibility or functionality of the store.

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) – visual stability

Buttons and other elements that shift just before a click or tap – causing users to miss their intended target – are a major source of frustration. The lower the CLS value, the more stable elements remain in place.

Target value: Under 0.1.

Ecommerce relevance: A high CLS leads to misclicks. In the worst case, customers abandon the purchase because they feel manipulated or frustrated by an unstable interface.

Interaction to Next Paint (INP) – responsiveness

INP replaced the older FID (First Input Delay) metric in March 2024. It measures how quickly the store responds to interactions, such as clicking “Add to cart.”

Target value: Under 200 milliseconds.

Ecommerce relevance: Delayed responses feel sluggish. In checkout flows, this often causes users to click multiple times or abandon the process altogether because they are unsure whether their input was registered.

Time to First Byte (TTFB) – server response

TTFB measures the time between the browser request and the first byte received from the server.

Target value: Under 800 milliseconds (often harder to achieve in ecommerce due to dynamic carts).

Ecommerce relevance: Poor TTFB indicates slow hosting or an overloaded database. If the foundation is weak, frontend optimizations can only do so much.

The biggest page speed killers in ecommerce

As a store operator, it is essential to identify what is slowing your store down. Often, the issue is not the core shop system, but elements added later – such as oversized images, scripts, or plugins.

Unoptimized images: High-resolution product images are critical for sales, but PNG or JPEG formats unnecessarily inflate page weight. Modern formats like WebP or AVIF reduce file size by 30–50% at the same quality.

Third-party scripts: Tracking pixels, chat widgets, review platforms, and social media embeds all load their own JavaScript. Each script blocks page rendering. In many stores, these external requests account for more than 50% of total load time.

Plugins: Every additional app or plugin loads its own stylesheets and scripts. Particularly problematic are plugins that run complex database queries on every page load without caching results.

Caching: Without caching, the server must rebuild the entire page on every click – querying databases, calculating prices, and assembling layouts. Full-page caching delivers a pre-rendered version instead, dramatically reducing response times.

CSS and JavaScript: Many themes load functionality site-wide, even if it is only needed on a single subpage. Browsers still have to download and process this unused code, significantly slowing mobile performance.

How to improve your ecommerce store’s page speed

Reducing load times requires minimizing file sizes, lowering the number of server requests, and implementing an effective caching strategy. This is achieved through image compression, disabling unnecessary plugins, and using modern protocols such as HTTP/2.

Step 1: Establish a baseline

Before making technical changes, you need a before-and-after comparison to understand the impact of each measure.

Approach: Use Google PageSpeed Insights. Enter your URL and run the analysis for mobile and desktop.

Tip: Take screenshots of the results or note LCP values and the overall score. Document every change in a simple list (e.g., “March 15 – image compression enabled”).

Step 2: Optimize image assets

Images can account for more than 60% of a page’s total data volume – making them the biggest optimization lever.

Action: Use modern formats like WebP instead of classic JPEGs.

Implementation: A small number of images can be converted manually using free browser-based tools.

Tip: Systems like Shopware automatically convert images into efficient formats.

Step 3: Audit extensions (plugins and scripts)

Every active plugin loads code that slows down page rendering. Over time, stores often accumulate extensions that are no longer used.

Approach: Review your plugin list from top to bottom in the admin panel. Ask yourself: “How does this plugin currently contribute to revenue?”

Check: Disable uncertain plugins in a staging environment and measure page speed again. Marketing pixels or unused design effects often block rendering. Remove unused plugins completely rather than simply deactivating them.

Step 4: The technical foundation

Some of the most powerful optimization levers sit deep within the server infrastructure.

Approach: Speak with your technical team – either your in-house IT administrator or your hosting provider’s support.

Important: Only contact your provider after completing steps 1–3. Otherwise, support will simply point to unoptimized content.

Ask specifically about the PHP version and whether server-side caching such as Redis or Varnish is active. In SaaS and cloud environments, many settings are already optimized, but reviewing the documentation is still worthwhile.

Automatic page speed optimization in Shopware

Shopware natively embeds many performance optimizations. The platform includes automated mechanisms to reduce server load and accelerate content delivery in the customer’s browser.

WebP generation: Shopware automatically converts uploaded source images into WebP, significantly reducing transferred data without manual effort.

Thumbnail sets: Shopware automatically generates multiple image sizes for each product, delivering the appropriate size for the user’s device.

Integrated HTTP cache: The system stores fully rendered pages. On repeat visits, the server delivers ready-made HTML instead of querying the database or executing PHP.

Intelligent cache invalidation: Shopware detects price or stock changes and clears only the affected pages, keeping the store fast without showing outdated information.

Shopware also bundles and optimizes the CSS and JavaScript required for the design.

Topics. resource optimization / The manual cleanup of residual Shopify app code: uninstalling an app does not always remove its injected scripts. Merchants must search theme.liquid, head.liquid, and footer.liquid (using tools like the Shopify Theme File Search Chrome extension) for app names (e.g., "loox") and delete lingering <script> tags to prevent external server requests. Image optimization: restricting file sizes to under 1MB, using JPEG instead of PNG (unless transparency is required), and replacing heavy, animated GIFs with compressed MP4 videos using HTML <video> tags. Lazy loading mechanics: applying preload="none" to videos and loading="lazy" to off-screen images, but strictly avoiding lazy loading for above-the-fold assets (like hero images), which instead require a preload link in the <head> to minimize LCP. Font optimization: ensuring all @font-face CSS declarations include font-display: swap so the browser renders text in a system font immediately rather than remaining blank while the custom font downloads. Script execution order: appending defer or async attributes to non-essential JavaScript tags in theme.liquid so they do not block HTML parsing, with the explicit exception of tracking pixels, which must not be deferred. CSS optimization: using the media="print" onload="this.media='all'" trick to load non-critical stylesheets asynchronously.

Look for. The file paths to check for residual app code: theme.liquid, head.liquid, and footer.liquid. The specific file format that should replace animated GIFs: MP4 videos inside an HTML <video> tag. The specific CSS property required to prevent "flash of invisible text" when using custom fonts: font-display: swap inside the @font-face rule. The specific HTML attribute used to delay non-essential JavaScript execution until the DOM is loaded: defer. The specific HTML attribute trick to load non-critical CSS without blocking rendering: <link rel="stylesheet" href="..." media="print" onload="this.media='all'">.

Skip. General complaints about "pushy apps" or "speed optimization specialists" who use tricks to spoof Google Lighthouse scores. The overly broad restaurant analogy regarding serving drinks before the main course.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 15 to 20.

By the end, your images will load faster, look professional, and help increase conversions. And if you're new here, my name is Christian and I help Shopify store owners improve their stores, boost conversions, and get better results. If that sounds like something you want for your store, hit that subscribe button and let's jump right into it. The first thing I always check when optimizing a Shopify store is the images. They are amongst the heaviest assets, and even though they are not the only thing that affects speed, they are one of the easiest problems to fix. So, what do we mean when we say image optimization on Shopify? Simply put, it's about preparing your images the right way before you upload them and keeping them in check once you have them on your store. The goal is to get the best quality possible while keeping the file size as low as possible. But why bother doing that? Because image optimization affects a lot more than just speed. It impacts how your store looks, how trustworthy it feels to visitors, and yes, it can affect the conversion rate. Get this part right, and your store will not only load faster, also look sharper, and perform better. And this is just one small part of my full Shopify speed optimization course. If you want your store to load faster, feel smoother, and convert better overall, I break everything down step by step in the full course. You can check that out by using the link in the description. So, how does Shopify actually handle our images? Well, Shopify does a couple of things for us. One of which is to serve our images from a CDN, which is a content delivery network. Instead of having all your files served from one server, what a CDN does is to actually copy the main server and all the files as they come from the user. So let's say you are updating your site and you add new images. Those images would go to the main server and from the main server will propagate to the copy servers. For example, if you have customers in North America, you're going to have a server there. If you have customers in South America, you're going to have a server there. And customers from those regions instead of downloading everything from the main server would download things from the local server for them. and that would speed up things significantly. Now, there are still websites and systems out there that still don't use CDNs and that's obviously a shame because customers that are far away from the server will have to wait more to download that and will have a worse experience. But Shopify does this automatically. On Shopify, you get a CDN automatically and things are smoother. So customers from far away will still have a good experience on your store. Now the second thing that Shopify does for us automatically is to actually serve multiple sizes from one single upload. So you're going to upload the image once and you can actually add filters on your theme in order to have the image displayed in the right format for the right screen. And this is more of a technical thing because this is done inside the code. But let's say you uploaded this image over here. So once you've uploaded an image to your store, you're going to have a link something like this. So this is the link that resulted from me uploading this image. And as you can see, it has the extension here. JPEG. But at the end, we have another part of the URL. And it actually says here 493. This is the width of the image right now. This is created with an image filter on the Shopify theme. And if I go and I remove this part over here, I'm going to actually access the original image that I've uploaded. So if I enter now, this is much larger. And now I can actually zoom. So if I click on the image now, I can see the full width of the image. This is the actual size that I've uploaded. But if I go back, I'm going to get the smaller version, a version that was created with Shopify filters. And that looks something like this. So I can go here to the documentation. And let's say this is one of our product images. As you can see, this is the liquid code that generates this link over here. And at the end, you're going to have the width as we had it on the other example. So 450. And at the end here we have 450. This would be the original file. And if I add this extension, I would get the one that this filter generated the same way I got this one over here. And that's why it's important to use newer Shopify themes because newer themes use these filters. And if you upload by mistake an image like I've uploaded here, this was 5,000 pixels, the original one. If I go here and I check it out, the intrinsic size is now 1,300 pixels. And this was resized by the theme itself. I didn't have to do anything. The theme itself took my original upload, rescaled it, and displayed the version of that image that is more manageable and that will help my users have a better experience. Another thing that Shopify actually does for us behind the scenes is to serve our images. No matter the format we are uploading like JPEG or PNG, it will automatically transform them in web which is a format that was developed by Google and it should be superior. So whenever our customers browser will support this new format, it will show web instead of JPEG or instead of PNG. So you don't have to actually go ahead and convert your JPEGs or your PGs into web. This is done automatically and I can show you that actually. So if I go and I try to save this image for example save image as you can see here at the end I'm going to have the web extension. This image was uploaded as JPEG but is automatically converted to web because my browser supports that. So what are the things Shopify cannot help us with? First of all, if you are uploading oversized images, images that are too large, you can actually resize them inside Shopify, but it won't be the same as if you would resize them in Photoshop or something that is more professional. It has more controls to resize an image that you already uploaded to your Shopify store. Let's say this is the image. And by the way, you should never upload an image that looks like this. You're going to click on it and you're going to have a bunch of adjustments that you can do. One of which is the resize option right here. So, I'm going to click that. You can go ahead and you can resize it from here. But, as you can see, there is no compression settings. So, if you want to do this right, you should do it before you upload the image because on a more professional image resizing tool, you're going to have compression settings as well. and you're going to be able to find that right balance between size and quality. This way you are just resizing the image. So if I change here the numbers, they will change and the image will be resized to that size but you won't have any compression settings in here. jobs.text:
08-SPD / speed and performance

Goes here. Loading performance, browser rendering, perceived performance, resource optimization, Core Web Vitals (CWV), caching strategies, and the technical mechanics of shrinking file sizes and reducing execution time. Specifically capturing the definitions and optimization tactics for Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), First Input Delay (FID), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

Not here.

Website security, SSL certificates, or DDoS protection -> 23-SEC

Google Analytics 4 installation and event tracking -> 06-MEA

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Provides baseline definitions for Core Web Vitals (LCP, FID, CLS) and explains mechanical optimization tactics like setting image aspect ratios, utilizing preload links, and analyzing performance across an entire domain using Unlighthouse.

modules: [SPD]

topics: [core web vitals]

tier: 3

scope_hint: baseline

Topics.

core web vitals / Understanding the three primary metrics of Google's Core Web Vitals. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): measures loading performance, tracking the time it takes to render the largest image or text block. LCP must occur within 2.5 seconds (anything over 4 seconds negatively impacts SEO). Optimizations include compressing images (using WebP formats), utilizing CDNs (like Firebase or Vercel), minimizing render-blocking JavaScript, and using HTML preload links and fetchpriority attributes on critical assets. First Input Delay (FID): measures interactivity, tracking the time from a user's first click to the browser's response. FID must be under 100 milliseconds. Optimizations include reducing JavaScript execution time via lazy loading, using frameworks like Qwik, or offloading scripts to Web Workers (via tools like Partytown). Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): measures visual stability, tracking unexpected page jumps. Optimizations include explicitly defining image dimensions (width and height) or using the CSS aspect-ratio property, and utilizing the srcset attribute for responsive images to reserve space before they load.

auditing tools / Using the Chrome Network Tab waterfall to identify asset bottlenecks. Installing the Web Vitals Chrome Extension to log specific DOM elements causing LCP or CLS issues directly in the browser console. Running Unlighthouse (npx unlighthouse --site <url>) to perform parallel Lighthouse audits across hundreds of URLs simultaneously to find outlier pages with poor performance.

Look for. The specific LCP threshold: good is <2.5 seconds, poor is >4.0 seconds. The specific FID threshold: good is <100 milliseconds, poor is >300 milliseconds. The CSS attribute used to prevent CLS without hardcoding exact pixels: aspect-ratio. The tool to offload third-party scripts to a Web Worker: Partytown. The exact terminal command to run site-wide audits: npx unlighthouse.

Skip. Plugs for Fireship Pro. The subjective analysis of Amazon, Reddit, or Astro's homepage scores.

Scope mix.

Almost all baseline.

Volume.

10 to 15.
