 Extensive testing by Starch Research has shown that placing more than one ad in the same issue of the same publication can be remarkably effective, and have a 1 + 1 = 3 effect that no single ad can replicate. If you want to make some waves in your market, here are 10 ways to do it. Ad-Agency Secrets 169 The 10 Most Effective Multi-ad Formations 1. Three single-page ads in sequence on the right side. 2. Two-single page ads in different sections of the same issue on the right side. 3. Double-page spread. 4. Single-page ads on the right. 5. Single-page ads on the left with strip ad on the right. 6. Single-page ads on the left. 7. Right-page checkerboard (one quarter-page ad in each of the page’s four corners). 8. Left-page checkerboard ads. 9. Half-page ad, upper right. 10. Half-page ad, lower right. Ad-Agency Secret #33: Guarantees That Guarantee Higher Response Do you believe in your product or service? How strongly? I offer a full one-year money-back guarantee on many of my products. Why? It instills confidence in buyers and puts them at ease. They think, “Drew must feel pretty confident about this product. I have a full year to return it and get all my money back. How can I lose?” Buyers feel vulnerable. In exchange for their hard-earned money, they take a leap of faith every time they give some of it away. They wonder if what they’re buying will be worth at least the value of the money they’ve exchanged for it. And between the time they release their legal tender and the time they experience the product, there’s a period of stress and uncertainty. The higher the dollar amount of the transaction, of course, the greater the stress. Buy a rotten apple, and it won’t ruin your day. But buy a house and find out five years later that the title was forged and you never really owned it, and say hello to an “Excedrin headache” that’ll span six seasons. During the Great Depression, people were extremely cautious about spending what little money they had. Counter to the logic of the times, Hormel ran a large ad in a Chicago newspaper featuring an illustration of an apron-clad grocer holding a can of soup in his outstretched hand. Here’s how it began: CA$HVERTISING 170 DOUBLE YOUR MONEY BACK ...if you don’t say this NEW Home-Style Vegetable Soup is the most delicious you ever bought. THE OFFER Friday and Saturday THE OFFER only. Go to your nearest food store. Pay the regular price of 13¢ for one big 20 oz. container of Hormel Flavor-Sealed Vegetable Soup, following instructions on the label. If you don’t agree that it’s the best vegetable soup you ever bought, return the empty container to your grocer...who is authorized to pay you back TWICE what you paid. It was the first time an advertiser had the courage to offer a “doubleyour-money-back” guarantee. Many fearful company execs warned, “Don’t do it! With the state of the economy, people are going to buy armloads of soup and return them all for a big profit!” The ad was a smashing success, and only 12 women took advantage of the guarantee. But the question is: Did the guarantee help close the sale? You better believe it did. It reduced buyers’ pre-purchase stress. And most importantly, it gave them the confidence to buy. Every time your prospect thinks about buying, her head becomes a battleground for two opposing forces: skepticism and the desire to believe. Now, imagine an old apothecary scale with skepticism on one side and the desire to believe on the other. Let’s say her level of skepticism is a 7 on a scale from 1 to 10, 10 being “most skeptical.” And her desire to believe is a 5. It’s up to you to throw more weight onto the desire to believe side in order to offset the amount of skepticism she now experiences. Including a strong guarantee helps lighten the skepticism side and press down on that desire side. Sometimes it’s all you need to clinch the sale. Not only do longer, stronger guarantees boost your sales, but they (ironically) also result in fewer returns. Why? Studies show that shortterm guarantees (30, 60, or 90 days) keep customers poised to make the return and force them to be more conscious of the return deadline. Longer guarantees (six months, one, five, 10 years, lifetime) give prospects confidence in the product and avoid the “beat the clock” mindset of using the product and sending it back within the short allotted time. CA$HVERTISING Tip: Offer the longest, strongest guarantee in your industry. (Your competition will hate you for this.) Such a guarantee conveys your confidence in what you sell, which in turn gives prospects the confidence to give you their money. As a bonus, it causes Ad-Agency Secrets 171 potential buyers to question your competitors’ weak—or absent!—guarantee. It also lets you ask—in big bold type—“Why Do Our Competitors Guarantee their [PRODUCT TYPE] for Only 90 Days?” Followed up with the insidious, “Do they know something about their [PRODUCT] that they’re not telling you?” A well-crafted guarantee isn’t an afterthought. It’s a damned powerful sales tool—one of your most important, especially if your competitors’ guarantee is weak by comparison. Show off your guarantee, don’t hide it! Surround it with a fancy certificate border and print your signature under it. Include it in your ads, on brochures, your Website, everywhere. Be proud of it! And watch it perform wonders for you. Ad-Agency Secret #34: The Psychology of Size Fact: Bigger ads attract more attention. This idea has been tested by various researchers using different methodologies, and they’ve all come to this same conclusion. What hasn’t been quantified, however, is just how much of a proportional increase in attention a larger ad will consistently deliver. Research has shown this: the attention value of ads is not in direct proportion to its increased size. In other words, increasing the size of your ad four times will not, in general, multiply the number of readers by four. So if your boss, client, partner, or spouse says, “Hey, we got 100 replies to our quarter-page ad. Blow it up to a full-page ad so we’ll get 400 replies,” you need to sit him or her down and have a little talk. In the following table, the attention value of a quarter-page ad is represented as 100 percent. Likewise, the attention value of both the half- and full-page ads are calculated as a ratio to the value of the quarter-page ad. Okay, let’s make this easy. In applied psychologist Walter Dill Scott’s experiment (first column, bold type), he had subjects read magazines at their own pace and later asked, “What ads do you remember?” Note that the half-page ad (which was two times the area of the quarter-page) scored 300 percent, or three times the attention. The full-page ad (which was four times the area of the quarter page) scored 666 percent, or more than six times the attention. Scott’s conclusion: Attention value exceeds increase of ad size. This would mean you could double your ad size and get far more than double the attention. Great, right? But wait... CA$HVERTISING 172 Stanford University researcher E.K. Strong (creator of The Strong Interest Inventory, used today to help people make career choices) believed that using real magazines would skew the test results. “Hey guys, it’s not just ad size that’s influencing your subjects...it’s the ads themselves!” So Strong created a dummy magazine—a mock-up—for his experiment. The results showed that the attention value for the larger ads did not increase as dramatically as in Scott’s experiment. Strong’s Conclusion: Attention value lags behind increase of ad size. New York University Professor G.B. Hotchkiss’s study had similar results. Without mentioning anything about the ads themselves, he instructed students in his class to read an article in a magazine, and later asked them to recall what ads they saw. How about our buddy Daniel Starch? In his classic Analysis of Over Three Million Coupons published in 1927, he collected 1,400,000 replies from 907 different ads from various advertisers. This mind-bogglingly extensive study produced results not unlike those of Strong, Hotchkiss, and Adams. Look at the Starch data and you’ll see that a half-page scores 68 percent better than a quarter-page and a full-page slightly more than 300 percent better than the quarter. Starch’s conclusion: Attention value lags behind increase of ad size. Starch said, “Advertisements brought replies very nearly in proportion to their size, although the smaller sizes had a slight advantage. This may have been due to the possibility that the smaller advertisements...placed more emphasis on securing responses.” University of Michigan psychology professor Henry Adams didn’t like anyone’s studies. He wanted to eliminate every possible variable that Ratio of Size to Attention Quarter-Page Control Ad Half Page (2x size) Full Page (4x size) W.D. Scott 100% 300% 666% E.K. Strong 100% 141% 215% G.B. Hotchkiss 100% 151% 213% D. Starch 100% 168% 314% H.F. Adams 100% 178% No Data Averages 100% 187.6% 352% Ad-Agency Secrets 173 didn’t directly concern size and attention. Magazines? Gone! Articles? Removed! Pictures? Eliminated! Instead, Adams whipped out his scissors and pasted up colored squares in four different sizes: one inch, one and a half, two, and three square inches. Talk about minimalism. Using a tachistoscope—a short-exposure projection device used to help train WWII fighter pilots to identify enemy aircraft—he exposed his subjects to the material four squares at a time. Long story short: His results were similar to all the others. So how can we make sense of all this crazy research in a way that’s practical for us as advertisers? It boils down to this: an ad’s attention value is approximately proportionate to the square root of the area. Huh? Okay, this means that if you want to double the attention your ad’s now getting, you need to enlarge it 400 percent. (So if it’s a quarter-page ad, you need to run a full-pager.) To triple the attention, blow it up 900 percent (which is practical only if you’re starting out with a very small ad such as a classified display). You’d otherwise have to go to a multipage ad, as described in Ad Agency Secret #32: Multi-Page Your Way to Success. So now you have a rule of thumb that tells you how to boost the number of eyeballs that roll across your ads. Start with a proven-effective ad and more attention = more reading = more convincing = more buying = more dollars in your pocket. Now that’s the kind of equation I like! Ad-Agency Secret #35: The Psychology of Page and Section Positioning Left page? Right page? Top? Middle? Bottom? Ask 100 different advertisers and you’ll get 100 different reasons why your ad should appear in a certain location within a publication. However, few, if any, will have any research to back up their recommendations, but boy oh boy, will they adamantly believe it! Multiple studies of hundreds of issues of magazines and scores of ads in dozens of industries have shown virtually no difference in the effectiveness of ads appearing on the inside pages toward the front, middle, or back of any issue, or whether they appeared on left- or right-hand pages. Researchers Starch, Stanton, Nixon, National Magazine, Lucas, and others, generally concluded that what matters most is the ad itself: the strength of its offer, and the execution of the copy and design. CA$HVERTISING 174 A good ad will get noticed irrespective of its position within the newspaper.* —Roper Starch Worldwide *But four of them get noticed more. See more “Ad-Agency Secret #36: The Fantastic Four.” Ad-Agency Secret #36: The Fantastic Four Although there are no clear winners of the left-page vs. right-page debate, as we just discussed, researchers at Starch INRA Hooper uncovered distinct ad-position advantages that are actually worth paying more for. They compared 618 magazine ads occupying cover positions to 10,789 single-page, four-color ads appearing on inside pages. They checked both men’s and women’s publications, business and consumer, and the findings were consistent. This “Fantastic Four” can help your message stand out in even the most crowded publications. Here are the results: ✸ Ads appearing on the inside front cover have the highest average “Noted” (seen and recalled) scores with the greatest increase—29 percent—over similar ads run anywhere else in the same issue. ✸ Ads placed opposite a table of contents earn up to 25 percent higher scores. ✸ Ads appearing on the back cover score 22 percent higher than ads inside. ✸ Ads placed on the inside back cover score a 6 percent advantage over inside pages. So stop fretting about where inside the publication your ad runs. That’s likely not to make a shred of difference, unless, of course, you choose to fork over more green stuff for the research-proven, higherattention cover slots. Ad-Agency Secrets 175 Ad-Agency Secret #37: Consumer Color Preferences and How Color Affects Readership Do you know what colors people like most? Dozens of experiments have been made by various researchers in the United States and abroad on the question of consumer color preferences. And as human psychology would have it, the results are pretty uniform across the board. Here, in a nutshell, are the compiled rankings. The number-one preference for most people tested is blue, with red a close second, then green, violet, orange, and yellow, ranked exactly in that order. Look at your current sales materials—online and off—and see if they reflect these worldwide findings. Unfortunately, not all graphic designers are aware of this research (they should be), so it’s up to you to specify the colors you’d like most prominently featured. Battles of the Oranges Men and women differ only slightly in color preferences. Based on 21,000 reports, the order of preference was the same for both men and women, except that men put orange in fifth place and yellow in sixth, whereas women put yellow in fifth place and orange in sixth. Color Preferences Change With Age Infants select red as their first choice. Next come yellow, green, and blue. At about 12 to 14 months this preference changes. Red remains in Ranking Color 1 Blue 2 Red 3 Green 4 Violet 5 Orange 6 Yellow CA$HVERTISING 176 first, yellow second, but blue leaps ahead of green. By the time children are 5 years of age, red, green, and blue are about equal in preference, but yellow is farther down the scale (less appealing). It’s during the grade-school years that blue gradually overtakes yellow. This preference direction continues through adulthood. While blue goes up in preference, yellow goes down, and continues to do so through as the individual ages. Preference for red, however remains high. The Older, the Bluer Why is blue preferred as we grow older? The universal preference for it may have some connection with what takes place inside the aging human eye. Look inside an old man’s (or woman’s) eye, and you’ll see that the optical lens has hazed, or yellowed. In fact, the lens of the child’s eye may absorb only 10 percent of the blue light, whereas an elderly eye may absorb 85 percent of blue light. One theory is that this is nature’s way of protecting the eye against painfully bright light as we age. Most-Loved Color Combos How much money is spent on multi-color ads every year? Billions. But are some color combinations actually preferred by more people than others? Let’s take a look… According to artists, the primary colors are red, yellow, and blue. Many insist that the best color combinations are those that do not “cross a primary.” Unlike artists, psychologists believe there are actually four primary colors: red, green, yellow, and blue. They insist that the best color combinations are those that employ complementary colors. Little experimentation has been done, so the jury is still out, but the studies that have been done do show similarities in results. In one experiment by our ol’ researcher buddy Daniel Starch, 10 ads of two predominant colors each were ranked in preference. The results showed that the most “complementary” color combinations weren’t the most preferred. Ad-Agency Secrets 177 Most Effective Paper and Ink Combos Readership studies confirm that white and yellow are the two best paper colors for easy reading. Use black, dark blue, and red inks for maximum impact. The best combination? Black ink on yellow paper. Worst? Red ink on green paper, an optically repulsive mix that’s practically unreadable—completely unreadable if you’re colorblind! Color Pairings Complementary Ranking Consumer Preference Ranking Red–Green Blue–Yellow 2 Violet–Green 3 5 Green–Yellow 4 9 Purple–Yellow 5 3 Purple–Orange 6 10 Red–Green 7 6 Blue–Orange 8 7 Red–Orange 9 8 Blue–Red 1 (most complementary) 4 1 (most preferred) 10 (least complementary) 2 CA$HVERTISING 178 Colorful Research Starch Research shows that color not only attracts readers, but also gets them more involved. What’s more, color also encourages more in-depth reading by: ✸ 60 percent over black-and-white only ads. ✸ 40 percent over two-color only ads. In fact, color does more to affect whether your ad gets seen than does size. So if it costs less to add color than it does to run a larger ad, opt for color. In fact, research says that there’s a bigger difference in readership between a black-and-white and a four-color ad than there is between a one- and two-page color ad! Black & white ads work best when emphasizing end benefits, demonstrating dramatic situations and appealing to the intellect. —Starch Research Ad-Agency Secret #38: The Psychology of Pricing What’s the difference between $19.98 and $20.00? No, I don’t mean two cents. (I can figure that out myself.) I mean, psychologically, motivationally, persuasively? It’s psychological pricing, and you see it used everywhere from department stores to restaurants to furniture retailers, even jewelers. WalMart is known for its heavy use of psychological pricing, with their favorite end digits being “97.” Odd-even pricing theory says that prices ending in odd amounts such as 77, 95, and 99 suggest greater value than prices rounded up to the next whole dollar. $9.77 seems like a better deal than $10.00. And 64 cents for a pound of bananas seems to be an okay price...but 70 cents? You gotta be kidding! But it’s more than the idea of saving a few cents. For advertisers like you and me, the effects of such a seemingly simple technique can be dramatic. Prestige pricing, by contrast, says that if you want something to be perceived as higher quality, you use only rounded whole numbers when pricing. For example, $1,000.00 suggests higher quality than $999.95, Ad-Agency Secrets 179 simply because we’ve been conditioned to interpret fractional pricing as suggestive of value. Upscale retailer Nordstrom department store uses prestige pricing, and so do many fine jewelers and other sellers of highend merchandise. Surf over to SaksFifthAvenue.com and you’ll see only 00s. In fact, the only cents you’ll see are in the prices of the few featured sale items. Fractional pricing is more widespread than you probably realize. Researchers Holdershaw, Gendall, and Garland (1997) found that approximately 60 percent of advertised retail prices ended in 9, 30 percent ended in 5, 7 percent ended in 0, and the remaining seven digits, combined, accounted for just more than 3 percent of the prices studied. But why does this work? Psychologists say that (1) fractional pricing suggests that the seller has calculated the lowest possible price, thus the odd number, and (2) we ignore the last digits rather than mentally rounding up. Doing so allows us to justify a purchase that may be teetering on the threshold of affordability. Schindler and Kibarian (1996) tested odd pricing using three versions of a direct-mail women’s clothing catalog. All three catalogs were identical, except for the prices, which ended in 00, 88, and 99. The winner? The 99 catalog produced 8 percent greater sales and more buyers than the 00 version. The 88 catalog pulled in as many sales and buyers as the 00 version. In 2000, Rutgers University did a study of people reading an ad for a woman’s dress. The subjects reported that the dress priced at $49.99 was of lower quality than the same ad featuring the exact same dress priced at an even $50. Interestingly enough, people make some fascinating rationalizations for fractional prices. For example, Schindler (1984) found that consumers who see a price ending in 98 or 99 are more likely to believe that the price was not recently raised. (How anyone jumps to that conclusion I’ll never understand.) According to Quigley and Notarantonio (1992), subjects who saw an ad with a 98 or 99 ending price were much more likely to believe the product was on sale than products with 00 end prices. What about prices ending in 95? Are they as effective as 99? Research shows they’re not. Likewise, 49, 50, and 90 are also not suggestive of low price. But evidence shows that prices ending in 79, 88, and 98 do convey value. CA$HVERTISING 180 Psychological pricing isn’t a random game of picking numbers out of a hat, it’s a well-researched topic with great implications for your bottom line. And now that you’ve read what consumers think and what research recommends, how do your prices look now? Ad-Agency Secret #39: The Psychology of Color Paint a prison’s walls pink, and there’s less inmate violence. Put a baby in a yellow room, and the crying begins. Want to suppress your appetite? Try the “Blue Wall Diet Plan.” Likewise, red classrooms hype kids up, blue rooms chill them out. Volunteer fundraisers who wear pink uniforms get bigger donations, and sage-green hospital corridors ease patients’ frazzled nerves. Color affects us strongly, including our perception of weight. For example, lifting and carrying boxes all day long can be a real drag. So to give its employees some relief, a manufacturer painted their heavy-looking black boxes light green. Voila! Psychologically “lighter” boxes. To make its packaging look heavier, a food manufacturer changed to a darkercolored package. Voila! “More” food inside. Don’t confuse this phenomenon with fashion experts’ advice to wear black for its “slimming” effect. Because of its ability to hide shadows caused by “beer and brownie bulges,” black clothing helps smooth the body’s contours. This in turn causes less attention to be paid to individual “problem areas” by presenting the body’s outline as a single optical unit without specific points of interest. That’s why bodybuilders look beefier in white and light-colored shirts. All those shadows— readily contrasted against the light-colored cloth—add depth to their musculature. This “darker is heavier” illusion is called apparent weight. And it’s simply a matter of choosing the right color to give you the weight perception you’re looking for. In an article in the American Journal of Psychology entitled “The Effect of Color on Apparent Size and Weight,” psychologists Warden and Flynn ran some tests. They put eight boxes—all the same size—in a glass display case. They had people randomly look at each box, in varying order, and asked them to rank the boxes according to how much they thought they weighed. Dr Pepper Snapple Group’s Barrelhead Sugar-Free Root Beer was advertised as full-bodied, draught-style root beer. When packaging experts Berni Corp. changed the background color on the cans of their sugar-free beverage to beige from blue, people reported that it tasted more like good-old-fashioned frosty-mug root beer, even though the recipe never changed. Similarly, consumers say that darker-colored orange drinks taste sweeter. Colors—if strongly associated with other products—can also confuse. In the beverage industry, for example, Coca-Cola “owns” the color red. When Berni Corp. designers changed Canada Dry’s sugar-free ginger ale can from red to green and white, sales shot up more than 25 percent. The red can had made consumers think “cola.” Because of its power to not only draw attention, but also alter perception in ways that even the experts can’t explain, ad agencies are hypersensitive to how they use color in their ads and packaging. It’s the power of white-wrap isolation. It’s another one of those littleknown and little-used agency secrets revealed by decades-old testing that can give your ad response a lift. Buy more ad space—say a half-page instead of a quarter—but instead of filling it with more copy and pictures, put your original quarterpage ad smack in the center of it, wrapping your ad with white space. Multiple experiments by researchers Poffenberger and Strong conclude that, for example, a white-wrapped quarter-page ad will get more attention than a fully fleshed-out half-page ad loaded with text and graphics. According to Strong, “If more than 60 percent is used, the increased cost will not be compensated by a corresponding increase in attention value. Furthermore, about 20 percent additional used as white space about the advertisement gives the greatest increase in effectiveness, cost considered.” Ad-Agency Secret #41: Give Yourself a “Cleverectomy” It’s frustrating. It’s the most colorful way I know to teach you this lesson. Scott: This headline stinks! “Powerful Web Pages Designed in 24 Hours by Famous Marketing Expert for $199” isn’t very creative! Drew: Agreed. Not at all. Scott: Well, can’t we do a little play on words, a pun, or give it a twist? Drew: Why give it a twist? Scott: To make it catchier. You know, so more people read it. Something like, “Only $250 Keeps You from Getting Caught in a Sticky Web on the Net.” Drew: [Suppressing a laugh] The purpose of your headline is not to be “catchy,” Scott. It’s to be effective. Being creative for the sake of being creative is a waste of time and money, and is a complete misunderstanding of the principles of creating a headline. Allowing yourself to be seduced by the thrill of creating a “clever” headline that will impress friends and family (but not your prospects) is a terrible mistake! Besides, that “Sticky Web” headline is ridiculous! It doesn’t tell the reader what you’re selling! And because 60 percent of people who read ads read only the headlines—they scan—you’ll lose at least 60 percent of your audience. I teach these ideas in my small-business audio seminar. Scott: I disagree. Major corporations create very catchy headlines and win awards for them all the time. Did you ever see the commercials during the Super Bowls? Very creative stuff. Drew: [Sigh] You’re right. They do win awards. And the Super Bowl commercials are very creative indeed. But “creative” does not mean “effective.” If you can develop a headline that contains all the elements of one that could be a potential winner, why would you want to junk it up by trying to be clever? Scott: Why not make it clever first, and then make it effective—that way you accomplish both things. The “Sticky Web” headline can get people curious to read more. Drew: But what happens to those who don’t get curious enough and don’t read any further than that headline? CA$HVERTISING 184 Scott: They weren’t prospects. Drew: Not true! They may have very well been prospects, but because they had no clue what you’re selling, they didn’t bother to read any further. You outright lost them! Scott: Yeah, well... Drew: Well nothing! Advertising is not supposed to be entertainment! You may be entertained by it, but that’s not its purpose. It’s not a creativity contest. It’s not meant to grace the walls of the Louvre in Paris. It’s also not poetry, comedy, or a riddle to be figured out. Advertising is not about winning awards for being tricky, off-the-wall, or ingenious. Advertising—plain and simple—is about selling products and services. It’s business communication with the goal to increase sales by interesting people enough in a product or service that they ultimately trade their money for it. Scott: But that doesn’t mean it has to be boring! Drew: Did I say anything about boring? It should always be interesting! But something doesn’t have to be clever or tricky to grab and hold a prospect’s attention. You don’t write copy to appeal to the masses that aren’t buyers for your product as a way to thank them for reading your ad! Scott: I still feel that we can do something more than simply state what we’re selling. Drew: Read it again, Scott. This headline does much more than just state what you’re selling. Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a highly specific, technical AI workflow for generating direct-response hooks, addressing the common failure of generic AI prompting by using an MCP to ground the LLM in scraped transcript data and precise grammatical analysis. modules: [ADC] topics: [copywriting, hook writing, AI workflows, Claude Desktop, Sandcastles MCP, prompt engineering, data analysis, direct response] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. the failure of generic AI hooks / explaining that standard LLMs are not optimized for short-form social data, resulting in generic copy, and why manual "copy-pasting" of viral hooks across niches fails due to mismatched psychology and formatting; the Hook Machine methodology / introducing a four-step process that combines hard social data (transcripts and metrics) with storytelling principles to generate original, high-performing hooks; technical setup / the requirement to use the Claude Desktop app and the Sandcastles Model Context Protocol (MCP) to build a data pipeline that automatically scrapes and analyzes video metrics and transcripts; automated competitive analysis / using the MCP to scrape the top 10 videos from the user's channel and three competitors, automatically filtering out personal vlogs and artificially inflated brand deals (below 2% engagement) to ensure pure hook data; sorting winners from losers / how the AI identifies natural "break points" in view counts to categorize the top videos as winners and the rest as losers, analyzing the differences to extract core hook principles; extracting psychological & grammatical patterns / generating a custom rubric by analyzing how winners frame concepts (e.g., attaching a concrete outcome to a constrained input) versus losers (e.g., using vague superlatives or delaying the payoff); the danger of cross-pollination / advising against mashing too many different competitors into one analysis, as combining distinct styles (e.g., a "yapper" vs. a concise speaker) dilutes the insights into an ineffective average; the hook grading and rewrite engine / inputting a new topic or draft hook into the established custom rubric, allowing Claude to grade the hook (e.g., giving a "B" for lacking specificity) and immediately generating optimized rewrites (e.g., adding a specific number or "dopamine ladder" reference).

Look for.

The Hook Machine Workflow: A technical AI process requiring the Claude Desktop app and the Sandcastles MCP to scrape competitor transcripts, sort winners from losers, and extract custom psychological and grammatical rules for hook writing.

Brand Deal Filtering: The crucial analytical rule to automatically screen out any video with below a 2% engagement rate, as these are likely paid brand deals whose artificially inflated view counts would corrupt the hook analysis data.

Winner vs. Loser Break Points: The method of evaluating a channel's top 10 videos by finding the natural drop-off in views (the "break point") to definitively isolate the true viral hooks from the average performers.

The Cross-Pollination Dilution: The warning that mashing too many different creator styles (e.g., a fast-paced editor vs. a slow storyteller) into a single AI analysis prompt will dilute the insights; it is better to build separate, creator-specific hook generators.

Skip. The promotional intro/outro regarding the creator's billion-view history, the request for "mustache chef" emojis in the comments, and the general "Wavy World" community plugs.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of AI and hooks), 85% growth (advanced prompt engineering, MCP integration, and algorithmic data analysis). Volume. ~400 words.

jobs.text:
10-MCR / paid social creative and content

Goes here. Paid social creative production, hook writing, direct response video frameworks, creator/UGC scripting, static ad design, messaging strategies, evaluating stages of awareness, identifying new ad formats/angles, advertorials, unique mechanisms, and creative strategist workflows.

Not here.

Paid advertising performance metrics, ROAS, scaling rules, bidding, or ad-platform specific attribution -> 11-ADC

Conversion rate optimization (CRO) on core website pages or general analytics -> 06-MEA

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details comprehensive direct-response copywriting masterclass strategies—emphasizing second-person ("you-focused") framing, simple conversational language, sentiment matching, email launch sequence structuring (the "triple close"), and sales page hero framing. modules: [MCR] topics: [creative strategy, messaging and positioning, video ads] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. creative strategy / Mastering direct-response copywriting principles for email sequences and sales pages. Eliminating first-person pronouns ("I", "me", "my", "we", "our") in favor of strict second-person ("you-focused") copywriting where the prospect remains the hero. Rejecting complex SAT-level vocabulary in favor of simple, conversational, and concrete language written at an accessible reading level. messaging and positioning / Utilizing sentiment matching by studying customer reviews and competitor feedback to uncover how prospects talk about their problems and desires. Structuring 10-day email launch sequences using distinct phases (introducing the product, short-win lessons, repurposed content, testimonials, FAQs, and a high-urgency "triple close" on closing day). video ads / Mapping out sales page architectures and PPC ad congruence. Ensuring full message match between social ad creative and landing page destination to eliminate bounce. Structuring hero sections with a compelling headline, subheadline, and primary call-to-action without mentioning product names prematurely.

Look for. The core copywriting rule regarding pronouns: eliminating first-person references ("I", "my") unless directly tied back to the reader, ensuring the customer stays the hero. The definition of sentiment matching: reviewing five-star and one-star customer testimonials to mirror the exact internal narrative prospects use to describe their problems. The structure of a 10-day email launch sequence: deploying value-driven lessons, repurposing content, addressing FAQs, and utilizing the high-converting "triple close" on the final day.

Skip. General consulting credentials, AMA finalist awards, or self-promotional coaching pitches.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 15 to 20.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the inner workings of the Google Ads auction algorithm (retrieval, elimination, ranking, and auction pricing) alongside advanced catalog expansion techniques ("surface area scaling") and simplified Performance Max configuration for e-commerce. modules: [ADC] topics: [algorithm mechanics, return on ad spend (ROAS), campaign setup and tracking] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. algorithm mechanics / Decoding Google Ads' internal four-step ranking process: retrieval (matching relevant ads), elimination (discarding non-viable entries based on the DOJ-disclosed ad score formula involving bids, predicted click-through rates [PCTR], and quality/experience penalties), ranking (ordering ads by ad score), and the auction (calculating dynamic cost-per-click [CPC] based on buyer intent and advertiser relevance). campaign setup and tracking / Structuring lean Performance Max (PMax) campaigns for e-commerce by removing distracting secondary placements (Gmail, Display, Maps, Discover) and focusing budget heavily on high-intent search and shopping. Leveraging automated bidding strategies like target ROAS (tROAS) or maximize conversion value only after baseline conversion histories are established. return on ad spend (ROAS) / Scaling e-commerce profitability through "surface area scaling"—multiplying product feed variations across diverse price tiers, image angles (targeting distinct buyer avatars), and keyword-stuffed titles. Maximizing impression share in top auction rankings to capture up to 40% of clicks from prime search positions.

Look for. The four core steps of the Google Ads algorithm: retrieval, elimination, ranking, and auction. The definition of "surface area scaling": duplicating product listings across distinct pricing tiers, lifestyle images, and keyword-rich titles to dominate multiple slots in search and shopping results. The formula for the ad score: a blend of bids, predicted click-through rates (PCTR), and a penalty variable (beta) reflecting user experience and landing page quality.

Skip. General personal background stories, college dorm room anecdotes, or vague agency promotional calls to action.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 15 to 20.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details advanced e-commerce scaling strategies via Google Ads and YouTube Ads—covering multi-tier campaign architectures, performance max execution, automated conversion tracking, AI-driven asset generation, and aggressive scaling through break-even unit economics and LTV expansion. modules: [ADC] topics: [campaign setup and tracking, algorithm mechanics, return on ad spend (ROAS)] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. campaign setup and tracking / Architecting a comprehensive e-commerce Google Ads and YouTube Ads ecosystem that blends top-of-funnel demand generation (Demand Gen, YouTube shorts/instream) with middle-of-funnel capture (Performance Max, Shopping) and bottom-of-funnel defense (Branded Search and Branded Shopping). Configuring advanced conversion tracking via Google Tag Manager, Shopify customer events, and server-side/enhanced conversion setups. algorithm mechanics / Leveraging Google's machine learning and automated bidding models (maximize conversion value, target ROAS, and absolute target impression share) while maintaining structural control through aggressive negative keyword lists, search-term pruning, and strict brand-exclusion isolation to prevent wasted budget on existing traffic. return on ad spend (ROAS) / Scaling ad spend based on break-even contribution margins, Average Order Value (AOV), and Customer Lifetime Value (LTV) rather than short-term front-end ROAS. Structuring campaigns to acquire new customers at break-even or slight losses on first purchase while capturing long-term profitability through automated backend retention and repeat-purchase flows.

Look for. The foundational prerequisite for running Google Ads successfully: having a proven, converting offer and product-market fit rather than treating Google as a magic fix for broken marketing. The structural rule for branded traffic isolation: strictly separating Branded Search and Branded Shopping campaigns from prospecting traffic to prevent algorithm distortion and ensure clean acquisition data. The scaling philosophy for high-growth e-commerce: scaling ad spend by evaluating break-even customer acquisition cost (CAC) against lifetime value (LTV) rather than restricting budgets to arbitrary front-end efficiency targets.

Skip. Promotional pitches for agency booking calls, software affiliate links, or generic marketing motivational commentary.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 15 to 20.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details Google Ads campaign strategies for e-commerce, covering campaign selection (Search and Shopping vs. Performance Max), product concentration, unit economics (AOV, LTV, margins), attribution tracking, and budget scaling. modules: [ADC] topics: [campaign setup and tracking, return on ad spend (ROAS), algorithm mechanics] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. campaign setup and tracking / Structuring Google Ads campaigns for e-commerce brands by starting with intuitive Search and Shopping (text and product carousel) campaigns before layering in Performance Max once the account reaches a baseline volume of conversions (ideally 100+ purchases). Utilizing proper attribution and tracking tools (such as Hyros) to maintain clear visibility into cross-platform lead and purchase data. return on ad spend (ROAS) / Evaluating and managing e-commerce unit economics. Balancing Average Order Value (AOV), gross profit margins, and Customer Lifetime Value (LTV) to determine sustainable customer acquisition costs (CAC). Leveraging backend repeat purchases and high-LTV models (such as subscription or consumable ecosystems) to afford higher initial acquisition costs and enable aggressive campaign scaling. algorithm mechanics / Managing product catalog focus and algorithmic bidding. Avoiding fragmented ad spend across too many SKUs on cold traffic; instead, isolating winning product heroes to feed the Google Ads algorithm clean conversion data. Deploying broad product catalogs and remarketing dynamic product ads selectively to warm audiences who have already interacted with the site.

Look for. The recommended starting campaign types for e-commerce on Google Ads: Search and Shopping campaigns because they are intuitive and easy to manage before introducing automated Performance Max campaigns. The baseline conversion threshold for adding Performance Max: at least 100 purchases in the ad account to provide sufficient machine-learning data. The core principle of product focus for cold traffic: concentrating ad spend on a single or select few winning products rather than spreading budgets thinly across an entire catalog of SKUs.

Skip. Promotional pitches for agency management services or tracking software affiliate links.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 15 to 20.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the technical mechanics of the Meta Ads algorithm in 2026, explaining how vector-based targeting, machine learning updates (Andromeda, Lattice, GEM), auction bidding, signal quality, and account consolidation directly dictate ad delivery and performance. modules: [ADC] topics: [campaign setup and tracking, algorithms and auction dynamics, scaling] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. campaign setup and tracking / Restructuring Meta ad accounts by abandoning deprecated interest and lookalike targeting in favor of "broad targeting with exclusions." Consolidating campaigns and ad sets to prevent data siloing, thereby feeding unified conversion data to the machine learning models. Ensuring high Event Match Quality (EMQ) via the Conversions API (CAPI) to accurately pass conversion data back to Meta, which directly improves the Estimated Action Rate and lowers CPMs. algorithms and auction dynamics / Deconstructing the 200-millisecond Meta auction into three distinct phases: Retrieval (the Andromeda algorithm scanning tens of millions of ads to shortlist a few thousand), Ranking (the Lattice algorithm scoring relevance), and the final Auction. Understanding that targeting is now vector-based (mapping users in high-dimensional space based on organic and paid interactions) rather than label-based. Recognizing the "Entity ID trap": if ads are too similar, the GEM algorithm groups them under one Entity ID, restricting unique reach and serving variations to the exact same cluster of users. scaling / Winning the Meta auction at scale by recognizing that the bid equation (Bid × Estimated Action Rate + Ad Quality) is fundamentally an economic competition. Leveraging superior unit economics—higher Average Order Value (AOV), strong LTV, and optimized gross margins—to sustain higher bids and out-scale competitors, rather than relying on tactical platform hacks. Understanding that Estimated Action Rate and Ad Quality are diagnostic metrics (rearview indicators) and that true scaling requires feeding diverse creative concepts to the algorithm to map to net-new audience clusters.

Look for. The definition of vector-based targeting: Meta plotting users and creatives in a high-dimensional space based on continuous interactions, replacing static interest labels. The three stages of the Meta ad delivery system: Retrieval, Ranking, and the Auction. The "Entity ID trap": when Meta's algorithm scans similar ads and groups them into a single entity, limiting their delivery to the exact same audience cluster. The primary driver of winning the auction: superior unit economics allowing for a higher sustainable bid, outperforming competitors regardless of minor platform tactics.

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a free account audit with Blue Sense Digital or recruitment calls for performance marketers.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Deconstructs Eugene Schwartz's Five Stages of Awareness applied to Meta Ads, detailing how to script and design creatives that match the user's specific mindset (from Unaware to Most Aware) to prevent ad accounts from getting stuck in high-frequency retargeting loops. modules: [MCR] topics: [messaging and positioning, creative strategy, static ad design] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. messaging and positioning / Applying the Five Stages of Customer Awareness (Unaware, Problem Aware, Solution Aware, Product Aware, Most Aware) to paid social ad scripting. Demonstrating that to reach cold audiences (Unaware/Problem Aware), ads must utilize pattern interrupts and problem agitation before introducing the product, whereas bottom-of-funnel ads (Product/Most Aware) can rely on proof, risk reversals, and offers. Warning against the common mistake of mixing stages within a single ad—such as pairing a Product Aware static image with Problem Aware body copy—which causes the creative to fail across all audiences. creative strategy / Managing creative volume across the marketing funnel by intentionally allocating 80% of ad production to the top stages (Unaware and Problem Aware) to scale, 10% to the middle (Solution Aware), and 10% to the bottom (Product/Most Aware). Understanding how Meta's Andromeda algorithm reads creative intent to determine targeting; if an account only produces Product Aware ads, the algorithm will restrict delivery to warm audiences, artificially inflating frequency and preventing the account from scaling to cold traffic regardless of targeting settings. static ad design / Executing top-of-funnel static ads that target Unaware audiences by using curiosity-driven imagery combined with long-form storytelling copy. Highlighting examples where a seemingly unrelated or vague image (e.g., a ring camera screenshot) forces the user to read the primary text, which then pulls them through an extensive problem-agitation narrative before redirecting to an advertorial landing page, bypassing the limitations of standard static ad real estate.

Look for. The definition of the Unaware stage of awareness: the user does not know they have a problem, requiring the ad to use a bold claim and pattern interrupt to reframe their thinking before any problem agitation can occur. The recommended distribution of creative volume: 80% of volume focused on Unaware/Problem Aware, 10% on Solution Aware, and 10% on Product/Most Aware. The definition of the "product awareness curve": the psychological trajectory of an ad where the viewer's awareness that they are being sold to should rise slowly over the course of the video, avoiding aggressive spikes or "bridges" into hard calls to action. The primary reason high-frequency issues occur in broad ad sets: the account is only producing Product Aware creatives, so Meta's algorithm refuses to push them to cold audiences and instead repeatedly serves them to the warm retargeting pool.

Skip. Nothing.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 10 to 15.

Topics. attribution and modeling / Deconstructing deceptive Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) metrics within Meta Advantage+ campaigns by demonstrating how a seemingly strong 13x ROAS often masks poor performance (e.g., a 1.7x incremental ROAS) once analyzed through the lens of audience breakdowns (existing vs. new customers) and attribution settings (7-day click vs. 1-day view). Differentiating between a true Conversion Lift Test (a geo-holdout experiment based on difference-in-difference design) and Meta's "incremental attribution" setting (an algorithmic estimate based on aggregated competitor data), advising against using the latter for campaign optimization. campaign setup and tracking / Establishing strict account structure guidelines to prevent top-of-funnel scaling campaigns from cannibalizing retargeting audiences. Mandating the use of a 7-day click attribution setting for optimization (ignoring view-throughs) and explicitly excluding existing customers from cold campaigns (with specific nuances for lapsed customers, e.g., excluding 2-year purchasers). Recommending that scaling efforts be measured against top-line revenue impact—specifically, new customer sales at the individual SKU level—rather than relying solely on in-platform ROAS.

Look for. The primary reason a top-spending ad in an Advantage+ campaign might actually be performing poorly: it is over-allocating budget to existing customers and relying heavily on 1-day view-through conversions rather than driving incremental new customers. The recommended attribution setting for campaign optimization: 7-day click. The distinction between a Meta Conversion Lift Test and Meta's "incremental attribution" setting: a lift test is a true holdout experiment, whereas the incremental setting is merely an algorithmic estimate based on competitor averages. The primary method to verify ad scaling success: measuring top-line new customer sales at the specific SKU level in Shopify.

Skip. General complaints about other agencies misinterpreting data.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 5 to 10.

Sounds pretty obvious, but exclude existing customers from your cold campaigns. Now, there are caveats here. For example, what about customers that haven't bought in 2 years? Topics. campaign setup and tracking / Architecting Meta ad accounts to support high-volume creative testing without oversegmenting or overconsolidating (e.g., avoiding the mistake of dumping all ads into a single Advantage+ campaign). Defining segmentation layers at the campaign level based on business complexity (e.g., distinct product categories with differing gross margins and budget caps) and at the adset level based on creative concepts (e.g., "persona + angle + offer"). Rejecting basic adset segmentation by "launch date" (which confuses the targeting algorithm) in favor of structuring adsets by concept to ensure clear, reliable performance data. algorithms and auction dynamics / Managing the Meta algorithm's inherent limitations regarding last-click attribution at the individual ad level, which falsely penalizes top-of-funnel creative while over-crediting bottom-of-funnel follow-up ads within a multi-touch sequence. Shifting the primary feedback loop and KPI evaluation from the ad level up to the adset level to mitigate this attribution distortion, using ad spend as a proxy for algorithmic success. Understanding how the Andromeda algorithm isolates learning within distinct adsets, meaning that grouping conflicting personas (e.g., men’s and women’s apparel) in one adset degrades delivery efficiency. scaling / Executing budget scaling and creative volume forecasting through structured adset management. Applying Pareto's principle to anticipate that 20% of concepts will command 80% of the spend, then utilizing that data to either double down on the winning concept's creative output (producing 120 variations instead of 50) or applying a maximum spend limit (e.g., 40%) to mitigate the business risk of overleveraging a single angle.

Look for. The primary flaw of evaluating performance at the individual ad level: Meta attributes via last-click, which masks the multi-ad customer journey and creates unreliable data for top-of-funnel creatives. The optimal level to evaluate creative performance and make budget decisions: the adset level. The definition of a "concept" for adset grouping: Persona + Angle + Offer. The fundamental rule of how Meta's algorithm learns within an account: each adset learns in isolation, meaning grouping unrelated creatives (e.g., men's and women's apparel) confuses the targeting model.

Skip. General complaints about generic agency coaching groups teaching universal account structures.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 10 to 15.

Here's how to structure your ad account for high volume creative. Everyone wants to test more. Everyone wants to put more creative in the account, but it causes one of two things. You either oversegment or you overconolidate. And both put you in a bad position because the goal isn't just to launch more ads, but it's to build an account structure that lets you test fast without destroying spend efficiency and while still getting learnings that you can feed back into future creative design. Common mistakes is people make way too many campaigns. They force budget way too thin across so many tests. You see this all the time. People test a hundred things but learn nothing. They judge ads too quickly when they really only spent$1 or $2. And they use one fully consolidated campaign and they just say, "Hey, Meta will figure it out." I see a lot of this these days. Hey, just run one Advantage Plus campaign and just put all your ads in there. Terrible idea. So, let's break down how you should be thinking through this problem and how you should be structuring your account. Step number one is we need to understand the complexity of the business because the complexity of the ad account is a product of the complexity of the business. If you sell one product to one persona and you're relatively small, maybe you can get away with just one advantage plus campaign where you're dropping asset, fair enough. But if you're two products, three products, if you have some complexity in the personas that you're targeting, if you have a really high volume of creative, which if you're watching this, this is the whole point of this video. Well, if product categories are treated meaningfully differently, what you then have to start to consider here is different product categories have different gross margin both in dollar value and percentages. They have different target demographics and they have different budgets in targeting particularly in large retail businesses. Now, why this is important is because segmentation allows us to do two things. It allows us to control budgets and it allows us to KPI better at the adset level. And so if you have a lot of different product categories, it makes sense to introduce some campaign level segmentation for those different product categories because they might have different KPIs. They might need different budgets. They might be treated differently by the business. And so if you have any of these things, you want to be thinking, okay, we should probably introduce a degree of segmentation at the campaign level here to be able to accommodate. Step number two is what variable do we want to gain insights on? Now probably doesn't make much sense. So let me explain. The reliability of rorowaz declines as you move down the account structure. When you look at campaign level rorowaz with 7-day click it's relatively reliable. It correlates to acquisition me in the business quite well. Once you go to the adset level becomes a little bit less reliable and once you're all the way down at the ad level it's very unreliable. The reason why it's very unreliable is because meta attributes based on last click despite meta optimizing across multi-click. So this ends up causing a lot of confusion where you're trying to optimize at the ad level. Let me give you an example. Two ads sorting by spend. Why is the highest spending ad here have a lower rorowaz? Why is meta putting spend here? Why wouldn't be putting spend into this second ad? Makes no sense. Why? What do we do in this circumstance? Firstly, do we turn the top one off? Do we go and take the second one and launch it in a second ads set? What do we do? How do we interpret the data? Well, we can't because it's unreliable. Now, why is it unreliable? Well, because we know that almost no one buys after one impression. And so if no one buys after one impression and it typically takes multiple different ads serving to you, potentially even multiple different clicks and all of the attribution just goes to the final click in the customer journey. Well then yes, this ad right here is doing well, but it might just be taking all the credit. But for most people watching this, you're probably spending at least $10,000 a month. In which case, don't run this. Doesn't make much sense. Okay. Well, what else can we do? But on dresses, oh sorry on tops we know we have to have a higher return on ad spend. And so then that indicates our spend distribution and our creative volume throughput on each of these adsets. For sure this is a good option. We do this sometimes. However, often this can just be done at the campaign level. It depends really on the complexity of the business. So running the same structure across everyone's accounts makes no sense at all. It should be bespoke to your individual commercial needs and outcomes. However, there's really two critical components that every single account structure requires. Number one, you now you need to be able to read data to make decisions effectively. And that data must have data integrity. You may have a specific segment of the m of the product category like your core range that needs to hit specific budgets. therefore needs a specific amount of spend behind it. The rule that tests must run on custom landing pages with isolated cold traffic (e.g., Meta only) to avoid contamination from email/warm channels. The common invalidation of "peeking": checking tests daily and stopping them immediately when a false positive appears.

The argument that Conversion Rate is a vanity metric and should be replaced by Revenue Per Visitor (RPV), which belongs in 06-MEA.

07-LPG / landing pages and funnels Goes here. A breakdown of Alex Hormozi's approach to Conversion Rate Optimization (CRO) and landing page design. Covers the financial impact of CRO, systematic A/B testing (specifically "above the fold"), and applying the "Value Equation" (Dream Outcome, Perceived Likelihood of Achievement, Time Delay, and Effort/Sacrifice) to landing page copy and layout. Not here. • Paid media campaign setup or ad account scaling -> 06-MEA • Brand strategy, logo design, or foundational positioning -> 04-BRD

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details how to directly apply a well-known behavioral framework (The Value Equation) to specific landing page elements, demonstrating how to systematically test and optimize the "above the fold" section to maximize ROI on ad spend. modules: [LPG] topics: [conversion rate optimization, landing pages, Alex Hormozi, Value Equation, A/B testing, above the fold, copywriting, B2B landing pages, e-commerce landing pages] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. the ROI of CRO / explaining that as ad costs (CPMs and CPCs) rise across Meta, TikTok, and Google, doubling the conversion rate is mathematically superior and more cost-effective than attempting to double traffic; systematic A/B testing / the importance of testing only one element per week to compound wins over time, using an AB testing calculator to ensure statistical significance for low-traffic sites; optimizing the "above the fold" / why the topmost section of a landing page is the highest-leverage area to test (since 100% of visitors see it and 60% never scroll past it), focusing primarily on testing the headline and the hero image; headline copywriting / ensuring the headline answers "who you are, what you do, and what's in it for me" in under 5 seconds, using the "so that" principle to arrive at the deepest customer benefit; the Value Equation on landing pages / translating Hormozi's four-part framework into page elements: (1) Dream Outcome: explicitly stating the end goal in the main headline; (2) Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (Risk): using trust badges, guarantees, and testimonials below the CTA to de-risk the purchase; (3) Time Delay: quantifying how fast the user will get results or receive the product (e.g., "Get funded fast" or "Ships in 24 hours"); (4) Effort and Sacrifice: writing copy that highlights "done-for-you" aspects or emphasizes how the product eliminates manual labor (e.g., "We reach out to thousands of influencers so you don't have to").

Look for.

The "Above the Fold" Rule: The statistical reality that 100% of visitors see the top of a page, but 60% never scroll down, making the main headline and hero image the most profitable elements to split-test.

The "So That" Principle: A copywriting technique to find the true Dream Outcome by asking "so that..." multiple times (e.g., "Warm up your emails so that you land in the inbox so that you close more deals").

The Value Equation Mapping: How to map Hormozi's framework directly to page elements: Dream Outcome (Headline), Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (Trust badges/guarantees under the CTA button), Time Delay (Shipping or result timelines), and Effort/Sacrifice (Copy explicitly stating what the user won't have to do).

Skip. Mentions of Microsoft Clarity, general complaints about rising ad costs on Meta/TikTok, and the podcast host's promotional intro/outro to other videos.

Scope mix. 20% baseline (general CRO definitions), 80% growth (advanced landing page psychology, specific A/B testing methodologies, and applying the Value Equation to UX design). Volume. ~400 words.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a tactical scaling playbook for Meta ads under the Andromeda algorithm, emphasizing the superiority of high-volume static creatives over VSLs, broad targeting mechanics, and optimizing for net free cash flow over vanity ROAS percentages. modules: [ADC] topics: [campaign setup and tracking, algorithm mechanics, return on ad spend (ROAS)] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. campaign setup and tracking / Scaling Meta ad campaigns by utilizing the "winning format clone" strategy and "zombie campaigns." Extracting winning ad variables (copy and creative) and feeding them into an LLM to generate hundreds of micro-variations tailored to specific demographic segments (e.g., 25-year-old women vs. 30-year-old women). Placing these variations into a Campaign Budget Optimization (CBO) structure to let the algorithm determine the winner. Reviving high-conviction ads that received zero initial spend by placing them into isolated "zombie campaigns" to force delivery and extract additional winning creatives. algorithm mechanics / Navigating the Meta Andromeda algorithm's preference for ad volume and specific targeting inputs. Countering the popular reliance on highly produced Video Sales Letters (VSLs) by pivoting to high-volume static ads, as Meta's algorithm favors statics due to its ability to serve a higher quantity per user session without causing ad fatigue. Demonstrating how inserting hyper-specific "identity triggers" or category keywords (e.g., "dental leads," "lawyer leads") directly into the ad copy and headline trains the algorithm to locate previously unreachable buyer pockets, completely replacing the need for manual backend interest stacking (i.e., broad targeting). return on ad spend (ROAS) / Shifting optimization strategies away from vanity platform ROAS percentages to focus entirely on blended net free cash flow. Identifying the business's break-even ROAS and scaling ad spend aggressively up to that maximum threshold to acquire market share. Explaining that while scaling may compress ROAS (e.g., from 15x down to 5x), the absolute volume of net cash generated from spending $100,000 versus $1,000 is the true driver of business growth.

Look for. The primary reason static ads currently outperform high-production VSLs on Meta: Meta's algorithm (Andromeda) can serve a much higher volume of statics per user session without causing ad fatigue. The definition of an "identity trigger": inserting a specific demographic or category keyword directly into the ad copy to feed the algorithm, replacing backend interest targeting. The definition of a "zombie campaign": an isolated ad set specifically designed to force spend on high-conviction ads that were ignored by the algorithm in the primary CBO campaign. The primary metric to scale against: net free cash flow and blended ROAS, rather than platform-specific ROAS percentages.

Skip. Promotional pitches to use the speaker's AI platform (Kong) for generating ad headlines.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 10 to 15.

why: Details fundamental copywriting and creative positioning principles—such as the three rules of visualization, falsifiability, and distinctiveness—alongside strategic copy frameworks used to craft high-converting static ads and marketing hooks.

modules: [MCR]

topics: [creative strategy, messaging and positioning]

tier: 2

scope_hint: core

Topics.

creative strategy / Applying the three core rules of high-performance copywriting to ad creative: visualizability (moving from abstract terms to concrete, mental images), falsifiability (writing statements that can be proven true or false rather than relying on empty adjectives), and distinctiveness (ensuring the copy uses positioning that competitors cannot replicate). Leveraging structured copywriting frameworks and visual hierarchy (such as layout parity with classic print ads) to craft stopping power for static ad creatives.

messaging and positioning / Utilizing precise messaging, contrast, and conflict to drive consumer decision-making. Shifting from vague feature-listing to concrete value communication by framing copy around clear arguments, distinct customer pain points, and memorable metaphors or analogies that instantly communicate a product's utility within seconds.

Look for.

The three fundamental rules of high-converting copy: "Can I visualize it?", "Can I falsify it?", and "Can nobody else say this?". The definition of moving from abstract to concrete: replacing vague qualitative adjectives with tangible objects or scenarios that a reader can mentally picture. The strategic value of distinctiveness: forcing copy to take a hard positioning stance that competitors cannot legitimately sign their name to.

Skip.

General podcast commentary or platform-specific ad account button-pushing guides.

Scope mix.

Almost all core.

Volume.

10 to 15.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details timeless direct-response advertising principles from Claude C. Hopkins' Scientific Advertising—focusing on ad-agency science, salesmanship-in-print, offering service over boasting, using specific facts, telling the full story, and employing traceable testing (coupons/samples) to optimize copy. modules: [MCR] topics: [creative strategy, messaging and positioning, video ads] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. creative strategy / Treating advertising as multiplied salesmanship-in-print rather than entertainment, literary art, or general brand awareness. Grounding creative strategy in scientific fundamentals and traced returns (keyed ads and coupons) rather than whims and fancies. Offering wanted information and service rather than empty boasts, using precise mail-order design principles (economy of space, small type, direct utility pictures), and avoiding negative advertising in favor of positive, bright-side appeals. messaging and positioning / Writing copy by placing yourself in the position of a typical buyer, addressing their selfish interests and desire for service, utility, or problem resolution. Eliminating platitudes and generalities in favor of extreme specificity (using exact figures, test results, and concrete details like percentages or formulas) to build instant consumer trust and authority. Telling the full story in every ad under the principle that "the more you tell, the more you sell," ensuring no important sales argument is omitted for unconverted prospects. video ads / Structuring long-form sales copy and video scripts around the functional laws of direct salesmanship. Utilizing precise headlines that pick out and hail only the interested target audience, employing curiosity and service-oriented offers (samples, approvals, trials) to induce immediate consumer action, and designing individualized personalities and distinctiveness into promotional assets.

Look for. The core definition of advertising from Hopkins: advertising is salesmanship-in-print, governed entirely by the rules of personal salesmanship and evaluated strictly by sales results. The strategic purpose of headlines: to pick out and attract only the specific percentage of readers who can be interested in the product, acting like a direct hail in a crowd. The principle of specific facts: replacing weak generalities and superlatives ("best in the world") with precise, verifiable claims ("softens the beard in one minute") to command belief.

Skip. General book forward commentary, historical printing metrics (e.g., 2-cent postage stamps), or out-of-date turn-of-the-century product examples (e.g., specific incubator or bicycle models) that do not translate to modern direct-response frameworks.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 15 to 20.
