13-ORG / organic content Goes here. An in-depth masterclass by Nicolas Cole on content strategy and writing in the AI era. It explores why generic writing becomes worthless ("AI slop"), the concept of "language as open source," the three tiers of content (commodity, personality, original), how to build a personal "digital brain" or personal language model (PLM), and how to leverage AI to repeat and remix approved thinking rather than generate net-new ideas. Not here. • Paid media campaign setup, Facebook Ads Manager, or ROAS optimization -> 10-MCR • Long-form direct-response sales letter copywriting or advertorial funnels -> 07-LPG • Email automation sequences or SMS flows -> 14-EML

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a foundational philosophy and tactical framework for writing, personal branding, and organic content in the AI era, focusing on building an owned "digital brain" (personal language model) to avoid generic commodity slop and achieve compounding organic leverage. modules: [ORG] topics: [content strategy, AI writing, digital brain, personal language model, copywriting, organic social media, content moats, thought leadership, storytelling] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. points of view as software and content moats / debunking the claim that SaaS or content has no moat in the AI era; explaining that a distinct "point of view" (a proprietary methodology or lens) forces competitors into perpetual catch-up mode; language as open source / examining how vocabulary, letters, and common sentence combinations are public domain, meaning true ownership in writing is merely "association" achieved via repetition and volume; the three tiers of content / delineating between (1) Commodity Content (universal, baseline facts like "eat healthy to lose weight"), (2) Personality Content (anchored in specific, unmade personal data points and identity details), and (3) Original Content (rare, distilled paradigms that fundamentally shift a category after years of deep crystallization); the "I" vs. "You" writing frame / how shifting from prescriptive second-person ("You should do X") to first-person experience ("I did X / I think X") instantly elevates copy from generic commodity advice to high-affinity personality content; the AI slop paradox & unmade datasets / defining "AI slop" as generic commodity output created because LLMs share the same training data; the human's role is to manually author their own "unmade dataset" (formative stories, unique failures, personal viewpoints) so AI has proprietary material to work with; robots repeat, humans write / the core paradigm that humans should do the heavy lifting of original thinking and writing, while AI agents should be restricted to repeating, remixing, and re-formatting "approved language" across platforms; timely vs. timeless content / balancing the content portfolio between hyper-timely posts (high 24-hour spike, zero long-term retention) and timeless essays (compounding assets that feed the digital brain for a decade); deconstructing voice and style / demystifying "voice" into measurable variables: specific word choice, adjective swapping, sentence length, and rhythmic pacing; the company brain as enterprise infrastructure / why modern companies must hire dedicated writers/thinkers to build central content libraries ("company brains") that feed automated social distribution pipelines.

Look for.

The Three Tiers of Content: The hierarchical framework classifying writing into Commodity Content (rehashed shared facts), Personality Content (grounded in personal biography and specific unmade datasets), and Original Content (novel category-defining insights).

"Robots Repeat, Humans Write": The operational rule that content creators should never outsource net-new thinking or initial phrasing to AI; instead, creators produce "approved language" and use AI strictly to remix, re-swizzle, and cross-post those validated ideas.

The Unmade Data Set: The concept that everyone uses the same LLMs trained on the same internet corpus, meaning a creator's only genuine moat is their proprietary personal history, specific failures, and unshared lessons.

The "I" Perspective Shift: The copywriting heuristic that writing from "I" ("I tested," "I believe") immediately produces personality content, whereas writing from "You" ("You need to," "You should") defaults to patronizing commodity advice.

Skip. The promotional intro sponsor read for Brex, personal banter about playing World of Warcraft, specific mentions of the host's agency LCA, and promotional plugs for TypeShare and the Ship 30 for 30 cohort.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of content marketing and social volume), 85% growth (intellectual property frameworks, LLM mechanics, voice deconstruction, and personal language modeling). Volume. ~400 words.

13-ORG / organic content Goes here. A framework for creating viral, story-driven organic and paid social media content. It covers the psychology of storytelling (neural coupling), identifying powerful narrative angles, "frame swiping" from out-of-niche competitors, and scaling content production to remove the founder bottleneck. Not here. • Paid media technical campaign setup or ad account scaling -> 10-MCR • Automated email marketing flows or SMS strategies -> 14-EML

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a specific, story-centric approach to organic and paid creative strategy, moving beyond generic hooks to explain the psychological necessity of storytelling and providing a structured method for ethically swiping and scaling creative formats. modules: [ORG] topics: [organic social media, storytelling, neural coupling, frame swiping, content scaling, open loops, Zeigarnik effect, emotional triggers, Founder Constraint] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. the power of storytelling (neural coupling) / explaining the neuroscience behind why stories go viral and drive sales: while facts only activate two areas of the brain, stories trigger "neural coupling" (activating the motor cortex or amygdala), making the content visceral and memorable; the old vs. new creative formula / discarding the outdated "Hook -> Body -> CTA" model in favor of the new formula: "Frame Swipe -> Create a Story -> Scale"; emotional triggers for virality / identifying the core emotions that drive shares and sales, including moral outrage, belonging, confusion, and visual shock, and pairing them with specific story angles (e.g., exposing counterfeiters to trigger moral outrage and drive $1M+ in sales); finding your viral story / prompting founders to uncover hidden narratives by asking: "What does everyone think is true about my product, but isn't?", "What is a controversial aspect of my industry?", and "What is the most inspiring customer success story?"; the "Frame Swiping" methodology / a structured process for ethically stealing content formats from out-of-niche competitors by breaking videos down into micro-elements: pacing, location, audio cues, text placement, lighting, and the viewer's emotional state (e.g., taking the pacing and camera angles of an e-commerce teeth whitening ad and applying them to a clothing brand); mastering the "Open Loop" (Zeigarnik Effect) / utilizing the psychological principle that humans remember incomplete tasks by opening a loop in the first sentence (e.g., "What's the secret to these plaques?") and refusing to close it immediately, forcing the viewer to watch the entire video; powerful language / replacing weak, corporate descriptions with exaggerated, emotionally charged language (e.g., changing "Here is a problem with ice baths" to "This is a national ice bath crisis") to trigger algorithmic prioritization; removing the "Founder Constraint" / diagnosing why sales plateau when founders burn out on content creation, and providing a playbook for scaling: hiring native creators (influencers/videographers with proven views, not corporate social media managers), building massive centralized Google Drive footage archives, and utilizing overseas editors incentivized by performance; life extension of viral assets / multiplying the ROI of a single successful story by altering its format (e.g., changing the hook, converting it to an AI voiceover, or translating a video script into a text carousel) and posting it across multiple brand or fan accounts.

Look for.

Neural Coupling: The neuroscientific concept that telling a story activates the viewer's motor cortex and amygdala, making the content visceral and memorable, whereas stating facts only activates the language processing centers.

The Zeigarnik Effect (Open Loops): The psychological principle that humans are wired to remember incomplete tasks or unresolved mysteries. In content, this means opening a loop in the first three seconds and deliberately withholding the answer until the end of the video.

Frame Swiping: The ethical method of analyzing an out-of-niche viral video by dissecting its structural elements (pacing, location, audio cues, visual text, and the viewer's emotional state) and applying that exact framework to your own product.

The Founder Constraint: The operational bottleneck where a brand's sales volume is entirely dependent on the founder's daily capacity to film content, necessitating a shift to hired creators, centralized footage drives, and overseas editors.

Skip. The intro hook regarding 7.5 billion impressions and comparing the speaker's reach to the 1970s New York Times.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of hooks and CTAs), 85% growth (advanced storytelling psychology, structured swiping frameworks, and operational scaling). Volume. ~450 words.

identifying the gap / using the Creator DNA to find a unique point of view or missing perspective in the proven competitive research, turning generic trends into proprietary content; visual professionalism / debunking the myth that "raw and authentic" means poor quality, emphasizing that practical background lights and a dedicated key light (e.g., a cheap softbox) are necessary to stop the scroll and lend credibility to the hook; conversational hook writing / abandoning obnoxious, "clever" marketing hooks (e.g., "3 mistakes you're making...") in favor of natural, conversational openers that bypass the viewer's psychological ad-blocker (e.g., "Did you know if you add oats..."); content batching / dividing the workflow into discrete stages—researching, writing 10-20 scripts in one sitting, and filming them back-to-back on a separate day—to eliminate the friction of daily overthinking; macro analytics / advising creators to ignore individual video flops and instead look for patterns across weeks of content to identify which specific formats drive views, which drive followers, and which drive deep engagement; owning the audience via lead magnets / shifting focus away from brand sponsorships and towards using automation tools like ManyChat (e.g., "Comment the word SEARCH") to deliver a free resource, moving organic viewers onto an owned email list where high-ticket sales occur.

Look for.

The Stranger-First Algorithm: The algorithmic reality that Instagram tests content on non-followers first. If strangers immediately swipe away, the Reel's reach dies, regardless of how much existing followers might like it.

The Creator DNA Formula: A fill-in-the-blank positioning statement: "I am [X]. I do [Y] for people who [Z]. And you should listen to me because [Proof/Authority]."

Conversational Hooks: The shift away from loud, generic hooks ("Stop doing this!") to natural, conversational openers ("Did you know if you...") that bypass the user's psychological resistance to being marketed to.

The ManyChat Lead Magnet Funnel: The explicit strategy of creating a free resource (e.g., a PDF blueprint) and asking viewers to comment a specific keyword on the Reel, triggering a ManyChat automation that delivers the resource in exchange for their email address.

Skip. The promotional intro hooks about $100k Reels, plugs for the creator's AI tool and mentorship program, and the outro teasing the next video.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (basic definitions of Reels and lead magnets), 85% growth (advanced algorithmic heuristics, conversational copywriting, and automated funnel mechanics). Volume. ~400 words.

Balancing email campaign frequency (recommending 3 to 4 campaigns weekly to maintain top-of-mind awareness without inducing list fatigue) and categorizing campaign content into seven key buckets (promotions, holidays, product launches, highlights, social proof, value/education, and company updates). Klaviyo flows / Architecting core automated email sequences. Building front-loaded Welcome Series flows (deploying two emails on day zero within the critical 72-hour purchase window), Browse Abandonment sequences (focusing on mid-funnel trust and objection handling rather than immediate discounts), Abandoned Cart/Checkout flows (using strategic non-buyer vs. returning customer splits), and Post-Purchase sequences (minimizing buyer's remorse and driving repeat purchases within 30 days). list growth / Optimizing website signup forms to lift conversion rates from the 1-3% industry standard to an 8-12% target. Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a complete content and copywriting framework for e-commerce email campaigns, providing actionable strategies for overcoming 3-second attention spans using infographics, text-based emails, and AI-assisted topic generation. modules: [EML] topics: [email marketing, non-discount campaigns, microtopics, copywriting, ChatGPT prompts, email sending frequency, e-commerce strategy, text-based emails, infographics] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. market evolution / explaining the shift from the high-spending 2020 e-commerce boom to the skeptical, saturated market of 2024-2026, necessitating trust-building through email content rather than just paid ads; the trust threshold / the concept that cold traffic requires multiple content touchpoints before converting, making email the most cost-effective channel for repeated brand exposure; sending frequency / advocating for a 3-4 times per week sending cadence to stay top-of-mind and build a dopamine-driven opening habit without causing list fatigue or high unsubscribe rates; microtopics / the strategy of breaking down broad macro topics (e.g., "holistic health") into hyper-specific, single-takeaway emails (e.g., "how adaptogens manage stress") to accommodate short attention spans; AI ideation and copywriting / utilizing ChatGPT with specific priming prompts (detailing brand voice, target audience, and unique selling propositions) to generate hundreds of microtopic ideas and draft structural copy; email formatting ratios / recommending a strategic mix of graphic-based to text-based emails (typically a 3:1 or 4:1 ratio), noting that plain-text emails from the founder often yield the highest engagement; copywriting principles / adhering to rules making emails Skimmable (no text blocks, bold main points), Clear & Concise (one takeaway, short), and Engaging (punchy, informational); infographics as copy / substituting dense paragraphs with checklists, icon graphics, feature diagrams, timelines, and comparison charts to visually communicate value propositions in seconds.

Look for.

The 3-4x Weekly Cadence: The specific recommendation that sending 3-4 non-discount, value-driven emails a week is the optimal frequency to maintain the "top-of-mind effect" and maximize revenue without burning the list.

The Microtopic Strategy: The copywriting framework of focusing on one specific problem, process, or solution per email rather than overwhelming the reader with a laundry list of product benefits.

The ChatGPT Priming Prompt: The exact two-step AI workflow: first, feeding the LLM all brand, product, and demographic context ("priming"), and second, instructing it to write a punchy headline, a sub-headline, and exactly 2-3 sentences of body copy leading to a CTA.

The 3-Second Attention Span: The design constraint recognizing that consumers do not read emails but skim them while multi-tasking, making infographics, bold headers, and short copy mandatory for conversion.

Skip. Plugs for the "inboxnewsletter.com" guide, promotional mentions of the creator's agency ("Well Copy"), and repetitive narration of scrolling through the custom ChatGPT interface.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (standard email marketing principles), 90% growth (advanced content strategy, AI prompt engineering, and conversion copywriting). Volume. ~400 words.

jobs.text:
09-EML / email and sms Goes here. A comprehensive masterclass on e-commerce email marketing and lifecycle automation (primarily built on Klaviyo and Figma). Covers high-converting pop-up form design (targeting 10%+ opt-in rates), foundational email flows (Welcome, Site Abandon, Browse Abandon, Cart vs. Checkout Abandon, Post-Purchase, Winback), non-discount campaign strategies (sending 3–4x weekly microtopics), inbox deliverability repair, advanced segmentation, and systematic A/B testing. Not here. • Paid media acquisition or cold traffic ad campaigns -> 06-MEA • Physical fulfillment, unboxing operations, or shipping logistics -> 21-OPS or 22-CXP

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the complete end-to-end framework for generating 20–40%+ of e-commerce store revenue through automated email flows and high-frequency, non-discount campaigns while maintaining high inbox deliverability. modules: [EML] topics: [email marketing, Klaviyo, email flows, cart abandonment, checkout abandonment, welcome series, post-purchase flows, deliverability, list building, pop-up forms, segmentation, copywriting] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. list growth & pop-up architecture / capturing 8–12% of traffic using large, mobile-optimized pop-ups (75%+ screen coverage) with a single input field, clear value proposition (e.g., dollars off for AOV >$100), 4–12 second time delay, and minimal copy; core lifecycle flows / building automated sequences that drive roughly 50% of total email revenue, specifically: Welcome (8 emails focusing on brand mission, USPS, and founder outreach), Site Abandon (1 email, best sellers), Browse Abandon (5 emails, dynamically pulling viewed items), and Winback (3 emails deployed at 2x the average order interval); Cart Abandonment vs. Checkout Abandonment / distinguishing between "Added to Cart" (custom JavaScript snippet required in Shopify) and "Checkout Started" (native integration), ensuring separate flows so top-of-funnel cart abandoners are not dropped; non-discount campaign engine / sending 3–4 non-promotional campaigns per week focused on a single "microtopic" (one feature, one benefit, or one FAQ) to build authority, stay top-of-mind, and preserve profit margins; flow optimization loop / using high-frequency email campaigns as an instant testing ground and cycling winning campaign angles directly into automated flows; email copywriting / writing skimmable, punchy, and concise copy (under two mobile scrolls) that uses bold headers and infographics (timelines, checklists, comparison tables) rather than dense text blocks; deliverability recovery protocol / executing a 6-week rehabilitation plan for sender reputations below 40% open rates by temporarily shutting non-essential flows and strictly sending 3x weekly to a 14-day engaged segment before gradually expanding to 30, 60, and 90 days; segmentation & suppression / maintaining list health by segmenting by engagement (30/60/90-day active), store behavior (VIPs, browse without purchase), and suppressing profiles with zero opens in 180 days or any hard bounce.

Look for.

Cart vs. Checkout Abandonment Separation: The critical technical distinction that "Added to Cart" requires an injected custom snippet into Shopify's liquid code and fires earlier than "Checkout Started"; treating them as identical drops up to 90% of cart abandoners.

The 6-Week Deliverability Rehabilitation Protocol: The specific step-by-step process of turning off non-essential flows and mailing exclusively to a 14-day engaged list 3x weekly until open rates hit 50%+, before incrementally widening to 30, 60, and 90 days.

The 10%+ Pop-up Blueprint: Form rules demanding single-input steps (never email + SMS on screen one), 4–12 second delay, hiding the standard top-right "X" to break reflexive closing habits, and using dollars-off rather than percentages if AOV is above $100.

The Microtopic Campaign Cadence: The strategy of sending 3–4 non-discount emails weekly by covering only one hyper-specific topic (e.g., an ingredient breakdown, myth vs. fact, or single customer review) to build a dopamine-driven opening habit without fatiguing the list with sales pitches.

Skip. Personal agency revenue disclaimers, video intro banter, self-promotional newsletter links (inboxnewsletter.com), and the live design/coding walkthrough in Figma/Klaviyo.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (standard Klaviyo setup and flow triggers), 85% growth (deliverability rehabilitation, non-discount retention frameworks, and advanced segmentation). Volume. ~450 words.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a foundational guide to SMS marketing for e-commerce, focusing on list growth via pop-ups, technical constraints (character limits, MMS costs), core automated flows, and structuring a balanced SMS campaign calendar. modules: [EML] topics: [SMS marketing, list growth, campaign strategy] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. SMS marketing / Navigating the technical and financial constraints of SMS marketing. Managing message frequency to prevent high unsubscribe rates (recommending 1–2 sends per week), keeping copy under the strict 160-character limit to avoid double billing, minimizing emoji use (which consumes 35–50 characters), and restricting expensive MMS (image) messages only to campaigns where the ROI justifies a 2–3x cost increase. Establishing five core automated flows: Welcome (2-3 messages), Browse Abandonment, Cart Abandonment, Checkout Abandonment, and Win-back. list growth / Driving SMS list growth by optimizing website pop-up forms to capture 8–10% of visitors. Implementing a two-step micro-commitment strategy: first asking for an email, and then prompting for the phone number with clear, benefit-driven copy (e.g., "finish signing up to get your discount"). Delaying the pop-up trigger to 6–10 seconds to ensure optimal visibility without hurting website conversions. campaign strategy / Structuring an SMS campaign calendar centered around transactional, high-urgency, and important announcements rather than nurture content. Planning monthly sends around product launches (teaser, launch, reminder), flash sales (launch, last chance), and strategic filler campaigns like social media giveaways or "restock" alerts to maintain a cadence of 1–2 messages per week. Testing optimal send times, typically finding success in the 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. or 4:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. windows.

Look for. The primary nuances/constraints of SMS marketing compared to email: higher cost, strict 160-character limits, emoji character consumption (35–50 characters per emoji), and the 2–3x higher cost of MMS (images) versus SMS. The recommended SMS campaign sending frequency: 1 to 2 times per week. The recommended pop-up form time delay trigger: 6 to 10 seconds.

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a consulting call with the speaker or download the free SMS swipe file document in the description.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 10 to 15.

Topics. SMS marketing / Developing a profitable SMS marketing strategy by treating the channel as a high-urgency, low-frequency communication medium rather than a nurture channel. Managing the technical costs of SMS (e.g., keeping character counts under 160, limiting emojis, and evaluating the ROI of expensive MMS image sends). Establishing core automated SMS flows, including a rapid Welcome sequence, strict single-message abandonment flows (Site, Browse, Cart, Checkout) due to compliance regulations, and precisely timed post-purchase replenishment/win-back messages. list growth / Optimizing pop-up forms to capture SMS subscribers at a high rate (e.g., aiming for 15%+ opt-in rates). Utilizing interactive quiz formats or micro-commitments on platforms like Alia before requesting contact information. Maximizing phone number capture by using action-oriented copy such as "Finish signing up with text to activate your discount" rather than generic prompts like "Sign up for texts." campaign strategy / Structuring SMS campaign blasts for maximum impact and minimal unsubscribe rates. Recommending a baseline frequency of two campaigns per week for standard brands, strictly reserving SMS for high-urgency events such as product launches, back-in-stock alerts, and flash sales rather than general nurture content. Simplifying segmentation by broadcasting to the entire subscriber list while only suppressing chronically unengaged users (e.g., users who have received 15+ texts with zero clicks).

Look for. The recommended SMS platform strategy: consolidate SMS and email within the same platform (e.g., Klaviyo, Omnisend) for ease of management. Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the exact visual, structural, and copywriting frameworks required to build high-converting e-commerce emails, including practical tutorials on using Figma to design and slice image-based emails for platforms like Klaviyo or Omnisend. modules: [EML] topics: [email marketing, email design, copywriting, Figma, Klaviyo, Omnisend, conversion rate optimization, email structure, image slicing] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. email structure / positioning the headline, copy, and primary CTA button "above the fold" to capture non-scrollers immediately, followed by a "bridge" section with infographics, and ending with a footer containing category navigation; visual design / creating a seamless, scrolling experience using background gradients and dynamic layouts (e.g., S-curves, GIF carousels) rather than blocky, disjointed sections; skimmable copywriting / optimizing for 3-second attention spans by using punchy headlines, extremely short body copy, bolded main points, and infographics (checklists, icons, timelines) instead of dense paragraphs; AI copywriting workflow / using ChatGPT to reverse-engineer competitor emails by pasting an example, asking for a reusable framework, and prompting it to generate new copy using that specific structure; the "button at the top" rule / the strict design requirement to place a large, easily clickable CTA button immediately below the hero copy, ensuring it is visible without scrolling; footer navigation / utilizing the footer to include "shop by category" buttons (e.g., Men/Women) to capture clicks from users who reached the bottom but did not want the specific product featured in the email; Figma to ESP workflow / the technical process of designing an email in Figma, using the "slice" tool to export sections as individual JPEGs, compressing them (via tools like iLoveIMG), and uploading them as stacked images into an Email Service Provider (ESP); the "hidden text" deliverability hack / placing invisible text (e.g., the brand's "About Us" copy set to size 5, 5% line spacing, and matched to the background color) at the bottom of image-heavy emails to pass spam filters that penalize text-to-image ratios.

Look for.

The "Button at the Top" Rule: The non-negotiable design principle of placing a massive CTA button immediately below the hero text so that it is fully visible "above the fold" when a user opens the email on mobile.

The Invisible Text Hack: The deliverability tactic of pasting a large block of text (like an "About Us" page) at the bottom of an image-only email, changing the font color to match the background, and shrinking it to trick Gmail's text-to-image spam filters.

The Figma Slicing Workflow: The process of exporting a long email design into multiple smaller image "slices" to optimize load times and allow for multiple, distinct hyperlinks (e.g., splitting a footer into separate slices for different social media icons).

The ChatGPT Reverse-Engineering Prompt: The copywriting strategy of feeding ChatGPT a successful competitor's email, asking it to extract the structural template, and then prompting it to write new copy for your brand using that exact formula.

Skip. Plugs for the creator's agency (Well Copy), the newsletter sign-up pitches, and the extended, repetitive clicks during the live Figma design tutorials unless they illustrate a core concept.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (standard email marketing principles), 85% growth (advanced Figma design, conversion-optimized layouts, and technical deliverability hacks). Volume. ~450 words.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a foundational shift in text-based selling for 2026, advocating for iMessage (blue bubble) outreach over traditional SMS, and outlines specific tactics for maximizing reply rates, maintaining human-to-human trust, and tracking conversational metrics. modules: [EML] topics: [SMS marketing, conversational commerce, list growth] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. SMS marketing / Shifting text-based selling from automated broadcast SMS to human-to-human conversational outreach, specifically emphasizing the transition to iMessage (the "blue bubble") to avoid the spam-associated limitations of traditional green SMS (e.g., mandatory "reply STOP to unsubscribe" language and A2P regulations). Optimizing lead capture funnels by reducing friction to ask only for a name and phone number, and utilizing a 5-minute delay before sending the initial text to simulate natural human behavior. conversational commerce / Driving inbound engagement by utilizing a two-part introductory text template: an introduction followed 5 seconds later by a low-friction, open-ended question designed solely to elicit a reply. Maintaining trust and a conversational tone by adhering to the "80-character rule" (avoiding walls of text), deliberately using common abbreviations or minor typos to appear authentic, and leveraging iMessage-specific features like text effects (e.g., lasers, invisible ink), voice notes, and video messages to build rapport. Mandating a "human handoff" where a live agent takes over the conversation immediately following the first automated reply. list growth / Tracking text-based sales funnels by shifting focus away from delivery and open rates toward engagement-centric metrics: the Reply Rate (the primary indicator of conversation initiation), the Show-Up Rate (for appointments and webinars), and the Close Rate (measuring whether conversational trust shortens the sales cycle and increases final conversions).

Look for. The fundamental shift in modern text-based selling: moving from automated, broadcast SMS to trust-based, conversational iMessage ("blue bubble") outreach. The recommended time delay for the first text message: a 5-minute delay after the lead opts in to simulate human response time. The "80-character rule": keeping text messages under 80 characters (one to two lines maximum) to maintain a natural, non-robotic tone. The "human handoff rule": an automated system handles the initial outreach, but a live human must take over the conversation the moment the lead replies.

Skip. Promotional pitches for the SendBlue iMessage tool, its templates, or links to book a consultation in the video description.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 1 to 5.

I've spent the last two years sending millions of texts for my clients, analyzing reply rates, and analyzing what actually makes people respond to a text message. And if you're thinking about SMS marketing, SMS outreach, or textbased selling in 2026, there are very important things you need to know to successfully reach your people and drive more sales. In this video, I'm condensing everything that I've learned, all of the breakthroughs, all the best practices, all the templates, all the data into a definitive guide on how to send better text in 2026. It doesn't matter if you're sending your very first text today or if you sent thousands of texts for your business. What I'm going to share is a fundamentally new way to think and go about your texting outreach in 2026 so that you drive more engagement, drive more replies, more trust, and conversions for your business. This video will be separated into five chapters. Chapter one being the foundation of texting in 2026. Chapter two being the art of getting a first reply. Chapter three being beginner level texting secrets. Chapter four being expert level texting secrets. And chapter five being texting metrics and reporting. So feel free to skip ahead to the chapter that interests you the most. Pro tip though, I'd highly recommend starting at chapter 1 because the fundamentals talked about in this section have never been talked about before in the texting industry. Listen up. 2025 marked a significant shift in the texting world where people are tired of getting SMS blasted. We are seeing deliverability of text tanking, people replying stop to text, and even worse, people fully marking your text as junk. All because people are tired of getting sent the exact same texts from all businesses all written with the exact same AI prompts. In 2026, the game is moving entirely towards trustbased human first conversations. If your text sound automated, you are cooked. We have to talk about the four fundamental shifts that will redefine your texting strategy because these secrets have never been discussed yet. This is the true foundation of modern textbased selling, and it starts with accepting four non-negotiable facts about texting in 2026. First, you must go blue. Let's be totally real. People are sick and tired of the green SMS text. They're sick of the text blast, the obvious automations, and the reply stop to unsubscribe line at the end of every single message that they receive. Businesses have somehow found a way to invade and ruin the one channel that people use for personal communications. And people are sick of it. North Americans have iPhones. It's a fact. If people have iPhones and you are texting them a green SMS text, you have to accept that you're not welcome. The only people that are welcome to iPhone users are other iPhone users. People who text blue eye messages and not businesses who text blue eye messages. people who text blue eye messages. This is the foundation of everything that we're going to cover today. So, let me repeat it again. You must start texting your leads, your prospects, and your clients via iMessage in 2026. Second, meet them where they live. You need to know this. Messages is the most used native app on the iPhone. People live in that app. It's where they talk to their friends. It's where they talk to their family. It's where they talk to their partners. And so, your job is to get in there. You need to forget about email. You need to forget about calling, about DMing, and you need to start texting people. Third, be a person and not a business. To get people to reply, you need to embody being a person who texts and not a business who texts. People don't care about a faceless brand sending out texts. They don't care about an automated appointment reminder. They don't care about an automated promotional text. They care about you sending out a text. So be you, be human and people will respond to that. Fourth, conversations not broadcast. In today's age, conversation leads to conversions. Trust leads to conversions. Therefore, we don't want to broadcast and bulk text. We want to build rapport with our leads. Every single text that you send out needs to be designed to open up a dialogue and not just deliver a message. Every message you send has to end with a follow-up question, an opportunity for the lead to bite and to give you one more piece of information about themselves or about their business or about their intentions. Okay, so you've accepted the fundamentals and you're ready to go blue and to be more human in your texting approach. But here's the truth. All that foundation is completely worthless if people don't reply to our texts. Or even worse, if they reply, stop. The entire game of textbased selling in 2026 comes down to one simple urgent metric. We need to get a relevant reply. And if we get that lead to engage with us via text, it's game on. So how exactly do we guarantee that reply? It comes down to these three things. First, reduce all friction. You need to redesign your entire marketing funnel to focus on getting that one single piece of data, which is their phone number. Stop asking for their email, their company, their job title on your lead capture form. That's friction. Reduce all friction. Just ask for their name and their phone number. That single piece of data unlocks a direct, personal, trustbased line of communication with the person who is ready to buy from you. Second, the 5-minute delay. Wait 5 minutes after they've opted into your funnel before texting them. A 5-minute delay feels natural. It feels like a real person saw their submission, took a moment, and then reached out. It removes the robotic instant reply feeling that triggers spam alerts in everyone's brain. And third, the two-part template. You need to use this exact template when you're sending out that first initial text message to a lead. Your first message should be, "Hey, prospect name, this is your name from company name." So for me, that would be, "Hey, John, this is Tristan from SendBlue." And then you need to send a second message 5 seconds later asking an open-ended question that's very simple and very low friction. For example, you could say, "Are you new to industry X? Have you done X type of offer before? How many X projects have you done this year?" The goal is not to tell them anything in the first text. The goal is to get them to engage. This is how you will guarantee that people will reply to you. All right, so you got the first reply and that's huge. But this is where most people completely drop the ball. They treat the first reply as a finish line when it's actually the starting gate. The goal now is to keep building trust until you get that prospect to the next stage of the pipeline. Trust is very fragile and we don't want to break it. So here are the three core rules to maintain that essential human connection once that conversation has begun. First, the 80 character rule. Your texts need to be under 80 characters, one maybe two lines maximum. You have to text like you normally text. If you send a brick text, a giant wall of words, you are cooked. Keep it short, keep it punchy, and keep it human like you normally text people. Second, the opt- out language rule. We are iPhone users. We don't need the reply stop to unsubscribe because we don't fall under A2P regulation that makes SMS feel spammy. By operating an iMessage, you are set free from having to finish all of your texts with a call to action. asking people to opt out of a conversation before it even happened. Third, the human handoff rule. The moment that you get that first reply, a real live person has to take over the conversation. The automation's job is to handle the perfectly timed first outreach. But the human's job is to build connection. This is how you scale your personal outreach without sacrificing that little personal touch. Now, let's take this one step further. What I'm about to share are expert level techniques that will ensure that your leads never think that you're sending them automated follow-ups. If your leads ever get the feeling that this is an automated conversation or that you used chat GPT or prompts to write out your text, you are cooked. We will lose their trust. We will lose their replies and we will lose their deal. First mistakes and abbreviations. No businesses write text with intentional mistakes in them. But we do because we aren't businesses texting, we are people texting. So make mistakes in your text and use common abbreviations. This is so minimal, but it's so human. It instantly breaks the formal and the corporate tone that so many businesses have. For example, just take a look at this text. Just got your call booked for Tuesday. What kind of business do you have? Notice the minimal just here and the abbreviated Tuesday. That's badass. It proves that you're a real person texting. And like I said, people get replies. Businesses don't. Second, use iMessage text effects. No business has ever sent a text message with a text effect in it. And so if you use them, I can guarantee you that people will stop the scroll and look at your message. My personal favorite text effects are lasers when you really want your follow-up to stand out. Or sometimes I like to use the invisible ink when someone's been ghosting me for a while. And another one that works really well is confettes when you really want to celebrate something. Maybe it's like a client sign up or a client win. Third, use videos and voice messages. These are the number one way for your prospects and your leads to feel familiar with you. You could use a video in so many different ways. It could be to introduce yourself before a call or to send a demo of your tool or your coaching program or it could even become your VSSL. Same thing for voice messages. Use them to remind people about upcoming appointments or to answer a question that would be over the 80 character limit that we talked about before. People consume content in all different shapes and forms and so we need to be accommodating and send them all types of content. So send texts, send videos, send voice messages, send memes, and send text effects. Okay, so we're getting pretty good at getting replies and maintaining trust at this point. But those replies are worthless if they don't lead to money. Our goal isn't just to make their phones ding. It's to fill up that pipeline with leads who are actually going to buy whatever you're selling. This is where we stop guessing and start tracking the data that actually prints cash. You could throw away all of the old metrics like delivery rates and open rates. In the texting world, here are the three metrics that we want to track. First, the reply rate. This is probably the most important metric to track. Are you actually starting conversations? You need to be split testing basically everything. Do I say hey versus hi versus hello versus what's up in my first introduction text? Do I wait five or seven minutes before texting them? Do they prefer voice messages or videos? Literally everything. Find the micro improvements that give you a huge lift in reply rates. But the most important split test is this one. You absolutely must track your iMessage versus SMS reply rates. I've been tracking this across thousands of clients and even for our own business for just about 2 years now. And I'm consistently seeing a 2x lift when texting via the blue bubble world. So, iMessage. Second, the show up rate. The conversation started, but did they commit? You know, did your leads commit to showing up to your appointment, to your demo, or to your webinars? Test that. Test your texts. Does a quick voice message 15 minutes before the call beat a simple text reminder? Or does a video perform better than a voice message? When you put in the effort to maintain trust and to religiously follow up with your people, they will become more purchase ready buyers and they will most probably honor their commitment to actually show up. Third, the close rate. This is the ultimate payoff. Am I getting people to actually close and buy my software, buy my course, or buy my product? You need to verify if the trustbased text selling has done two things. Did it shorten my sales cycle because of the constant personal follow-ups? and did I increase my close rate because the lead trusts me and the lead actually told me about their problems and gave me the opportunity to help them in the purchasing cycle. This relationship building isn't just nice, it's a measurable competitive advantage that hits your bottom line. All right, you made it. Now you have everything you need to send better text to your leads in 2026. Following this blueprint is really what's going to make the difference between your audience replying stop to you via text and them actually engaging with you back and forth in a conversation. But I want to leave you with this one final essential truth. iMessage will be the biggest needle mover for marketing and sales teams in 2026. And if your business starts using iMessage today, you are guaranteed to be one of the first to use a tool that will make all of the difference in generating more revenue for your business. SMS is becoming a saturated and regulated industry, and your crowd is tired of getting texted with those green spammy SMS texts. Move it to iMessage, though, and you'll see response rates fly off the roof. Like, literally. If you want to be part of the very selective group of people that text with iMessage, check out the link in the description of this video. My team has built tons of iMessage texting templates and workflows for appointment reminders, opt-in funnels, abandoned cart recovery, webinar reminders, appointment cancellations, and so much more. We can even sit down with you to determine how to tailor your texting habits to your crowd so that you drive more replies. Thank you so much for watching and I really hope you enjoyed this video as much as I did making it.

Look for. The recommended campaign sending frequency: 3 to 4 campaigns per week. The critical purchase window for welcome flows: the first 72 hours (with day zero driving the highest conversion volume). The core Klaviyo automated flows: Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Abandoned Cart, Abandoned Checkout, and Post-Purchase. The list cleaning benchmark: suppressing unengaged subscribers who have been inactive for 180 days.

Skip. Promotional pitches for the speaker's agency booking links, the free email marketing course download, or external tool affiliate links (e.g., Aaliyah, Clock Apps).

Scope mix. Almost all core.

So, in this full email marketing course, I'm going to walk you through the exact setup I'd focus on to build a high performing email system from the ground up. We will start with list growth because none of the rest of this matters if you're not consistently adding new email subscribers to your list. So it serves as the gateway to turning those casual visitors into potential customers for your brand. So by capturing their details through an engaging and well-placed signup form, you're not just collecting data, you're creating an opportunity for ongoing communication. This means that you can nurture those leads with your welcome series flow and with your email campaigns. And this way you can build trust with them and guide them towards that first purchase. And from there you can nurture them into a repeat customer. So it's a key tool for lowering your customer acquisition and making sure that the traffic that you're paying for doesn't just vanish. So this is the typical e-commerce funnel that I often see and that's that brands are running top of funnel paid ads. People will visit your website. 2% of them on average will be converting and actually buying from you. But 98% of the people are leaving your store without actually purchasing. And of course underneath there you'll run some retargeting ads which are super expensive and of course there will be some people that will be revisiting your website but a lot of them again will leave your store without buying and maybe you'll convert just a small portion of it another 2%. But the end result is that your cost per acquisition is sky high. So that's why I always recommend this optimized e-commerce funnel where still you will be running the top of funnel paid ads. People will still visit your store via those paid ads and still only 2% of the people will actually convert straight away and 98% of the people will leave your store. But now you have a high converting signup form in place which will capture 8 to 12% of your website traffic. And these new email subscribers, you can nurture them with your welcome series flow which will convert 10 to 20% of your new email subscribers. and the rest of your new email subscribers, you can nurture them with your autoflows and with your email campaigns, which will convert even more email subscribers. So, in the end, you will have a lot more people who will actually buy from you and your customer acquisition will go down. 09-EML / email and sms Goes here. A breakdown of Alex Hormozi's e-commerce and B2B email marketing playbook, focusing on the "Mosie Money Minute" format. Covers the strategy of high-value, text-only emails, optimal sending frequency, subject line split testing, and maximizing click-through rates (CTR) over open rates. Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a high-leverage, text-heavy email marketing strategy designed to bypass the Gmail "Promotions" tab, build long-term reader habits, and generate massive ROI by prioritizing short, actionable content over traditional graphic-heavy sales emails. modules: [EML] topics: [email marketing, newsletter strategy, deliverability, click-through rate, A/B testing, copywriting, B2B email, B2C email] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. the ROI of email / explaining how email marketing generates a 35-45x return on investment because the lead acquisition cost is already paid, making it the highest-leverage retention and conversion tool available; deliverability and the promotions tab / detailing the 2011-era tactic of using plain-text formatting, minimal links, and avoiding "money" words to ensure emails land in the primary inbox rather than the Gmail promotions tab (noting that 16.9% of B2B marketing emails fail to reach the inbox entirely); the "Mosie Money Minute" format / breaking down Hormozi's specific email structure: an immediate quote/reward at the top, a single 200-word tactical nugget, a contextual Call to Action (CTA), and a P.S. statement that rewards the reader for finishing; maximizing Click-Through Rate (CTR) / shifting focus from open rates (which are increasingly inaccurate due to Apple Privacy changes) to CTR, emphasizing that training the audience to click by offering high-value hidden content (e.g., Google Drive links to VSLs) is critical for algorithm health; opt-in and engagement loops / utilizing the "Reply Yes" strategy during the lead magnet opt-in process to force engagement, which signals to email servers that the sender is highly reputable; email sending cadence / confirming that a frequency of roughly 3x per week is the sweet spot for maximizing conversions without burning out the list, provided the content remains strictly value-driven; A/B testing subject lines / using split testing to determine the winning subject line on a small percentage of the list before blasting the remainder, while also optimizing the first 150 characters (the preview text) to spike open rates by up to 24%; optimal send times / highlighting data that B2C emails perform best on Mondays and Tuesdays, B2B emails peak on Wednesdays, and the ideal send windows generally fall between 10:00 AM–Noon and 1:00 PM–3:00 PM.

Look for.

The "Reply Yes" Deliverability Hack: The onboarding strategy of requiring new subscribers to physically reply "Yes" to the welcome email to receive their lead magnet, instantly signaling to email providers (like Gmail) that the sender is a trusted contact and bypassing the Promotions tab.

The Plain-Text Paradigm: The deliberate choice to format marketing emails exactly like a message from a friend—heavy text, zero images, and minimal links—to avoid triggering AI spam filters that penalize graphic-heavy "Vegas Strip" style e-commerce templates.

Preview Text Optimization: The tactical focus on meticulously crafting the preview text (the first 150 characters visible before opening) rather than letting it default to generic greetings, which is proven to lift open rates by up to 24%.

The "Contextual CTA" Rule: The principle that Call to Actions must naturally bridge from the specific educational content of the email, rather than using generic, copy-pasted buttons that train readers to ignore them.

Skip. Plugs for the acquisition.com scaling workshops, the School community, and personal anecdotes about Hormozi's hesitation to start an email list.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (standard email formatting), 90% growth (advanced deliverability hacks, copywriting structure, and algorithmic engagement loops). Volume. ~450 words.

jobs.text:
09-EML / email and sms Goes here. A strategic framework for e-commerce email copywriting, emphasizing deep audience research and a modular approach to constructing emails using specific, conversion-focused building blocks rather than traditional long-form direct response copy. Not here. • Paid media creative strategy or video ad scripting -> 06-MEA • Foundational brand identity or tone-of-voice creation -> 04-BRD

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Simplifies e-commerce email copywriting by breaking it down into manageable visual modules and provides a systematic research process to uncover deep customer insecurities and objections before drafting. modules: [EML] topics: [email copywriting, audience research, review mining, Facebook Ad Library, email building blocks, objection handling, risk reversal, guarantees, consumer psychology] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. audience research / utilizing the Facebook Ad Library to analyze top-performing competitor video ads and identify primary marketing angles and claims; review mining / scanning Amazon, Trustpilot, and YouTube podcast comments to uncover specific customer objections (e.g., bad taste, difficulty of use, ingredient concerns) and raw voice-of-customer data; psychological extrapolation / the process of mapping surface-level product benefits (e.g., clearer skin or muscle gain) to deep-seated human insecurities (e.g., social anxiety or feeling inferior) to write highly empathetic copy; the blame shift / an ethical copywriting tactic that redirects the blame for a customer's problem away from their own habits and onto external factors (e.g., chemical corporations or standard market practices); modular email blocks / treating e-commerce emails as an assembly of functional components—including Banners, CTAs, Reviews, Product Displays, Benefit Highlights, Content/Stories, Countdowns, and Guarantees; objection-handling reviews / intentionally selecting specific customer testimonials that neutralize known pre-purchase anxieties rather than relying on generic, unhelpful praise; risk reversal / implementing unconditional guarantees to eliminate the fear of loss.

Look for.

The Modular Block Approach: The strategy of constructing e-commerce emails by stacking specific, pre-defined copy blocks (e.g., Banner, CTA, Review, Benefit Highlight) rather than writing traditional, long-form direct response letters.

Objection-Handling Reviews: The tactic of strategically selecting customer reviews that directly answer common pre-purchase anxieties (e.g., "Is it easy to swallow?") instead of using generic "I love it" reviews.

The 180-Day Guarantee Paradox: The counterintuitive insight that offering a longer guarantee window (180 days) actually results in fewer returns than a shorter 30-day window, because customers feel less immediate urgency and eventually forget to process the return.

Deep Psychological Extrapolation: The process of mapping a basic product benefit to a core human insecurity (e.g., social anxiety due to acne) to write highly empathetic copy that blames external factors (chemical corporations) rather than the consumer.

Skip. Plugs for the creator's agency, specific navigational instructions for using Chrome Developer tools to view mobile sites, and the promotion of the upcoming Canva design module.

Scope mix. 20% baseline (copywriting and audience research basics), 80% growth (e-commerce specific modular copy structure and psychological tactics). Volume. ~400 words.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides an introductory guide to setting up an e-commerce SMS marketing channel within Klaviyo, covering platform configuration, list growth via two-step pop-ups, campaign cadence, flow restrictions, and core performance KPIs. modules: [EML] topics: [SMS marketing, list growth, campaign strategy] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. SMS marketing / Implementing a foundational SMS marketing channel for e-commerce brands, utilizing platforms like Klaviyo to consolidate email and SMS operations. Managing technical and compliance constraints: adhering to the 160-character limit per message to avoid double billing, recognizing the high cost of MMS (images) compared to standard text, restricting abandonment flows to a single compliant message, and observing legal "quiet hours" (e.g., avoiding sends before 8:00 a.m. or after 9:00 p.m.). list growth / Expanding the SMS subscriber base by separating email and SMS opt-ins into a two-step pop-up flow to minimize friction. Using clear, action-oriented copy for the SMS step, such as "finish signing up with text to activate 20% off," to maximize conversion rates without offering additional discounts beyond the initial email incentive. campaign strategy / Structuring an SMS campaign calendar centered around high-impact, direct events (e.g., flash sales, restocks, new product launches) rather than broad nurture content. Maintaining a low frequency of 1 to 2 SMS campaigns per week to prevent high unsubscribe rates, testing optimal send times (typically late morning or early afternoon), and shifting performance evaluation away from vanity metrics (open rates) toward click rates (aiming for 5–15%) and unsubscribe rates (maintaining below 1%).

Look for. The recommended time delay for website pop-ups: 6 to 10 seconds after page load. The primary compliance rule regarding SMS abandonment flows: you are only allowed to send one SMS message per abandonment flow. The key SMS KPIs to monitor: target a click rate of 5–15% and keep the unsubscribe rate below 1%. The legal limitation on SMS send times: avoiding sends prior to 8:00 a.m. and post 9:00 p.m.

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a consulting call with the speaker's agency or download the free swipe file of 500 SMS templates.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 5 to 10.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides an end-to-end technical, operational, and strategic blueprint for scaling DTC e-commerce email revenue from list building to advanced deliverability and campaign segmentation. modules: [EML] topics: [email marketing, Klaviyo, DMARC, DNS setup, popup forms, automated flows, welcome series, cart abandonment, email campaigns, segmentation, copywriting, A/B testing] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. technical deliverability setup / executing Google's 2024 requirements by configuring a dedicated sending domain (DNS records: CNAME/NS) and a DMARC record to protect sender reputation; high-converting popup architecture / deploying single-opt-in popups with 4–10 second time delays, 60% scroll triggers, contrasting button sizes (70px+), and a micro-yes step to achieve 8–12% list growth; essential lifecycle flows / building the 7 core automations: Welcome Series (discount delivery, brand story, bestsellers, social proof, USBs, and urgency), Site Abandon (guide traffic to products), Browse Abandon (personalized product reminders and delayed reviews), Cart Abandonment (using Shopify's "Added to Cart" custom snippet rather than checkout triggers), Checkout Abandonment, Post-Purchase (reducing buyer's remorse, product education, loyalty introduction, and review requests), and Winback; campaign strategy / maintaining a 10:1 non-discount to discount ratio, sending 3–4 targeted campaigns per week across diverse content buckets (promos, holidays, product highlights, social proof, values); email copywriting framework / utilizing short, fifth-grade reading level copy, the "inverted triangle" or "Z-pattern" visual hierarchies, and emotion-driven hooks; list hygiene and segmentation / creating dynamic segments for engagement (30/60/90/120-day active), purchase history (VIPs, 1x/2x/3x buyers), and suppressing hard bounces or unengaged profiles; A/B testing methodology / optimizing campaigns and flows for placed order rate rather than open rates, split-testing send times, product blocks, and time delays.

Look for.

The "Added to Cart" vs. "Checkout Started" Distinction: The critical technical warning that Shopify's default checkout trigger is not a cart abandonment flow; true cart abandonment requires installing a custom JavaScript snippet to track "Added to Cart" events.

The DMARC and DNS Mandate: The technical requirement to set up a branded sending domain and a DMARC policy (reporting mode p=none moving to quarantine/reject) to comply with Gmail and Yahoo's 2024 inbox standards.

The 10:1 Non-Discount Ratio: The strategic rule to protect brand margins by sending at least ten value-driven, educational, or social proof campaigns for every single promotional discount.

Placed Order Rate A/B Testing: The analytical directive to evaluate campaign and flow split tests strictly by placed order rate or net revenue, rather than vanity metrics like open rates or click-through rates.

Skip. Self-promotional agency pitches, introductory course overviews, repetitive walkthroughs of creating demo Klaviyo accounts, and long lists of basic definitions.

Scope mix. 15% baseline (Klaviyo UI navigation and basic email terminology), 85% growth (technical DMARC setup, advanced lifecycle flow architecture, and conversion-optimized design/segmentation). Volume. ~450 words.

Topics. technical SEO / simplifying requirements to just indexability, zero broken links, mobile UX, and clear hierarchy, debunking the obsession with meta descriptions and minor speed fixes; money pages / prioritizing transactional category and product pages over informational blogs that drive vanity traffic but zero revenue; link building / prioritizing "link insertions" (niche edits) on existing high-traffic pages over new guest posts due to lower costs ($100-$400) and proven page authority; SEO tools / utilizing Semrush for all-in-one competitor analysis, Google Ads Keyword Planner for free intent/CPC data, and Screaming Frog for technical crawling.

Look for.

The Anti-Blog Rule: Shifting focus away from informational blog content (e.g., "why should I use natural face wash") toward transactional "money pages" (collections), because traffic without conversions is a sunk cost for e-commerce.

The Link Insertion Strategy: Prioritizing buying link insertions on pages that already have established traffic rather than writing new guest posts, as it is 20-30% cheaper and immediately leverages existing page authority.

The 80/20 SEO Focus: Acknowledging that while reporting and technical fixes take up time, 80% of actual revenue growth comes from just 20% of the effort: optimizing money pages and acquiring quality backlinks.

The Essential Tool Stack: Using Semrush for keyword gap analysis, Google Keyword Planner as a free alternative to gauge commercial intent via CPC, and Screaming Frog (free under 500 URLs) for technical audits (finding 404s, missing H1s, canonicals).

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a discovery call with the agency, specific dollar amounts of past client case studies, and generic platitudes about "making good content."

Scope mix. 20% baseline (basic tool stack), 80% growth (revenue-focused prioritization, link insertion tactics).

Volume. ~350 words.

Topics. technical SEO / correcting Shopify’s default URL structure (removing the collection path from product URLs), managing product/blog tag indexing, utilizing custom robots.txt, handling product variants (merging vs. canonical tags), redirecting deleted products, and implementing structured data (schema); site speed / choosing lightweight themes, optimizing image formats (WebP) and sizes, implementing lazy loading, async/deferring non-essential scripts, and minifying code; keyword research / building topical maps using tools like Semrush and Keyword Cupid, prioritizing bottom-of-funnel pages via Google Search Console impressions, conducting keyword gap analysis, and matching search intent; site structure / optimizing main menus, featuring high-volume collections on the homepage, utilizing faceted navigation (with caution), and implementing breadcrumbs and related product links; on-page SEO / optimizing key elements (Title, H1, URL) for collection and product pages, adding detailed descriptions (splitting descriptions above and below grids), incorporating FAQ accordions, and leveraging rich snippets; content strategy / building topical authority through comprehensive blog content, internally linking to shopping pages, and embedding product CTAs; link building / building foundational links (citations, social profiles), executing guest posts and niche edits (prospecting, outreach, negotiation), and utilizing platforms like HARO/Connectively for PR and media backlinks.

Look for.

The URL Structure Fix: Editing the Shopify theme code (specifically the product grid snippet) to remove the within collection parameter, ensuring product URLs always point to the primary /products/product-name path rather than creating duplicate URLs with the collection path.

Topical Mapping: Building out comprehensive content covering all subtopics related to a main keyword to establish the site as an authority, enabling it to outrank larger, broader competitors like Amazon.

The "One Topic Per Page" Rule: Ensuring that no two pages on the site target the exact same keyword (keyword cannibalization), assigning distinct topics to collections, products, and blog posts based on search intent.

Guest Posting Strategy: The specific process for scraping a competitor's backlink profile using Semrush, filtering for domains with >1,000 monthly visits, and executing cold email outreach to secure contextual links.

Skip. Plugs for the agency's done-for-you services or the School community.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (basic Shopify navigation), 90% growth (advanced technical SEO, link building strategies). Volume. ~450 words.

16-AEO / answer engine optimization Goes here. A comprehensive masterclass on utilizing Claude Code and SEMrush to execute an end-to-end SEO and AI search strategy. Covers generating static sites via Claude Code, filtering low-difficulty keywords, scraping competitor formulas, incorporating personal voice/humor into AI-generated content, setting up automated SEO skills, optimizing Lighthouse performance scores (technical SEO), and deploying via GitHub and Vercel. Not here. • Paid ad campaign strategies or Meta Ads tracking -> 06-MEA • Shopify backend configurations (inventory, taxes, shipping) -> 05-SET

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a cutting-edge approach to modern SEO and AI search optimization by leveraging AI coding assistants (Claude Code) to automate technical setup, content writing, and site performance optimization at scale. modules: [AEO] topics: [Claude Code, static site generation, keyword research, SEO automation, technical SEO, Lighthouse optimization, content scaling] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. site generation / using Claude Code and a foundational Claude.md file to rapidly build static-site-generation (SSG) web apps optimized for crawler indexing; keyword research / utilizing SEMrush Keyword Magic Tool to find keywords with a difficulty under 30 and search volume over 100, focusing on informational queries and service-city commercial intent; competitor analysis / analyzing top-ranking competitor pages to extract winning content structures, word counts, and heading distributions; content scaling / training Claude on personal voice, brand stories, and humor (avoiding AI slop) and prompting it to reverse-engineer top competitors; service page architecture / implementing the "zipper" method to combine service offerings with municipal locations to capture local intent; technical SEO / using Google Lighthouse performance reports to identify and feed performance issues back into Claude Code until the site hits 100/100 scores across SEO, accessibility, best practices, and performance; deployment / pushing repositories to GitHub and deploying instantly via Vercel before submitting XML sitemaps to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.

Look for. * Static Site Generation (SSG): The technical requirement to build sites using static site generation rather than client-side rendering, ensuring Google and AI crawler bots can instantly access and index fully rendered HTML without waiting for JavaScript execution.

The Claude.md SOP File: Utilizing a core instruction markdown file (Claude.md) to train the AI coding agent on standard operating procedures, design references (via Dribbble screenshots), and formatting rules before scaffolding the site.

Competitor Content Reverse Engineering: Prompting Claude to analyze the top-ranking search results for a target keyword, calculate average word counts and heading structures, and synthesize a superior draft based on the winning formula.

Lighthouse Score Remediation: The automated loop of running a Google Lighthouse audit in Chrome Developer Tools, copying the performance/SEO error report, pasting it directly into Claude Code, and commanding the AI to rewrite the code until hitting a 100% score.

Skip. Promotional pitches for Pexels API setups, Namecheap domain purchases, and the creator's paid agency/community programs.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (traditional SEO metrics), 90% growth (AI-driven development, Claude Code automation, and modern tech stack deployment). Volume. ~450 words.

06-MEA / measurement and analytics

Goes here. SEO tracking, search engine analytics, rank tracking, tracking organic search performance, monitoring technical site health, analyzing keyword performance, backlink profile tracking, competitor keyword gap analysis, and tracking AI visibility (AEO/GEO) benchmarks across LLMs.

Not here.

Paid advertising performance, ROAS, or attribution -> 06-MEA (other sub-topics) or 11-ADC

Writing and executing optimized blog content or copy -> 10-MCR

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details tracking answer engine optimization (AEO) and generative engine optimization (GEO) performance, managing data from Google Search Console, monitoring indexation status, checking website speed performance via GTMetrics and Google PageSpeed Insights, and performing keyword gap analysis. modules: [MEA] topics: [seo analytics, rank tracking, site auditing] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. seo analytics / Tracking organic search and generative engine performance by extracting data from Google Search Console and Google Analytics, evaluating transactional vs. informational keyword gaps, and assessing competitor traffic profiles, rankings, and backlink volumes. rank tracking / Monitoring keyword positioning shifts, click-through rates (CTR), and impressions over time across traditional search engine result pages (SERPs) and AI-driven platforms. site auditing / Monitoring technical site health by auditing website loading speed (using GTMetrics and Google PageSpeed Insights), analyzing core web vitals, inspecting missing metadata or structured data (schema markup), and evaluating local SEO parameters via Google Business Profile metrics.

Look for. The metrics to evaluate in Google Search Console: total clicks, impressions, average CTR, and average position. The recommended speed testing metrics: evaluating performance via GTMetrics and Google PageSpeed Insights. The key components of local SEO audits: NAP consistency, primary/secondary categories, and local citations.

Skip. Step-by-step instructions on setting up automated workflows in Pabbly, prompt engineering copy via ChatGPT/Claude Canvas, or purchasing paid backlink packages via Get Me Links, which belong in 11-ADC, 10-MCR, or other tactical execution modules.

Scope mix. Baseline mixed with edge (AI answer engine measurement frameworks).

Volume. 15 to 20.

jobs.text:
15-SEO / search engine optimization Goes here. A complete Shopify SEO guide focusing on the SEO cycle, keyword clustering, intent validation (commercial vs. informational), on-page optimization mapping (H1s, titles, descriptions), and content creation workflows using ChatGPT for blogs and product descriptions. Not here. • The technical setup of Shopify payment gateways or tracking -> 05-SET • Designing the landing page visual aesthetics -> 07-LPG

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a practical monthly SEO cycle tailored for e-commerce, explicitly breaking down keyword clustering, commercial intent validation using Semrush, and mapping keywords to Shopify backend fields. modules: [SEO] topics: [keyword research, commercial intent, SEO cycle, on-page optimization, AI content generation, search engine listing] tier: 2 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. the SEO cycle / understanding SEO as a long-term gardening process, consisting of a monthly cycle: researching keywords, updating pages, feeding the search engine (adding content/blogs), and acquiring links; keyword strategy / moving away from single-keyword stuffing to "keyword clustering" (building relevance around a hero keyword with related cluster keywords); intent and validation / using Semrush (Keyword Magic Tool) to validate search volume (>1,000/mo), keyword difficulty (<40%), and commercial intent (indicated by a CPC > $1), explicitly avoiding high-difficulty informational keywords when trying to sell products; rank tracking / setting up projects in Semrush to track keyword position movements over time; on-page optimization / mapping keywords to Shopify's backend fields: Title (H1), Description (SEO paragraph containing hero and cluster keywords), and Search Engine Listing (optimizing the Title Tag and Meta Description to drive clicks, not just rank); feeding the search engine / maintaining relevance by publishing blogs, new products, and reviews; AI content creation / using ChatGPT to generate blog titles and articles by providing strict prompts defining the target audience (e.g., "environmentally conscious women under 30") and author persona (e.g., "handmade soap maker with 15 years experience"); AI detection / using tools like CopyLeaks to detect AI content and manually rewriting the last 10-20% to avoid Google's AI content penalties.

Look for.

The Semrush Validation Rule: Only targeting keywords that meet specific criteria: Commercial intent (C), Volume >1,000, Keyword Difficulty (KD) <40%, and a Cost Per Click (CPC) >$1 (proving the keyword generates revenue).

The Search Engine Listing Tweak: Optimizing the Shopify Search Engine Listing (Meta Title and Description) not just with the keyword, but with a Call to Action (CTA) like "Fast Delivery" or "Buy Online" to optimize for the click-through rate.

The ChatGPT Persona Prompt: Instead of a generic prompt, explicitly instructing ChatGPT on the author's persona (e.g., "a soap maker with 15 years experience") and the audience's persona (e.g., "women 25-35 who are environmentally conscious") to generate non-generic blog content.

The Human Touch Rule: Mandating that AI-generated content must be checked against an AI detector (like CopyLeaks) and manually rewritten (10-20%) to prevent Google from de-ranking the site for spam.

Skip. The promotional pitch for the $99 SEO course and the Semrush free account bypass trick.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (standard Shopify SEO execution and planning). Volume. ~400 words.

Topics. category dominance / restricting focus to a single product cluster for 90 days rather than optimizing the entire site to prevent dilution; technical audit / analyzing Google Search Console and Analytics data specifically through the lens of the chosen cluster; customer awareness funnel / reverse-engineering content strategy starting with the "Most Aware" bottom-funnel phase (e.g., "best creatine for vegans," "First Form vs Thorne"), using ChatGPT grounded with 5 competitor URLs to generate topic ideas; Generative Engine Optimization (GEO/AEO) / analyzing AI platform answers (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok) to identify and export the exact domains frequently cited as retrieval sources; earned off-site SEO / executing a parasite SEO strategy by aggressively pursuing citations and sponsored posts on frequently retrieved domains (e.g., Healthline, Reddit, Amazon, YouTube); owned off-site SEO / syndicating content natively across owned platforms (LinkedIn company pages, YouTube, TikTok) and utilizing employee amplification to force indexation; competitor comparison formatting / structuring content as "Alternatives to [Competitor]," "[Competitor] Reviews," and "[Brand] vs [Competitor]" to hijack branded search; AI content generation / creating AI briefs grounded in brand voice and competitor gaps, generating listicles that explicitly state unique selling propositions (USPs) and rank the owned brand as #1; agentic website optimization / optimizing code specifically for AI crawlers (CCBot) to ensure the brand's data is ingested into future Large Language Models (LLMs), identifying outdated code (e.g., file freshness), and ensuring fast page load speeds.

Look for.

The Single Cluster 90-Day Rule: The explicit instruction to avoid trying to rank the entire website at once, and instead focus all SEO efforts on absolutely dominating one specific product category (e.g., "Creatine") for a full 90-day quarter.

The AI Citation Scraping Method: The specific process of querying AI tools (like ChatGPT), inspecting the specific domains they cite as sources for their answers (e.g., Healthline, Men's Health), and exporting those domains into a spreadsheet to prioritize for off-site outreach and sponsored posts.

The Parasite SEO LinkedIn Strategy: Republishing articles on the company's LinkedIn page and having employees (especially founders with large followings) share and engage with the post, using LinkedIn's massive domain authority to rank in the top 5 of traditional search results.

The Agentic Optimization Check: Using tools to verify that the website's code is easily readable by CCBot (Common Crawl's bot), ensuring the site's data is scraped and baked directly into the training models of future AI like ChatGPT and Claude.

Skip. Plugs for the Rankability software platform or generic explanations of what an AI prompt is.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (Google Search Console), 90% growth (AEO, Generative Engine Optimization, Parasite SEO, AI Agent indexing). Volume. ~450 words.
