 In this actual example, we would only have 375 unengaged, which is a much better ratio than this brand had initially. Then we split the remaining 375 into random samples. So, I might split this into 10 random samples each of 37.5,000 people. And then I can slowly add these small segments into our engaged sends. So, when we send an email out and we focus on making an elite piece of content, we go, "Cool. I'm going to get my 375,000 engaged. I'm going to add back in 37500 unengaged." And my total segment now is whatever the quick math is here, something like 410,000 people. So, now our engaged sending has gone from 375 to 410,000. Now, not all of these people are going to open, but you might get say 20 or 30% of these people open. Ideally, closer to 30, but realistically maybe 20. And then 7,000 of these people have now become engaged. And our new engaged segment size is 382,000 people. Then we keep chipping away at that. And you do that over 6 7 8 9 months. And you have really clear goals in mind of being able to expand your reach through the email channel. And before you know it, you might end up with an engaged audience of say 450, 550, 650 out of your 750,000 people. For this particular brand, we did this exact method for, we ended up being able to send to the whole 750,000 during their big sale launch at the end of 2025, which was for Black Friday. And they beat their Black Friday results by 40% yearonear. And a big part of that was because they had re-engaged a whole bunch of dormant subscribers who hadn't purchased in a long time, who weren't opening emails, and pretty much just weren't interacting with the brand whatsoever across any channels. able to get them back involved over email and SMS, which is free to do because you're already paying for those profiles, and then get good offers out in front of them when it matters most, and rely on those marketing calendar peaks to convert those subscribers. And I have brands all the time ask me, "But hey, isn't providing a personalized onetoone experience better?" You know, if I'm sending people really, really good content that's super relevant to them, of course, that's going to isn't that obviously going to perform better than more general broad content. The way I like to think about it is our flows is where we do the personalization at scale. Flows are behavior based. They trigger when someone does something specific and we have real data to back it. We know when someone's just bought a protein powder so we can send them more relevant content about a protein powder. We know when someone's just left a certain product behind at checkout so we can send them relevant content about that if we need to. Of course, if you think back to when we were talking about flows, we always want to split out by where the customer is in their journey first. But then once you've done that, you can split out and be as personalized as you need to depending on what sort of products or collection split you have. Our campaigns is where we worry about reach moments messaging. The reason for this too is because out of our email list, like I said, only certain amount are going to be engaged, but only a certain amount are ready to buy today. You might only have 3% of your email list ready to buy right now today. And if all you do is focus on onetoone personalization, you're inherently just trying to sell them stuff based on what they've bought in the past. where if we focus on reach moments, good marketing messages, educational content, entertaining content, and getting that in front of as many people as possible, we're actually inherently appealing not just to the 3% of people who are ready to buy, but the 97% of people who aren't ready to buy today, but may still interact with our emails. Now, moving on, where do our VIPs come into this? If you cast your mind back to earlier, I mentioned that your VIPs should be driving 50% or more of your revenue. And this usually correlates to 80% of profit for your business because these people come back more often, buy more frequently, don't use discounts, etc., etc. In practice, the best way to use this segment is to reward them with exclusive stuff. You don't want to just be treating them like everyone else. And we want to split this out into our campaigns and flows. in our flows. We might want to we might want to focus on a loyalty program, which I'll talk about later, but but we might also just want to bake in some VIP pathways within our flows, which we spoke about much earlier, too, and have some dedicated VIP flows here where we give them particular perks. But for the purpose of our campaigns, this is really going to depend on our strategy. And this would fall into that 20% bucket. Like I said, 80% is for reach. Broader campaigns, 20% is for more specific goals. So, if your goal is to drive more VIP revenue, then you can use your campaigns to exactly do that. It can be exclusive stuff for VIPs. Whether that's products, sales, early access. It could be offline experiences. So maybe this is event or community stuff you have on for VIPs. This works really well. Or maybe it's reminders about perks and loyalty program stuff that they may have attached to their account. But my general rule with VIPs is we only want to be focusing on driving additional revenue here if this is our constraint. If you're a business that's already easily getting 50% or more of your revenue from VIPs and 80% or more of your profit from VIPs and you're actually say struggling with first to second order conversion then trying to drive further incrementality through our VIPs is not the highest leverage thing we should be doing right now and instead our efforts should be focused on our real constraint first to second order conversion. So, it's important to know how you can be spec it's important to know how you can be segmenting out your VIPs, but to be honest, most ecom brands say doing under $10 to $20 million a year. VIP revenue is not their biggest constraint. Realistically, it's first to second order conversion. If you're doing above $10 to $20 million a year, this segment becomes a lot higher leverage and we probably should be focusing on driving further value here. But again, only focusing on this if it's our actual constraint. Now, what does RFM analysis look like? RFM analysis is an extremely effective way to split out our lists, our segments, our life cycle cohorts into really easy definitions that we can use all throughout our Clavio account and in our business. So RFM essentially scores people based on how recently they purchased, how frequently they're purchasing, and how much money they're spending with your business when they do. So if someone's purchased, and this is all relative to other people on your email list. So it's actually scoring it based on real behaviors within your business, not some external benchmark. So how often is someone purchasing? Sorry. How recently is someone purchasing compared to the average person in your subscriber base? How frequently is someone purchasing compared to the average in your subscriber base? And how much money is someone spending compared to the average? So someone who is in say the top 10% of all of these things is going to score very high and they're going to be considered a champion customer. RFM grades people like this. So you have your champions, like I just said, these are the people who are scoring in the top percentiles of all of those definitions. You have loyal, which is just the step under champions. You have recent, so people who have purchased recently, but maybe aren't necessarily purchasing super frequently or spending tons of money with you. You have at risk. These are subscribers who are showing signs of slowing in these metrics. So maybe say they purchase every 3 months usually on average, but now it's got to 3 and 1/2 months since their last purchase, and now they're at risk of churning and needs attention. These are people we need to get in front of, give attention before they churn. To be honest, the way I use this in practice is at risk and needs attention very much the same. If the average score needs attention, we just need to be getting in front of them and making sure they place an order, especially if they were previously a champion. So, where you can actually do this in Claio is once you've set this up, which is just in the Claio marketing analytics tab, and I know a bunch of other softwares that do this as well. So, you might already have this available to you elsewhere. But having this in Clavio is great because you can create segments based on this. You can go, okay, who is X champion? So, they were a champion customer, but they're now at risk or needs attention. This would be a really great segment that we can use for those 20% of spends where we want to get more specific. So, if our goal is more VIP revenue, we can go, okay, cool. Who was a previous champion customer who's now at risk or needs attention? They're showing they're showing signs of churning, we can get some campaigns out to this cohort this month to try re-engage them. You can also set up really good flows off the back of this. So rather than having some arbitrary win back flow, which is okay, anyone who hasn't purchased in 120 days, you can do this just when real subscribers show signs of being at risk or needs attention and they're actually going to churn based on their data. Because say what if you have a customer who only shops every 200 days on average and they spend a lot of money. Do you want them getting your win back campaign at day 120 with some random 20% discount? No. You only want to be sending that stuff when you need to based on that customer's actual data. So this is where that hyperpersonalization comes into play. We can actually use the real customer data based on their purchasing patterns and their purchasing history to make better decisions with the way that we segment our campaigns and our flows here. Make better win back flows and then come up with creative campaign ideas to drive revenue where we need to. For example, recent customers who aren't loyal or champions. This would be a really good first or second order conversion segment where we go, okay, who's purchased recently? How can we elevate them into loyal status? What can we offer them? or who's purchased recently and is now also at risk or needs attention. And what could and what do we need to offer them to save them from becoming a lapsed first-time customer and joining that dreaded list of people who only shop with us once. And you can use these definitions in all of your flows. So it could be in post purchase, abandoned cart, abandoned checkout, whatever it is. You can always segment people based on this. I like to do it for winbacks, maybe replenishment. And then you can use these segments in your campaigns as you need. Now that sort of takes us to the end of segmenting. Just to recap for our campaigns, we want to be focusing on reach and engagement. How can we keep the most amount of people on our email list engaged? How can we create elite content and get in front of them 80% of the time and then 20% of the time focusing on the more personalized touch points to maybe drive a specific goal or to help us unblock our constraint. You can use RFM analysis here. You can use simple Clavio definitions. Whatever you do, but I would be measuring the size of your engaged segments and ensuring that's growing over time. And then we leave the hyperpersonalization. We leave the onetoone stuff to our flows where we can segment based on triggers and real data within our flows. so we're not wasting our time with campaigns trying to send super micro niche campaigns. There's a couple more things I want to talk about which is going to be post-purchase surveys and a bit of loyalty stuff, but I'll save that to the end for now. I'm going to pass back over to Nathan. Nathan's going to be going over the role of paid media in your retention. So, we'll pass back over to him and then I'll see you in a little bit. >> In this last section of the video, we'll be going through paid media's involvement in driving retention. Should you be spending on paid ads, on existing customers, on even website visitors? What should that allocation look like? and how can you employ the best strategies possible here? So firstly, a very big part of our content is always focusing on acquisition. Paid ads is primarily an acquisition tool. That is the reason why you were spending on ads. You are not spending to get existing customers to purchase again. However, there's obviously a time and place for that and we have been wrong on this core assumption before. About two maybe 3 years ago, we were of the position that you should spend nothing on existing customers. All of your ads should go towards acquisition. And this is ultimately what grows the business. Retention is what makes you really profitable, but acquisition is what's going to compound growth in a DTOC or a retail business. Now, one of the caveats where this actually doesn't apply and where this kind of thinking and structure will be flawed is within fashion. And the reason being is that in fashion, you're constantly dropping new products. It needs to get surfaced to the existing customer base. And unless you have retail stores where they're walking past the store every single day seeing the new products, then it is actually hard to surface weekly product launches in front of an existing customer base just through email and SMS. You're not going to hit the entire existing customer base. People are going to miss some emails. People might not read the emails and therefore they're going to miss out on a lot of product. So that's where paid ads surfacing new arrivals starts to make a lot of sense. So you want a dedicated spend towards existing customers surfacing new arrivals constantly surfacing new campaign shoots that are relevant to what's currently live. This is incremental. Now when you actually measure the success of this campaign you want to do two things. Number one, you don't want to have the same KPI measurements as you do on new customers. So if you have, let's say, a $40 CPA target on new customers, you want to drop this down to $20 or lower for existing customers. And the reason being is that you should be way more efficient when you're serving to a warm audience. If you're going and spending the same kind of efficiency on existing customers as you are on new, you're just overspending on the existing or your ads are terrible. One or the other. The concept to really understand here in existing customer targeting is that as you layer more and more spend in, you're not really getting any more incremental conversions. So, let's say that this is your spend at $1,000 a day on existing customers. And this bar represents how many conversions you're getting. So let's say you're getting 50 a day. Then if you go and cut that spend down and you actually only spend $700 a day, you would still get 47 conversions because continuing to spend more and more on a small existing customer base doesn't actually force people to buy more. There's actually not much more squeeze available here. So, if we look at the incremental returns, you're spending an extra $300 a day for an extra three conversions, which is $100 a conversion, which is probably way off what you actually want to be spending to acquire these customers. It's probably unprofitable for you. And so, you want to be thinking about this, which is that most people are overspending on existing customers. And if you can pull back spend while maintaining conversion volume, you're just saving money that you can reallocate into acquisition. On top of this, a lot of people think through spend allocation towards retention in a percentage. They say, "What percentage of my media spend should be going to existing customers?" But you should instead reframe into what dollar amount should we be putting to existing customers. Because ultimately, the equation here is the frequency per month that you want to serve on these existing customers times by the amount of new customers that you have times by the CPMs that it cost in the platform to actually acquire these people divided by a,000. And so if you know the frequency, which should be between 4 to a 7, if you know how many existing customers you have, and then you know what your CPMs are, you can calculate directly the dollar amount that you should be putting into an existing customer campaign. One other important note on paid ads actually goes into acquisition, but it directly ties into your LTV performance, which is acquiring customers on a discount. Now, this isn't always true, and actually we have some large 9 figure retailers where this doesn't apply at all. So this is why it's so important to understand how to look at your own data and how to pull out your own insights. But as a generalization to say that maybe 60% of the brands that we work with when you acquire customers on a discount, so there's a high discount rate, the LTV of these customers is typically substantially worse. And the reason for this is that when you go into a discounting period like Black Friday or end of financial year or any kind of activation and you pull your prices down, you are opening up to a wider target demographic, which is those that weren't purchasing due to price. And then when your prices go back up, guess what? They don't repeat buy because they only bought because it was on discount. And so you end up with worse repeat rates on cohorts that come through with a discount. This is where you have to be very cognizant of the paid ad strategy and how it ties into acquisition. Because on the paid ad side of things, when we discount, everything looks better. Rowz goes up, efficiency goes up, new customer volume goes up, everything looks really good. But until we dive into the economics of the offer, and then until we dive into the lifetime value and the quality of these customers, only then do we start to see the full picture and go, "Oh, maybe this isn't actually as good of a strategy as we thought." So, make sure you pull your own numbers, look at a cohort analysis, look at a customer breakdown based on discount codes taken and start to get insights into whether people on discount are actually worse customers because sometimes they're not, but for your brands, they might be. Then the last important note here where retention, LTV, email strategies really ties into improving acquisition is getting what's called zeroarty data off of customers. So, first party data is email address, phone number, name, etc. Zero party data is personal information about the user or the customer. And so this is asking them what do they do on the weekend? What kind of problem are they trying to solve with this product? What do they actually like about the brand? All of these questions gives us granular information about who the customer actually is. Now why does any of that matter for paid? Surely that's the kind of information that you use in segmentation or email flows. Well, the reason why it matter is impaid is because that builds the fundamentals of what personas we're actually talking to, what angles we're actually pushing, and what offers we're going to put in front of these people. Because if we can understand the top 20% of customers, which typically drive 80% of revenue in most businesses, what persona they are, what angles they resonate with, and what offer they came in and purchased, then we can ensure that all of this is forced into paid ads. we overallocate spend here so that we get more top 20% customers and vice versa. Looking at the bottom 20% customers, what were their personas? What angles did they come in on to try to solve? And what was their offer? And what you'll often end up finding is that the bottom 20% of customers are people are returning, refunding, not spending a lot. They probably came in on an angle that was a little bit sketchy for your product, right? And so you sell some kind of supplement that helps with skin health, but they've come in while you are running an angle on meta about energy production. And as a consequence of that, your product hasn't really actually solved the problem. So they don't repeat buy. They might even refund or return because the packaging is all about skin health, not energy. And therefore, these are bad customers. And you shouldn't run this in the front end of ads. Now, on the front end of ads, your rorowaz might have looked good. You might have run this concept. The ad team saw a five rorowaz and went, "Oh, this is actually something that's working. Let's continue cranking this. let's continue getting it to work. But the only piece of feedback aside from a survey would have been the customer support team picking up on this. And if they don't pick up on it, then it never would have been picked up on. And you continue to pump lowquality customers into the database. Same thing for personas. Same thing for offers. So if you can figure out the type of person that is becoming the top 20%, you want to continue to speak to that person. Even if returns are slightly lower on acquisition, if LTV is much better, then that's where you want to focus your effort. If you made it this far in the video and you're an e-commerce brand doing at least $5 million a year, click the link in the description. Reach out for an audit where we'll provide you with a road map on how to scale. If you're a performance marketer with at least 2 years experience in meta and Google ads, reach out to us. There'll be a hiring link as well. We're always hiring for incredible performance marketing talent. And lastly, Angus, who was about 70% of this video. All of his socials will be below where you can reach out to him directly. you can watch his YouTube or if you're an email marketer, you can go and work with the biggest email marketing agency in Australia.

05-SET / store setup and tech Goes here. A high-level overview of customer experience (CX) management principles, emphasizing purpose-driven business, emotional connections, and transitioning from random to intentional customer experiences. Not here. • Paid media campaign setup -> 06-MEA • Landing page optimization for conversions -> 07-LPG

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides foundational concepts for understanding the importance of customer experience and the methodology behind customer journey mapping. modules: [SET] topics: [customer experience, CX strategy, customer journey mapping, emotional connection, intentional experiences, purpose-driven business] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. defining customer experience / explaining that CX is an expertise and mindset ensuring a great journey for both customers and employees; emotional impact / highlighting that customer experiences are defined by how they make people feel, which directly influences future behavior and commercial benefits; customer-centricity / emphasizing the need to place the customer at the center of the organization, referencing Amazon's practice of keeping an empty "customer chair" in meetings; market shifts / noting the rise of customers, employees, and investors who prioritize companies that "do good" and solve social problems; intentional vs. random experiences / describing the evolutionary phases of CX, moving from inconsistent "random" experiences to designed "intentional" experiences, and finally to "differentiated" experiences; the CX framework / introducing a three-part framework consisting of strategy (defining the desired experience), measurement (using journey mapping to focus improvements), and people (creating a culture that enables employees to act in the customer's interest).

Look for.

The Amazon "Customer Chair": The anecdote about Amazon leaving an empty chair in every meeting room to represent the customer, ensuring their perspective is considered in all decisions.

Intentional vs. Random Experiences: The concept that organizations must actively design their customer interactions rather than leaving them to chance, a transition that can take years to fully achieve.

18-COG / COGS and supplier Goes here. Cutting landed cost on something you already sell. BOM and should cost, supplier discovery and vetting, MOQ and price breaks, incoterms and landed cost, negotiation levers, quality control, dual sourcing. Not here. • Finding a supplier for a product that does not exist yet -> 01-PRD • Working capital and inventory financing -> 20-FIN Header. url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SCJ9XYOQ-ho rights: public_reference why: Transforms the factory relationship from a transactional cost center into a banking instrument using hyper-granular BOM breakdowns and utilization price breaks. modules: [COG] topics: [BOM and should cost, MOQ and price breaks, negotiation levers] tier: 2 scope_hint: growth Topics. BOM and should cost, supplier discovery and vetting, MOQ and price breaks, incoterms and landed cost, negotiation levers, quality control, dual sourcing. Sub-vendor component transparency, capacity utilization credits. Look for. Cost structures by component type. Volume break points. Negotiation levers and what each one is worth. Explicit line items for factory labor, factory overhead, and sub-vendor costs within the BOM. Skip. Negotiation advice with no benchmark behind the ask. Scope mix. Mostly growth. Baseline: every supplier change is gated on a sample approval and a 90 day return rate watch. Volume. 15 to 20.

20-FIN / finance and accounting Goes here. How the money actually works over time. Cash flow and the cash conversion cycle, working capital and inventory financing, P&L structure and chart of accounts, bookkeeping and inventory accounting, forecasting and budgeting, funding options and cost of capital, runway and burn, and financial reporting for lenders or investors. Not here. • Contribution margin per order and the profit formulas the ranking engine uses -> 06-MEA • Negotiating landed cost down -> 18-COG Header. url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SCJ9XYOQ-ho rights: public_reference why: Details the exact mechanics of using dividend recaps and supplier-financed consignment (via credit insurance) to maximize free cash flow distributions. modules: [FIN] jurisdiction: global topics: [cash conversion cycle, working capital and inventory financing, funding options and cost of capital, exit and valuation basics] tier: 2 scope_hint: growth Topics. cash conversion cycle, working capital and inventory financing, chart of accounts and P&L structure, inventory accounting and COGS recognition, bookkeeping practice and reconciliation, forecasting and budgeting, funding options and cost of capital, runway and burn, financial reporting for lenders and investors, exit and valuation basics. Factory credit insurance factoring, dividend recaps. Look for. Formulas with every term defined. Timing above all: how many days between paying a supplier and being paid by a processor. The exact mechanism of Chinese factories using state-backed credit insurance (e.g., Sinosure) to factor invoices at ~6% APR to pass Net 90+ terms to the brand. Dividend recap requirements (e.g., $2M+ EBITDA, 2x interest expense ratio covenants). Skip. Generic personal finance and get-rich content. Do not capture personal stock market investment strategies (e.g., buying Meta or AppLovin stock). Scope mix. Everything about financing, tax and forecasting is growth and jurisdiction-gated. Volume. 20 to 30.

21-OPS / operations and team

Goes here. Hiring methodologies, interviewing frameworks, offshore vs. onshore labor arbitrage, organizational structure, daily reporting cadences, and internal accountability systems.

Not here.

• OPEX as a fixed cost line item on the P&L -> 20-FIN

• The creative output or ad copy generated by the team -> 10-MCR

Header.

Look for. The exact trap questions used in screening (e.g., "What are you not good at?", "If I call your last 5 managers right now, how would they rate you 1-10?"). The criteria for geographic routing of roles based on context requirements (e.g., generalists onshore, highly specialized procurement or PPC offshore). Scope mix. 100% baseline.

The Reference Sample Tactic: Getting a physical sample of a high-quality product the client currently buys but finds too expensive, and shipping it directly to China for a factory to reverse-engineer and replicate.

18-COG / sourcing Goes here. A comprehensive guide to e-commerce product sourcing and supply chain management. Covers creating Tech Packs, vetting suppliers (Alibaba vs. sourcing agents), understanding True Landed Costs, managing freight (Air vs. Sea) and 3PL fulfillment, executing quality control (QC) checks, and calculating inventory reorder points. Not here. • Team management, hiring, or internal business operations -> 21-OPS • SEO or organic search strategies -> 15-SEO

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the entire lifecycle of physical product sourcing for e-commerce, moving from product definition (Tech Packs) through manufacturing, freight, 3PL logistics, and inventory forecasting. modules: [COG] topics: [sourcing, supply chain, Tech Packs, supplier vetting, landed cost, freight forwarding, 3PL, inventory forecasting, quality control] tier: 2 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. product definition / utilizing a "Tech Pack" as a strict product blueprint containing exact materials, GSM, trims, Pantone codes, and measurements to prevent factory shortcuts; supplier vetting / using Alibaba to shortlist 10-15 verified suppliers, executing video calls to spot red flags, and progressing through strike-off samples to pre-production and final production samples; True Landed Cost / calculating the actual unit cost by factoring in the X-factory price plus freight, duties, taxes, insurance, warehousing, and 3PL pick/pack fees; freight and logistics / blending Air freight (fast, expensive) with Sea freight (slow, 30-40 days) to balance inventory speed and margin; quality control / mandating a $200 third-party QC inspection before the container leaves the factory to prevent receiving damaged stock; 3PL management / selecting third-party logistics partners based on accuracy, speed, communication, and scalability, emphasizing the need for proactive communication during Q4 surges; inventory forecasting / tracking Daily Sales Velocity and Lead Times to determine exact reorder points, calculating it as: (Daily Sales Velocity x Total Lead Time) + Safety Stock.

Look for.

The Tech Pack Requirement: The explicit instruction to never manufacture a product without a detailed Tech Pack (blueprint) outlining exact GSM, Pantone colors, trims, and packaging folds, preventing the factory from making cheap assumptions.

True Landed Cost: The definition that the "X-factory price" is just the beginning, and profitability must be calculated using "Landed Cost" (Cost of Goods + Freight + Duties + 3PL fulfillment + Platform fees).

The Pre-Shipment QC Check: The hard rule to hire a third-party Quality Control inspector for ~$200 to check random units and carton weights before the container leaves the port, as problems cannot be fixed once the stock is on the water.

The Reorder Point Formula: The specific calculation for when to reorder stock: Reorder Point = (Daily Sales Velocity x Total Lead Time in days) + Safety Stock.

Skip. Plugs for the Daily Mentor program and the story about the Oodie selling out during COVID unless used to define forecasting.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (standard supply chain and sourcing execution). Volume. ~350 words.

The biggest reasons brands go out of business isn't marketing. [music] It's actually sourcing. Sourcing is difficult. You're dealing with late suppliers, wrong samples, shifting prices, and constant delays. I've lived through it all. After building the Udie, past $850 million in sales, I can tell you that operations is the hardest part of e-commerce, but also the most rewarding once it's done right. That's why today I'm going to give you an ultimate product guide [music] and sourcing guide and operations guide. This is the exact kind of guide that I wish I had when I started. You'll learn how to make your product factory ready. Find and vet suppliers, negotiate prices, and build systems that keep your margins strong and your brand in control. Let's start with the foundation. How to make your product truly factory ready before you even message a supplier. Chapter one, product definition. Most sourcing problems don't start at the factory. They start with the product itself. [music] If you aren't crystal clear on specifications of your product, you're asking for trouble. Suppliers will guess, cut corners, and you'll end up with inconsistent stock, wasted cash, and frustrated customers. Back when I started calming blankets, I remember getting our first big shipment after weeks of waiting. We opened the containers and instantly realized something was wrong. The blankets were all different. Same skew, same fabric, but three completely different shades of gray and different weights. They didn't mess up. We did. We had never given the factory a clear spec sheet. [music] They just made assumptions. It was an expensive mistake that could have been avoided with one proper thing, a proper tech pack. [music] A tech pack is your product's blueprint. It's the single document that defines how your product should be built. From materials all the way to packaging. Without it, every reorder becomes a gamble. You might get lucky once, but you'll never build consistency with your product without a tech pack. When I first learned about tech packs, I realized how many variables I'd been leaving open for the supplier. The thickness of the fabric, the exact drawstring length, even how the packaging was folded. Every one of those details matters because factories don't see your brand the way you do. They care about throughput and efficiency. If something isn't defined, they'll choose whatever is easiest for them, and they'll try to sneak things in. So, if you're serious about product quality, your tech pack isn't optional. Here's what a solid tech pack should definitely include. Detailed product drawings or photos from every angle. Exact materials and finishes, including GSM, trims, and hardware. Measurements for every size or variant, colorways, and pantone codes, label, packaging, and care instructions, clear product name, version, and date. If you're not a designer, that's fine. Hire someone that is. On Upwork, you can find experienced product designers who will build your tech pack for $200. It's worth [music] every cent. You can also use tools like Figma, Canva, or Notion templates to keep your specs always up to date. When you reach this stage, sourcing becomes way easier. You're no longer guessing and suppliers can't take shortcuts. You're in control of the process. So, now your product is truly factory ready. Let's talk about how to actually find the right suppliers to bring it to life. Chapter two, suppliers and sampling. This is where sourcing becomes real because a good supplier will make you more money for years and a bad one can sink you in a single order. So, how do we vet and find suppliers? Most founders start on Alibaba, which is totally fine. It's still the easiest way to get a feel for pricing, materials, and minimum order quantities, but you have to treat it like research, not a final decision. Don't just click the first link that looks professional. You need to verify everything. The first step is building a short list. Search by your exact product type. Filter by verified suppliers and trade assurance and message at least 10 to 15 factories. You'll lose some along the way and that's fine. You're testing for responsiveness, professionalism, and whether they produce similar products before. Once you've shortlisted a few, get on a video call. Ask them to walk you through their facility or show you some sample products. You'll quickly spot some red flags such as vague answers, poor communication, or someone clearly operating from their living room. Then comes the verification step. check how long they've been active, their export countries, and request documents like their ISO or BSCI certifications. Now, if you're planning on scaling using a sourcing agent or like a platform like Quimma or Easy IMAX, they'll inspect factories in person for you. It's also worth diversifying outside of China depending on your product type and your age of business. If you're an older business, maybe you can consider other countries like Vietnam, India, and Turkey. But you need to make sure you're at the right size to do this. Now, a good supplier relationship starts with clarity. Send them your tech pack and ask for quotes that include things like your unit cost for each skew or variation, your minimum order quantity, your lead time to manufacture, and packaging details and payment terms. Now, we've got that covered. This is where sampling comes into play. When you find a few potential suppliers, get samples from all of them. It's not just about quality. It's about communication and reliability. who follows instructions the best, who sends updates without being asked who can match your tech pack precisely. Start with a strike off or small test sample for materials and prints, and once that's approved, move to a pre-production sample, which should match your tech pack perfectly. Treat this as your gold standard. When you move to bulk, this is the reference you'll compare against. For apparel, this is also where you confirm grading. Make sure your sizes, small, medium, and large, scale correctly. Get multiple samples in the pre-production round to confirm proportions. Once you're happy, keep one sample inhouse and then keep one of these samples in the factory for reference. When you've chosen your final supplier, move to a production sample. This is a final test built right before mass production. If it doesn't match your pre-production standard, don't proceed. Building long-term supplier relationships. A good supplier isn't just a vendor, they're a partner. Once you find someone reliable, treat them like part of your team. Share your forecasts early, pay on time, and reward good performance with repeat business. Factories will always prioritize their best clients first. Just become one of them. And protect your product as you scale. Always keep your original tech packs, artwork, and source files on your side. Once you're at volume, get a manufacturing agreement signed and register all of your trademarks. When you follow this process completely, you turn chaos to control. You'll know who you're working with, what to expect, and how to keep your standards high every single order. So, now that you understand how to find a reliable supplier and what a production ready sample looks like, chapter three, price,QS, terms, and POSOS. You can have a great product and reliable supplier, but if you don't understand your numbers, you're building on sand. I see this time and time again with founders designing an amazing product with great branding, but everything falls apart when production begins because they never account for pricing or profit properly. Even larger companies make this mistake. They rush from design straight into manufacturing without ever checking if the numbers actually make sense. Let's say we designed an Udie with a built-in heated pockets and Bluetooth temperature controls. Something crazy. That might be something that people would line up for and we want to sell it for say $50, but that product might cost $40 or something to make up. Meaning that I'd have to sell the product for $200. That instantly kills the idea. Understanding your costs upfront is what decides whether your product is even viable. Understanding true unit cost. When you're new to manufacturing, it's easy to think you're making great margins until you realize how many hidden costs are actually under the quote. The number your supplier gives you is rarely the full picture. That's the X factory price, [music] meaning it only covers the physical production. But the second that the product leaves the factory, a whole new layer of costs begin. There's freight, which can fluctuate wildly depending on fuel and global shipping rates. Then duties and taxes, which differ from country and product type. You've also got insurance, warehousing, packaging, and fulfillment fees. each one nibbling at your profits until what looked like 60% margin turns into 20%. When I first started scaling my dog bed business, what seemed like a very very profitable business, all of these costs started to add up and it was nowhere near as profitable as I thought. That's when I learned the concept of landed cost. The total cost of your product once it's in your warehouse and ready to sell. It's the only number that really matters with sourcing. Here's the thing. Most people don't do this math until it's too late. They make decisions on what feels affordable, not what's actually profitable. This is why it's important to build out a detailed spreadsheet breaking down everything: product, freight, packaging, duties, taxes, warehousing, platform fees, transaction costs, and payment transfer fees. If you want to understand your landed cost for customers, you'll also need courier fees. If you need help building the spreadsheet, just go to Chat TBT and prompt it asking for all of these hidden costs and then fill out the template. Alternatively, you can join Daily Mentor. We've got so many templates like this. So, when you know your real cost per unit, you can start making smarter choices everywhere else. Marketing spend, ad testing, even offer strategy, pricing, and negotiation. Once you understand your costs, it's time to focus on how pricing and negotiation really works. Most founders chase the lowest possible unit cost, thinking it's the key to profit, and end up sitting in warehouses full of unsold products. Sure, they saved $2 a unit, but they killed their cash flow in the process. Because you see, early on, flexibility is worth more than margin. Paying slightly more per unit gives you room to test, pivot, and adjust without overcommitting. Your first few production runs might not be about maximizing profit. They might be about learning, such as how fast does the stock sell, how consistent is quality, and where delays happen. Once you know those answers, that's when you can negotiate confidently. And remember, negotiation isn't just about price. It's about partnership. If you squeeze a supplier too hard, they'll make up the difference somewhere else, such as cheaper materials, skipped quality control, or sometimes even slower timelines. Factories have margins, too. And when they're under pressure, your brand usually pays for it later. Good negotiation means balancing what works for both sides. Now, no factory will ever lower their price or offer better payment terms unless they know that you have options. That's why it's smart to get quotes or samples from at least one other supplier. It keeps the conversation honest and gives you leverage without hostility. Be transparent about your goal. Share your forecast and show them your serious about scaling. Now that you know your margins and have your deal locked in, it's time to learn how to move that product. And that's where freight and fulfillment come in next. Chapter four, freight, customs, and fulfillment. Getting your product from the factory floor to your hands of your customers without losing your sanity or your profit can be very, very painful. Logistics is the bloodstream of your business. Every day your inventory sits idle, it's burning cash. Every time you touch it, it's burning cash. The faster and cleaner you can move your stock through the supply chain, the stronger your cash flow and the calmer your business will feel. Freight forwarders and planning lead times. There are really only two ways to move your product. Air or C. Air is fast and expensive, which is perfect for small or urgent batches or if you've got a tiny product. C is slower but dramatically cheaper. It's what keeps your margins healthy once you're scaling. Most successful brands use a hybrid strategy. Air freight, a small batch to start selling quickly, then follow up with C shipments to restock at lower cost. But this really depends on your product size and weight. For small items, a mix works well. For larger or heavier items, C freight is almost always the best option. But moving stock isn't just about picking a transport method. It's about planning lead times backwards. Freight isn't instant. Sea can take 30 to 40 days doortodoor. Air might take 7 to 10 and production itself can often add another 20 or 30 days. That means that if you wait until you are nearly out of stock to reorder, you're already too late. Start planning your next shipment the moment your current one lands. The biggest reason brands panic ship or run out of stock isn't bad luck, it's just bad forecasting. From the moment your PO is signed, your countdown begins. You need visibility from factory to warehouse at all times. That's where freight forwarders come in. These companies manage the complex stuff for you. Booking containers, handling customs, and coordinating delivery to your warehouse. A good forwarder will update you before problems happen and help you navigate global delays. If you've ever tried to handle shipping yourself, you know it's chaos. Different time zones, customs forms, endless email chains. A strong forwarder simplifies all of that. They'll quote you based on route, wait, and deadlights. And more importantly, they'll tell you what's realistic. And again, don't always chase the cheapest rate. The cheapest freight forer might leave your goods sitting at a port for weeks and fill a container instead. Finally, before that container leaves the factory, book your final inspection. This is your last chance to catch mistakes before they multiply. A $200 QC check, quality control check, can save $20,000 in damage or inconsistent stock in that last check stage. Your QC agent will test random units, check measurements, verify packaging, labeling, and carton weight. And they'll take photos of everything. [music] They'll flag even small inconsistencies that could become massive issues later. If they find problems, the factory can fix them before the shipment leaves. Once it's on the water, it's just too late. You need to think beyond just product quality and more about protecting your reputation and customer experience. Think of it like insurance, a small cost that keeps your entire operation safe. You approve or reject the shipment based on that report and only release final payment once everything passes. Fulfillment and 3PLs. If all goes smoothly and your goods arrive, your job still isn't finished. It's now just shifted from production to delivery. Disorganization can kill brands at this step. You need to learn more about 3PL's. A 3PL, also known as third party logistics provider, is the bridge between your factory and your customers. They store, pick, pack, and ship your orders, manage returns, and often integrate directly with Shopify or your warehouse management tools. However, the difference between a good 3PL and a bad one can make or break your experience with e-commerce. When we were scaling the Udy, fulfillment became our biggest threat overnight. During one of our Q4, we were forecasting record numbers, $45, $50 million in sales, and everything looked perfect until one of our 3PL collapsed under the pressure. We lost tens of millions in potential revenue and even ended up in the news because customers thought we were scamming them. It was one of the hardest lessons that I've ever learned. That experience made me realize how critical fulfillment partners are. You can do everything right, product, marketing, sourcing, and still lose it all if your logistics partner fails you. So, how do you pick the right one? Don't just compare prices or promises. Ask questions that really expose how they operate, such as accuracy. What's their error rate on orders shipped? Speed. How fast do they process during peak volume and how do they do that? Communication. Who's your direct contact when problems [music] actually hit? Scalability. How have they handled previous Q4 surges for other brands? And never skip going to visit their warehouse to see how it all operates. Once you've seen two or three, you realize who the true players actually are. You also want to ask them how do they handle returns, damages, and restocks. Do they flag issues proactively or wait for you to notice? Those answers tell you who will protect your brand when orders start flying. Our coaches at Daily Mentor always hammer home that fulfillment isn't a set and forget system. It's a living part of your business. The best operators track inventory turnover weekly, maintain shared dashboards with their warehouses, and hold monthly reviews with their 3PL partners. These habits prevent the exact disaster we went through. Once you built a setup like this, your logistics should start to feel very, very calm. And that's the goal, predictable, repeatable, and reliable. When fulfillment runs on autopilot and nothing feels urgent, that's when you know it's working. Next, let's look at the final piece of the puzzle. Forecasting, cash flow, and reordering. How do you actually keep up this whole system running without ever running out of stock again? [music] Chapter 5, forecasting and planning. You might think the hardest part of sourcing is over once your product is shipping smoothly and orders are being fulfilled. But that's actually where most brands slip. Everything you've built up to this point, your supplier relationships, your logistics, your product quality, only matters if you can keep it consistent. A lot of founders treat forecasting like an afterthought, but it's one of the most important parts of sourcing. Because sourcing isn't just about finding great products. [music] It's about keeping them in stock, profitable, and moving through your supply chain. If you followed everything up to now, this is the final step that ties it all together. This part will decide whether your sourcing process scales or collapses. The real cost of poor planning. Back in the early days of the Udie, I thought we had it all figured out. Our products were selling fast, ads were converting, and everything looked like it was working perfectly. But then co hit. I remember watching sales skyrocket overnight, $200,000 days back to back and thinking we'd hit the jackpot. But I didn't realize how big the demand spike would be. Within a week, we were completely sold out. It doesn't sound like a problem, right? Wrong. We had zero stock, monthsl long production lead times, and no forecasting system in place to keep catching up. For almost two months, we couldn't fulfill orders, couldn't capitalize on demand, and lost millions in potential sales. Worse, it damaged the momentum. Customers got frustrated, and our performance tanked. That experience taught me one thing. If you're not forecasting, you're gambling. You can't grow what you can't plan. That experience forced me to completely rethink forecasting and operations. We didn't just fail to reorder. We failed to plan at all. There was no one inside the business dedicated to looking ahead, checking lead times, or adjusting our forecast regularly. And that's why we missed the moment. Looking back, if we had someone focused purely on operations and planning, the Udie could have been 30, 40% bigger. But the truth is, you don't need a full team right away to get this right. You just need discipline. Whether you're a solo founder or have a small crew, you can still build a forecasting rhythm that protects your sourcing. Create a simple system that forces you to review performance and stock levels every single week and communicate these with your suppliers before problems appear. This goes handinhand with what I mentioned on credibility. Here's a simple version of what this forecasting sheet should look like. It should have daily sales velocity, such as how fast your products actually sell, measured over time. This shows how quickly inventory is moving. You should have lead time, how long it takes from paying your supplier to the stock arriving at your warehouse or 3PL, including production, shipping, and clearance. Then you also need to have safety stock, which is basically your insurance buffer. When sales spike or freight gets delayed, this keeps you selling. Then you can just use this simple equation. Your reorder point equals the daily sales velocity times total lead time plus safety sold. For example, if you sell 50 units a day, your total lead time is 60 days and you keep 500 units as safety stock. Your reorder point is 3500 units. When your inventory hits that level, it's time to reorder. Shopify already gives you almost everything you need. Use your order history to spot sales velocity, slow movers, and seasonal spikes. Make sure to check those insights weekly and feed them into your reorder plan. If this video helped you, go check out all of the mistakes that I made in this video on the screen. And make sure you like and subscribe. Peace.

jobs.text:
18-COG / sourcing Goes here. A practical guide and list of lessons learned by an e-commerce entrepreneur transitioning from dropshipping to bulk sourcing products from China via Alibaba. Covers negotiating volume discounts, executing quality control, managing shipping methods, maintaining supplier relationships, and navigating payment gateways. Not here. • Marketing, scaling ads, or storefront design -> 04-BRD or 06-MEA • Domestic 3PL warehouse setup and operations -> 21-OPS

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details practical, hard-learned lessons for bulk importing e-commerce products from China, emphasizing risk mitigation through quality checks, secure payment gateways, and calculated supplier transitions. modules: [COG] topics: [sourcing, Alibaba, bulk purchasing, supplier negotiation, quality control, freight logistics, trade assurance] tier: 2 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. bulk purchasing / leveraging high-volume orders (e.g., 10k units) to negotiate per-item costs down significantly (e.g., reducing a $7.80 item to $2.00); quality control / emphasizing the need to order a 10% surplus or hire a $200 third-party inspector to account for the inevitable defective products in bulk shipments; shipping logistics / planning ahead for heavy items by choosing sea containers over expensive air cargo, and negotiating premium shipping (FedEx/UPS) for large orders instead of relying on ePacket; supplier relationships / avoiding sudden supplier switches by maintaining multiple vendor options and testing new, cheaper suppliers with smaller batches to verify defect rates; communication and payments / securing direct contact methods (WeChat/WhatsApp) to avoid supplier ghosting, and strictly using Alibaba's Payment Gateway (Trade Assurance) for buyer protection rather than direct transfers like PayPal.

Look for.

The 10% Buffer Rule: The recommendation to order at least 10% more units than needed to safely account for the inevitable defective products found in bulk Alibaba shipments.

Alibaba Payment Mandate: The strict advice to only use Alibaba's built-in Payment Gateway (Trade Assurance) and avoid PayPal or direct WeChat transfers to ensure grievance redressal and buyer protection.

Multi-Channel Communication: The necessity of securing a supplier's WhatsApp or WeChat, as they often go offline without notice on the native Alibaba chat platform.

Slow Supplier Transitions: The strategy of maintaining your original supplier while testing a new, cheaper supplier with a smaller test batch (e.g., 500 units) to verify their quality before fully migrating your supply chain.

Skip. Automated moderator comments, deleted comments, subreddit rules, and generic compliment replies in the comment section.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (standard bulk sourcing and operational execution). Volume. ~350 words.

What I learnt from sourcing e-commerce products from China.

DISCLAIMER: The intention of this to increase cautiousness and practice best practices between the entrepreneurs that are importing from China.

So I have been running an e-commerce store for a very long time, not a drop-shipping particularly but we would order the products in bulk to the country and then ship from there (For faster shipping).I wanted to do drop-shipping but then it halted back in 2019, right after the COVID and ePacket was banned (ePacket is a shipping agreement between US and China to reduce shipping times, it uses passenger planes to carry the parcel, hence faster shipping) .

Anyway getting back to the point, We were selling jewellery in the United States, firstly we used to just order from Aliexpress (a bunch of 500 every week) to our warehouse, do the quality check and then we would ship it from there. However the price per item was $7.80 and it was selling for $25.99 with a good profit margin.

We decided to scale that store (I shared the scaling strategy in a different blog post) by going to a supplier and ordering 10K since Q4 was coming up and we were trying to scale up, the item was selling like a hot dog. We posted a few Request For Quotation on Alibaba and got some quotations and here are my learnings.

You will get the same product for less.

The item we were getting for $7.80 was available for as low as $4.00 if we ordered in bulk, and as high as $10, so it varies. If you order $10K units then it will be available for $2.00. The more volume you ask for the lesser the cost will be - I mean it's normal, but the cost can go very low. I mean compare $7.80 to $2.00

You will have to do your own quality check.

Alibaba is not like Amazon where they do the quality check for you, you will have to do your quality check before you ship the items to your customers. We ordered 10K and got around 300 defective items from the supply. (either they were broken, or of a bad quality). And then you have to send them to the supplier, the supplier will usually ask you to send the items back but it's not worth the time. So make sure that you order at least 10% more of what you need.

Plan your shipments accordingly and choose the correct method

Unrelated to the store, we saw a great kitchen product that we thought could do really good in the American market, but the problem? It was 1.2Kgs. It was a really large item made out of stainless steel. We wanted it faster but AIR CARGO was expensive (it was charging $2000) as we did not have time since Q4 was already around the corner, however the affordable option was ship containers but the transit time was 1 month. So make sure if you plan to order large items, do it beforehand and make sure you choose the right shipping service to save costs.

Trust your negotiation skills.

You got to trust your negotiations skills and don't be shy when negotiating with your suppliers, we got down the per product cost from $6 to $4.80. While it may not seem a lot but it saved around $3500 per order. So negotiation works! I mean just like any other business.

Never ditch a supplier too early.

If you find a better price somewhere then don't move your orders at once, we got a supplier that was giving the exact same product for almost 20% less, and ordered 500 units from them. Most of the units were defective, so always maintain multiple suppliers until you do the quality check of both of the suppliers.

Have multiple modes of communication

If you're using Alibaba chat to communicate with your suppliers then make sure you have their emails and WhatsApp, WeChat or anything they use because they will go offline without prior notice.

You will get free FedEX/UPS shipping

Don't hesitate to ask for premium shipping if you maintain a good relationship, the supplier we had used to send the items using ePacket which used to take 10-14 days, talked to the supplier and he offered a premium FedEX shipping for large orders which delivered the order in 4-5 days max (to California)

Always use AliBaba Payment Gateway

Never use PayPal, or WeChat or anything else to send the funds, it's just not worth the hassle. Even though you have the escrow services at place. I would just avoid PayPal or anything and just go with Alibaba's gateway. It is seamless and has a great grievance redressal system.

Product Sourcing Agents are great but be careful

There are a lot of product sourcing agents are great, they will get in touch directly with the manufacturer for you and can get any type of customisation done for you and can get you better prices. But be careful and use a better sourcing agent.

I guess that was it. I will edit this post if I find more points to address.

3y ago

Good write up.

I am a US based Sourcing Agent/ contract mfg and work with similar companies to yours.

One objection I would have us with Alibaba Trade Assurance. The grievance system in my experience is a joke. Seen a lot of times people get denied that clearly should have been refunded. I personally would rather TT the payment and negotiate a discount because they no longer have to pay the fee. But that is just me. Sourcing is my expertise and have confidence in the suppliers and products I chose. I have a manufacturing and engineering background, so way easier for me.

I will also say about volume discounts.

If there are any unused discounts you aren't taking advantage of, volume or even other discounts like lower cost/ consolidated freight. Maybe because buying a higher volume would be to hard on your cash flow. Those discounts can be leveraged to your advantage in other ways. And that advantage could be significantly more valuable to you than the discount itself.

One thing I do for a couple Clients is. Normally they would pay their supplier 30% deposit to start production, then 70% balance before it ships. And they would re-order the same product multiple times a year with say a landed cost of $10.00.

What I would do is when the Client was going to order next for $10.00, I would add my own money to the mix to increase that order to say a year supply. Basically what that does is makes the cost of their units $10.00 like normal, but my units are cheaper because of the discount my money unearthed. Then the full year supply is shipped to the Client. Once they burn through the inventory they paid for, they then order from me that is already in their warehouse for the same $10.00 they would have paid anyway. Only now there is no lead time and no MOQ. They just pay me for what they use of my inventory when they use it. Which helps their cash flow significantly.

Then we discuss reorder. Sometimes I just take it from there, other times we repeat the above.

Basically, leveraging those unused discounts to help their cash flow.

The reason I say this, is there is probably distributors or investors in your area that might do the same for you.
