Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides explicit, practical guidance on how e-commerce brands must classify operational expenses versus Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) to accurately track gross margins and profitability. modules: [FIN] topics: [COGS, e-commerce accounting, freight classification, landed cost, gross margin, inventory management, drop shipping, customs duties] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. defining COGS / defining Cost of Goods Sold as every expense incurred to bring a product up to the point it sits on the warehouse shelf ready to sell ("all in until it's in"); freight and duty classification / clarifying that inbound freight, shipping container costs, and customs tariffs are strictly included in COGS; outbound shipping classification / noting that outbound shipping to the customer is an operating expense unless it's a drop-shipping model or explicitly baked into a "free shipping" retail price; packaging classification / distinguishing between "product packaging" (the retail box sitting on the shelf), which is COGS, and the "shipping packaging" (the brown cardboard box), which is an operating expense; platform fees / explicitly stating that Amazon PPC fees, Shopify transaction fees, advertising, and warehouse rent (3PL storage) are operating expenses, not COGS; returns accounting / explaining that the cost of shipping a return back is an overhead expense, but the cost to repackage or refurbish the item to make it sellable again can be classified as COGS; inventory management / recommending software over spreadsheets to automatically attribute and weight lump-sum freight and duty invoices down to the individual SKU level to calculate true landed cost.

Look for.

The "All in until it's in" Rule: The guiding accounting principle that any cost incurred before the product is ready to be sold on the shelf is COGS, and any cost incurred after the sale is an operating expense.

The Packaging Distinction: The specific rule that the retail box (e.g., the white Apple iPhone box) is part of COGS, but the brown cardboard shipping box it goes into for delivery is a shipping expense.

The Drop-Shipping Exception: Noting that outbound shipping is usually an expense, except in drop-shipping models where the supplier charges the merchant a bundled outbound freight fee, which is then counted as COGS.

The Repackaging Rule for Returns: Clarifying that return shipping is an overhead expense, but the labor and materials used to repackage that returned item to make it sellable again are classified as COGS.

Skip. Plugs for the A2X software tool and Outserve accounting services.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (standard accounting and reporting principles). Volume. ~350 words.

everyone and welcome. Today we're diving into the world of COGS. That's cost of goods sold. And we're going to talk about why it's such a crucial part of accurate accounting for e-commerce businesses. I'm joined by Phil Oakley from Outserve, one of the UK's top accounting integrators. outserve work with many well-known Amazon and Shopify brands, some you might recognize, and they help them to streamline their accounting and get their inventory management sorted out. Phil is a real expert in this space. So, if you are an e-commerce brand looking to get a handle on your numbers, you're in the right place. So, Phil, great to have you here. And tell us a little bit about yourself. >> Thank you very much. Thank you for that great introduction. No pressure there there at all. But yes, uh at outserve we have a specialist team working with scaling e-commerce businesses and and brands. And because I think we have a real focus on inventory management, inventory accounting with some of the software and the tools, we do spend a lot of time uh looking at at COGS and COGS calculations and all of those things. So really really really excited to get into a discussion uh about how we can yeah help some businesses understand. Great. So, before we get into the nuts and bolts of cost of goods sold, let's talk about why it's important to get it right in the first place. Why is close enough not good enough for e-commerce brands? Um, Phil, you tell us a bit more about that. >> I think, you know, for us, it it we talk about COGS all the time, but what we're really talking about is margin and profit. And of course hopefully that's what all the all the businesses uh are are in this in this for um especially in these you know challenging challenging times. Um, if you don't know your cogs, then you don't know your your profit margin. You you can't calculate your profit. And and I think, you know, when we think about strategy and and all businesses need to be thinking about their strategy so much at the time once you've decided what problem you're solving, you know, what great product you've got, then your cost of goods sold and your margin is really going to dictate so much of your strategy from what channels you sell on, how you promote. um it's it's really going to be the anchor of of everything in in your business uh to understand how you're going to going to make money, how you're going to be profitable, how you're going to be successful and and deliver maximum value. Um and you know, it feels to me so many times that businesses without understanding COGS are really flying blind, flying by the seat of their pants and and uh understandably giving themselves some sleepless nights maybe. >> Yes, I can imagine. So um okay so from the accounting side just tell us to start with what exactly does cost of goods sold cover and how would you go about calculating it? Yeah. And I think we could all say straight away, Ellsworth, it's complicated. It's it's complex. It's not always straightforward. And for different businesses, it it can be quite different. I think if we just try and focus at the moment on on many of the types of businesses that we would uh have as as A2X clients who are buying products in and selling products, we can touch a bit, you know, obviously if you're manufacturing, then your cost of goods sold is going to have another layer and level to it. But if we just sort of build it up and we think about business that that's buying in in in that cost of goods sold, you know, we we're we're really thinking in that calculation of of everything you've paid for that product up to the point that you've got it onto your shelf. Um, you know, think from the supplier door onto your shelf um before it's sold. And that's thinking, okay, let's always start with I've got to buy the product. there's a purchase price for that product. Hopefully, we've all know what that is. It might be, you know, sometimes even for some some of our clients that's not clear and until it's uh later on prices fluctuate and change, especially in some commodity markets, currencies change. But then, of course, the big ones we often think about is freight. It's the freight cost to bring that product in. So if you were bringing say a product in from China, which of course is is very common and popular with some e-commerce businesses, you're going to have uh probably a container maybe uh coming over by container, you're going to have that container cost, which is is going to be included in the cost of goods sold. And then of course you're going to have to think about how do you actually allocate that that complete container cost to each product. Um duties uh is is another one that we we spend a lot of time thinking about. you know a lot of discussion on on tariffs at the moment and and that affects everybody. So tariff is the percentage of the the import duty and then the actual import duty is what what you pay and of course for you know so many of the American North American uh A2X users there looks like there could be some very interesting tariffs and calculations all of that that tariff all of those import duties are going to be included in in the cost of goods sold. So, it's increasing that uh that that product product cost and and anything really to get it into your warehouse onto your shelf is going to be included in there. Um, so I think that's that's really the starting point, but also it's not just okay, what's in there then how how is it calculated? because you might have that those duties and those freight in sort of big lumps on invoices from different people and then it's all got to be attributed across essentially down to a unit by by unit cost. So you can see a total cost of of of the unit. Does that does that make sense? >> Yeah. So there's there's a few moving parts there. >> There is >> in reality we do know that a lot of e-commerce sellers struggle with this. um tell us some of the common pitfalls that you see when businesses are trying to calculate their costs. >> Yeah, and and I think you know obviously some really just do struggle to to to calculate it at all and and they're they're left with a you know sort of a zero or a QuickBooks or a Netswuite without having clear figures in their tool. So maybe they've just put all of their purchase invoices uh in there and they're not even making a making a stock adjustment. But I think some of the um you know some of the the common areas as I've sort of touched on before is that they're not actually allocating those costs to each unit or trying to understand how how those costs would would apply. I think there's a some confusion on sort of okay I've got uh inbound freight but actually I've got shipping costs out and those shipping costs in in most cases are not included. >> Yes. >> In in costs of goods sold. Maybe some people start to think that they've got to put their fees, their Amazon fees or their advertising. And it's really, you know, we start to get into this conversation, what's above the line of gross profit. Um, so what is really that gross profit margin and what's below the line and in below the line we're talking what's an overhead? you know, we might be thinking what's, you know, opex, what's an operating e expense and classifying that so you can really have some good comparison figures and and I think shipping income as in uh outbound shipping, shipping income and uh shipping expenses confuses people even you know to the point of of packaging. So, if it's a box which is actually part of of the product, so it's the product box with the picture on, that's part of your cost of goods sold as as you would expect. Um, you know, if someone over here, you can see that Apple box, that box is part of the cost of goods sold. But the brown box that it goes into when it actually leaves and gets delivered, that is not part of the cost of goods sold. That that's part of the shipping cost to go out. So suddenly you might have an invoice with with you know packing boxes on or or product boxes and they might be on the same invoice and then you've got to start splitting it down to go actually that is part of the product and that is not. And of course at every level we can get a little bit more complicated. >> You know in when we've got clients in fashion and apparel then they can have a lot of returns and many businesses can have returns and then when stuff comes back in you've got to start understanding the cost there. If if the if the cost is actually to repackage that product into that maybe to make it sellable again, that could be part of the cost of goods sold. If it's part of bringing it back and then actually then just getting it ready to to ship it out again, then that's not. So, you know, there's those that fine line between there's lots of costs going on and just really understanding which which part of of it is it is it to get it ready up to that to sell it and then it's a co cost after sale and that's what you've you've got to think sometimes is really the the shipping cost to send it out is after you've sold it. >> Yes. >> Um the brown box that it goes in is a cost after you sold it. the, you know, the product box was a cost before you sold it and and start to think about things. There's a few little rules that you can follow as in would you have incurred this cost anyway if you hadn't have bought that item. So, it's a bit like the rent of your warehouse. You would have incurred that cost whatever. Even if you didn't buy that shipment, you would have still had that cost. Whereas the container, the duty, the freight, you would not have had that cost if you hadn't have bought those products. Um, you know, one of the phrases, you know, all in until it's in. So, all of the costs in until it's in, and then when it's in, things after that point are then expenses. >> Yeah. Okay. That's that's a really good rule of thumb. Um, okay. So, I think we've got a little bit of a quick fire for you here. We're going to ask you, we're going to um give you a transaction type and you're going to tell us where it fits. Okay. >> And Yeah. And if I get it right, you'll leave it in the video. If I get it wrong, you just edit me out and make me look really good. >> Yeah. >> Okay. Here we go. So, first one, inbound shipping and duty. >> Yeah. So, we've touched on this a bit nearly in every single case that is included in your cost of goods sold. you know, all in until it's in, you wouldn't have had that cost till then. So, inbound freight and duty um is in your cost of goods sold. >> Outbound shipping to customers. >> Okay. So, I will go into a little bit of of detail here. As a general rule, and as you know, there's there's no think that's 100%. As a general rule, it's an expense. There's a couple of scenarios you can think about where you can consider it as part of your COGS. that could be where it's actually included in the price. So, you're not you're not charging for it. It's actually free shipping, then that could be considered as part of your COGS. And then a slight nuance, if you're in drop shipping, and you know, obviously we know a few businesses in e-commerce are in drop shipping and your supplier is charging for what is effectively outbound freight, but that could also be being uh considered a cost of goods sold. So, if we're not talking about drop shipping and we're not talking about a product which has free shipping included, then then generally that is that is not in COGS, that's an expense. >> Good point on the drop shipping though because we do have quite a few sellers that that are doing that. Okay, next one. Amazon and Shopify fees. >> Amazon Shopify fees very important to the profitability of your business. Very important that A2X is there doing that for you, but it's an expense, not part of the cost of goods sold. Okay, advertising and coupons. >> Um, so obviously if it's an advertising cost, it's going to be an expense. It's if it's actually a a coupon which would reduce the price, then that could obviously be reducing the sale price. So it's not in it's not in COGS. It could be reducing your revenue, your turnover, your sales. Um, but you think anything in advertising, marketing, so when we think about the, you know, the the the the pay-per-click fees on Amazon, anything they might do in marketing, that's all to do with with overheads and expenses. >> Okay. And the next one, we have touched on this already, but um, we'll do it again just quickly. Packaging materials. >> Yeah. So, the distinction in packaging materials, when you're thinking of packaging materials, is this actually product packaging? So, it's the nice pretty box or the inner and and everything that actually makes up that that product that you you see and buy. Or is it and I know they're not always brown, but think if it's the brown shipping box, if it's actually just there to be part of the shipping, um it's it's not it's not part of the cost of goods sold. So, product packaging is part of the cost of goods sold. Think of it sitting on the shelf looking pretty. If you were in a retail environment and that's where a lot of this stems from even for e-commerce businesses make you know sitting on a shelf makes product look pretty that's cost of goods sold brown box to actually get it there or equivalent then it's a shipping expense >> good distinction there okay next one warehouse rent or 3PL storage >> yeah all all overheads all expenses again falls into that category you're going to have that expense whatever pretty pretty much and it's a cost after you've sold if the 3PL's charging you to to ship again. So, it's it's expense after it's got in again. All in until it's in, it's in. Now, if you've got warehouse rent, if if you got a 3PL who's charging, that's not in cost of goods sold. >> Okay, that's a good one. Now, this one, a little bit more of a gray area. Supplier discounts or credits. >> Um, yeah, I think, you know, it depends. I'd say generally speaking if a supplier has given you a discount on a product that you are you are buying then that's in in cost of goods sold. So it's reduced the cost. Um obviously if they're giving you a credit depends what they've given you a credit might be that you've given them the stock back. So we're going to have the stock movement anyway. So we got movement in stock and there's a credit note from that. I would say generally speaking um we'd we'd be looking at cost of goods sold from those supplier costs. >> Okay. And last one on the list customer returns. So customers of returns are are really interesting. Um I mentioned apparel obviously very high returns but so many e-commerce businesses we need to expect that there'll be returns and generally the cost of returning the item that's that's really an overhead. Um and uh but if there's repackaging or again it needs a new box then that can go into cost of goods sold. and and you know some of these things we're talking strictly for maybe some statutory accounts or compliance accounts in in any of the different countries. There is no doubt some interesting KPIs that different businesses can have and definitely we see this in apparel businesses that they they will have a look at slightly different margin figures as well as cost of goods sold, gross profit margin. We can have sort of contribution margin. We can have some really interesting stats on returns understanding what it's cost on that. But really strictly speaking for statutory accounts then it's you know there's a distinction between the cost to return the goods in and anything you need to do to get the cost the goods ready to sell them again. >> Yeah. And that's a really interesting piece because we're seeing some Shopify brands are doing some clever things in Shopify to try and reduce that returns rate based on what they can see. Um, which is I think that's the way some of these Shopify stores are going right now. >> Yeah, I think there's a great opportunity to possibly offer a voucher or a discount or even trade up on the sale and that can make the accounting even even more tricky to do to try and understand what was actually sold, what was the margin. Then you've got maybe a discount and a voucher. But there's great success we see in people actually encouraging them to make a purchase when they're making the return. Um, and actually making sure that that there is there is a sale. And uh, you know, when people purchase an item, sometimes we see that they actually did want to purchase something, but that one wasn't quite right. So maybe offering them an alternative or an upsell or a discount can be a great thing to do. >> I've noticed a prepaid return that you get a slightly discounted rate if you prepay it as well, which is quite a nifty way to do it. Yeah, I think we we're seeing it's harder and harder to offer, you know, free postage and free returns, which of course is cutting into your profits significantly. And this again is the key reporting everybody needs to know. COGS margin very important, but we need to consider all of the the cost of doing business and and how that affects profitability. >> Yeah, 100%. Okay, great. So, that's been brilliant. There's one more question just to ask you around is around what do you think the best practices are for e-commerce businesses that are trying to get a handle on their cost of goods sold. Phil, >> um obviously I'm I'm a little bit biased and when we really need to, you know, those businesses have the best calculations they can is is probably having inventory management software. You know, we know uh many of the A2X uh clients now starting to look at inventory management and and then really having that controlled process and and really is about people and process before it is about systems and software and and really understanding, okay, when I place a purchase order for for goods, I'm going to be very clear on on what price it is and checking that that price that it comes through to the actual invoice that I get that goes into financials. But actually, I'm actually going to start catch capturing freight and duty costs actually relevant to those products. Um, what we've seen businesses, you know, do over over the time is sort of just have a pile of freight and duty invoices and then actually never quite work out what products were they for. You know, best practice is capture those freight costs, those duty costs and any other relevant costs at at the right point attributed to the right purchases. And that can be challenging. You could definitely try and do that in a spreadsheet, but I think as the business scales and grows, you need software that's going to help you actually calculate the the the landed cost by really giving you the the system and the process to attribute those those additional costs and sometimes again they need to be weighted across. You could have ordered three or four things and that duty or the freight cost needs to be weighted or attributed differently across those and that and that's where you know some of this great software can really help. >> Okay, that's that's really helpful. Thank you, Phil. So, if you want to learn more about things like acrruel accounting or calculating your landed costs like we've been speaking about or choosing a cost flow method, which we're going to talk about in another quick video, we have included links to some of that content um down in the description. You'll also find a link there to get in touch with Phil and the outserve team if you want to chat with them. So, Phil, thank you for joining us today. It's always great to hear your insights on these types of topics. Uh it's been brilliant having you. Thank you. >> Thank you for having me. Be very enjoyable. Thank you.

why: Deconstructs the full e-commerce P&L, providing precise formulas for gross margin, AMER, and Contribution Margin 3, while detailing how to build causal inference models and run Geo-Lift tests to escape ROAS attribution illusions.

modules: [MEA]

topics: [profit and contribution formulas, incrementality and holdouts, return rate]

tier: 1

scope_hint: baseline

Topics. profit and contribution formulas / differentiating between gross revenue and net revenue (which deducts refunds, discounts, and chargebacks). The difference between product margin and gross margin, where gross margin accounts for the total landed cost, shipping/fulfillment, transaction fees, and a refund/discount allowance. Defining the Contribution Margin waterfall (CM1 = product margin, CM2 = gross margin, CM3 = total revenue minus cost of delivery and marketing). 20-FIN / finance and accounting

Goes here. Cash flow management, P&L interpretation, balance sheet mechanics, capital expenditures, inventory cash cycles, unit economics modeling, and calculating the financial impact of discount strategies versus Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC).

Not here.

Ad account structuring, creative testing, or media buying tactics -> 11-ADC

Setting up website pop-ups or optimizing the checkout UI -> 07-LPG

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Details how to model unit economics to determine whether offering deep discounts is more profitable than paying higher Customer Acquisition Costs (CAC), using a mathematical breakdown of post-marketing contribution margins.

modules: [FIN]

topics: [unit economics, discount strategy]

tier: 2

scope_hint: core

Topics. unit economics / Defining the Unit Economics Framework as the financial breakdown of a relationship with one single customer, including revenue, discounts, COGS, and profits. Evaluating the true cost of acquisition by adding the customer discount and the Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) together into one combined metric. Demonstrating mathematically that offering a $60 discount can yield the exact same $25 post-marketing contribution margin per customer as offering a $0 discount, provided the discount generates a proportional lift in website conversion rate (e.g., jumping from 1.5% to 3.8%) that equivalently lowers the CAC (e.g., dropping from $100 to $40). discount strategy / Managing discounts and marketing budgets as one combined financial pool rather than separate expenses. Recognizing that giving $100 to an advertising platform or giving $100 to a customer via a discount has the exact same profitability impact on a per-unit basis. Leveraging deep discounts strategically as an on-ramp into subscription or loyalty programs to guarantee high customer lifetime value (LTV), rather than wasting them on one-off flash sales. Maximizing total company profit by modeling which discount scenario yields the highest total volume of customers, showing how an optimized discount strategy can drive total company profit from $25,000 to $63,000 utilizing the exact same $100,000 ad spend.

Look for. The definition of Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC): the average marketing or advertising invested to get one customer to buy for the very first time. The mathematical insight on discounts versus CAC: if a discount increases conversion rates enough to lower the CAC by the exact same dollar amount, the per-unit post-marketing contribution margin remains completely identical. The strategic rule for deep discounts: they should be explicitly attached to an on-ramp into a loyalty or subscription program rather than utilized for standard flash sales.

Skip. Promotional pitches for Ordergroove (transcribed as Order Group) and their capabilities for enterprise brands like Dollar Shave Club or L'Oreal. The line-by-line reading of the hypothetical $1.50 Cost Per Click grid.

Scope mix.

Almost all core.

Volume.

15 to 20.

01-FPM / Four-Quarter Accounting & Financial Planning Goes here. P&L segmentation rules, fixed vs. variable cost definitions (Cost of Delivery, CAC, OPEX, Profit), baseline OPEX targets (10-12% of revenue), and the "13-week cash flow" management model. url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RHJSO4eVJVA rights: public_reference why: Defines the exact financial accounting boundaries (the four quadrants) required to isolate and optimize cash flow in an e-commerce business. modules: [01-FPM] topics: [Financial Planning, P&L Structure, Cash Flow, OPEX Management] tier: 1 scope_hint: baseline cost_ceiling: N/A jurisdiction: N/A

Topics.

The Four Quarters: Cost of Delivery (COGS + Shipping), CAC (Variable Marketing), OPEX (Fixed Costs), Profit.

Cost of Delivery: Target 30-40%.

OPEX Scaling: Target 10-12%. Rule: Base full-time payroll at 12% of the absolute lowest revenue month of the year; everything above that is flex/variable labor.

Cash Flow vs. P&L: Trading P&L margin for cash velocity (e.g., liquidating aged inventory below cost to free up working capital).

Vendor as Lender: Negotiating net terms (Net 60, Net 90, Net 120) aligned with the manufacturing timeline so inventory is sold before the invoice is paid.

Look for. Strict definitions of where specific costs sit. For instance, distinguishing between a variable creative expense (CAC) and a fixed agency retainer (OPEX). Look for the exact baseline metrics for OPEX (10-12%) and Cost of Delivery (30-40%).

Skip. General adages about "saving money" or basic accounting principles not specific to the four-quarter DTC model.

Scope mix. 80% baseline (structuring the math), 20% growth (leveraging terms for capital). Volume. ~500 words.

02-MED / The Hierarchy of Metrics & Media Measurement Goes here. The exact sequence of metric prioritization from Contribution Margin down to in-platform ROAS. The rules connecting platform algorithms to business objectives, and the protocol for expanding media measurement beyond a single channel (e.g., .com + Amazon incrementality). Not here. • [Content creation processes] -> [04-CRE] • [Inventory liquidation rules] -> [05-INV]

url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RHJSO4eVJVA rights: public_reference why: Establishes a rigid hierarchy of truth for e-commerce performance, preventing optimization toward proxy metrics (ROAS) at the expense of actual cash flow (Contribution Margin). modules: [02-MED] topics: [Metric Hierarchy, Contribution Margin, Measurement, Incrementality, Channel Expansion] tier: 2 scope_hint: baseline

Topics.

The Pyramid: 1. Contribution Margin (Top), 2. Business Metrics (Revenue, Spend, blended MER), 3. Customer Metrics (New vs. Returning), 4. Channel Level (ROAS, in-platform proxy metrics).

Daily Contribution Margin: The primary daily focus for the team: Net Sales minus Product Cost minus Variable Expense minus Ad Spend. Fixed costs (OPEX) are excluded from the daily view to prevent false signals to cut spend.

Returns Accrual: Applying an estimated return rate to current daily revenue rather than processing cash-basis returns, preventing false negative signals in high-return months like January.

Measurement and Optimization: Why MTA (Multi-Touch Attribution) models matter less than the signal passed back to the Meta algorithm. You must optimize for what the platform uses to allocate dollars.

Channel Expansion Measurement: When moving beyond Meta to YouTube/CTV/TikTok, measurement must expand beyond .com to include Amazon/Retail lift. E.g., YouTube drives almost 1:1 value on Amazon as it does on .com.

Look for. The explicit formula for Contribution Margin. The specific rules for when to run incrementality tests (when expanding beyond a single channel like Meta).

Skip. Generic platform setup guides (how to launch a Facebook campaign).

Scope mix. 90% baseline (setting the rules). Volume. ~600 words.

03-MER / Product Segmenting, Peaks, & Expansion Goes here. The "Product MVP" evaluation matrix (Margin, Volume, Cash). The strategy for building the marketing calendar around forced demand spikes ("Progressive Peaking"). Methods for de-risking new category expansion. Not here. • [Supply chain net terms] -> [01-FPM] • [Creative iteration cycles] -> [04-CRE]

url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RHJSO4eVJVA rights: public_reference why: Shifts e-commerce growth from a media buying problem to a merchandising and demand-creation problem. modules: [03-MER] topics: [Product Development, Demand Creation, Marketing Calendar, Merchandising] tier: 3 scope_hint: growth

Topics.

Progressive Peaking: Engineering four distinct peaks a year (one per quarter). Creating a cultural or narrative reason for a consumer to buy today, increasing conversion rates while holding CPMs constant. E.g., attaching to International Women's Day or Veterans Day to spike demand outside of BFCM.

Product MVP Matrix: Evaluating SKUs by Margin Expansion, Volume Velocity, or Cash Flow correction.

The Four SKU Types:

Champions: High volume, high efficiency.

Growth Drivers: Increasing investment to find the ceiling.

Hidden Gems: Low investment, disproportionately high efficiency (needs more spend).

Underperformers (Aged Inventory): Liquidate quickly to recover cash.

De-risking Category Expansion: Using small-batch manufacturing or pre-orders to validate demand before committing media budget or large POs. Mapping the required media spend before placing the inventory order.

Look for. The criteria for defining a "peak." The criteria for categorizing a SKU into one of the four types (Champions, Gems, etc.).

Skip. General advice on "listening to your customer" for product ideas.

Scope mix. 30% baseline, 70% growth. Volume. ~600 words.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides a clear, foundational understanding of how COGS and Gross Margins differ between CPG and SaaS businesses, including common accounting misclassifications that distort valuations. modules: [FIN] topics: [COGS, SaaS accounting, CPG accounting, gross margin, financial valuation, unit economics, AWS server costs, freight classification] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. unit economics / how COGS determines the remaining capital available for marketing and R&D per unit sold; valuation / why venture capitalists and private equity firms obsess over gross margin (which is dictated by COGS) when valuing a business; CPG COGS / calculating tangible COGS using raw materials, direct labor on the manufacturing floor, factory overhead, freight-in, and packaging; SaaS COGS / calculating intangible COGS using server costs (AWS/Azure), third-party delivery APIs, customer support wages, and onboarding/implementation wages; accounting flow / how CPG inventory hits the balance sheet as an asset before flowing to the P&L as COGS upon sale, whereas many SaaS costs (like wages) hit the P&L immediately; gross margin expectations / expecting 20-40% gross margins for manufacturing/CPG versus 70-90% for SaaS; freight misclassification / the common accounting error of recording "freight-out" (shipping to customers) as COGS, when it should be recorded as a selling/operating expense; SaaS misclassifications / incorrectly recording Customer Success wages (which are sales/upsell functions) or third-party revenue shares as COGS instead of operating expenses.

Look for.

The Freight Classification Rule: The strict accounting rule that "freight-in" (bringing materials to the factory) is part of COGS, but "freight-out" (shipping the final product to the customer) is an operating/selling expense and should NOT be in COGS.

The Customer Success Misclassification: Noting that while Customer Support and Implementation wages belong in SaaS COGS, Customer Success teams (who handle upsells and renewals) are a sales function and belong in operating expenses.

Gross Margin Benchmarks: The rule of thumb that traditional CPG/manufacturing businesses operate at 20-40% gross margins, whereas SaaS businesses operate at 70-90% gross margins.

SaaS Server Depreciation: The explanation that if a company owns its physical servers, the cost enters COGS as depreciation over time, but most modern companies rent via AWS/Azure and log the monthly fee directly as COGS.

Skip. Plugs for the creator's "Controller Academy" website and generic requests to like/subscribe.

Scope mix. 100% baseline (fundamental accounting definitions and reporting rules). Volume. ~350 words.

In this video, we'll go over why CFOs obsess over COGS or cost of good sold. And the reason why this conversation is important to you as a finance leader or even a business founder is this can help guide the discussion that you have with auditors and investors. So, if this sounds good to you, let's dive right in. Hey everyone, this is Bill Hannah, your favorite financial controller, bringing about 20 years of experience in corporate accounting and finance leadership. and I teach my experience here in this YouTube channel as well as on my website, the Controller Academy, for which I'll leave a link down below. In today's video, we're discussing why CFOs obsess over COGS. But before jumping into the various elements of the video, I want to quickly address why CFOs spend a lot of time thinking about COGS. The first reason is going to be unit economics. So from each unit that we sell, say we sell something for $10, the COGS is going to determine how much money is left over that we can spend on marketing and research and development. So that's reason number one. Reason number two is valuation. Uh when VCs and private equity values a business, they think of revenue growth and gross margin. Gross margin is dependent on COGS. That's why it becomes a highly important thing for a valuation of a business. All right. So to structure today's video, we'll be talking about two main industries. The first one is going to be CBG or consumer package goods and the other one is SAS or software as a service because cost of goods sold is going to be different in these industries. So overall when we talk about CPG the cost of goods sold is going to be tangible. So the product is tangible. It's something that you can touch. So think of a company like Nike that manufactures sneakers and athletic attire. So their inventory is tangible, something that you can touch and therefore their cogs is going to be tangible. It's something that you can touch with the software as a service. An example of that is Salesforce. So Salesforce sells the platform of sales and marketing businessto business. So it's a B2B SAS business. In their case, their product is not tangible. So, it's a cloud-based product and most of the cogs that goes into it is going to be labor based, which is the salaries of the people who are supporting the delivery of that service. Okay, so let's go ahead and break that down. So, for a company that is CPG, let's say Nike, the COGS is going to be raw material plus direct labor plus overhead. raw material. If you're making a pair of sneakers, it's going to be uh rubber, uh leather, maybe laces. Uh direct labor is going to be the labor of the person who's standing on the manufacturing floor processing the actual manufacturing of the sneakers. The overhead is going to be the other costs such as the rent of the factory, uh depreciation of the factory if you own it, uh depreciation of the equipment, uh maintenance, utilities and things that uh keep the manufacturing operation running. Uh the second thing is going to be the freight in the cost to bring in the inventory uh and then packaging at the end when you make the pair of sneakers, you need to put it in a box and that is part of your cogs as well. Okay, so this is the breakdown for a CPG. What is about the breakdown for a SAS company? Uh these are the common costs that go into COGS. So the first one is server cost. So to deliver the service to your customers, you need to have a server and that server could be something physical that you own. So if you own an actual server, uh then the cost that goes here is going to be the depreciation over time of that server. Uh but most companies nowadays don't have their own physical server. We're talking about small businesses. uh what you do in this case is you go to AWS, Amazon Web Services or you go to Azure and uh lease or rent a server space and pay a monthly rent for that and that's going to be your server cost that goes here. Uh the second item that goes into cost is going to be tools to deliver the service. Um these are things like API or thirdparty tools that you need to have in place to be able to deliver that uh SAS uh product to your customers. Uh the third thing is going to be customer support wages. This is the wages that you pay uh to your customer support uh staff. Implementation wages. This is the salaries and the benefits that you pay to the team within your company that implements or on board the client uh with the new product that they just purchased. Okay. Let's spend some time talking about the recording and the timing of that recording for COGS. And for those of you who are accountants, it's really helpful to understand how information goes from data to populate the financial statements. And for that, I created an Excel file that actually helps you uh take a sample set of data and create financial statements from it. I'll leave a link down below for you to download that file. But for the recording of COGS for CPG, typically the information goes into the balance sheet. So when you create inventory that becomes an asset on the balance sheet and then that gets recorded to the P&L as COGS when when the inventory is sold when you make a sale right for a SAS business uh you also have a similar mechanic. So there is a flow from the balance sheet to the P&L and that has to do with your fixed asset. So a lot of times you have a fixed asset that relates to the actual delivery of the service which could be a computer cost, server cost and these are fixed assets that flows into COGS after that. But you also have a fair amount of COGS that gets recorded directly into COGS and these are things like customer support wages and implementation wages. And if this video is providing you with real value, don't forget to hit the like and subscribe button which will pay me back from my efforts that I'm doing here. Okay, so the next item is going to be gross margin. So typically with a CPG manufacturing based business, you have high cogs and low gross margin. Typically it's between 20 to 40%. Um so when I worked at a manufacturing company that made baby food products, uh the gross margin was about 30% and that's typical for that kind of business. With a SAS company, you typically have lower cogs in relation to revenue. you have lower COGS and you have high gross margin. So typically it's between 70 and 90% gross margin. So you might say maybe I should go into business here in SAS uh instead of going into a CPG product business. And the answer is yes. A SAS has higher gross margin, but in the end it's going to depend on the skill that you have. Maybe you have a killer idea for a CBG product that's going to have a very quick and high distribution and you'll have a small slice of the pie, but you're going to have a huge pie to get a small slice from. So, at the end, you win. Uh, but if of course if you have a really good idea for a SAS product, the gross margins are really appealing. Okay. Now, let's talk about the final point which is really most important is the common mistakes. What are the common mistakes that finance leaders and business founders make in relation to the cogs of the products? So the first thing is going to be waste. Uh the first item is going to be expired goods. So you need to keep tabs on the expiration and the obsolescence uh dates of your goods. Uh because if you're getting close to the expiration date, you should be moving the products with the near expiration first before you touch the products that have a longer expiration window or obsolescence window. Right? And if you get to the point that you're very close to expiration, sometimes you have to do a fire sale uh so that you can sell the product quickly with a much lower margin uh so that you can get the product moving. Uh with the uh stolen products, um what I see the mistake is being made is not implementing inventory controls that logs when the inventory leaves the warehouse. So you need to be logging the inventory when it comes in and logging it when it when it goes out and doing a periodic inventory count to make sure that nobody is stealing the inventory. Uh another mistake that I see is mclassification of freight. So freight is tricky because um the cost of freight in to bring in material direct material uh to your or and packaging to your factory. The freight in is part of COGS, but the freight out when you're shipping the product out to customers isn't part of COGS. Freight out is a selling cost that goes into operating expenses. So, this is a mistake that I see often. Uh what are the mistakes that I see under SAS? So, with the SAS businesses, the first one is going to be mclassification of customer success. So within the customer or the delivery organization in a SAS company, you typically have customer uh support, customer success and implementation. These are the three functions that you typically see within the delivery organization of a SAS business. Customer success isn't part of COGS. Customer success is a selling function, right? These are the teams that are making sure that the uh user is able to use the product and is buying more. So they upsell the customer on other products as well. That's why they're called customer success. Their cost typically is not part of COGS and it should be part of operating expenses. Uh server cost increase. So typically what I see is that the cost that you're paying to AWS or Azure is left unchecked. It rises quickly. So you need to tie it to usage of the business. So when you're if you're B2B and you're adding in a new uh enterprise uh client or account, you need to be able to tie the cost of that to uh an element of the cost in AWS or Azure so that uh your economics are moving uh in the right way and not paying double for an additional customer that you add into your platform. So for that to happen you need to have periodic meetings uh with the engineering team. So the finance organization and the engineering organization need to be in sync into deciding how the cost should be moving up for the business. The other element that I see is revenue share. So if you are a B2B SAS company and you are partnering with a third party um company that's going to be marketing your product and you're paying them a revenue share. A lot of times I see that revenue share being booked into COGS which is a mistake because uh the revenue share for a third-party company promoting the business um if that company is not involved in the delivery of the service then that's not COGS because COGS is only about the delivery of the service. But if all they're doing is marketing your product then this is a marketing cost that operating expenses are not part of your COGS. So to zoom back out and remember the why, the why behind CFOs, why do you obsess over COGS in general, is because if you get the recording correctly and the timing correctly, and you record the correct elements that go into it and you pay attention to the waste and the mclassification and all of these things combined, you can arrive at the correct gross margin for the business. that's going to help you decide the unit economics and that drives whether you can make more of the same product or maybe discontinue and create a new product and it's going to help you with the valuation of the business overall. So, if you like this video, give it a big thumbs up and I'll see you on the next one.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details the organizational and operational structure of an 8-figure e-commerce brand, outlining strict product development (Tech Packs), forecasting variables (lead times, safety stock), and 3PL Service Level Agreements (SLAs). modules: [OPS] topics: [supply chain, tech packs, 3pl management, unit economics, organizational design, customer service] tier: 1 scope_hint: core

Topics. supply chain / Establishing a "Critical Path" for product development and launch, detailing every sequence from fabric strike-offs and first samples to Quality Control (QC) inspections and Purchase Orders (POs). The necessity of hiring a QC agent (e.g., via Alibaba or SGS) for the first few production runs. Managing Freight Logistics by comparing rates from 2-3 freight forwarders simultaneously, and logging the Estimated Departure Date, Estimated Arrival Date (ETA), Vessel Number, and Bill of Lading in an internal master spreadsheet that is restricted from supplier manipulation. tech packs / The absolute necessity of creating a Technical Pack (Tech Pack) to prevent supplier discrepancies and protect IP. Components include: 1) Complete drawings (to clarify details like print placement), 2) Fabric specifications (including GSM for thickness/density and treatment rules like acid washing), 3) Measurements (crucial for sizing and grading), 4) Graphics, 5) Hardware (zips, pockets), and 6) Labels and packaging. Utilizing Tech Packs to prove supplier undercutting (e.g., weighing fabrics) and facilitate easy manufacturer transitions. 3pl management / Managing Third-Party Logistics (3PLs). Conducting a Request for Pricing (RFP) by providing product dimensions, forecasts, and historical data to multiple 3PLs to enforce competition. Identifying red flags (e.g., using stolen shopping carts to move goods). Mandating barcode usage for accurate inventory tracking. Breaking down 3PL pricing into Pick/Pack, Inbounds (unloading containers), Outbounds (courier rates, which vary drastically based on the 3PL's total volume), and Storage. The necessity of a Service Level Agreement (SLA) outlining exact "Picked on Time" metrics with financial penalties for failures, especially during Q4 peaks. Auditing 3PL bills monthly using a custom spreadsheet based on Shopify order volume. unit economics / Calculating the true cost of a product before marketing. Formula: Sale Price - Cost of Product - Freight (per unit) - Courier Cost (pick/pack + shipping) - Storage - Duties (sunk costs based on region, distinct from sales tax) - Payment Fees. Inputting this landed cost into Shopify's "Cost per item" field to enable accurate, automated daily profit reporting via tools like Triple Whale. organizational design / Structuring the executive team. The CEO oversees the CFO (Finance), CMO (Marketing), and COO (Operations). The COO manages Product, Supply Chain (forecasting/planning), Fulfillment, and Customer Service. Recognizing that operations act as "weeding the garden"—if neglected, the revenue seeds planted by marketing will be choked out by stockouts or fulfillment disasters. customer service / Operating a blended local/international customer service team (using international agents for basic tickets and local agents for nuanced, complex escalations). Tracking operational efficiency through customer service metrics: Resolution Time, Touchpoints, and Cost Per Service (total CS expenses divided by ticket volume). Using the "Cost Per Service" metric to forecast hiring needs during peak seasonal sales.

Look for. The definition of a Tech Pack: a comprehensive document detailing drawings, fabric GSM, measurements, hardware, and labels, used to hold manufacturers accountable. The specific components of unit economics: Sale Price, Cost of Goods (COGS), Freight, Courier, Storage, Duties, and Payment Fees. The definition of a 3PL RFP: Request for Pricing, where a brand submits forecasts and dimensions to multiple warehouses to force competitive bids. The distinction between sales tax and duties: duties are a sunk cost based on import regions and must be factored into unit economics, whereas sales tax is collected and remitted. The specific components of a 3PL SLA: Picked on time guarantees, delivered on time tracking, and mandated bi-annual cycle counts.

Skip. General complaints about the BBC calling the creator a scammer. Plugs for Daily Mentor or the Oodie brand unless specifically explaining an operational concept (like weighted blanket discrepancies).

Scope mix. Baseline (Tech Packs, unit economics formulas) mixed with Growth (3PL negotiations, global CS team structures).

Volume. 20 to 30.

21-OPS / team and operations

Goes here. Sourcing, interviewing, and hiring talent. Creating Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), onboarding flows, setting KPIs and incentives. Managing remote teams, maintaining company culture, leadership, establishing organizational structures, executing daily huddles, team building, conflict management, and scaling payroll parameters.

Not here.

Financial modeling or accounting -> 20-FIN

Customer support or post-purchase experience -> 17-CXP

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: A comprehensive handbook detailing the mechanics of team building, stages of team development, structural roles, conflict management strategies, and techniques for assessing and leading effective operational teams. modules: [OPS] topics: [team building, leadership and culture, organizational scaling] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. team building / Understanding the stages of team development (Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, and Adjourning) to systematically build cohesive work groups. Differentiating between various types of teams (e.g., cross-functional, self-managing, task forces, and virtual teams) and establishing strong communication norms to prevent information sludge and build trust. Identifying constructive versus destructive conflict and utilizing strategies like confronting, smoothing, and compromising to manage team differences. leadership and culture / Exploring core leadership styles (Authoritarian/Autocratic, Participative/Democratic, and Delegative/Free Reign) to effectively manage team dynamics. Understanding the Belbin Team Roles (Coordinator, Shaper, Plant, Monitor Evaluator, Implementer, Team Worker, Resource Investigator, Completer, and Specialist) to balance task-focused, quality-focused, and process-focused responsibilities within an organization. Fostering a high-morale culture by setting positive examples, enabling open 360-degree feedback, and delegating effectively. organizational scaling / Diagnosing the root causes of poor team performance (structural, communication, and personal factors) to prevent project derailment. Utilizing structured intervention techniques such as the Role Analysis Technique, Responsibility Charting, and Force Field Analysis to clarify expectations, assign actionable behaviors, and move an organization from its current condition to a desired, stabilized state. Executing ongoing team effectiveness assessments to track team vibrancy, meeting management, and behavioral indicators.

Look for. The five stages of team development: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, and Adjourning. The nine Belbin Team Roles framework used to categorize behavioral contributions: Coordinator, Shaper, Plant, Monitor Evaluator, Implementer, Team Worker, Resource Investigator, Completer, and Specialist. The three primary leadership styles: Authoritarian, Participative, and Delegative. The four classes of behavior in Responsibility Charting: Responsibility (R), Approval required (A-V), Support (S), and Inform (I).

Skip. Detailed scoring rubrics and numerical questionnaires intended for self-assessment (e.g., the 5-point scale worksheets for Team Vibrancy, Meeting Management, and Behavior Indicators).

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 15 to 20.
